topics.short: Metals give electrons to nonmetals, and the oppositely charged ions hold each other in a lattice.

topics.title: Formulas of Ionic Compounds
topics.short: Choose the ratio of ions that makes the total charge zero.

topics.title: Naming Ionic Compounds
topics.short: Name the metal, then the nonmetal ending in -ide; add a Roman numeral for metals with more than one charge.

topics.title: Polyatomic Ions
topics.short: Groups such as NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻ act as single ions; use parentheses when you need more than one.

topics.title: Covalent Bonds
topics.short: Nonmetal atoms share pairs of electrons in single, double or triple bonds.

topics.title: Naming Molecular Compounds
topics.short: Use prefixes to count atoms: N₂O₄ is dinitrogen tetroxide.

topics.title: Lewis Structures
topics.short: Count all the valence electrons, connect the atoms, then complete octets with lone pairs and multiple bonds.

topics.title: Molecular Shapes (VSEPR)
topics.short: Electron groups around an atom spread as far apart as they can, and lone pairs help set the shape.

topics.title: Polar and Nonpolar Bonds
topics.short: The bigger the electronegativity difference, the more unevenly the bonding electrons are shared.

topics.title: Polar and Nonpolar Molecules
topics.short: A molecule is polar when its bond dipoles do not cancel out.

topics.title: Ionic, Molecular, Network and Metallic Solids
topics.short: The kind of particles and the forces between them explain melting point, hardness and conductivity.

topics.title: Intermolecular Forces
topics.short: Dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds pull whole molecules toward each other.

topics.title: Predicting Boiling Points
topics.short: Stronger forces between molecules mean a higher boiling point and a lower vapor pressure.

topics.title: The Mole
topics.short: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, a count chosen so that a mole of atoms has a mass in grams equal to its atomic mass.

topics.title: Molar Mass
topics.short: Add up the atomic masses in a formula to get the mass of one mole in grams.

topics.title: Grams, Moles and Particles
topics.short: Divide a mass by the molar mass to get moles; multiply moles by Avogadro's number to count particles.

topics.title: Percent Composition
topics.short: Each element's share of a compound's molar mass, as a percent.

topics.title: Empirical Formulas
topics.short: Turn masses into moles, then into the simplest whole-number ratio.

topics.title: Molecular Formulas
topics.short: A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found from the molar mass.

topics.title: Atoms Are Conserved
topics.short: In a reaction atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same.

topics.title: Coefficients and Subscripts
topics.short: Subscripts say what one molecule is made of; coefficients say how many molecules there are.

topics.title: Balancing Equations
topics.short: Change coefficients, never subscripts, until every element has the same count on both sides.

topics.title: Types of Reactions
topics.short: Synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement and combustion.

topics.title: Predicting Single Replacements
topics.short: A more active metal replaces a less active one in a compound; the activity series tells which is which.

topics.title: Mole Ratios
topics.short: The coefficients of a balanced equation give the ratio of moles that react and form.

topics.title: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry
topics.short: Go from grams of one substance to moles, across the mole ratio, then back to grams of another.

topics.title: Limiting Reactant
topics.short: The reactant that runs out first decides how much product can form.

topics.title: Theoretical and Percent Yield
topics.short: Compare the product you actually got with the most the limiting reactant allows.

topics.title: Gas Pressure
topics.short: Pressure is the push of particle collisions on each square meter of wall, measured in atm, kPa or mmHg.

topics.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory
topics.short: The particles of a gas move fast and randomly, and the kelvin temperature measures their average kinetic energy.

topics.title: Boyle's Law
topics.short: At constant temperature, squeezing a gas into half the volume doubles its pressure: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

topics.title: Charles's Law
topics.short: At constant pressure, a gas's volume is proportional to its kelvin temperature.

topics.title: Gay-Lussac's Law and the Combined Gas Law
topics.short: At constant volume, pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature, and P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ joins all three laws.

topics.title: Avogadro's Law and Molar Volume
topics.short: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of particles: 22.4 L per mole at 0 °C and 1 atm.

topics.title: The Ideal Gas Law
topics.short: PV = nRT connects the pressure, volume, moles and temperature of a gas.

topics.title: Why Things Dissolve
topics.short: Water's polar molecules pull ions and polar molecules apart and surround them: like dissolves like.

topics.title: Solubility and Solubility Curves
topics.short: A solubility curve shows the most solute that dissolves at each temperature.

topics.title: Molarity
topics.short: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution.

topics.title: Dilution
topics.short: Adding water spreads the same moles of solute through more volume: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

topics.title: Precipitation and Solubility Rules
topics.short: Mixing two solutions can make an insoluble solid fall out, and solubility rules predict when.

topics.title: Acids and Bases
topics.short: In water, acids make hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) and bases make hydroxide ions (OH⁻).

topics.title: Proton Donors and Acceptors
topics.short: An acid gives an H⁺ to a base, leaving a conjugate pair on each side of the equation.

topics.title: The pH Scale
topics.short: pH counts powers of ten: each step down the scale means ten times more H₃O⁺.

topics.title: pH, pOH and the Ions in Water
topics.short: In water [H₃O⁺] × [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pH + pOH = 14.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Acids
topics.short: A strong acid ionizes completely and a weak acid only partly; strength is not the same as concentration.

topics.title: Neutralization
topics.short: An acid and a hydroxide base react to make water and a salt.

topics.title: Titration
topics.short: Add base drop by drop until it exactly uses up the acid, then work out the acid's concentration.

topics.title: Heat and Temperature
topics.short: Temperature measures the particles' average kinetic energy; heat is energy that flows from hotter to colder.

topics.title: Specific Heat
topics.short: q = mcΔT: some substances need more energy per gram to warm by one degree.

topics.title: Calorimetry
topics.short: In an insulated cup, the heat lost by the hot object equals the heat gained by the cold one.

topics.title: Heating Curves and Phase Changes
topics.short: While a substance melts or boils, the added heat pulls particles apart and the temperature stays flat.

topics.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
topics.short: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions take it in.

topics.title: Bond Energy and Reaction Energy
topics.short: Breaking bonds takes energy and forming bonds releases it; the difference is the energy change of the reaction.

topics.title: Collision Theory and Reaction Rate
topics.short: Particles must collide hard enough and lined up the right way, so temperature, concentration and surface area change the rate.

topics.title: Activation Energy and Catalysts
topics.short: A catalyst opens a path with a lower energy barrier and is not used up.

topics.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
topics.short: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions run at equal rates, so the amounts stop changing.

topics.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
topics.short: A system at equilibrium shifts to partly undo a change in concentration, pressure or temperature.

topics.title: Radioactive Decay and Nuclear Equations
topics.short: Alpha, beta and gamma decay change the nucleus, and both the mass numbers and the charges balance.

topics.title: Half-Life
topics.short: In each half-life, half of the remaining nuclei decay; use it to find amounts left and ages.

topics.title: Fission and Fusion
topics.short: Splitting heavy nuclei and joining light ones both release energy as a little mass disappears.

topics.title: Definite and Multiple Proportions
topics.short: A compound has a fixed mass ratio of elements; when two elements make several compounds, their mass ratios compare as small whole numbers.

topics.title: Mass Spectra of Elements
topics.short: Each peak is an isotope: its position gives the mass and its height gives the abundance.

topics.title: Combustion Analysis
topics.short: Burn a compound, weigh the CO₂ and H₂O, and work back to its empirical formula.

topics.title: Composition of Mixtures
topics.short: Use the measured mass of one element to find how much of each compound a mixture holds.

topics.title: Wavelength, Frequency and the Spectrum
topics.short: Light's speed is its wavelength times its frequency: c = λν.

topics.title: Photons and the Photoelectric Effect
topics.short: Light comes in packets of energy E = hν, and only photons above a threshold frequency can free an electron from a metal.

topics.title: Hydrogen's Energy Levels
topics.short: Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J / n², and each spectral line is a jump between two levels.

topics.title: What Light Does to Molecules
topics.short: Microwaves set molecules rotating, infrared makes bonds vibrate, and visible and ultraviolet light move electrons to higher levels.

topics.title: Quantum Numbers
topics.short: The numbers n, l, mₗ and mₛ name an electron's shell, subshell, orbital and spin.

topics.title: Orbital Diagrams and Magnetism
topics.short: Pauli's rule and Hund's rule place the arrows, and unpaired electrons make an atom paramagnetic.

topics.title: Configurations of Ions and Exceptions
topics.short: Transition metals lose their 4s electrons first, and chromium and copper break the filling pattern.

topics.title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy
topics.short: Each peak shows the energy needed to remove electrons from one subshell, and its height counts those electrons.

topics.title: Coulomb's Law in Atoms
topics.short: The attraction between charges grows with the size of the charges and weakens with distance.

topics.title: Shielding and Effective Nuclear Charge
topics.short: Core electrons screen the nucleus, so a valence electron feels roughly the protons minus the core electrons.

topics.title: Successive Ionization Energies
topics.short: Each electron removed costs more, and a huge jump appears once the valence electrons are gone.

topics.title: Exceptions in Ionization Energy
topics.short: The dips at boron and oxygen come from starting a new subshell and from the first paired electron.

topics.title: Sizes of Ions
topics.short: Cations are smaller than their atoms and anions larger; in an isoelectronic series, more protons make a smaller ion.

topics.title: Potential Energy and Bond Length
topics.short: Two bonded atoms settle at the distance where their potential energy is lowest.

topics.title: Lattice Energy
topics.short: Higher ion charges and smaller ions hold an ionic crystal together more tightly.

topics.title: Metals and Alloys
topics.short: Metals are cations in a sea of shared electrons; alloys mix in other atoms by substitution or in the gaps.

topics.title: Formal Charge
topics.short: Assign each atom its share of the electrons; the best Lewis structure has formal charges closest to zero.

topics.title: Resonance
topics.short: When more than one Lewis structure fits, the real molecule is a blend with in-between bonds.

topics.title: Exceptions to the Octet Rule
topics.short: Odd-electron molecules, electron-poor boron and beryllium, and atoms past period 2 with more than eight electrons.

topics.title: Shapes with Five and Six Electron Groups
topics.short: The trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral families, and where their lone pairs go.

topics.title: Hybrid Orbitals, Sigma and Pi Bonds
topics.short: sp, sp² and sp³ orbitals match two, three and four electron groups; a double bond is one σ bond and one π bond.

topics.title: Molecular Orbital Diagrams
topics.short: Atomic orbitals combine into bonding and antibonding orbitals that give the bond order and the magnetism.

topics.title: Comparing Intermolecular Forces
topics.short: Size, polarizability and shape set the strength of dispersion forces, which can outweigh dipole forces.

topics.title: Vapor Pressure and Boiling
topics.short: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure above it.

topics.title: The Clausius–Clapeyron Equation
topics.short: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) links vapor pressure to temperature.

topics.title: Phase Diagrams
topics.short: Read the phase at any temperature and pressure, and find the triple point and the critical point.

topics.title: Crystal Structures and Unit Cells
topics.short: Count the atoms in simple, body-centered and face-centered cubic cells, and find a crystal's density.

topics.title: Separating Mixtures
topics.short: Distillation sorts by boiling point, and chromatography sorts by attraction to the paper or column.

topics.title: Electrolytes and Ions in Solution
topics.short: Strong electrolytes split completely into ions, weak electrolytes partly, and nonelectrolytes not at all.

topics.title: Concentrations of Ions
topics.short: One formula unit can release several ions: 0.20 M CaCl₂ is 0.40 M in Cl⁻.

topics.title: The Energy of Dissolving
topics.short: Pulling solute apart and pulling solvent apart cost energy, forming new attractions releases it, and the total is ΔH of solution.

topics.title: Gas Solubility and Henry's Law
topics.short: More pressure dissolves more gas (C = kP), and warmer water holds less gas.

topics.title: Molality, Mole Fraction and Parts per Million
topics.short: Other ways to state concentration, each suited to a different job.

topics.title: Converting Concentration Units
topics.short: Use the solution's density to switch between molarity, molality and mass percent.

topics.title: The Beer–Lambert Law
topics.short: Absorbance is proportional to concentration, A = εbc, so a calibration line reveals an unknown concentration.

topics.title: Vapor Pressure Lowering
topics.short: A nonvolatile solute lowers the solvent's vapor pressure: P = χ(solvent) × P°.

topics.title: Freezing Point Depression and Boiling Point Elevation
topics.short: ΔT = iKm: dissolved particles lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point.

topics.title: Osmotic Pressure
topics.short: Π = iMRT: water moves through a membrane toward the more concentrated side.

topics.title: Molar Mass from Colligative Properties
topics.short: Measure ΔT or Π, find the moles of solute, then divide its mass by those moles.

topics.title: Gas Density and Molar Mass
topics.short: d = PM/RT, so the density of a gas reveals its molar mass.

topics.title: Gas Stoichiometry
topics.short: Use PV = nRT to turn a volume of gas into moles inside a stoichiometry problem.

topics.title: Partial Pressures and Mole Fractions
topics.short: Each gas in a mixture pushes as if it were alone: Pᵢ = χᵢ × P(total).

topics.title: Molecular Speeds and Effusion
topics.short: At one temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy, so lighter molecules move faster and effuse faster: rate ∝ 1/√M.

topics.title: The Maxwell–Boltzmann Distribution
topics.short: Molecular speeds spread over a curve that flattens and shifts toward faster speeds as the temperature rises.

topics.title: Real Gases
topics.short: The particles' own volume and their attractions make real gases stray from PV = nRT at high pressure and low temperature.

topics.title: Net Ionic Equations
topics.short: Write dissolved strong electrolytes as ions, then cancel the spectator ions.

topics.title: Solution Stoichiometry
topics.short: Molarity times volume gives moles, which go straight into a mole ratio.

topics.title: Gravimetric Analysis
topics.short: Weigh a precipitate to find how much of an ion a sample held.

topics.title: Titration Calculations
topics.short: Use the volume at the equivalence point and the mole ratio to find a concentration, a molar mass or a percent purity.

topics.title: Oxidation Numbers
topics.short: Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping charges that track electrons; in a neutral compound they add to zero.

topics.title: Oxidation and Reduction
topics.short: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain; one never happens without the other.

topics.title: Balancing Redox Reactions
topics.short: Split the reaction into half-reactions, balance atoms and charge with electrons, then add them back together.

topics.title: Redox Titrations
topics.short: Titrate with permanganate or another oxidizing agent, using the electron-balanced mole ratio.

topics.title: The First Law and Sign Conventions
topics.short: ΔU = q + w: energy that enters the system counts as positive, and energy that leaves counts as negative.

topics.title: Pressure–Volume Work
topics.short: A gas that expands against an outside pressure does work on the surroundings: w = −PΔV.

topics.title: Enthalpy and Thermochemical Equations
topics.short: ΔH is the heat at constant pressure; it scales with the equation and changes sign when the reaction is reversed.

topics.title: Heat from Amounts of Reactant
topics.short: Multiply moles by ΔH per mole of reaction, using the mole ratio to the substance you were given.

topics.title: Heat for Warming and Phase Changes Together
topics.short: Add mcΔT for each warming step and nΔH for each phase change along the way.

topics.title: Calorimetry for Reactions
topics.short: Find ΔH from a temperature change: q(reaction) = −q(solution), divided by the moles that reacted.

topics.title: Bomb Calorimetry
topics.short: At constant volume, the heat the calorimeter takes up, C(cal) × ΔT, measures the energy released by burning a sample.

topics.title: Hess's Law
topics.short: Add chemical equations like algebra, and add their ΔH values the same way.

topics.title: Standard Enthalpies of Formation
topics.short: ΔH°(reaction) = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants).

topics.title: Born–Haber Cycles
topics.short: Add up the steps that build an ionic solid from its elements to find its lattice energy.

topics.title: Measuring Reaction Rates
topics.short: A rate is the change in concentration per unit time, divided by each substance's coefficient so that every substance gives the same rate.

topics.title: Rate Laws and Reaction Order
topics.short: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, where the orders m and n are found by experiment.

topics.title: The Method of Initial Rates
topics.short: Compare experiments in which only one concentration changes to find each order, then k and its units.

topics.title: First-Order Reactions
topics.short: ln[A] falls in a straight line with time, and the half-life, t½ = 0.693/k, never changes.

topics.title: Zero- and Second-Order Reactions
topics.short: [A] or 1/[A] changes in a straight line with time, and the half-life depends on the starting concentration.

topics.title: Finding the Order from a Graph
topics.short: Plot [A], ln[A] and 1/[A] against time; the straight one gives the order, and its slope gives k.

topics.title: The Arrhenius Equation
topics.short: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT), so rate constants at two temperatures reveal the activation energy.

topics.title: Elementary Steps and Molecularity
topics.short: For a single elementary step, the rate law comes straight from its coefficients.

topics.title: Reaction Mechanisms
topics.short: The steps add up to the overall equation; intermediates are made and then used, and catalysts are used and then remade.

topics.title: The Rate-Determining Step
topics.short: When the first step is slow, its rate law is the rate law of the whole reaction.

topics.title: A Fast Equilibrium Before a Slow Step
topics.short: Set the forward and reverse rates of the fast step equal to replace an intermediate's concentration.

topics.title: Energy Profiles for Multistep Reactions
topics.short: Each step is a hump: intermediates sit in the valleys and transition states at the peaks.

topics.title: Catalysis
topics.short: Homogeneous, heterogeneous and enzyme catalysts open a new mechanism with a lower barrier.

topics.title: The Equilibrium Constant
topics.short: K is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, with pure solids and liquids left out.

topics.title: What the Size of K Tells You
topics.short: A large K means mostly products at equilibrium; a small K means mostly reactants.

topics.title: Reversing, Scaling and Adding Reactions
topics.short: Reversing gives 1/K, multiplying by n gives Kⁿ, and adding reactions multiplies their K values.

topics.title: Kp and Kc
topics.short: For gases, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn counts only moles of gas.

topics.title: The Reaction Quotient
topics.short: Compare Q with K to see which way a reaction will go.

topics.title: Calculating K with an ICE Table
topics.short: Use the change in one amount and the coefficients to find every amount at equilibrium, then K.

topics.title: Finding Equilibrium Concentrations
topics.short: Set up an ICE table and solve for x, using the quadratic formula when needed.

topics.title: The Small-x Approximation
topics.short: When K is tiny, x is small next to the starting amount; check that it is under 5%.

topics.title: Le Chatelier's Principle with Q and K
topics.short: Changes in concentration or volume move Q away from K; only a temperature change alters K itself.

topics.title: pH of Strong Acids and Bases
topics.short: Use logarithms to find the pH and pOH of any strong acid or base solution.

topics.title: Acid and Base Constants
topics.short: Ka and Kb measure strength, pKa = −log Ka, and Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair.

topics.title: pH of a Weak Acid
topics.short: Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for [H₃O⁺], then take the pH.

topics.title: Percent Ionization
topics.short: The share of a weak acid that ionizes grows as the solution is diluted.

topics.title: pH of a Weak Base
topics.short: Solve Kb for [OH⁻], then change pOH to pH.

topics.title: Acidic, Basic and Neutral Salts
topics.short: Ions from weak acids or weak bases react with water and shift the pH.

topics.title: Polyprotic Acids
topics.short: Each proton comes off with a much smaller Ka, so the first step sets the pH.

topics.title: Molecular Structure and Acid Strength
topics.short: Bond strength, bond polarity and resonance in the conjugate base explain which acids are stronger.

topics.title: How Buffers Work
topics.short: A weak acid and its conjugate base use up added acid or base, so the pH barely moves.

topics.title: The Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation
topics.short: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) for a buffer.

topics.title: pH, pKa and Which Form Dominates
topics.short: Below the pKa the acid form dominates; above it the base form does.

topics.title: Adding Acid or Base to a Buffer
topics.short: Do the neutralization stoichiometry first, then use the new ratio in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

topics.title: Buffer Capacity and Choosing a Buffer
topics.short: Pick an acid whose pKa is near the pH you want; more of both parts means more capacity.

topics.title: Strong Acid–Strong Base Titration Curves
topics.short: Find the pH before, at and after the equivalence point.

topics.title: Weak Acid–Strong Base Titration Curves
topics.short: Halfway to equivalence the pH equals the pKa, and at equivalence the pH is above 7.

topics.title: Choosing an Indicator
topics.short: Choose an indicator whose color change falls on the steep part of the titration curve.

topics.title: The Solubility Product
topics.short: Ksp describes a slightly soluble salt in equilibrium with its ions, and gives its molar solubility.

topics.title: Comparing Solubilities
topics.short: Ksp ranks solubility directly only for salts that release the same number of ions.

topics.title: The Common-Ion Effect
topics.short: A salt dissolves less in a solution that already holds one of its ions.

topics.title: Will a Precipitate Form?
topics.short: Compare Q with Ksp after mixing, remembering that mixing dilutes both solutions.

topics.title: pH and Solubility
topics.short: Salts with basic anions, such as hydroxides and carbonates, dissolve better in acid.

topics.title: Lewis Acids and Complex Ions
topics.short: Metal ions accept electron pairs from ligands, and Kf measures how tightly the complex holds together.

topics.title: Entropy and Microstates
topics.short: Entropy counts the ways to arrange particles and energy: S = k ln W.

topics.title: Predicting the Sign of ΔS
topics.short: Entropy rises with more moles of gas, with melting, boiling and dissolving, and with warming.

topics.title: Absolute Entropies and ΔS°
topics.short: ΔS°(reaction) = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants), and the S° of an element is not zero.

topics.title: The Second Law
topics.short: A process is favored when the entropy of the universe increases, and ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH/T.

topics.title: Gibbs Free Energy
topics.short: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and a negative ΔG means the process is thermodynamically favored.

topics.title: Temperature and Favorability
topics.short: The signs of ΔH and ΔS decide whether heating helps, and the crossover is at T = ΔH/ΔS.

topics.title: Favored but Slow: Kinetic Control
topics.short: A high activation energy can keep a favored reaction from happening at a useful rate.

topics.title: Free Energy and Equilibrium
topics.short: ΔG° = −RT ln K, and ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.

topics.title: Coupled Reactions
topics.short: An unfavored reaction can run when it is paired with a strongly favored one, as ATP does in cells.

topics.title: Galvanic Cells
topics.short: A redox reaction split into two half-cells pushes electrons through a wire from the anode to the cathode.

topics.title: Standard Reduction Potentials
topics.short: E°(cell) = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), and E° is never multiplied by a coefficient.

topics.title: Cell Potential, Free Energy and K
topics.short: ΔG° = −nFE°, so a positive E° means a favored reaction with K > 1.

topics.title: The Nernst Equation
topics.short: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q gives the cell voltage away from standard conditions, even for concentration cells.

topics.title: Electrolytic Cells
topics.short: An outside power source drives an unfavored redox reaction.

topics.title: Electrolysis Calculations
topics.short: Charge equals current times time; divide by Faraday's constant to count moles of electrons.

topics.title: Batteries, Fuel Cells and Corrosion
topics.short: Batteries and rusting are redox reactions, and a more active metal can protect iron.

topics.title: Nuclear Stability and Decay Modes
topics.short: The neutron-to-proton ratio predicts whether a nucleus will beta decay, emit a positron, capture an electron or alpha decay.

topics.title: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
topics.short: A nucleus weighs less than its separate parts, and the missing mass times c² is its binding energy.

topics.title: Radioactive Decay Rates
topics.short: Radioactive decay is first order: N = N₀e^(−kt), even between whole half-lives.

topics.title: Coordination Compounds
topics.short: A central metal ion, its ligands and its coordination number; find the metal's oxidation state.

topics.title: Naming Coordination Compounds
topics.short: Name the ligands in alphabetical order with prefixes, then the metal and its oxidation state.

topics.title: Isomers of Complexes
topics.short: Cis and trans arrangements and mirror-image pairs give complexes with the same formula but different properties.

topics.title: Crystal Field Theory and Color
topics.short: Ligands split the d orbitals; the size of the gap sets the color and the number of unpaired electrons.

topics.title: Preferences and Their Axioms
topics.short: Completeness, transitivity, more-is-better and a taste for variety let us rank bundles of goods consistently.

topics.title: Indifference Curves
topics.short: All bundles a person likes equally lie on one curve; when more is better, the curves slope down and never cross.

topics.title: Utility Functions
topics.short: A utility function gives preferred bundles bigger numbers; any increasing transformation of it describes the same preferences.

topics.title: Marginal Utility as a Partial Derivative
topics.short: MUx = ∂U/∂x is the extra utility from a little more x with y held fixed.

topics.title: The Marginal Rate of Substitution
topics.short: MRS = MUx/MUy, the amount of y a person would give up for one more x, is the size of the indifference curve's slope.

topics.title: Substitutes, Complements, Cobb-Douglas and Quasilinear
topics.short: Four common utility functions and the shapes of their indifference curves.

topics.title: Budget Sets
topics.short: p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ ≤ m, and how prices, income, taxes and rationing reshape the set of affordable bundles.

topics.title: The Best Affordable Bundle
topics.short: At an interior optimum the MRS equals the price ratio; substitute the budget into the utility function and maximize.

topics.title: Cobb-Douglas Demand
topics.short: With U = xᵃyᵇ a person spends the fixed share a/(a + b) of income on x.

topics.title: Corners and Kinks
topics.short: Perfect substitutes lead to buying only the good with more utility per dollar; perfect complements are bought in fixed proportions.

topics.title: The Lagrange Method for Consumers
topics.short: Maximize utility subject to the budget with a Lagrange multiplier, which measures the marginal utility of income.

topics.title: Minimizing Spending for a Target Utility
topics.short: The cheapest way to reach a utility level is also a tangency, and it gives compensated (Hicksian) demand.

topics.title: Revealed Preference
topics.short: If you chose bundle A when B was affordable, you should never choose B when A is affordable.

topics.title: Income Changes and Engel Curves
topics.short: The income offer curve and the Engel curve show normal goods, inferior goods, luxuries and necessities.

topics.title: Price Changes and the Demand Curve
topics.short: Rotating the budget line traces the price offer curve and the demand curve; doubling all prices and income changes nothing.

topics.title: Substitution and Income Effects
topics.short: Split a price change into a move along the original indifference curve and a shift from the change in buying power.

topics.title: Point Elasticity with Calculus
topics.short: ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) at a point; demand Q = AP^(−k) has elasticity −k everywhere.

topics.title: Adding Up to Market Demand
topics.short: Market demand adds the quantities all buyers want at each price, a horizontal sum.

topics.title: Consumer Surplus as an Integral
topics.short: Consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve and above the price, an integral over quantity.

topics.title: Compensating and Equivalent Variation
topics.short: Money measures of a price change: how much to hand back afterward (CV) or take away beforehand (EV) to leave utility the same.

topics.title: Labor Supply and Leisure
topics.short: A higher wage makes leisure more costly but also makes you richer, so labor supply can bend backward.

topics.title: Present Value
topics.short: A dollar later is worth less than a dollar now: PV = FV/(1 + r)ᵗ, with shortcuts for annuities and perpetuities.

topics.title: Saving and Borrowing over Time
topics.short: The budget c₁ + c₂/(1 + r) = m₁ + m₂/(1 + r) shows when it pays to save and when to borrow.

topics.title: Expected Utility
topics.short: Compare risky choices by the probability-weighted average of their utilities, not of their dollar amounts.

topics.title: Risk Aversion and Certainty Equivalents
topics.short: With concave utility, a sure amount below the expected value is as good as the gamble; the gap is the risk premium.

topics.title: Insurance
topics.short: A risk-averse person offered actuarially fair insurance buys full coverage.

topics.title: Production Functions and Marginal Products
topics.short: Q = f(K, L); the marginal product of labor is ∂Q/∂L.

topics.title: Isoquants and the MRTS
topics.short: An isoquant shows the input mixes that make the same output; the size of its slope is MRTS = MPL/MPK.

topics.title: Returns to Scale
topics.short: Doubling every input may more than double, exactly double, or less than double output.

topics.title: Cost Minimization
topics.short: The cheapest input mix sets MRTS = w/r, the producer's version of the consumer's tangency.

topics.title: Cost Functions and Marginal Cost
topics.short: C(q) gives the least cost of making q; MC = C′(q) and AC = C(q)/q.

topics.title: Short-Run and Long-Run Cost
topics.short: With capital fixed, short-run cost is never below long-run cost; the long-run curve is the lower envelope of the short-run curves.

topics.title: Where Average Cost Is Lowest
topics.short: Average cost is lowest where it equals marginal cost, and the quotient rule shows why.

topics.title: The Competitive Firm's Supply Curve
topics.short: Maximize pq − C(q): set p = MC on the rising part of MC above minimum average variable cost.

topics.title: Producer Surplus as an Integral
topics.short: Producer surplus is the integral of p − MC, which equals revenue minus variable cost, or profit plus fixed cost.

topics.title: Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
topics.short: With free entry, price falls to minimum average cost, and the number of firms is market quantity over each firm's output.

topics.title: Tax Incidence with Elasticities
topics.short: Buyers bear the share εS/(εS + |εD|) of a small per-unit tax, so the less elastic side pays more.

topics.title: Deadweight Loss of a Tax
topics.short: The deadweight loss is about ½·t·ΔQ, so it grows with the square of the tax.

topics.title: Monopoly with Calculus
topics.short: Maximize p(q)·q − C(q): set MR = p + q·p′(q) equal to MC.

topics.title: Markups and the Lerner Index
topics.short: (p − MC)/p = 1/|ε|, so a monopoly with positive marginal cost never prices where demand is inelastic.

topics.title: Pricing in Separate Markets
topics.short: Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost in each market; the less elastic market pays the higher price.

topics.title: Two-Part Tariffs
topics.short: With identical customers, charge a per-unit price equal to marginal cost and an entry fee equal to each customer's consumer surplus.

topics.title: Monopsony with Calculus
topics.short: An employer facing the wage curve w(L) hires where marginal revenue product equals the marginal cost of labor, w + L·w′(L).

topics.title: Best Responses and Nash Equilibrium
topics.short: Mark each player's best responses; any cell where both are best responses is a Nash equilibrium, and there may be several.

topics.title: Mixed Strategies
topics.short: In a mixed-strategy equilibrium each player mixes so as to make the other player indifferent between their choices.

topics.title: Sequential Games and Backward Induction
topics.short: Solve a game tree from the end: each player looks ahead to how others will respond, which rules out empty threats.

topics.title: Repeated Games and Cooperation
topics.short: When a game repeats with no known last round, cooperation can last if players value the future enough.

topics.title: Cournot Competition
topics.short: Firms choose quantities; each firm's best response depends on the other's output, and equilibrium output lies between monopoly and competition.

topics.title: Bertrand Competition
topics.short: Two firms selling identical goods and competing on price drive the price down to marginal cost.

topics.title: Stackelberg Leadership
topics.short: A leader who moves first, knowing the follower's best response, produces more and earns more than in Cournot.

topics.title: Auctions
topics.short: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy; in a first-price auction bidders shade their bids.

topics.title: The Edgeworth Box and Pareto Efficiency
topics.short: An allocation is Pareto efficient when no trade can help one person without hurting the other; there the two MRSs are equal.

topics.title: Competitive Equilibrium in Exchange
topics.short: Find the price ratio at which both people's demands, paid for with the value of their endowments, add up to what is available.

topics.title: The Welfare Theorems
topics.short: Competitive equilibria are Pareto efficient, and with convex preferences any efficient allocation can be reached with lump-sum transfers.

topics.title: The Efficient Amount of an Externality
topics.short: Set marginal benefit equal to marginal social cost; a tax equal to the marginal external damage at that quantity gets the market there.

topics.title: The Coase Theorem
topics.short: With clear property rights and low bargaining costs, the parties reach the efficient outcome whoever holds the rights; only who pays whom differs.

topics.title: Providing Public Goods Efficiently
topics.short: Provide more of a public good while the sum of everyone's marginal benefits is above its marginal cost.

topics.title: Common Resources
topics.short: Open access draws users until the average return equals the cost, which uses the resource more than is efficient.

topics.title: Adverse Selection and Lemons
topics.short: When sellers know quality and buyers don't, good products can be driven out of the market.

topics.title: Moral Hazard and Incentives
topics.short: When actions are hidden after a deal, deductibles, copays and pay tied to results can restore incentives.

topics.title: Signaling
topics.short: A costly signal can separate types when it costs the high type less, even if it adds nothing to productivity.

topics.title: The Circular Flow
topics.short: Households and firms meet in product and factor markets, with money flowing one way and goods and resources the other.

topics.title: What GDP Counts
topics.short: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.

topics.title: GDP = C + I + G + NX
topics.short: Sort spending into consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, then add.

topics.title: Value Added and the Income Approach
topics.short: Adding the value each stage of production adds, or adding everyone's income, gives the same total as final spending.

topics.title: GDP per Person and Its Limits
topics.short: GDP per person helps compare living standards, but it leaves out work at home, leisure, the environment and how income is shared.

topics.title: Nominal and Real GDP
topics.short: Real GDP values output at base-year prices, so it grows only when production grows.

topics.title: The GDP Deflator
topics.short: The deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100, and it turns nominal values into real ones.

topics.title: Who Is in the Labor Force
topics.short: The labor force is everyone working plus everyone without a job who is looking for one.

topics.title: The Unemployment Rate
topics.short: Divide the number unemployed by the labor force, not by the whole population.

topics.title: Frictional, Structural and Cyclical Unemployment
topics.short: The natural rate is frictional plus structural unemployment; cyclical unemployment comes from recessions.

topics.title: Price Indexes and the CPI
topics.short: A price index compares the cost of a fixed basket of goods with its cost in a base year, set to 100.

topics.title: Inflation, Deflation and Disinflation
topics.short: The inflation rate is the percent change in a price index from one period to the next.

topics.title: Converting Nominal to Real
topics.short: Divide a dollar amount by the price index over 100 to compare dollars from different years.

topics.title: Who Gains and Loses from Inflation
topics.short: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders and people on fixed incomes; all inflation brings menu costs and shoe-leather costs.

topics.title: The Business Cycle
topics.short: Real GDP moves through expansion, peak, contraction and trough around its long-run trend.

topics.title: Aggregate Demand
topics.short: AD slopes down because of the wealth, interest-rate and exchange-rate effects, not because buyers switch to other goods.

topics.title: What Shifts Aggregate Demand
topics.short: A change in consumption, investment, government purchases or net exports at every price level shifts AD.

topics.title: Marginal Propensities to Consume and Save
topics.short: MPC is the share of an extra dollar of income that is spent, MPS the share that is saved, and MPC + MPS = 1.

topics.title: The Spending Multiplier
topics.short: New spending becomes someone's income and is partly spent again, so GDP rises by 1/(1 − MPC) times the first change.

topics.title: The Tax Multiplier
topics.short: A tax cut raises GDP by MPC/MPS times its size, less than the same increase in government purchases.

topics.title: Short-Run Aggregate Supply
topics.short: SRAS slopes up because wages and some prices are slow to adjust; input prices, productivity and supply shocks shift it.

topics.title: Long-Run Aggregate Supply
topics.short: LRAS is vertical at full-employment output, which resources and technology set, not the price level.

topics.title: Equilibrium and Output Gaps
topics.short: Where AD meets SRAS, output may sit below full employment (a recessionary gap) or above it (an inflationary gap).

topics.title: Demand Shocks and Supply Shocks
topics.short: A demand shock moves the price level and output the same way; a supply shock moves them in opposite directions.

topics.title: Long-Run Self-Adjustment
topics.short: Over time, wages and other input prices adjust and SRAS shifts until output returns to full employment.

topics.title: Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy
topics.short: Raising spending or cutting taxes pushes AD right to close a recessionary gap; the reverse closes an inflationary gap.

topics.title: How Big a Fiscal Change?
topics.short: Divide the output gap by the right multiplier to find the change in spending or taxes needed.

topics.title: Progressive, Regressive and Proportional Taxes
topics.short: Marginal and average tax rates, and what happens to the average rate as income rises.

topics.title: Automatic Stabilizers
topics.short: Progressive income taxes and programs like unemployment insurance cushion recessions without any new law.

topics.title: Budget Deficits and the National Debt
topics.short: A deficit is one year's shortfall; the debt is the running total of past deficits minus surpluses.

topics.title: Bonds, Stocks and Interest Rates
topics.short: When market interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall.

topics.title: Nominal and Real Interest Rates
topics.short: The real interest rate is about the nominal rate minus the inflation rate.

topics.title: What Money Does
topics.short: Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.

topics.title: Measuring Money: M1 and M2
topics.short: M1 holds the most liquid forms of money; M2 adds less liquid ones such as small time deposits.

topics.title: Bank Balance Sheets
topics.short: Assets (reserves, loans, securities) equal liabilities (deposits) plus owners' equity; reserves split into required and excess.

topics.title: How Banks Create Money
topics.short: When banks lend out excess reserves, new deposits appear; the simple money multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio.

topics.title: The Money Market
topics.short: The demand for money and the supply the central bank provides set the nominal interest rate.

topics.title: The Central Bank's Tools
topics.short: Open market operations, the discount rate, reserve requirements and the interest rate paid on reserves.

topics.title: Setting Rates with Ample Reserves
topics.short: When banks hold plenty of reserves, the Fed steers the federal funds rate mainly through the interest rate it pays on reserves.

topics.title: Monetary Policy and the Economy
topics.short: Lower interest rates raise investment and consumption, shifting AD right; higher rates do the reverse.

topics.title: The Loanable Funds Market
topics.short: Saving supplies and borrowing demands loanable funds, and together they set the real interest rate.

topics.title: Fiscal and Monetary Policy Together
topics.short: Combine two policies' effects on output, the price level and interest rates, and spot which result is uncertain.

topics.title: The Short-Run Phillips Curve
topics.short: In the short run, lower unemployment comes with higher inflation; an AD shift moves the economy along the curve.

topics.title: The Long-Run Phillips Curve
topics.short: In the long run, unemployment returns to its natural rate whatever the inflation rate, so the curve is vertical.

topics.title: Money Growth and Inflation
topics.short: MV = PY: in the long run, money growing faster than output raises prices.

topics.title: Crowding Out
topics.short: Government borrowing can raise the real interest rate and reduce private investment.

topics.title: Schools of Macroeconomic Thought
topics.short: Classical, Keynesian, monetarist and newer schools agree on much and differ on how fast markets adjust and how active policy should be.

topics.title: Productivity and Growth
topics.short: Output per hour of work rises with physical capital, human capital and technology.

topics.title: Compound Growth and the Rule of 70
topics.short: At a growth rate of g percent a year, a quantity doubles in about 70/g years.

topics.title: Policies for Long-Run Growth
topics.short: Policies that build physical capital, skills and technology shift LRAS and the PPC outward.

topics.title: The Balance of Payments
topics.short: The current account and the capital and financial account record a country's dealings with the rest of the world, and they balance each other.

topics.title: Exchange Rates
topics.short: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another; a currency appreciates when it buys more of the other.

topics.title: The Foreign Exchange Market
topics.short: Demand for dollars comes from foreigners buying U.S. goods and assets; supply comes from Americans buying foreign ones.

topics.title: What Moves Exchange Rates
topics.short: Tastes, relative incomes, relative price levels and relative interest rates shift the demand for and supply of a currency.

topics.title: Exchange Rates and Net Exports
topics.short: A stronger currency makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, lowering net exports and AD.

topics.title: Interest Rates and Capital Flows
topics.short: A higher real interest rate draws in foreign financial capital, which raises demand for the currency.

topics.title: Saving, Investment and the Trade Balance
topics.short: Private saving plus the government's budget balance equals domestic investment plus net exports.

topics.title: Scarcity and the Factors of Production
topics.short: Wants outrun resources, so land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship must be rationed somehow.

topics.title: Opportunity Cost
topics.short: The cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up, including your time.

topics.title: Positive and Normative Statements
topics.short: A positive statement can be checked against facts; a normative statement says what ought to be.

topics.title: Economic Systems
topics.short: Markets, command and tradition each answer what to make, how to make it and who gets it; real economies mix them.

topics.title: Budget Constraints
topics.short: A budget line shows every affordable combination of two goods, and its slope is an opportunity cost.

topics.title: The Production Possibilities Curve
topics.short: Points on the curve are efficient, points inside waste resources, and points outside cannot be produced yet.

topics.title: Opportunity Cost Along the PPC
topics.short: A straight PPC means constant opportunity cost; a bowed-out PPC means the cost rises as you make more.

topics.title: Growth and Shifts of the PPC
topics.short: More resources or better technology push the curve out; idle resources put the economy at a point inside it.

topics.title: Absolute and Comparative Advantage
topics.short: Comparative advantage goes to whoever gives up less of the other good, not to whoever makes more.

topics.title: Specialization and the Terms of Trade
topics.short: Trade helps both sides when the price lies between the two producers' opportunity costs.

topics.title: Marginal Benefit, Marginal Cost and Sunk Costs
topics.short: Keep going while the next unit's benefit is at least its cost; money already spent should not change the choice.

topics.title: Total and Marginal Utility
topics.short: Each extra unit usually adds less satisfaction than the one before it.

topics.title: Marginal Utility per Dollar
topics.short: Spend so the last dollar on each good adds the same utility: MUx/Px = MUy/Py.

topics.title: The Law of Demand
topics.short: Other things equal, a higher price means a smaller quantity demanded.

topics.title: Demand Equations Both Ways
topics.short: Q = 20 − 2P and P = 10 − Q/2 describe the same demand curve, drawn with price on the vertical axis.

topics.title: Change in Demand vs Change in Quantity Demanded
topics.short: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; any other change in buying plans shifts the whole curve.

topics.title: What Shifts Demand
topics.short: Tastes, income, expectations and the number of buyers shift demand; more income raises demand for normal goods and lowers it for inferior goods.

topics.title: Substitutes and Complements
topics.short: A higher price for coffee raises demand for tea (a substitute) and lowers demand for coffee filters (a complement).

topics.title: The Law of Supply
topics.short: Other things equal, a higher price brings a larger quantity supplied, because extra units cost more to make.

topics.title: What Shifts Supply
topics.short: Input prices, technology, taxes and subsidies, expectations and the number of sellers shift supply.

topics.title: Market Equilibrium
topics.short: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, found on a graph or by setting the two equations equal.

topics.title: Shortages and Surpluses
topics.short: Below the equilibrium price there is a shortage, above it a surplus, and each pushes the price back toward equilibrium.

topics.title: When One Curve Shifts
topics.short: Decide which curve shifts and which way, then read the new equilibrium price and quantity.

topics.title: When Both Curves Shift
topics.short: With two shifts, either price or quantity changes in a definite direction and the other depends on which shift is larger.

topics.title: Price Elasticity of Demand
topics.short: Divide the percent change in quantity demanded by the percent change in price, using the midpoint method.

topics.title: Elastic, Inelastic and What Decides It
topics.short: Close substitutes, luxuries, a large share of the budget and more time to adjust all make demand more elastic.

topics.title: Elasticity and Total Revenue
topics.short: A higher price raises revenue only when demand is inelastic; revenue is largest where demand is unit elastic.

topics.title: Price Elasticity of Supply
topics.short: Supply is more elastic when firms have time, spare capacity and easy access to inputs.

topics.title: Income and Cross-Price Elasticity
topics.short: The sign tells the story: normal or inferior goods for income elasticity, substitutes or complements for cross-price elasticity.

topics.title: Consumer and Producer Surplus
topics.short: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and the price; sellers gain the gap between the price and their cost.

topics.title: Total Surplus and Deadweight Loss
topics.short: A competitive market with no spillovers maximizes total surplus; trading too little or too much loses some of it.

topics.title: Price Ceilings and Price Floors
topics.short: A binding ceiling sits below equilibrium and causes a shortage; a binding floor sits above it and causes a surplus.

topics.title: Per-Unit Taxes
topics.short: A tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep, raising revenue and causing a deadweight loss.

topics.title: Who Really Pays a Tax
topics.short: The less elastic side of the market bears more of a tax, no matter who sends the money to the government.

topics.title: Per-Unit Subsidies
topics.short: A subsidy lowers the price buyers pay, raises the price sellers get, costs taxpayers money and leads to more than the efficient quantity.

topics.title: Trade at the World Price
topics.short: When a country opens to trade, the world price decides whether it imports or exports, and who gains and who loses.

topics.title: Tariffs and Import Quotas
topics.short: A tariff or quota raises the domestic price, helps domestic producers, costs consumers more and creates deadweight loss.

topics.title: Accounting and Economic Profit
topics.short: Economic profit subtracts implicit costs too, so zero economic profit is a normal return.

topics.title: Short-Run Production
topics.short: Adding workers to a fixed plant eventually adds less output each time: diminishing marginal returns.

topics.title: Short-Run Costs
topics.short: Fixed, variable and total cost, and the average and marginal costs computed from them.

topics.title: How Marginal and Average Costs Relate
topics.short: Marginal cost crosses average variable cost and average total cost at their lowest points.

topics.title: What Shifts the Cost Curves
topics.short: A change in fixed cost, such as a license fee or lump-sum tax, moves only ATC and AFC; a change in variable cost moves MC, AVC and ATC.

topics.title: Economies and Diseconomies of Scale
topics.short: In the long run every input can change; average cost may fall, stay flat, then rise as the firm grows.

topics.title: Perfect Competition and Price Takers
topics.short: Many sellers of an identical product each face a flat demand curve at the market price, so P = MR.

topics.title: Profit-Maximizing Output: MR = MC
topics.short: Produce every unit whose marginal revenue covers its marginal cost, and stop where MR = MC.

topics.title: Profit and Loss on the Graph
topics.short: Profit equals (P − ATC) × Q, a rectangle between the price and average total cost.

topics.title: The Shutdown Rule
topics.short: In the short run, keep producing if price covers average variable cost, even at a loss.

topics.title: Entry, Exit and the Long Run
topics.short: Profits draw new firms in and losses push firms out until price equals minimum average total cost.

topics.title: Allocative and Productive Efficiency
topics.short: Allocative efficiency means P = MC; productive efficiency means producing at minimum ATC.

topics.title: Monopoly and Barriers to Entry
topics.short: Economies of scale, legal protection such as patents, control of a key resource and network effects can keep rivals out.

topics.title: Why Marginal Revenue Is Below Price
topics.short: To sell one more unit, a single-price seller must lower the price on every unit, so MR < P.

topics.title: The Monopolist's Price and Output
topics.short: Find the quantity where MR = MC, then go up to the demand curve to read the price.

topics.title: Monopoly and Deadweight Loss
topics.short: A monopoly sells less at a higher price than a competitive market would, so P > MC and some surplus is lost.

topics.title: Regulating a Natural Monopoly
topics.short: When one firm can serve a market most cheaply, regulators may set P = MC (efficient but loss-making) or P = ATC (a fair return).

topics.title: Price Discrimination
topics.short: Charging different buyers different prices for the same good can raise both output and profit while shrinking consumer surplus.

topics.title: Monopolistic Competition
topics.short: Many firms with differentiated products earn zero economic profit in the long run and have excess capacity.

topics.title: Payoff Matrices and Dominant Strategies
topics.short: A dominant strategy is a player's best choice no matter what the other player does.

topics.title: Nash Equilibrium and the Prisoner's Dilemma
topics.short: In a Nash equilibrium no player can do better by changing alone, which is why cartels are hard to hold together.

topics.title: Marginal Revenue Product and Hiring
topics.short: Hire workers until the marginal revenue product of the last one equals the wage.

topics.title: Shifts in Labor Demand and Supply
topics.short: Product prices, productivity and other inputs shift labor demand; population, preferences and pay elsewhere shift labor supply.

topics.title: The Least-Cost Mix of Inputs
topics.short: Use inputs so the last dollar spent on each adds the same output: MPL/w = MPK/r.

topics.title: Monopsony
topics.short: A single buyer of labor must raise the wage for everyone to hire one more worker, so it hires fewer workers at a lower wage.

topics.title: Negative Externalities
topics.short: When a cost spills onto bystanders, the market produces more than the efficient amount.

topics.title: Positive Externalities
topics.short: When a benefit spills onto bystanders, the market produces less than the efficient amount.

topics.title: Correcting Externalities
topics.short: A per-unit tax equal to the marginal external cost, a subsidy, tradable permits or direct rules can move output toward the efficient amount.

topics.title: Rival and Excludable Goods
topics.short: Private goods, public goods, common resources and club goods differ in whether people can be kept out and whether one person's use leaves less for others.

topics.title: Public Goods and Free Riders
topics.short: Because no one can be kept from using a public good, people can ride free, and markets tend to supply too little.

topics.title: Measuring Income Inequality
topics.short: The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient show how evenly income is shared.

topics.title: Earth's Four Spheres
topics.short: Sort the parts of Earth into geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere, and spot where they interact.

topics.title: Latitude and Longitude
topics.short: Find any place on Earth by its degrees north or south of the equator and east or west of the prime meridian.

topics.title: Reading Topographic Maps
topics.short: Read elevations from contour lines, and tell steep slopes from gentle ones and hills from valleys.

topics.title: Earth's Spin: Day and Night
topics.short: Earth turns once a day, so the Sun seems to rise in the east, cross the sky and set in the west.

topics.title: Why We Have Seasons
topics.short: Earth's tilted axis changes the Sun's height in the sky and the length of the day through the year.

topics.title: Phases of the Moon
topics.short: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun; as the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half.

topics.title: Solar and Lunar Eclipses
topics.short: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, which the Moon's tilted orbit allows only a few times a year.

topics.title: Gravity and Orbits
topics.short: Gravity pulls every mass toward every other mass; an orbit is falling around a body while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.

topics.title: Tides
topics.short: The Moon's pull makes two bulges of ocean, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours 50 minutes.

topics.title: Planets, Moons and Small Bodies
topics.short: Tell the rocky inner planets from the giant outer planets, and place moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.

topics.title: The Scale of the Solar System
topics.short: Use astronomical units and scale models to see how small the planets are and how far apart they lie.

topics.title: Light-Years, Stars and Galaxies
topics.short: A light-year is a distance; the Sun is one ordinary star among hundreds of billions in the Milky Way galaxy.

topics.title: Density
topics.short: Density is mass per volume; it decides what floats and what sinks, and how Earth sorted itself into layers.

topics.title: Earth's Layers
topics.short: The crust, mantle, outer core and inner core differ in what they are made of, how dense they are and whether they are solid or liquid.

topics.title: Lithosphere and Asthenosphere
topics.short: The rigid lithosphere, the crust plus the top of the mantle, rides on the hot, softer asthenosphere below.

topics.title: Convection
topics.short: Warm fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises while cooler, denser fluid sinks, making a loop.

topics.title: What Makes a Mineral
topics.short: A mineral is a natural, inorganic solid with a definite chemical makeup and an orderly crystal structure.

topics.title: Identifying Minerals
topics.short: Use hardness, streak, luster, cleavage and density to identify a mineral, since color can fool you.

topics.title: Igneous Rocks
topics.short: Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools; slow cooling underground grows large crystals, and fast cooling at the surface makes small ones.

topics.title: Sedimentary Rocks
topics.short: Sediments settle in layers, then are pressed together and cemented into rock; rocks made of grains are named by grain size.

topics.title: Metamorphic Rocks
topics.short: Heat and pressure change a rock's minerals and texture without melting it.

topics.title: The Rock Cycle
topics.short: Any rock can become any other kind through melting, weathering, burial, heat and pressure, driven by Earth's inner heat and the Sun.

topics.title: Mechanical and Chemical Weathering
topics.short: Rock breaks into smaller pieces (mechanical weathering) or changes into new substances (chemical weathering).

topics.title: What Speeds Up Weathering
topics.short: More surface area, more water and warmth, and minerals that break down easily make rock weather faster.

topics.title: How Soil Forms
topics.short: Soil is weathered rock mixed with water, air and living and once-living matter, built up slowly in layers called horizons.

topics.title: Erosion and Deposition
topics.short: Water, wind, ice and gravity carry sediment away and drop it where they slow down.

topics.title: Landforms Made by Water, Wind and Ice
topics.short: Read a landscape: V-shaped valleys and deltas from rivers, U-shaped valleys and moraines from glaciers, dunes from wind.

topics.title: Slow and Fast Changes
topics.short: Tiny changes each year add up over millions of years, while a few changes, like landslides, happen in minutes.

topics.title: Fossils
topics.short: Fossils are remains or traces of past life, usually kept when remains are buried quickly in sediment.

topics.title: Superposition: Reading Layers in Order
topics.short: In layers that have not been disturbed, the oldest is at the bottom and the youngest is at the top.

topics.title: Cross-Cutting Relationships
topics.short: A fault or a body of igneous rock that cuts through other rock is younger than the rock it cuts.

topics.title: Half-Life and Absolute Age
topics.short: Radioactive atoms decay at a steady rate, so the fraction left tells a rock's age in years.

topics.title: The Geologic Time Scale
topics.short: Earth's 4.6-billion-year history is divided into eons, eras and periods, marked by big changes in life.

topics.title: The Evidence for Moving Continents
topics.short: Matching coastlines, fossils, rock layers and scratches from ancient ice show the continents were once joined.

topics.title: Seafloor Spreading
topics.short: New ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges, so the rock gets older the farther it lies from a ridge.

topics.title: Three Kinds of Plate Boundaries
topics.short: Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries, push together at convergent ones and slide past each other at transform ones.

topics.title: What Forms at Each Boundary
topics.short: Match ridges, rift valleys, trenches, volcanic arcs, mountain ranges and long faults to the boundaries that make them.

topics.title: How Fast Plates Move
topics.short: Plates move a few centimeters a year, which adds up to hundreds of kilometers over millions of years.

topics.title: Earthquakes and Seismic Waves
topics.short: Rock snaps along a fault and sends out P waves first, then S waves, then slower surface waves.

topics.title: Earthquake Magnitude
topics.short: Each step up in magnitude means waves 10 times taller on a seismogram and about 32 times more energy.

topics.title: Kinds of Volcanoes
topics.short: Runny, low-silica lava builds broad shield volcanoes; sticky, gas-rich magma builds steep cones and erupts explosively.

topics.title: Hot Spots and Island Chains
topics.short: A plate sliding over a fixed hot spot leaves a line of volcanoes that get older with distance, which shows the plate's speed.

topics.title: Forecasting Natural Hazards
topics.short: Records and warning signs tell where hazards strike and how often, even when the exact day can't be known.

topics.title: Where Earth's Water Is
topics.short: About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean; most fresh water is frozen in ice or held underground.

topics.title: The Water Cycle
topics.short: Energy from the Sun lifts water by evaporation, and gravity brings it back down as precipitation and runoff.

topics.title: Groundwater and Aquifers
topics.short: Rain soaks into spaces in soil and rock; below the water table they are full, and wells draw water from aquifers.

topics.title: What Air Is Made Of
topics.short: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% argon, with small but important amounts of carbon dioxide.

topics.title: Layers of the Atmosphere
topics.short: Temperature falls, rises, falls and rises again with height, marking the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere.

topics.title: Air Pressure
topics.short: Air has weight, so it presses on everything around it; pressure is highest at sea level and drops as you go up.

topics.title: Wind and Local Breezes
topics.short: Uneven heating makes differences in pressure, and air flows from high to low pressure, as in sea breezes by day and land breezes at night.

topics.title: Global Winds and the Coriolis Effect
topics.short: Earth's spin bends moving air, turning the rising and sinking air of the tropics and poles into the trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.

topics.title: Air Masses and Fronts
topics.short: Large bodies of air take on the warmth and moisture of where they formed; where two meet, a front brings a change in weather.

topics.title: Surface Ocean Currents
topics.short: Steady winds drive surface currents into giant loops that carry warm water toward the poles and cool water toward the equator.

topics.title: Deep Ocean Currents
topics.short: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks near the poles, driving a slow current that winds through every ocean.

topics.title: Weather and Climate
topics.short: Weather is the state of the air at a time and place; climate is the pattern of weather over 30 years or more.

topics.title: What Sets a Place's Climate
topics.short: Latitude, elevation, distance from the sea, ocean currents and mountains together set a region's climate.

topics.title: The Greenhouse Effect
topics.short: Sunlight warms the ground, the ground gives off infrared light, and greenhouse gases absorb some of it and send part back down.

topics.title: Evidence of a Warming World
topics.short: Thermometer records, rising seas, shrinking ice and the rising carbon dioxide record show that Earth has warmed over the last century.

topics.title: Renewable and Nonrenewable Resources
topics.short: Some resources renew within a human lifetime; others, like fossil fuels and metal ores, took millions of years to form where they are.

topics.title: People and Earth's Systems
topics.short: Total use equals the number of people times the use per person, so growth in either one raises the impact.

topics.title: How Earth Formed and Layered
topics.short: Earth grew from colliding rock and metal about 4.54 billion years ago and, while hot, sorted itself by density into core, mantle and crust.

topics.title: Seeing Inside Earth with Seismic Waves
topics.short: S waves can't cross the liquid outer core and P waves bend at its edge, leaving shadow zones that map the core.

topics.title: Heat Flow and the Geothermal Gradient
topics.short: Temperature rises about 25 °C per kilometer in the upper crust, fed by heat left from Earth's formation and by radioactive decay.

topics.title: Isostasy: How Crust Floats
topics.short: Crust floats on the mantle like ice on water, so high mountains have deep roots and land rises when an ice sheet melts.

topics.title: Earth's Magnetic Field in Rocks
topics.short: Earth's field flips now and then, and iron-rich minerals in cooling lava record its direction, building a timeline of reversals.

topics.title: Atoms, Ions and Crystals
topics.short: A mineral is ions stacked in a repeating pattern, and ions of similar size and charge can trade places, so a mineral's makeup can vary.

topics.title: The Silica Tetrahedron
topics.short: One silicon bonded to four oxygens, SiO₄ with a charge of −4, is the building block of most minerals in the crust.

topics.title: Silicate Families
topics.short: Tetrahedra link as singles, chains, double chains, sheets or 3-D frameworks, which sets each mineral's silicon-to-oxygen ratio and how it breaks.

topics.title: Carbonates, Oxides, Sulfides and Other Groups
topics.short: Sort minerals by their negative ion: carbonates (CO₃), oxides (O), sulfides (S), sulfates (SO₄), halides (Cl, F) and native elements.

topics.title: How Rocks Melt
topics.short: Rock in the mantle melts when the pressure drops, when water is added, or when hot magma heats the crust around it.

topics.title: Bowen's Reaction Series
topics.short: As magma cools, minerals crystallize in order: olivine and calcium-rich feldspar first, quartz last.

topics.title: Mafic to Felsic
topics.short: Magmas range from mafic (low in silica, hot, runny and dark) to felsic (high in silica, cooler, sticky and light).

topics.title: Naming Igneous Rocks
topics.short: Name an igneous rock from its texture and composition: granite and rhyolite, diorite and andesite, gabbro and basalt.

topics.title: Plutons, Dikes and Sills
topics.short: Magma that cools underground forms batholiths, dikes that cut across layers and sills that slip between them.

topics.title: Gentle and Explosive Eruptions
topics.short: Viscosity and gas decide whether magma oozes out as lava or blasts out as ash; the VEI rates eruptions by volume, ten times more per step.

topics.title: Volcanic Hazards and Monitoring
topics.short: Pyroclastic flows, lahars, ash, gases and lava each threaten in their own way; swelling ground, gas and small earthquakes can give warning.

topics.title: Chemical Weathering Reactions
topics.short: Feldspar turns to clay, iron minerals rust and calcite dissolves, while quartz resists and piles up as sand.

topics.title: Grain Size and the Wentworth Scale
topics.short: Sort sediment by size, from clay under 1/256 mm to boulders over 256 mm, and use the phi scale, φ = −log₂ d.

topics.title: How Flowing Water Moves Sediment
topics.short: Faster water moves bigger grains; the Hjulström diagram shows when a grain is picked up, carried or dropped.

topics.title: Sorting, Rounding and Maturity
topics.short: The farther sediment travels, the better sorted and rounder it gets and the more of it is quartz.

topics.title: Naming Sedimentary Rocks
topics.short: Name clastic rocks by grain size and shape (conglomerate, breccia, sandstone, shale) and chemical and biochemical rocks by makeup (limestone, rock salt, chert, coal).

topics.title: Reading Sedimentary Structures
topics.short: Cross-beds, ripple marks, mud cracks and graded beds show current direction, waves, drying out and which way was up.

topics.title: Depositional Environments
topics.short: Match rocks and structures to the place they formed: river, delta, beach, reef, deep sea, desert dunes or glacier.

topics.title: Heat and Pressure with Depth
topics.short: Pressure grows by about 26 MPa for each kilometer of rock overhead (P = ρgh), and temperature rises along the geotherm.

topics.title: Foliation and Metamorphic Grade
topics.short: As heat and pressure rise, shale becomes slate, phyllite, schist and then gneiss, and index minerals like garnet appear in order.

topics.title: Naming Metamorphic Rocks
topics.short: Name a metamorphic rock by its foliation and its parent: marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone, gneiss from granite or shale.

topics.title: Where Metamorphism Happens
topics.short: Contact metamorphism bakes rock beside magma, regional metamorphism comes with mountain building, and subduction makes high-pressure, low-temperature rocks.

topics.title: Stress and Strain
topics.short: Rocks are squeezed, stretched or sheared; near the surface they break (brittle), while deep and hot they bend (ductile).

topics.title: Anticlines, Synclines and Domes
topics.short: Folds arch up (anticlines) or sag down (synclines); once eroded, an anticline shows its oldest rocks in the middle.

topics.title: Normal, Reverse and Strike-Slip Faults
topics.short: Name the hanging wall and footwall and read the slip: pulling apart makes normal faults, squeezing makes reverse and thrust faults, and shearing makes strike-slip faults.

topics.title: Strike and Dip
topics.short: Strike is the compass direction of a level line on a tilted layer, dip is its downward tilt, and with trigonometry they give how deep the layer lies.

topics.title: Steno's Principles and Faunal Succession
topics.short: Original horizontality, lateral continuity, inclusions and the order of fossils extend superposition to read any outcrop.

topics.title: Unconformities
topics.short: A buried erosion surface marks missing time: an angular unconformity, a nonconformity or a disconformity.

topics.title: Correlating Rock Layers
topics.short: Match layers from place to place by rock type, by key beds such as volcanic ash, and by index fossils.

topics.title: Reconstructing a Region's History
topics.short: Put a cross-section's events in order: deposition, folding, faulting, intrusion, erosion and more deposition.

topics.title: Radiometric Dating
topics.short: From the ratio of daughter to parent atoms, find how many half-lives have passed: a ratio of 1 means one half-life, 3 means two, 7 means three.

topics.title: Choosing a Radioactive Clock
topics.short: Match the clock to the job: carbon-14 for recent remains, potassium–argon and uranium–lead for igneous rock millions to billions of years old.

topics.title: Combining Relative and Absolute Ages
topics.short: Date a sedimentary layer by the dated igneous rocks around it: younger than what lies below it, older than what cuts it or covers it.

topics.title: Major Events in Earth's History
topics.short: Place the big events on the time scale: the oldest minerals, first life, oxygen in the air, the Cambrian explosion and the great mass extinctions.

topics.title: Magnetic Stripes and Spreading Rates
topics.short: Match seafloor stripes to the reversal timeline to find how fast a ridge spreads, as a half rate or a full rate.

topics.title: Measuring Plate Motion with GPS
topics.short: GPS stations move millimeters to centimeters a year; subtracting their velocity vectors shows how two plates move relative to each other.

topics.title: What Drives the Plates
topics.short: Sinking slabs pull plates, high ridges push them, and the mantle convects beneath; the pull of sinking slabs is the largest force.

topics.title: Subduction Zones
topics.short: The denser plate sinks, earthquakes trace the slab hundreds of kilometers down, and water from the slab melts the mantle above to feed arc volcanoes.

topics.title: Continental Collisions and Rifts
topics.short: Continents are too buoyant to sink far, so they crumple into high mountains when they meet and stretch into rift valleys when they split.

topics.title: Transform Faults
topics.short: Transform faults offset mid-ocean ridges and let plates slide past each other, and only the part between the ridge segments is active.

topics.title: The Wilson Cycle
topics.short: Oceans open and close in a cycle (rift, young ocean, wide ocean, subduction, closing and collision), with supercontinents like Pangaea in between.

topics.title: Elastic Rebound
topics.short: Rock on both sides of a locked fault bends slowly, then snaps back in an earthquake; slip rate and slip per quake give the average time between quakes.

topics.title: Distance from the S–P Time
topics.short: P waves outrun S waves, so the gap between their arrivals grows with distance: d = Δt·vP·vS/(vP − vS).

topics.title: Finding the Epicenter
topics.short: Draw a circle of the right distance around each of three stations; the epicenter is where all three circles meet.

topics.title: Moment Magnitude and Energy
topics.short: Magnitude grows with the logarithm of the fault's area times its slip, and each step up means about 32 times more energy.

topics.title: Intensity and Ground Shaking
topics.short: Intensity measures the shaking at one place on the Modified Mercalli scale; it depends on distance, depth and soft ground, not only on magnitude.

topics.title: Earthquake Forecasts as Probabilities
topics.short: Turn a yearly chance into the chance of at least one event in n years: 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ.

topics.title: Tsunamis
topics.short: A sudden jolt of the seafloor lifts the whole water column; the wave crosses deep ocean as fast as a jet (v = √(gd)) and slows and grows tall near shore.

topics.title: Landslides and Slope Stability
topics.short: A slope fails when the downhill pull beats the friction and strength holding it; water and steeper slopes tip the balance.

topics.title: Stream Gradient and Discharge
topics.short: A stream's gradient is its drop per distance, and its discharge is width × depth × speed, in cubic meters per second.

topics.title: Meanders, Floodplains and Base Level
topics.short: Rivers wear away the outside of bends and build on the inside, spread floodplains, and cut down toward base level.

topics.title: What a 100-Year Flood Means
topics.short: Rank a river's yearly peak flows to find recurrence intervals; a 100-year flood has a 1% chance of happening in any year.

topics.title: Groundwater Flow and Darcy's Law
topics.short: Groundwater flows from high head to low head, and Darcy's law, Q = K·A·Δh/L, tells how much.

topics.title: Glaciers: Mass Balance and Flow
topics.short: A glacier gains snow up high and loses ice down low; its end advances or retreats with the balance, but the ice always flows downhill.

topics.title: How Ore Deposits Form
topics.short: Ores are rare places where geology concentrated a metal; magma, hot water, weathering, evaporation and rivers can all do it.

topics.title: How Oil, Gas and Coal Form
topics.short: Buried remains of tiny sea life cook into oil at about 60 to 120 °C and collect under a seal in a trap, while buried swamp plants become coal.

topics.title: Resources, Reserves and How Long They Last
topics.short: Reserves are the part of a resource that can be produced at a profit today, so the years they last change with price, technology and discovery.

topics.title: Measuring Air Pressure
topics.short: Pressure is force per area; read it in hectopascals, millibars and inches of mercury.

topics.title: How Pressure Falls with Height
topics.short: Pressure drops by about half for every 5.5 km you climb, because less air is left above you.

topics.title: The Gas Law for Air
topics.short: Pressure, density and temperature are tied together by P = ρRT, so at the same pressure warm air is less dense than cold air.

topics.title: Sunlight In, Infrared Out
