topics.short: The Sun's light peaks in the visible and Earth's glow peaks near 10 μm in the infrared, so air can let sunlight through yet absorb Earth's heat.

topics.title: Hotter Things Glow Much More
topics.short: The energy a surface gives off grows with the fourth power of its temperature in kelvins: E = σT⁴.

topics.title: Sun Angle and Sunlight on the Ground
topics.short: A low sun spreads the same beam over more ground, so each square meter gets less energy.

topics.title: Albedo: How Much Sunlight Bounces Off
topics.short: Albedo is the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects: fresh snow reflects most of it and open ocean very little.

topics.title: Earth's Energy Balance
topics.short: Earth warms until the infrared it sends to space equals the sunlight it absorbs, which predicts about −18 °C with no greenhouse gases.

topics.title: How Greenhouse Gases Warm the Surface
topics.short: Air that absorbs infrared sends part of it back down, so the surface must warm until it gives off more.

topics.title: Why Coasts Stay Mild
topics.short: Water takes about five times more energy than dry sand to warm by one degree, so oceans warm and cool slowly and coastal places swing less in temperature than inland ones.

topics.title: Latent Heat: Energy Hidden in Water Vapor
topics.short: Evaporating water takes in a lot of energy and condensing vapor gives it back, warming the air inside clouds and powering storms.

topics.title: Water Vapor and Saturation
topics.short: Air is saturated when vapor condenses as fast as water evaporates; the saturation amount climbs steeply with temperature.

topics.title: Relative Humidity
topics.short: Relative humidity compares the vapor in the air with the saturation amount at the air's temperature.

topics.title: Dew Point
topics.short: The dew point is the temperature air must cool to for saturation; a higher dew point means more water vapor.

topics.title: Rising Air Cools
topics.short: A rising parcel expands as the pressure drops and cools about 10 °C per kilometer while it stays unsaturated.

topics.title: What Lifts the Air
topics.short: Air rises when the ground heats it, when it is forced over mountains, when it is pushed up at fronts and when winds crowd together.

topics.title: Finding the Cloud Base
topics.short: A rising parcel's temperature closes in on its dew point by about 8 °C per kilometer, so the cloud base is about 125 m up for each degree of difference.

topics.title: Saturated Air Cools More Slowly
topics.short: Once a parcel is saturated, condensation releases latent heat, so it cools more slowly, about 6 °C per kilometer on average.

topics.title: Rain Shadows and Warm Downslope Winds
topics.short: Air that drops its rain on the way up a mountain warms faster on the way down, so the far side is warmer and drier.

topics.title: Stable and Unstable Air
topics.short: Lift a parcel and compare it with the air around it: if it ends up warmer it keeps rising, and if colder it sinks back.

topics.title: Cloud Types
topics.short: Name clouds by height and shape: cirrus are high and wispy, stratus lie in flat layers, cumulus pile up in heaps, and nimbus means rain.

topics.title: How Raindrops Grow
topics.short: A raindrop holds about a million cloud droplets; drops grow by bumping and joining, or from ice crystals that grow at the droplets' expense.

topics.title: Rain, Snow, Sleet and Freezing Rain
topics.short: The temperatures a falling snowflake meets on the way down decide whether it lands as snow, rain, sleet or freezing rain.

topics.title: The Pressure Gradient Force
topics.short: Air is pushed from high toward low pressure, harder where the isobars are close together.

topics.title: The Coriolis Effect
topics.short: On a spinning Earth, moving air turns to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, more strongly toward the poles.

topics.title: Winds Aloft Follow the Isobars
topics.short: High above the ground, the pressure push and the Coriolis turn balance, so the wind blows along the isobars.

topics.title: Winds around Highs and Lows
topics.short: Near the ground, friction lets air spiral into lows, where it rises and builds clouds, and out of highs, where it sinks and clears the sky.

topics.title: Hadley, Ferrel and Polar Cells
topics.short: Air rises near the equator and sinks near 30° latitude, which explains rainy tropics, desert belts and the trade winds.

topics.title: The Jet Stream
topics.short: A fast river of wind about 10 km up forms where warm and cold air meet, and its dips and bulges steer storms.

topics.title: El Niño and La Niña
topics.short: When the Pacific trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east (El Niño); when they strengthen, cool water wells up in the east (La Niña), and weather shifts around the world.

topics.title: Reading a Station Model
topics.short: Decode a weather station's plot: temperature, dew point, pressure, wind barbs and cloud cover.

topics.title: Air Masses and How They Change
topics.short: Name air masses by their source (cP, mT and others) and see how they change over new ground, as in lake-effect snow.

topics.title: Cold Fronts
topics.short: A cold front lifts warm air sharply, bringing a narrow band of showers and storms, then cooler, drier air and a shift in the wind.

topics.title: Warm Fronts
topics.short: Warm air glides up a gentle slope over cold air, so high clouds come first and steady rain spreads over a wide area.

topics.title: Life of a Mid-Latitude Storm
topics.short: A low forms on a front, winds up into a comma of cold and warm fronts, occludes and fades over a few days.

topics.title: Reading a Surface Weather Map
topics.short: Use isobars, fronts, highs and lows to say where the wind blows, where it is raining and what is coming next.

topics.title: Thunderstorms
topics.short: Moisture, unstable air and a lift build a thunderstorm through its cumulus, mature and dissipating stages.

topics.title: Lightning and Thunder
topics.short: Lightning heats the air so fast that it expands with the boom we call thunder; sound takes about 3 seconds to travel a kilometer.

topics.title: Supercells and Tornadoes
topics.short: Winds that change with height can set a storm's updraft spinning; tornadoes are rated by their damage on the Enhanced Fujita scale.

topics.title: Hurricanes
topics.short: Warm ocean water feeds a hurricane through latent heat; its Saffir–Simpson category rates only its wind.

topics.title: Wind Chill and Heat Index
topics.short: Wind makes cold air feel colder and humid air makes heat feel hotter, by changing how fast your body loses heat.

topics.title: Weather Instruments
topics.short: Match each instrument to what it measures: thermometer, barometer, hygrometer, anemometer, wind vane, rain gauge and weather balloon.

topics.title: Radar and Satellite Images
topics.short: Visible images show sunlit clouds, infrared images show how cold cloud tops are, and radar shows where rain and snow are falling.

topics.title: Computer Forecasts and Chaos
topics.short: Models step the laws of physics forward on a grid; small errors grow, so forecasters run many versions and look at how far they spread.

topics.title: What a 40% Chance of Rain Means
topics.short: The chance of rain is the probability that measurable rain falls at any given spot in the forecast area during the forecast period.

topics.title: Climate Normals and Anomalies
topics.short: A climate normal is a 30-year average, and an anomaly is how far a value is from its normal.

topics.title: Reading Climographs
topics.short: A climograph shows a place's average monthly temperature and precipitation, enough to tell its hemisphere and climate type.

topics.title: Climate Zones
topics.short: Classify a climate from its monthly numbers with the Köppen groups: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar.

topics.title: The Carbon Cycle
topics.short: Carbon moves among air, ocean, living things and rock, quickly through photosynthesis and decay and slowly through rocks and fossil fuels.

topics.title: Tracking Carbon from Emissions to the Air
topics.short: About 2.1 billion tonnes of carbon raise the air's carbon dioxide by 1 ppm, and a little under half of what we emit stays in the air.

topics.title: The Rising Carbon Dioxide Record
topics.short: Measurements at Mauna Loa since 1958 show a yearly wiggle from plant growth on top of a rise that has reached 2 to 3 ppm a year.

topics.title: What Changes Climate: Forcings
topics.short: Changes in sunlight, volcanic haze, greenhouse gases, pollution particles and land cover push climate warmer or cooler.

topics.title: Climate Feedbacks
topics.short: A change can strengthen itself, as when melting ice uncovers darker water, or weaken itself, as when a warmer Earth gives off more heat.

topics.title: Orbital Cycles and Ice Ages
topics.short: Slow changes in the shape of Earth's orbit, its tilt and the direction of its axis, over tens of thousands of years, pace the ice ages.

topics.title: Reading Past Climates
topics.short: Ice cores, tree rings, ocean mud and corals record temperatures and gases from long before thermometers.

topics.title: How Much Warming per Doubling
topics.short: Each doubling of carbon dioxide adds about 3.7 W/m² of push, and the long-run warming is likely 2.5 to 4 °C per doubling.

topics.title: Why Sea Level Rises
topics.short: Seas rise as warming water expands and as ice on land melts or slides into the ocean.

topics.title: Climate Models and Projections
topics.short: Climate models project long-term averages, not the weather on a date, for different paths of future emissions.

topics.title: Statements
topics.short: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false; questions, commands and exclamations are not statements.

topics.title: Arguments and Non-Arguments
topics.short: An argument offers reasons (premises) meant to support a claim (the conclusion); a report, description, warning or bare opinion does not.

topics.title: Arguments and Explanations
topics.short: An argument tries to show that something is true; an explanation tells why something we already accept is true.

topics.title: Premises and Conclusions
topics.short: Find the conclusion first by asking what the speaker wants you to believe; the premises are the reasons given for it.

topics.title: Indicator Words
topics.short: Words like "therefore" and "so" usually mark a conclusion; "because", "since" and "for" usually mark a premise.

topics.title: Standard Form
topics.short: Rewrite an argument as numbered premises followed by its conclusion, leaving out filler, repeats and side remarks.

topics.title: Linked and Convergent Premises
topics.short: Linked premises support the conclusion only together; convergent premises each give a separate reason on their own.

topics.title: Chains of Reasoning
topics.short: A claim can be the conclusion of one step and a premise of the next; the last claim supported is the main conclusion.

topics.title: Unstated Premises
topics.short: Many arguments leave a premise unsaid; supply the most reasonable one that connects the stated premises to the conclusion.

topics.title: Deductive and Inductive Arguments
topics.short: A deductive argument claims its conclusion must be true if the premises are; an inductive argument claims only that it is probably true.

topics.title: Validity
topics.short: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false.

topics.title: Testing Validity with a Counterexample
topics.short: To show a form is invalid, give an argument with the same form whose premises are plainly true and whose conclusion is plainly false.

topics.title: Soundness
topics.short: A sound argument is valid and has all true premises, so its conclusion must be true.

topics.title: Validity and Truth Together
topics.short: Every mix of true and false premises and conclusions is possible for a valid argument except one: true premises with a false conclusion.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Inductive Arguments
topics.short: An inductive argument is strong when its premises, if true, make the conclusion likely; a strong argument with true premises is cogent.

topics.title: Generalizing from a Sample
topics.short: A generalization is only as good as its sample: large enough, chosen fairly, and like the whole group in the ways that matter.

topics.title: Arguments from Analogy
topics.short: An analogy argues that two things alike in some ways are alike in another; it is strong when the likenesses are relevant and the differences are not.

topics.title: Reasoning about Causes
topics.short: Two things happening together does not show that one causes the other; look for a common cause, reverse direction, or coincidence.

topics.title: Ambiguity and Vagueness
topics.short: A word is ambiguous when it has two distinct meanings in context, and vague when its boundary is fuzzy.

topics.title: Kinds of Definitions
topics.short: Lexical definitions report how a word is used, stipulative ones assign a new meaning, precising ones sharpen a vague word, and persuasive ones slant it.

topics.title: Definition by Genus and Difference
topics.short: A classical definition names the larger kind (genus) and the feature that sets this thing apart within it (difference).

topics.title: Rules for Good Definitions
topics.short: A good definition is neither too broad nor too narrow, not circular, not negative when it can be positive, and not figurative or obscure.

topics.title: Emotive and Loaded Language
topics.short: Words can carry feelings as well as facts; loaded words try to win agreement by attitude instead of by reasons.

topics.title: Verbal and Factual Disagreements
topics.short: Some disagreements are about the facts; others vanish once people notice they are using a word in different senses.

topics.title: What a Fallacy Is
topics.short: A fallacy is a common pattern of bad reasoning that can look persuasive; formal fallacies are flaws in form, informal ones in content.

topics.title: Attacking the Person
topics.short: Ad hominem rejects a claim by attacking the person who made it (insults or their circumstances) instead of the reasons given.

topics.title: You Too (Tu Quoque)
topics.short: Tu quoque dismisses an argument because the arguer does not follow their own advice.

topics.title: Straw Man
topics.short: A straw man swaps the opponent's real position for a weaker or exaggerated version, then knocks that down.

topics.title: Red Herring
topics.short: A red herring changes the subject to a different issue, then treats the original question as settled.

topics.title: Appeal to Force
topics.short: An appeal to force tries to win agreement by a threat of harm instead of by reasons.

topics.title: Appeal to Pity
topics.short: An appeal to pity asks us to accept a claim because of sympathy, when the sympathy has no bearing on whether the claim is true.

topics.title: Appeal to the People
topics.short: The bandwagon fallacy argues that a claim is true, or a choice good, because many people believe it or do it.

topics.title: Appeals to Authority: Fair and Unfair
topics.short: Citing an expert in their own field, where experts agree, is reasonable; citing someone outside their expertise, or one voice against a consensus, is not.

topics.title: Appeal to Ignorance
topics.short: An appeal to ignorance argues that a claim is true because it has not been shown false, or false because it has not been shown true.

topics.title: Begging the Question
topics.short: An argument begs the question when a premise assumes the very conclusion it is supposed to prove, often in other words.

topics.title: Complex Question
topics.short: A complex question has a hidden assumption built in, so that any direct answer grants it.

topics.title: False Dilemma
topics.short: A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones when others exist.

topics.title: Hasty Generalization
topics.short: A hasty generalization draws a conclusion about a whole group from a sample that is too small or not typical.

topics.title: False Cause
topics.short: False cause claims one thing caused another only because it came first (post hoc) or because the two occur together.

topics.title: Slippery Slope
topics.short: A slippery slope claims one step will set off a chain of bad results, without good reason to think each link will happen.

topics.title: Weak Analogy
topics.short: A weak analogy rests on likenesses that do not matter for the conclusion, or ignores differences that do.

topics.title: Suppressed Evidence
topics.short: Suppressed evidence leaves out an important fact that would change the conclusion.

topics.title: Accident
topics.short: Accident applies a general rule to a special case that the rule was never meant to cover.

topics.title: Equivocation
topics.short: Equivocation uses a word in one sense in one premise and in another sense elsewhere, so the argument only seems to connect.

topics.title: Amphiboly
topics.short: Amphiboly draws a conclusion from a sentence whose grammar allows two readings.

topics.title: Composition
topics.short: Composition reasons that because every part has a property, the whole must have it too.

topics.title: Division
topics.short: Division reasons that because the whole has a property, each part must have it too.

topics.title: Affirming the Consequent and Denying the Antecedent
topics.short: From "if P then Q", you may infer Q from P, and not-P from not-Q; inferring P from Q, or not-Q from not-P, is a fallacy.

topics.title: Telling Look-Alike Fallacies Apart
topics.short: Name the fallacy by the job the faulty step does: distorting a view, changing the subject, leaping from a sample, or assuming the conclusion.

topics.title: Good Reasoning That Looks Like a Fallacy
topics.short: Many fallacy names have fair cousins: trusted experts, well-supported chains of causes, and real either-or choices are good reasoning.

topics.title: The Principle of Charity
topics.short: Before judging an argument, state it in its strongest reasonable form, the way its author would accept.

topics.title: Evaluating an Argument Step by Step
topics.short: Find the conclusion and premises, check whether the reasoning is valid or strong, then check whether the premises are true.

topics.title: Objections and Replies
topics.short: A strong case answers the best objection to it; an objection attacks a premise or the link from premises to conclusion.

topics.title: Simple and Compound Statements
topics.short: A simple statement has no other statement as a part; a compound statement is built from simpler ones with words like not, and, or, if.

topics.title: The Five Connectives
topics.short: Negation ¬, conjunction ∧, disjunction ∨, conditional → and biconditional ↔ build compound formulas from statement letters.

topics.title: The Main Connective and Scope
topics.short: Parentheses group a formula; the main connective is the one with the widest scope, applied last, and it decides what kind of statement the formula is.

topics.title: Translating Not, And and Or
topics.short: "But", "although" and "yet" are ∧; "neither p nor q" is ¬(p ∨ q) or ¬p ∧ ¬q; "not both" is ¬(p ∧ q).

topics.title: Translating Conditionals
topics.short: "If p, q", "q if p", "p only if q", "q provided that p", "p is sufficient for q" and "q is necessary for p" are all p → q; "p unless q" is ¬q → p, or p ∨ q.

topics.title: Biconditionals and Longer Sentences
topics.short: "p if and only if q" and "p just in case q" are p ↔ q; longer sentences are translated from the main connective inward.

topics.title: From Symbols Back to English
topics.short: Read a formula aloud in plain English that keeps its grouping, using "either…or", "both…and" and "it is not the case that".

topics.title: Truth Values of the Connectives
topics.short: Each connective is a truth function: the truth value of the compound depends only on the values of its parts.

topics.title: Computing a Truth Value
topics.short: Given the values of the letters, work from the innermost parts outward to find the value of the whole formula.

topics.title: Building a Truth Table
topics.short: A formula with n letters has 2ⁿ rows; list them in a fixed order and fill a column for each part, ending with the main connective.

topics.title: Tautologies, Contradictions and Contingent Statements
topics.short: A tautology is true in every row, a self-contradiction false in every row, and a contingent statement true in some rows and false in others.

topics.title: Logical Equivalence
topics.short: Two formulas are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row; then their biconditional is a tautology.

topics.title: De Morgan's Laws
topics.short: ¬(p ∧ q) is equivalent to ¬p ∨ ¬q, and ¬(p ∨ q) to ¬p ∧ ¬q: moving a negation inside flips ∧ and ∨.

topics.title: Converse, Inverse and Contrapositive
topics.short: p → q is equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p, but not to its converse q → p or its inverse ¬p → ¬q.

topics.title: Consistent, Inconsistent and Contradictory
topics.short: Statements are consistent if some row makes them all true; two statements are contradictory if they have opposite values in every row.

topics.title: Validity by Truth Table
topics.short: An argument is valid when no row makes every premise true and the conclusion false.

topics.title: The Short Truth Table Method
topics.short: Assume the premises true and the conclusion false, then work out the forced values; if that leads to a contradiction, the argument is valid.

topics.title: Valid and Invalid Argument Forms
topics.short: Modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical and disjunctive syllogism are valid forms; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid.

topics.title: What a Formal Proof Is
topics.short: A proof is a numbered list of lines; each is a premise or follows from earlier lines by a rule, written beside it with the line numbers it uses.

topics.title: Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens (MP, MT)
topics.short: MP: from p → q and p, infer q. MT: from p → q and ¬q, infer ¬p. The letters can stand for any formulas.

topics.title: Hypothetical and Disjunctive Syllogism (HS, DS)
topics.short: HS: from p → q and q → r, infer p → r. DS: from p ∨ q and ¬p, infer q.

topics.title: Simplification, Conjunction and Addition (Simp, Conj, Add)
topics.short: Simp: from p ∧ q, infer p. Conj: from p and q, infer p ∧ q. Add: from p, infer p ∨ q for any q at all.

topics.title: Constructive Dilemma (CD)
topics.short: CD: from (p → q) ∧ (r → s) and p ∨ r, infer q ∨ s.

topics.title: Matching a Rule to Whole Lines
topics.short: A rule of inference applies only to whole lines whose main connectives match the rule's pattern, with any formulas in place of p, q, r and s.

topics.title: Justifying Proof Lines
topics.short: Name the rule and the earlier lines that justify each line of a finished proof.

topics.title: Building Short Proofs
topics.short: Supply the missing lines of short proofs, choosing each step by what the conclusion needs.

topics.title: Proof Strategy: Working Backward
topics.short: Find the conclusion inside the premises, then plan which rule would produce it and what that rule needs.

topics.title: Rules of Replacement
topics.short: A replacement rule says two forms are equivalent, so either can replace the other anywhere, even inside a line, in either direction.

topics.title: De Morgan and Double Negation (DM, DN)
Commutation, Association and Distribution (Com, Assoc, Dist)
topics.short: Com swaps the sides of ∧ or ∨; Assoc regroups three parts joined by the same connective; Dist spreads ∧ over ∨ and ∨ over ∧.

topics.title: Transposition and Material Implication (Trans, Impl)
topics.short: Trans: p → q :: ¬q → ¬p. Impl: p → q :: ¬p ∨ q.

topics.title: Equivalence, Exportation and Tautology (Equiv, Exp, Taut)
topics.short: Equiv: p ↔ q :: (p → q) ∧ (q → p), or (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q). Exp: (p ∧ q) → r :: p → (q → r). Taut: p :: p ∧ p and p :: p ∨ p.

topics.title: Proofs with All Eighteen Rules
topics.short: Combine rules of inference and replacement, often reshaping a line with replacement until an inference rule fits.

topics.title: Conditional Proof (CP)
topics.short: To prove p → q, assume p, derive q inside an indented subproof, then close it and write p → q.

topics.title: Indirect Proof (IP)
topics.short: To prove p, assume ¬p, derive a contradiction q ∧ ¬q, then close the subproof and write p.

topics.title: Nested Subproofs
topics.short: Subproofs can sit inside other subproofs; each must be closed, innermost first, and a theorem can be proved this way from no premises at all.

topics.title: Predicates and Names
topics.short: A predicate letter stands for a property (F: is friendly) and a lowercase name for an individual (a: Ava); Fa says that Ava is friendly.

topics.title: The Quantifiers ∀ and ∃
topics.short: ∀x Fx says everything is F; ∃x Fx says at least one thing is F. A variable is bound when a quantifier covers it.

topics.title: Translating A, E, I and O
topics.short: A: ∀x(Sx → Px). E: ∀x(Sx → ¬Px). I: ∃x(Sx ∧ Px). O: ∃x(Sx ∧ ¬Px).

topics.title: Translating Harder Quantified Sentences
topics.short: Handle "only", "none but", "all except", complex subjects (red cars) and complex predicates (fast or loud) inside one quantifier.

topics.title: Quantifier Negation
topics.short: ¬∀x Fx is equivalent to ∃x ¬Fx, and ¬∃x Fx to ∀x ¬Fx: moving a negation across a quantifier flips ∀ and ∃.

topics.title: Truth in a Small World
topics.short: In a world with a few named objects, ∀x Fx is true when every object is F, and ∃x Fx when at least one is.

topics.title: Counterexample Worlds
topics.short: Show an argument invalid by describing a small world where all its premises are true and its conclusion false.

topics.title: Universal Instantiation and Existential Generalization (UI, EG)
topics.short: UI: from ∀x Fx, infer Fa for any name. EG: from Fa, infer ∃x Fx.

topics.title: Existential Instantiation (EI)
topics.short: EI: from ∃x Fx, infer Fa only for a name a that is new: not in any earlier line, the premises or the conclusion.

topics.title: Universal Generalization (UG)
topics.short: UG: from Fy, infer ∀x Fx only when y is a variable standing for any object, not a name and not one introduced by EI.

topics.title: Proofs with Quantifiers
topics.short: Strip the quantifiers (EI before UI), reason with the propositional rules, then put quantifiers back with UG or EG.

topics.title: Conditional and Indirect Proof with Quantifiers
topics.short: CP, IP and quantifier negation (QN) work in predicate logic too, as long as each quantifier rule's restrictions are kept.

topics.title: Relational Predicates
topics.short: A relational predicate links two or more objects in order: Lab says a likes b, which is not the same as Lba.

topics.title: Quantifier Order
topics.short: ∀x∃y Lxy (everyone likes someone) differs from ∃y∀x Lxy (someone is liked by everyone); the order of mixed quantifiers matters.

topics.title: Properties of Relations
topics.short: A relation can be reflexive (Rxx for all x), symmetric (Rxy → Ryx) and transitive (Rxy ∧ Ryz → Rxz), or fail any of them.

topics.title: Identity
topics.short: a = b says a and b are the same object; identity lets us say "only", "someone other than" and "the same".

topics.title: At Least, At Most and Exactly
topics.short: With identity we can count: "at least two F" is ∃x∃y(Fx ∧ Fy ∧ x ≠ y); "at most one" and "exactly one" follow the same pattern.

topics.title: Proofs with Identity
topics.short: The identity rules: a = a may be written anywhere, a = b gives b = a, and from Fa and a = b infer Fb.

topics.title: Soundness and Completeness
topics.short: Provable (⊢) is about rules; valid (⊨) is about truth. A system is sound if everything provable is valid, and complete if everything valid is provable; our rules are both.

topics.title: The Three Acts of the Mind
topics.short: Simple apprehension grasps a term, judgment joins terms into a proposition, and reasoning moves from propositions to a conclusion.

topics.title: Terms
topics.short: A term is a word or phrase that names a class or an individual; singular terms name one thing, general terms name a class.

topics.title: Extension and Comprehension
topics.short: A term's extension is the set of things it applies to; its comprehension (intension) is the set of features it implies.

topics.title: Genus and Species
topics.short: A genus is a wider class divided into species; the same class can be a species of one genus and a genus of narrower species.

topics.title: The Predicables
topics.short: A predicate can relate to its subject as genus, species, difference, property (always goes with it) or accident (may or may not).

topics.title: Logical Division
topics.short: A good division splits a genus into species by one principle, so that the parts are exclusive and together exhaustive.

topics.title: Categorical Propositions
topics.short: A categorical proposition relates two classes: quantifier, subject term, copula (are or are not) and predicate term.

topics.title: The Four Forms: A, E, I, O
topics.short: A: All S are P. E: No S are P. I: Some S are P. O: Some S are not P. Quantity is universal or particular; quality is affirmative or negative.

topics.title: Putting Statements in Standard Form
topics.short: Turn verbs into "are" plus a class, singular statements into "All S are P", and words like "every", "none" and "a few" into the four quantifiers.

topics.title: Only, None But and All Except
topics.short: "Only S are P" and "None but S are P" become "All P are S"; "All except S are P" makes two claims.

topics.title: Distribution of Terms
topics.short: A term is distributed when the proposition says something about every member of its class: A distributes S, E both, I neither, O the predicate.

topics.title: Venn Diagrams for Propositions
topics.short: Shade a region to show it is empty; put an X in a region to show something is there. A and E shade; I and O place an X.

topics.title: Existential Import
topics.short: In the modern (Boolean) reading, A and E say nothing about whether S exists; I and O do. The traditional reading assumes the subject class is not empty.

topics.title: The Square of Opposition
topics.short: A, E, I and O with the same terms sit at the corners of a square; its sides and diagonals name how their truth values are tied.

topics.title: Contradictories
topics.short: A and O, and E and I, are contradictories: exactly one of each pair is true.

topics.title: Contraries and Subcontraries
topics.short: A and E cannot both be true but can both be false; I and O cannot both be false but can both be true.

topics.title: Subalternation
topics.short: On the traditional square, truth flows down from A to I and from E to O, and falsity flows up from I to A and from O to E.

topics.title: Inferences on the Square
topics.short: Given the truth value of one corner, work out each other corner as true, false or undetermined.

topics.title: The Modern Square
topics.short: Without existential import only the contradictory diagonals survive; contrariety, subcontrariety and subalternation can fail when a class is empty.

topics.title: Term Complements
topics.short: The complement of a class is everything outside it: non-P. The complement of non-P is P.

topics.title: Conversion
topics.short: Conversion swaps subject and predicate. It is valid for E and I, not for A or O (A converts only by limitation, on the traditional reading).

topics.title: Obversion
topics.short: Obversion changes the quality (affirmative to negative or back) and replaces the predicate with its complement; it is valid for all four forms.

topics.title: Contraposition
topics.short: Contraposition swaps subject and predicate and replaces both with their complements. It is valid for A and O, not for E or I.

topics.title: Chains of Immediate Inference
topics.short: Combine conversion, obversion, contraposition and the square to decide whether one proposition follows from another.

topics.title: The Parts of a Syllogism
topics.short: A categorical syllogism has three propositions and three terms: the major term (predicate of the conclusion), minor term (subject of the conclusion) and middle term.

topics.title: Standard-Form Syllogisms
topics.short: In standard form the major premise (with the major term) comes first, then the minor premise, then the conclusion.

topics.title: Mood
topics.short: The mood is the three letters of the major premise, minor premise and conclusion, in that order, such as AII or EAE.

topics.title: Figure
topics.short: The figure (1 to 4) records where the middle term sits: subject then predicate, predicate twice, subject twice, or predicate then subject.

topics.title: Testing Syllogisms with Venn Diagrams
topics.short: Draw three circles, diagram both premises, and the syllogism is valid when the conclusion is already shown without drawing anything more.

topics.title: Venn Tests with Particular Premises
topics.short: Diagram universal premises first; place an X in a region only if the other region it could go in is shaded, otherwise put it on the line.

topics.title: Rules of the Syllogism: Distribution
topics.short: The middle term must be distributed at least once, and a term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise.

topics.title: Rules of the Syllogism: Quality
topics.short: Two negative premises prove nothing; a negative premise requires a negative conclusion, and a negative conclusion requires a negative premise.

topics.title: Naming a Syllogism's Fallacy
topics.short: Each broken rule has a name: undistributed middle, illicit major, illicit minor, exclusive premises, affirmative from a negative, the existential fallacy, four terms.

topics.title: The Valid Forms and Their Names
topics.short: Fifteen mood-and-figure combinations are valid on the modern reading, such as AAA-1 (Barbara), EAE-1 (Celarent) and AII-3 (Datisi).

topics.title: Conditionally Valid Forms
topics.short: Nine more forms, such as AAI-1 and EAO-2, are valid only if a class is assumed to have members; the Venn test shows which class.

topics.title: Reducing the Number of Terms
topics.short: When an argument seems to have four or more terms, use synonyms, complements and obversion to bring it down to three.

topics.title: Syllogisms in Everyday Language
topics.short: Put each statement in standard form, find the three terms, arrange the syllogism, then test it by the rules or a Venn diagram.

topics.title: Enthymemes
topics.short: An enthymeme is a syllogism with a premise or the conclusion left unstated; supply the missing part so the syllogism is valid, then judge whether it is true.

topics.title: Sorites
topics.short: A sorites is a chain of premises that leads to one conclusion through several hidden intermediate conclusions; it is valid when every link is a valid syllogism.

topics.title: Hypothetical Propositions
topics.short: A hypothetical proposition joins an antecedent and a consequent: "If P, then Q". "Q if P", "P only if Q" and "Q provided that P" say the same.

topics.title: Affirming the Antecedent (Modus Ponens)
topics.short: From "If P, then Q" and "P", conclude "Q".

topics.title: Denying the Consequent (Modus Tollens)
topics.short: From "If P, then Q" and "not Q", conclude "not P".

topics.title: The Two Conditional Fallacies
topics.short: Affirming the consequent (Q, so P) and denying the antecedent (not P, so not Q) are invalid; the consequent can come about some other way.

topics.title: Pure Hypothetical Syllogism
topics.short: From "If P, then Q" and "If Q, then R", conclude "If P, then R"; the links must run in the same direction.

topics.title: Disjunctive Syllogism
topics.short: From "P or Q" and "not P", conclude "Q". From "P or Q" and "P", nothing follows about Q unless the "or" is exclusive.

topics.title: Conjunctive Syllogism
topics.short: From "Not both P and Q" and "P", conclude "not Q". From "not P", nothing follows.

topics.title: Dilemmas
topics.short: A constructive dilemma reasons from "If P then Q, and if R then S" and "P or R" to "Q or S"; a destructive dilemma from "not Q or not S" to "not P or not R".

topics.title: Answering a Dilemma
topics.short: Escape between the horns (show a third option), grasp a horn (deny a conditional premise), or offer a counterdilemma.

topics.title: Why Etiquette Exists
topics.short: Etiquette rests on three ideas: consideration for others' feelings, respect for every person, and honesty; its customs exist to put people at ease.

topics.title: Manners and Etiquette
topics.short: Manners are the spirit (kindness and consideration); etiquette is the specific code (which fork, how to address an envelope), and it changes with time and place.

topics.title: When Customs Differ
topics.short: Customs vary by region, country and family; as a guest, follow your host's way, and never mock or correct another family's customs.

topics.title: Reading a Place Setting
topics.short: Bread plate on the left, drinks on the right; forks to the left of the plate, knives and spoons to the right, used from the outside in.

topics.title: The Formal Place Setting
topics.short: Each course has its own utensils, set in the order of use from the outside in, with dessert utensils above the plate and glasses above the knives.

topics.title: Using the Napkin
topics.short: Place the napkin on your lap after the host does, blot rather than wipe, leave it on your chair if you step away, and set it loosely left of the plate at the end.

topics.title: Bread and Glasses
topics.short: Tear off one bite-size piece of bread at a time and butter it over your bread plate; hold a stemmed glass by the stem and drink only from your own.

topics.title: American and Continental Styles
topics.short: American style: cut, set the knife down, switch the fork to the right hand, eat tines up. Continental style: keep the fork in the left hand, tines down, and the knife in the right.

topics.title: Resting and Finished Positions
topics.short: Resting: utensils on the plate, never on the table (in Continental style, crossed near the tips like an upside-down V, fork tines down). Finished: fork and knife side by side, diagonally, handles toward the lower right.

topics.title: Courses and Service
topics.short: Wait until everyone is served or the host begins; at a large table, start when the host invites you. Food is traditionally served from the left and plates cleared from the right.

topics.title: Tricky Foods
topics.short: Spoon soup away from you, twirl long pasta against the plate or a spoon, eat finger foods with fingers, and remove a pit or bone the way it went in.

topics.title: Toasts
topics.short: The host usually gives the first toast; stand or raise your glass, keep it short and kind, and if the toast is to you, stay seated and don't drink to yourself.

topics.title: Restaurant Manners
topics.short: Reserve if needed, arrive on time, be courteous to every server, order at a similar pace and price as your host, and raise problems quietly.

topics.title: Who Pays and Splitting the Bill
topics.short: Traditionally whoever invites pays; with friends, agree before ordering whether to split evenly or pay for what you ordered.

topics.title: Tipping in the U.S.
topics.short: At a sit-down restaurant in the U.S., about 15 to 20 percent of the bill before tax is customary, more for great service; tipping customs differ abroad.

topics.title: Making Introductions
topics.short: Say the honored person's name first: an older person, a guest, a client, or a senior colleague; at work, rank decides, not age or gender.

topics.title: Forms of Address
topics.short: Use titles such as Mr., Ms., Mrs., Mx. or Dr. with a last name until invited to use a first name, and use the name and title a person prefers.

topics.title: Handshakes and Other Greetings
topics.short: In the U.S., stand and shake hands firmly; elsewhere a bow, a nod or a cheek kiss may be usual, and some people prefer not to shake hands at all.

topics.title: Small Talk
topics.short: Small talk uses safe shared topics (the event, travel, books, food, the weather), open questions and real listening, and it leads to bigger conversations.

topics.title: Invitations
topics.short: A good invitation says who is hosting, what, when, where, what to wear if it matters, and how and by when to reply.

topics.title: Replying to an Invitation
topics.short: Reply by the date asked, in the way asked; "RSVP" asks for a reply either way, and "regrets only" asks only those not coming to reply.

topics.title: Arriving and Leaving
topics.short: Arrive on time for a dinner (not early), within a reasonable window for a party, and leave before the host looks tired; thank the host at the door.

topics.title: Host Gifts
topics.short: A small host gift such as flowers in a vase, a treat or something for the pantry is welcome; it is for the host to enjoy later, not to serve that night.

topics.title: Hosting a Dinner
topics.short: Greet and introduce guests, ask about food needs ahead, seat the guest of honor at the host's right, keep the talk moving, and put guests at ease.

topics.title: Overnight Guests
topics.short: A good guest agrees on dates, follows the house routine, keeps their space tidy, offers to help, and sends a thank-you afterward; a good host gives towels, a key and a plan.

topics.title: Thank-You Notes
topics.short: Write soon, name the gift or kindness, say how you will use or enjoy it, add a personal line, and close warmly; a handwritten note is still the warmest.

topics.title: Condolence Notes
topics.short: Say you are sorry for the loss, share a memory or a good quality of the person, offer specific help if you can, and close with sympathy; keep it short.

topics.title: Writing a Letter
topics.short: A letter has the date, a greeting ("Dear Ms. Grant,"), the body in short paragraphs, a closing ("Sincerely," or "Warmly,") and your signature.

topics.title: Addressing an Envelope
topics.short: The recipient's name and address go in the center, your return address in the upper left, and the stamp in the upper right; use titles and full names.

topics.title: Email Manners
topics.short: Write a clear subject, open with a greeting, keep it brief, proofread, reply within a day or two, and use "reply all" only when everyone needs it.

topics.title: Phones in Company and in Public
topics.short: Silence the phone at meals, meetings and performances, step away for calls, and keep speakerphone and videos off in shared spaces.

topics.title: Texting and Messaging
topics.short: Mind the hour, the tone and the length; don't send important or sad news by text when a call or visit is possible; answer within a reasonable time.

topics.title: Social Media
topics.short: Ask before posting photos of others or their children, don't announce other people's news, and remember that posts are public and lasting.

topics.title: Video Calls and Meetings
topics.short: Join on time, check your sound and background, mute when not speaking, look at the camera, and give the meeting your attention.

topics.title: Job Interviews
topics.short: Arrive a few minutes early, dress a step above the job's usual dress, greet everyone kindly, listen, ask good questions, and send a thank-you within a day.

topics.title: Dress Codes Decoded
topics.short: Social dress codes run from white tie and black tie to cocktail, smart casual and casual; at work, from business formal to business casual and casual. When unsure, ask the host.

topics.title: Meetings
topics.short: Be on time, come prepared, let others finish, keep to the topic, credit others' ideas, and follow up on what you promised.

topics.title: The Office Kitchen and Shared Spaces
topics.short: Clean up after yourself, label and clear out your food, don't take what isn't yours, keep calls and smells modest, and refill what you empty.

topics.title: Wedding Guests
topics.short: Reply on time, bring only the guests named on the invitation, follow the dress code, give a gift (often from the registry), and let the couple shine.

topics.title: Funerals and Memorials
topics.short: Dress in quiet colors, arrive early, sign the guest book, follow the family's customs, and offer the family short, sincere words: "I'm so sorry. She was a wonderful teacher."

topics.title: Visiting the Bereaved
topics.short: Keep visits short, listen more than you talk, offer specific help ("I'll bring dinner Tuesday"), and keep in touch in the weeks after.

topics.title: Hospital Visits and New Babies
topics.short: Ask before visiting, keep it short, stay home if you are sick, wash your hands, and offer help with meals or errands rather than asking to hold the baby.

topics.title: Gifts and Regifting
topics.short: Choose with the person in mind, include a gift receipt when it may help, and thank every gift; regifting is debated, and most agree it must be new and never go back to the same circle.

topics.title: Borrowing and Lending
topics.short: Ask, return the item on time in as good shape or better, replace what you break or use up, and lend only what you can afford to lose.

topics.title: Being a Good Neighbor
topics.short: Greet neighbors, keep noise, pets and yard tidy, park considerately, warn them about a party or project, and talk to them directly about a problem.

topics.title: Travel Courtesy
topics.short: On planes and trains, store bags quickly, recline gently, share the armrest (the middle seat gets both), keep calls short and quiet, and thank the crew and hotel staff.

topics.title: Customs Abroad
topics.short: Before traveling, learn a greeting and "thank you" in the language, how people dress for sacred and formal sites, and the local customs on tipping, greetings and shoes.

topics.title: Forgetting a Name
topics.short: Admit it lightly ("I'm so sorry, your name has slipped my mind"), or introduce yourself first so they offer theirs; help others when they forget yours.

topics.title: Spills and Accidents
topics.short: Apologize briefly, help clean up, offer to pay for damage, and move on; as a host, reassure the guest and make light of it.

topics.title: When Someone Else Slips
topics.short: Tell someone privately about spinach in their teeth or an open zipper; never correct another person's table manners or grammar in front of others.

topics.title: Answering a Rude Remark
topics.short: Stay calm; ask "Why do you ask?", give a short neutral answer, change the subject, or simply say "I'd rather not discuss that."

topics.title: Declining and Saying No
topics.short: Decline invitations, food and requests kindly and briefly ("Thank you for asking; I can't make it"); a long excuse isn't needed, and a lie isn't either.

topics.title: Asking and Answering
topics.short: Ask clearly and in person or by call, make plans specific, and accept a "no" gracefully; answer kindly and truthfully either way.

topics.title: Courtesy on a Date
topics.short: Be on time, put the phone away, listen, be kind to staff, and settle who pays ahead; customs range from the inviter paying to splitting, and both are polite.

topics.title: Posture and Presence
topics.short: Stand tall and relaxed, sit upright, rise to greet, look people in the face, and keep hands still; presence means giving people your full attention.

topics.title: Starting a Conversation
topics.short: Open with a greeting and a simple question or comment about something you share, like the class, the game or the food.

topics.title: Asking Good Questions
topics.short: Open questions ("What was the best part of your trip?") keep a conversation going; yes-or-no questions often stop it.

topics.title: Listening Well
topics.short: Good listeners look at the speaker, let them finish, and ask a follow-up question about what they just said.

topics.title: Sharing the Conversation
topics.short: A conversation is a game of catch: say a little, then toss it back with a question, and bring quiet people in.

topics.title: Topics to Skip
topics.short: Remarks about someone's body, weight, money or a private family matter make people uncomfortable; leave those out.

topics.title: Ending a Conversation Politely
topics.short: End with a kind closing line, like "It was good to talk with you; I need to find my mom," and a goodbye.

topics.title: Introducing Yourself
topics.short: Stand, smile, look at the person, say "Hi, I'm Leo," and add one detail that gives them something to talk about.

topics.title: Eye Contact
topics.short: In the U.S., looking at someone's face while you greet and listen shows interest and respect; in some cultures, less direct eye contact is the respectful way.

topics.title: A Good Handshake
topics.short: Stand, reach out your right hand, meet palm to palm, grip firmly but not hard, shake two or three times, and let go.

topics.title: Remembering and Using Names
topics.short: Repeat a new name right away ("Nice to meet you, Grace"), use it once more, and ask again soon if you missed it.

topics.title: Introducing Two People
topics.short: Say the name of the older or honored person first, then present the other person to them, and give each a detail to talk about.

topics.title: Addressing Adults
topics.short: Use Mr., Ms., Mrs. or Dr. with a last name unless an adult invites you to use a first name; sir and ma'am are customary in many regions.

topics.title: Standing with Poise
topics.short: Stand tall and easy: weight on both feet, shoulders relaxed and back, head up, hands still at your sides.

topics.title: Sitting Well
topics.short: Sit back in the chair, upright and relaxed, with feet on the floor and hands in your lap or on the table edge.

topics.title: Walking into a Room
topics.short: Walk in at an easy pace, look up, smile, greet the people there, and wait to be shown where to sit if you are a guest.

topics.title: Standing to Greet
topics.short: Stand up when an adult or a guest enters the room or comes to meet you, and when you are introduced.

topics.title: Setting the Table
topics.short: Fork on the left, knife on the right with the blade toward the plate, spoon to the right of the knife, glass above the knife, napkin on the left.

topics.title: Holding the Fork and Knife
topics.short: In the American style, cut with the fork in the left hand and the knife in the right, then set the knife down and switch the fork to eat; the Continental style keeps the fork in the left hand.

topics.title: Passing Food
topics.short: Pass dishes to the right (counterclockwise), offer them to your neighbor first if you are starting, and pass the salt and pepper together.

topics.title: Serving Yourself
topics.short: Use the serving spoon, not your own fork, take a fair share so there is enough for everyone, and put the spoon back in the dish.

topics.title: Reaching and Elbows
topics.short: Ask for what is out of reach, keep elbows off the table while eating, and keep phones, toys and hats away from the table.

topics.title: Dropped Forks and Other Mishaps
topics.short: At home, pick up a dropped fork and get a clean one; at a restaurant, leave it and quietly ask for another; wipe a small spill and say "excuse me."

topics.title: Thanking the Cook
topics.short: Say something kind about the meal and thank whoever cooked it, and offer to help clear the table.

topics.title: Making a Phone Call
topics.short: Greet the person, say who you are, ask if it is a good time, say why you are calling, and say goodbye before you hang up.

topics.title: Answering and Taking a Message
topics.short: Answer with a greeting, ask "May I tell them who's calling?", and write down the name, number and message.

topics.title: Video Calls
topics.short: On a video call, find a quiet spot with light on your face, look at the camera, mute when you are not talking, and give the call your attention.

topics.title: Texting Courtesy
topics.short: Text at reasonable hours, write clearly, read your message before you send it, and remember tone is hard to hear in text.

topics.title: Group Chats
topics.short: In a group chat, stay on topic, don't share screenshots or private messages without asking, and never use the chat to leave someone out or gang up.

topics.title: Phones Around People
topics.short: When someone is talking with you, put the phone down; at meals, visits and conversations, the people in front of you come first.

topics.title: Having a Friend Over
topics.short: As a host, greet your friend and their parent, offer a snack and a choice of what to do, and include everyone who is there.

topics.title: Sleepovers
topics.short: At a sleepover, follow the family's rules and bedtime, offer to help, keep things tidy, and thank the parents in the morning.

topics.title: Birthday Party Invitations
topics.short: Reply to an invitation by the date it asks, and don't hand out invitations or talk about a party in front of people who were not invited.

topics.title: Giving a Gift
topics.short: Choose a gift with the person in mind, take the price tag off, add a card with your name, and let them open it when they like.

topics.title: Receiving a Gift Graciously
topics.short: Read the card first, look at the giver, thank them warmly, and say something kind, even if you already have one or it is not your style.

topics.title: Writing a Thank-You Note
topics.short: A thank-you note has a greeting, a thank-you for the specific gift or kindness, a line about how you will use or enjoy it, a warm closing and your signature.

topics.title: Apologizing Well
topics.short: A good apology says what you did, says you are sorry without a "but," offers to make it right, and does better next time.

topics.title: Disagreeing Kindly
topics.short: Disagree with the idea, not the person: listen first, say what you agree with, and say your view with "I think" instead of "You're wrong."

topics.title: Sportsmanship
topics.short: Play fair, follow the referee's calls, cheer for your team without jeering the other one, and shake hands after the game, win or lose.

topics.title: At School and with Teachers
topics.short: Greet your teacher, raise your hand and wait, listen when others speak, and ask for help respectfully.

topics.title: Respect for Elders
topics.short: Offer older people your seat, your help with doors and bags, and your attention; listen to their stories and stand when they enter.

topics.title: Helping at Home
topics.short: Do your share of chores without being asked twice, notice what needs doing, and thank family members for what they do.

topics.title: Lines and Crowds
topics.short: Join a line at the end, leave a little space, keep your bag close, and don't save places for friends who arrive later.

topics.title: Doors and Elevators
topics.short: Hold a door for the person behind you, let people off an elevator before you get on, and press the button for others.

topics.title: Sidewalks and Shared Spaces
topics.short: Walk on the right, don't spread out across the whole path in a group, step aside to stop or check your phone, and clean up after yourself.

topics.title: At the Movies and Shows
topics.short: Arrive on time, silence your phone and keep the screen dark, save talking for afterward, and clap at the right moments.

topics.title: The Pledge and the National Anthem
topics.short: Under the U.S. Code, during the Pledge and the anthem people stand, face the flag, place the right hand over the heart, and take off hats other than religious head coverings (people in uniform salute).

topics.title: Displaying the Flag
topics.short: On a wall, horizontal or vertical, the flag's blue union goes at the top and to the flag's own right, which is the viewer's left.

topics.title: Respect and Care for the Flag
topics.short: The Flag Code asks that the flag not touch the ground, fly from sunrise to sunset unless lit at night, and be retired in a dignified way when worn.

topics.title: Saying Please
topics.short: We say "please" when we ask for something, because asking is kinder than telling.

topics.title: Saying Thank You
topics.short: We say "thank you" when someone gives us something or does something for us, so they know we noticed.

topics.title: You're Welcome
topics.short: When someone thanks us, we answer "You're welcome" or "Glad to help," so the kindness goes both ways.

topics.title: Saying Excuse Me
topics.short: We say "excuse me" when we need to get past someone, when we bump into someone, or after a burp.

topics.title: Saying I'm Sorry
topics.short: When we hurt someone, even by accident, we say "I'm sorry," say what we did, and try to help.

topics.title: When Someone Says Sorry
topics.short: When someone says sorry to us, we can say "Thank you for saying sorry" or "It's okay," and let it go.

topics.title: Kind Words, Not Unkind Ones
topics.short: Calling names, teasing about how someone looks and saying "you can't play" hurt; kind words help everyone feel welcome.

topics.title: Saying Hello
topics.short: Look at the person, smile, and say "hello" or "hi," and answer when someone says hello to you.

topics.title: A Wave, a Hello or a Handshake
topics.short: There are many polite ways to greet someone: a wave, a hello, a high five or a handshake. You may choose one that feels right.

topics.title: Saying Goodbye
topics.short: When we leave, we say goodbye to the people we were with, and thank our host if we were visiting.

topics.title: What to Call Grown-Ups
topics.short: Many grown-ups are called Mr., Mrs., Ms. or Miss with their last name, or Dr. for a doctor; families and places have their own ways too.

topics.title: It's Okay to Say No and Tell
topics.short: If anyone makes you feel scared or uncomfortable, it is okay to say no, move away and tell a grown-up you trust.

topics.title: Taking Turns
topics.short: Taking turns means one person goes, then the next, so everyone gets a chance.

topics.title: Sharing
topics.short: Sharing means letting others use something too, or using it together, so everyone can have fun.

topics.title: Joining In and Letting Others In
topics.short: Ask "Can I play too?" to join a game, and say "Sure, come play!" when someone asks you.

topics.title: Asking Before You Borrow
topics.short: Ask before you use something that belongs to someone else, take care of it, and give it back.

topics.title: Good Winners and Good Losers
topics.short: A good winner does not brag, and a good loser does not pout; both say "Good game!" and play again.

topics.title: Tattling or Telling?
topics.short: Telling is getting help when someone is hurt, in danger or being unkind; tattling is trying to get someone in trouble over something small.

topics.title: Listening Ears
topics.short: To listen well, look at the person talking, keep your body still, and wait until they finish.

topics.title: Waiting to Talk
topics.short: When grown-ups are talking, wait for a pause, say "Excuse me," and wait to be called on, unless something is wrong.

topics.title: Inside Voice, Outside Voice
topics.short: Use a soft inside voice in homes, classrooms and stores, and save loud voices for the playground.

topics.title: Saying Hello on the Phone
topics.short: Answer with "Hello," speak clearly, and if the call is for a grown-up, say "Please wait" and go get them.

topics.title: Clean Hands for Meals
topics.short: We wash our hands before we eat, so our food stays clean and our hands are nice to sit beside.

topics.title: Sitting at the Table
topics.short: Sit on your bottom with your chair pulled in, feet down, and stay in your seat until the meal is over.

topics.title: Napkin on Your Lap
topics.short: Put your napkin on your lap when you sit down, and use it to wipe your mouth and fingers.

topics.title: Waiting Until Everyone Is Served
topics.short: We wait to start eating until everyone has food, or until the cook or a grown-up says to begin.

topics.title: Chewing with Your Mouth Closed
topics.short: Take small bites, chew with your lips closed, and finish chewing before you talk.

topics.title: Please Pass the Peas
topics.short: If something is out of reach, ask "Please pass the peas" instead of reaching across someone's plate.

topics.title: No, Thank You
topics.short: If you don't want a food, say "No, thank you" instead of "Yuck," because someone worked to make it.

topics.title: May I Please Be Excused?
topics.short: When you are done, ask "May I please be excused?", thank the cook, and help carry your plate if you can.

topics.title: Being a Good Guest
topics.short: At a friend's house, greet the grown-ups, play nicely, and help clean up before you go.

topics.title: Being a Good Host
topics.short: When a friend comes over, greet them at the door, let them choose a game first, and walk them to the door at the end.

topics.title: Other Houses, Other Rules
topics.short: Every family has its own rules, like shoes off at the door or no snacks on the couch; at their house, follow theirs.

topics.title: Thanking Your Host
topics.short: Before you leave a visit, find the grown-up and say "Thank you for having me."

topics.title: Waiting in Line
topics.short: In a line, go to the end, wait your turn, keep your hands to yourself, and don't cut in front.

topics.title: At the Store
topics.short: At the store, stay close to your grown-up, use a quiet voice, touch only what you plan to buy, and say thank you to the cashier.

topics.title: At the Library
topics.short: At the library, use a whisper voice, handle books gently, and put books where the librarian asks.

topics.title: Quiet Places
topics.short: In quiet places like a concert, a play, a waiting room or a place of worship, we sit still, keep our voices low and follow the place's customs.

topics.title: At the Doctor's Office
topics.short: At the doctor's office, wait calmly, answer the doctor's questions, and say thank you when the visit is over.

topics.title: Holding the Door
topics.short: Look behind you when you go through a door, and hold it for anyone close behind, especially someone with full hands.

topics.title: Covering Coughs and Sneezes
topics.short: Cough or sneeze into a tissue or your elbow, turn away from people and food, and wash or clean your hands after.

topics.title: Tidying Up
topics.short: When we finish playing, we put toys back where they belong, even when a friend helped make the mess.

topics.title: Noticing How Others Feel
topics.short: Manners are kindness: notice when someone is sad, left out or hurt, and ask "Are you okay?" or invite them in.

topics.title: Opening a Gift Kindly
topics.short: When you open a gift, look at the giver, say thank you, and say something kind, even if it is not what you hoped for.

topics.title: A Thank-You Picture or Note
topics.short: After a gift or a kind deed, draw a picture or write a few words to say thank you, and sign your name.

topics.title: Egypt in Greek and Roman Eyes
topics.short: Herodotus, Diodorus and Strabo described Egypt; their accounts mix good observation with hearsay.

topics.title: A Script Forgotten
topics.short: After the 4th century AD no one could read hieroglyphs; writers like Horapollo and later Athanasius Kircher read them as pure symbols.

topics.title: Obelisks on the Move
topics.short: Romans carried obelisks to Rome, and later ones went to Paris, London and New York, spreading interest in Egypt.

topics.title: Napoleon's Expedition
topics.short: Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798 with scholars who measured and drew the monuments; their Description de l'Égypte appeared from 1809.

topics.title: The Rosetta Stone
topics.short: Found at Rosetta in 1799, the stone carries a decree of 196 BC in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, and went to the British Museum in 1802.

topics.title: Thomas Young
topics.short: Thomas Young showed that cartouches held royal names, read part of Ptolemy's name, and saw that Demotic used sound signs too (1814–1819).

topics.title: Champollion's Breakthrough
topics.short: In 1822 Champollion read Ptolemy and Cleopatra, then Ramesses and Thutmose in older cartouches, and announced his results in the Lettre à M. Dacier.

topics.title: How the Code Was Cracked
topics.short: The keys were a bilingual text, royal names that could be matched across scripts, and Coptic, which gave the sounds of Egyptian words.

topics.title: A Mixed System
topics.short: In his Précis (1824), Champollion showed that hieroglyphs mix sound signs, word signs and determinatives.

topics.title: Proving It: Lepsius and the Canopus Decree
topics.short: Richard Lepsius refined the system, and the Canopus Decree, found in 1866, another bilingual text, confirmed it.

topics.title: Collectors and the Antiquities Trade
topics.short: In the early 1800s adventurers like Giovanni Belzoni shipped statues to Europe; much was lost because no one recorded where things were found.

topics.title: Mariette and the Antiquities Service
topics.short: Auguste Mariette founded Egypt's Antiquities Service in 1858 and a national museum at Bulaq to keep finds in Egypt.

topics.title: Flinders Petrie's Methods
topics.short: Petrie excavated with care from the 1880s, recording small finds and pottery, and published his results quickly.

topics.title: Seriation (Sequence Dating)
topics.short: Petrie put Predynastic graves in order by the changing styles of their pottery, giving "sequence dates" before any calendar dates existed.

topics.title: Stratigraphy
topics.short: Layers of soil pile up over time, so lower layers are usually older; recording layers lets archaeologists date finds by their context.

topics.title: Carter and KV62
topics.short: In 1922 Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) and spent about ten years recording and clearing it.

topics.title: Context and Recording
topics.short: An object's value to history depends on its context: where it lay, with what, in which layer. Excavation destroys a site, so records are everything.

topics.title: Relative and Absolute Dates
topics.short: Relative dating puts things in order (older or younger); absolute dating gives a date in years, with a margin.

topics.title: Radiocarbon Dating
topics.short: Living things take in carbon-14, which decays at a known rate after death; measuring what is left dates plant and animal remains, after calibration.

topics.title: Luminescence Dating
topics.short: Thermoluminescence can date when pottery was last fired, by the light trapped energy gives off when heated.

topics.title: Dating by Texts and Styles
topics.short: Inscriptions with regnal years and royal names, and the style of objects, date finds to a reign or period.

topics.title: Recording Inscriptions
topics.short: Epigraphers copy inscriptions exactly as they are, damaged parts included; Chicago's Epigraphic Survey has worked at Luxor since 1924.

topics.title: From Tracing to 3-D Scanning
topics.short: Methods range from hand tracing checked against the wall, to photogrammetry and laser scanning.

topics.title: Brackets for Damage and Restoration
topics.short: Editions mark restored text with [ ], partly visible signs with ⸢ ⸣, and words the scribe left out with ⟨ ⟩.

topics.title: Where Egyptian Objects Are
topics.short: Great collections are in Cairo (the Egyptian Museum and the Grand Egyptian Museum), London, Paris, Berlin, Turin and New York, among others.

topics.title: The Debate Over Returning Objects
topics.short: Some argue that famous objects taken in colonial times should go back to Egypt; others argue they were acquired legally, are well kept and seen by many. This topic sets out both sides.

topics.title: Laws on Antiquities
topics.short: Egypt's laws now keep antiquities as state property (Law 117 of 1983), and the 1970 UNESCO Convention works against illegal trade.

topics.title: Survey from the Air and Space
topics.short: Archaeologists find and map sites with field survey, aerial photographs, satellite images and geophysics, often without digging.

topics.title: Science in the Lab
topics.short: CT scans look inside mummies without unwrapping them; studies of ancient DNA, residues and isotopes are newer and still debated in places.

topics.title: The Nubian Rescue
topics.short: When the Aswan High Dam was built, a UNESCO campaign (1960–1980) moved temples such as Abu Simbel and Philae and surveyed Nubia before the flood.

topics.title: Egyptian Egyptologists
topics.short: Egyptian scholars, from Ahmed Kamal and Selim Hassan in the early 1900s to today's excavators, have led the study of their own past.

topics.title: What Hieratic Is
topics.short: Hieratic is the cursive form of hieroglyphs, written with a brush and ink, used from the earliest dynasties alongside hieroglyphs.

topics.title: What Was Written in Hieratic
topics.short: Letters, accounts, legal records, literature and religious texts were written in hieratic on papyrus, wood and ostraca.

topics.title: Reading Hieratic
topics.short: Egyptologists read hieratic by transcribing it, sign by sign, into hieroglyphs, then transliterating.

topics.title: Late Egyptian
topics.short: Late Egyptian, the everyday language of the New Kingdom, uses articles (pꜣ, tꜣ, nꜣ) and new verb forms.

topics.title: Late Egyptian Texts
topics.short: Late Egyptian texts include letters, the tomb-robbery papyri, the story of Wenamun and love poems.

topics.title: The Demotic Script
topics.short: Demotic grew out of hieratic in the 7th century BC; it is very cursive, written right to left, with many signs joined.

topics.title: Demotic Texts
topics.short: Demotic was used for contracts, letters, tax receipts and stories like the tales of Setne Khamwas.

topics.title: Demotic on the Rosetta Stone
topics.short: The Demotic text of the Rosetta Stone (32 lines) is the best preserved of its Egyptian texts and was key to Young's work.

topics.title: Where Coptic Comes From
topics.short: Coptic is the last stage of Egyptian, written from about the 3rd century AD by Egyptian Christians in Greek letters plus letters from Demotic.

topics.title: The Coptic Alphabet
topics.short: Coptic uses the 24 Greek letters, from alpha to omega, for Egyptian sounds.

topics.title: The Letters from Demotic
topics.short: Sahidic Coptic adds six letters from Demotic, ϣ ϥ ϩ ϫ ϭ ϯ, for sounds Greek lacked; Bohairic adds ϧ.

topics.title: What Coptic Tells Us
topics.short: Because Coptic writes vowels, it shows how Egyptian words sounded late in their history: rn "name" is ⲣⲁⲛ, ran.

topics.title: Coptic Dialects and Coptic Today
topics.short: Coptic had dialects, chiefly Sahidic in the south and Bohairic in the north; Bohairic is still used in Coptic Church services.

topics.title: The Last Hieroglyphic Inscription
topics.short: The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae on 24 August AD 394, beside a figure of the god Mandulis.

topics.title: The Last Demotic
topics.short: The last dated Demotic inscription, also at Philae, comes from AD 452.

topics.title: Meroitic, the Script of Kush
topics.short: The kingdom of Kush wrote its own language in Meroitic script; its sounds were worked out in 1909, but much of the language is still not understood.

topics.title: The Nile Valley and the Delta
topics.short: Egypt was the Nile valley, a strip of farmland rarely more than 20 km wide, and the fan-shaped Delta, between deserts.

topics.title: The Inundation
topics.short: Summer rains in Ethiopia raised the Nile each year, flooding the valley and leaving silt; the height of the flood decided the harvest.

topics.title: The Two Lands and the Nomes
topics.short: Egyptians called their country the Two Lands, Upper (south) and Lower (north) Egypt, divided into provinces called nomes.

topics.title: Sources for Egyptian History
topics.short: Historians use monuments and inscriptions, papyri and ostraca, archaeology, foreign records and later Greek writers, each with its own biases.

topics.title: Kingdoms and Intermediate Periods
topics.short: Modern historians divide Egyptian history into kingdoms (times of one strong state) and intermediate periods (times of division).

topics.title: King Lists
topics.short: Ancient king lists, like the Palermo Stone, the Turin Canon and the lists at Abydos and Saqqara, give kings in order, but leave some out.

topics.title: Manetho's Dynasties
topics.short: Manetho, an Egyptian priest of the early 3rd century BC, wrote a history in Greek that grouped the kings into the 30 dynasties we still use.

topics.title: Dating by Regnal Years
topics.short: Egyptians dated events by the year of the king's reign ("Year 5 of His Majesty"), so dates have to be added up king by king.

topics.title: Astronomical Dates
topics.short: A few texts record the rising of the star Sirius or the phases of the moon, which can tie reigns to absolute dates; scholars still debate how to read them.

topics.title: Radiocarbon and Egyptian Dates
topics.short: Radiocarbon dating of plant remains from dated contexts largely agrees with the standard chronology and is most useful for the earliest periods.

topics.title: How Sure Are the Dates?
topics.short: Dates are fixed from 664 BC on; before that they are approximate, uncertain by decades in the New Kingdom and by a century or more in the Old Kingdom.

topics.title: Before the Kings: Badari and Naqada
topics.short: Farming villages appeared along the Nile in the 5th millennium BC; the Naqada culture spread across Egypt and grew into chiefdoms.

topics.title: The First Writing
topics.short: Small labels from a tomb at Abydos (tomb U-j, c. 3200 BC) carry some of the earliest known Egyptian writing.

topics.title: The Joining of the Two Lands
topics.short: Around 3000 BC the Nile valley and the Delta came under one king; the Narmer Palette shows King Narmer in the white crown on one side and the red crown on the other.

topics.title: The First Dynasties
topics.short: Kings of Dynasties 1 and 2 ruled from Memphis, were buried at Abydos, and built the tools of the state: writing, taxes and royal titles.

topics.title: Djoser and the Step Pyramid
topics.short: Djoser of the 3rd Dynasty built the first large stone building, the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, credited to his official Imhotep.

topics.title: Sneferu, Khufu and the True Pyramid
topics.short: In the 4th Dynasty, Sneferu built the first true pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur, and Khufu the Great Pyramid at Giza.

topics.title: The State That Built the Pyramids
topics.short: Pyramids needed an organized state: a vizier, scribes, taxes in grain and labor, quarries, boats and a fed, housed workforce.

topics.title: The Sun Kings and the Pyramid Texts
topics.short: Kings of the 5th Dynasty built sun temples for Ra, and Unas, the last of them, had the first Pyramid Texts carved in his tomb.

topics.title: The 6th Dynasty and the Provinces
topics.short: Under the 6th Dynasty, provincial governors grew richer and more independent; officials like Weni and Harkhuf left autobiographies of their careers.

topics.title: Why Did the Old Kingdom End?
topics.short: Historians debate the causes: a weaker central government, very long reigns, and perhaps low Nile floods and a drier climate.

topics.title: The First Intermediate Period
topics.short: After the Old Kingdom, rival dynasties ruled from Herakleopolis in the north and Thebes in the south.

topics.title: Mentuhotep II Reunites Egypt
topics.short: Mentuhotep II of Thebes defeated the Herakleopolitan kings and reunited Egypt (c. 2055 BC), beginning the Middle Kingdom.

topics.title: The 12th Dynasty
topics.short: Amenemhat I founded the 12th Dynasty and a new capital, Itjtawy; its kings, named Amenemhat and Senusret, ruled about two centuries.

topics.title: Senusret III and Nubia
topics.short: Senusret III built a chain of forts at the Second Cataract, fixed the southern border, and reduced the power of provincial governors.

topics.title: The Classic Age
topics.short: The Middle Kingdom was the classic age of Egyptian literature, such as the Tale of Sinuhe and the teaching texts, written in Middle Egyptian.

topics.title: The Hyksos
topics.short: The Hyksos, rulers of western Asian origin, governed the north from Avaris as the 15th Dynasty (c. 1650–1550 BC).

topics.title: The Kingdom of Kush at Kerma
topics.short: South of Egypt, the kingdom of Kush, centered at Kerma, grew strong and allied with the Hyksos.

topics.title: The Theban War
topics.short: Theban kings Seqenenre Tao and Kamose fought the Hyksos, and Ahmose took Avaris and drove them out (c. 1550 BC).

topics.title: Ahmose and the New Kingdom
topics.short: Ahmose founded the 18th Dynasty; his successors pushed into the Levant and Nubia and built Egypt's empire.

topics.title: Hatshepsut
topics.short: Hatshepsut ruled first as regent for Thutmose III and then as king (c. 1473–1458 BC), building at Karnak and Deir el-Bahari.

topics.title: Thutmose III and Megiddo
topics.short: Thutmose III won the battle of Megiddo and led many campaigns into the Levant, making Egypt the leading power of the region.

topics.title: Amenhotep III and the Amarna Letters
topics.short: Amenhotep III ruled a rich and peaceful empire; his letters with the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and others survive in the Amarna archive.

topics.title: Akhenaten and Amarna
topics.short: Akhenaten made the Aten, the sun disk, the center of worship, closed temples of other gods and built a new capital at Amarna.

topics.title: Tutankhamun and the Restoration
topics.short: Tutankhamun, Ay and Horemheb brought back the old gods and left Amarna; later kings erased the Amarna kings from their lists.

topics.title: Ramesses II
topics.short: Ramesses II of the 19th Dynasty reigned 66 years (1279–1213 BC), built more than any other king and moved his capital to Pi-Ramesses.

topics.title: Kadesh and the Peace Treaty
topics.short: At Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw; years later the two powers signed a peace treaty.

topics.title: Ramesses III and the Sea Peoples
topics.short: Ramesses III fought off the Sea Peoples; in his reign came the first known strike, by the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina.

topics.title: The End of the New Kingdom
topics.short: Under the later Ramesses, Egypt lost its empire, tombs were robbed, and the high priests of Amun at Thebes grew powerful.

topics.title: A Divided Egypt
topics.short: In the Third Intermediate Period, kings at Tanis and then Libyan dynasties ruled the north while the priests of Amun held Thebes.

topics.title: The Kushite Kings
topics.short: Kings from Kush, such as Piye and Taharqo, conquered Egypt and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty until the Assyrians drove them out.

topics.title: The Saite Revival
topics.short: Psamtek I became king at Sais in 664 BC and had reunited Egypt by 656 BC; the 26th Dynasty copied Old Kingdom art and welcomed Greek traders and soldiers.

topics.title: Persian Rule
topics.short: In 525 BC Cambyses of Persia conquered Egypt; Persian kings ruled it as the 27th Dynasty until 404 BC.

topics.title: The Last Native Kings
topics.short: Egyptian kings ruled again from 404 BC until Persia returned in 343 BC; Nectanebo II was the last native pharaoh.

topics.title: Alexander in Egypt
topics.short: Alexander the Great took Egypt from Persia in 332 BC, visited the oracle of Amun at Siwa and founded Alexandria.

topics.title: The Ptolemies and Alexandria
topics.short: Ptolemy I and his heirs ruled from Alexandria, with its Library, Museum and lighthouse, as Greek kings and as pharaohs.

topics.title: Cleopatra VII
topics.short: Cleopatra VII, allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony, lost to Octavian at Actium (31 BC); after her death in 30 BC Egypt became Roman.

topics.title: Roman Egypt
topics.short: Rome ruled Egypt as a special province, and its grain fed the city of Rome.

topics.title: Christian and Byzantine Egypt
