topics.short: Christianity spread through Egypt; monks like Antony and Pachomius founded monastic life, and Coptic became the Christian Egyptians' written language.

topics.title: The Arab Conquest
topics.short: Arab armies under Amr ibn al-As took the fortress of Babylon in AD 641 and then Alexandria, ending Byzantine rule.

topics.title: Divine Kingship and the Titulary
topics.short: The king was Horus on earth and son of Ra, standing between the gods and the people; his five names expressed this role.

topics.title: The Vizier and the Officials
topics.short: A vizier ran the government with scribes and officials who counted harvests, collected taxes and kept records.

topics.title: An Economy Without Coins
topics.short: Until the Late Period Egyptians did not use coins; they traded goods valued in units of copper (deben) or grain, and wages were paid in bread and beer.

topics.title: The People of Egypt
topics.short: Most Egyptians were farmers; above them were craftsmen, scribes, priests and officials; there were servants and some slaves, especially war captives.

topics.title: Deir el-Medina, the Workmen's Village
topics.short: The craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs lived at Deir el-Medina; thousands of their notes on pottery and stone survive.

topics.title: Women in Ancient Egypt
topics.short: Egyptian women could own and sell property, make contracts, go to court and inherit, though few held office.

topics.title: The Army
topics.short: Egypt's army grew from local levies into a standing army of the New Kingdom, with chariots and foreign troops.

topics.title: Egypt and Nubia
topics.short: For three thousand years Egypt traded with, fought and ruled parts of Nubia, and Nubian kings once ruled Egypt.

topics.title: Egypt and the Near East
topics.short: Egypt traded with Byblos for cedar, ruled parts of Canaan, and dealt with Mitanni, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylon and Persia.

topics.title: Egypt and the Bible: What Scholars Debate
topics.short: Historians debate how stories of Joseph and the Exodus relate to Egyptian evidence; many identify Shishak with Shoshenq I, though some doubt it.

topics.title: The Nile River
topics.short: Egypt was a long, narrow green strip along the Nile, with dry desert on both sides.

topics.title: A River That Flows North
topics.short: The Nile flows from south to north and empties into the Mediterranean Sea through the Delta.

topics.title: Upper and Lower Egypt
topics.short: Upper Egypt is the south, up the river; Lower Egypt is the north, where the Delta spreads out.

topics.title: The Yearly Flood
topics.short: Every summer the Nile rose over its banks and left rich, dark mud that made the fields fertile.

topics.title: Three Seasons
topics.short: The Egyptian year had three seasons: the flood (Akhet), growing (Peret) and harvest (Shemu).

topics.title: Boats on the Nile
topics.short: The Nile was Egypt's road: boats floated north with the current and sailed south with the wind.

topics.title: Farming by the River
topics.short: Farmers grew wheat, barley and flax in the black mud and lifted water with a bucket on a pole, the shaduf.

topics.title: What Is a Pharaoh?
topics.short: A pharaoh was the king (or sometimes queen) of all Egypt; the word comes from per-aa, "Great House".

topics.title: Crowns, Crook and Flail
topics.short: The white crown stood for Upper Egypt, the red crown for Lower Egypt, and the double crown for both; kings held a crook and a flail.

topics.title: One Kingdom
topics.short: Around 3000 BC, Upper and Lower Egypt were joined into one kingdom; a carved palette shows King Narmer wearing the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other.

topics.title: Hatshepsut, a Woman King
topics.short: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as king for about fifteen years, built a great temple and sent ships to the land of Punt.

topics.title: Ramesses the Great
topics.short: Ramesses II ruled for 66 years, built huge temples like Abu Simbel, and had many children.

topics.title: Tutankhamun, the Boy King
topics.short: Tutankhamun became king at about nine and died young; his small tomb was found nearly untouched in 1922.

topics.title: Cleopatra, the Last Pharaoh
topics.short: Cleopatra VII was the last ruler of a Greek family that ruled Egypt; after her, Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.

topics.title: Why Pyramids?
topics.short: Pyramids were tombs for kings, built to protect the king's body and help him live forever.

topics.title: From Steps to Smooth Sides
topics.short: The first pyramid, King Djoser's, had steps; later kings like Sneferu and Khufu built smooth-sided pyramids.

topics.title: The Pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx
topics.short: Three great pyramids at Giza belong to Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure; the Great Sphinx guards them.

topics.title: How They Were Built
topics.short: Teams of skilled Egyptian workers cut stone with copper tools, dragged it on sledges and raised it on ramps; just how the ramps ran is still unknown.

topics.title: Many Gods
topics.short: The Egyptians believed in many gods, each caring for part of the world: the sun, the river, the sky, the home.

topics.title: Gods with Animal Heads
topics.short: You can tell gods apart by their heads: Horus the falcon, Anubis the jackal, Thoth the ibis, Bastet the cat, Hathor the cow, Sobek the crocodile.

topics.title: The Story of Osiris and Isis
topics.short: In the old story, Osiris was a good king; his wife Isis brought him back to rule the land of the dead, and their son Horus became king.

topics.title: Mummies
topics.short: Egyptians dried and wrapped the bodies of the dead so they would last for the afterlife; this is called mummification.

topics.title: Tombs and Grave Goods
topics.short: Tombs held food, furniture, games and little helper figures called shabtis for life after death.

topics.title: The Weighing of the Heart
topics.short: Egyptians believed a dead person's heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, truth, to see if they had lived a good life.

topics.title: Homes and Families
topics.short: Most families lived in houses of mud brick, with a flat roof for sleeping on hot nights.

topics.title: Bread, Beer and Onions
topics.short: Everyday food was bread, thick beer, onions, beans, fish and fruit like dates and figs.

topics.title: Clothes, Wigs and Eye Paint
topics.short: People wore light linen clothes; many wore wigs, and men and women lined their eyes with dark paint.

topics.title: Toys and Games
topics.short: Children played with balls, dolls and toy animals, and families played board games such as senet.

topics.title: Jobs Along the Nile
topics.short: Most people were farmers; others were bakers, potters, builders, painters, soldiers, priests and scribes.

topics.title: Scribes and School
topics.short: Scribes learned to read and write at school, using reed pens, ink and sheets of papyrus.

topics.title: Signs for Sounds
topics.short: Many hieroglyphs stand for sounds: the owl is m, the water is n, the mouth is r.

topics.title: Signs for Ideas
topics.short: Some signs show what a word means, and some go at the end of a word to give a hint, like walking legs for "go".

topics.title: Which Way to Read
topics.short: Hieroglyphs can go left to right, right to left or top to bottom; people and animals face the start of the line.

topics.title: Write Your Name
topics.short: You can write your name with sound signs, one sign for each sound.

topics.title: Reading a Cartouche
topics.short: A cartouche is an oval loop around a king's or queen's name.

topics.title: Egyptian Numbers
topics.short: Egyptians wrote numbers with a stroke for 1, a hobble for 10, a coil of rope for 100 and a lotus for 1,000, repeating signs to add up.

topics.title: The Rosetta Stone
topics.short: The Rosetta Stone has the same message in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, which helped people read hieroglyphs again.

topics.title: Champollion Cracks the Code
topics.short: In 1822, Jean-François Champollion showed how hieroglyphs work, using names in cartouches and the Coptic language.

topics.title: Finding Tutankhamun's Tomb
topics.short: In 1922, Howard Carter found the steps to Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings, full of treasures.

topics.title: What Archaeologists Do
topics.short: Archaeologists dig carefully, write down where everything was found, and study it to learn how people lived.

topics.title: What Egyptian Is
topics.short: Egyptian is an Afroasiatic language, related to the Semitic and Berber languages, written for more than 4,000 years.

topics.title: The Stages of Egyptian
topics.short: Egyptian changed over time: Old, Middle and Late Egyptian, then Demotic and Coptic.

topics.title: Why Learn Middle Egyptian
topics.short: Middle Egyptian was the classical language: spoken in the Middle Kingdom and used for formal inscriptions for two thousand years after.

topics.title: Three Kinds of Signs
topics.short: Signs either write sounds (phonograms), write whole words (logograms), or classify a word without being read (determinatives).

topics.title: Reading Direction
topics.short: Hieroglyphs run right to left, left to right, or in columns; signs of people and animals face the beginning of the line.

topics.title: Groups and Quadrats
topics.short: Signs are grouped into neat imaginary squares; within a group, read top before bottom and front before back.

topics.title: Writing Without Vowels
topics.short: Hieroglyphs write consonants only; the vowels of Egyptian words are mostly lost and partly known from Coptic.

topics.title: The Alphabet I: ꜣ j y ꜥ w
topics.short: The vulture ꜣ, the reed j, the two reeds y, the forearm ꜥ and the quail chick w.

topics.title: The Alphabet II: b p f m n
topics.short: The foot b, the stool p, the horned viper f, the owl m and the water n.

topics.title: The Alphabet III: r h ḥ ḫ ẖ
topics.short: The mouth r, the shelter h, the wick ḥ, the placenta ḫ and the belly ẖ: four different h sounds.

topics.title: The Alphabet IV: z s š q k g
topics.short: The door bolt z, the folded cloth s, the pool š, the hill slope q, the basket k and the jar stand g.

topics.title: The Alphabet V: t ṯ d ḏ
topics.short: The bread loaf t, the tethering rope ṯ, the hand d and the cobra ḏ.

topics.title: Transliteration and Its Order
topics.short: Egyptologists write Egyptian in a fixed alphabet, ꜣ j y ꜥ w b p f m n r h ḥ ḫ ẖ z s š q k g t ṯ d ḏ, which is also dictionary order.

topics.title: Typing Transliteration (the Manuel de Codage)
topics.short: On a keyboard, Egyptologists type A i y a w b p f m n r h H x X z s S q k g t T d D.

topics.title: Saying Words Aloud
topics.short: By convention Egyptologists say ꜣ and ꜥ as "a", j as "i", w as "u", and put "e" between other consonants: nfr is "nefer".

topics.title: Biliteral Signs
topics.short: Many signs write two consonants, like pr (house), mn (game board), wr (swallow) and nb (basket).

topics.title: More Biliterals
topics.short: More common biliterals: zꜣ (pintail duck), kꜣ (raised arms), jr (eye), ms (fox skins), ḥm (club), mꜣ (sickle).

topics.title: Triliteral Signs
topics.short: Some signs write three consonants: ꜥnḫ, nfr, ḥtp, nṯr, ḫpr, ḥqꜣ, wsr.

topics.title: Phonetic Complements
topics.short: One-consonant signs often repeat sounds of a bigger sign beside them, as a reading aid: nfr written with f and r.

topics.title: Reading Whole Words
topics.short: To read a word, read each sign in order, drop complements, and stop at the determinative.

topics.title: One Word, Many Spellings
topics.short: Scribes could spell a word in several ways, with more or fewer complements and different signs.

topics.title: Logograms and the Stroke
topics.short: A logogram writes a whole word by its picture, usually marked with a stroke: the house with a stroke is pr "house".

topics.title: Determinatives
topics.short: A determinative at the end of a word is not read; it shows the word's class of meaning and marks the end of the word.

topics.title: Common Determinatives
topics.short: The seated man and woman, the god, walking legs, the man with hand to mouth, the papyrus roll, the house, the town, the hills and water.

topics.title: Honorific Transposition
topics.short: Words for the king and the gods are written first out of respect but read in their normal place: ḥtp-dj-nsw is written with nsw first.

topics.title: Writing the Plural
topics.short: The plural is shown with three strokes, by writing a sign three times, or with the ending -w.

topics.title: Masculine and Feminine
topics.short: Nouns are masculine or feminine; most feminine nouns end in -t (the bread loaf): zꜣ "son", zꜣt "daughter".

topics.title: The Plural
topics.short: Masculine plurals end in -w and feminine plurals in -wt: nṯr "god", nṯrw "gods"; nṯrt "goddess", nṯrwt "goddesses".

topics.title: The Dual
topics.short: Egyptian has a dual for pairs: masculine -wj and feminine -tj: nṯrwj "the two gods", ꜥwj "the two arms".

topics.title: The Direct Genitive
topics.short: Putting two nouns side by side means "A of B": pr nsw "the house of the king".

topics.title: The Indirect Genitive
topics.short: "Of" can also be written with n, which agrees with the first noun: n (masculine), nt (feminine), nw (plural).

topics.title: Adjectives
topics.short: Adjectives follow the noun and agree with it: z nfr "a good man", zꜣt nfrt "a good daughter".

topics.title: Nisbe Adjectives
topics.short: Adding -j to a noun or preposition makes an adjective (a nisbe): njwt "town", njwtj "of the town"; ḥr "on", ḥrj "upper, who is on".

topics.title: nb, "Every"
topics.short: nb after a noun means "every" or "all" and agrees with it: tꜣ nb "every land", ḫt nbt "everything".

topics.title: This and That
topics.short: pn and tn follow a noun ("this"): z pn "this man"; nn "these" comes first, joined by n: nn n rmṯ "these people"; pꜣ, tꜣ and nꜣ also come first.

topics.title: Suffix Pronouns
topics.short: Suffix pronouns attach to the end of a word: =j "I, my", =k "you, your" (man), =ṯ (woman), =f "he, his", =s "she, her", =n, =ṯn, =sn.

topics.title: Using Suffix Pronouns
topics.short: On a noun a suffix means "my, your, his": pr=f "his house"; on a preposition it is the object: n=f "to him".

topics.title: Dependent Pronouns
topics.short: Dependent pronouns are objects or follow certain words: wj "me", ṯw "you", sw "him", sj "her", st "it, them", sn "them".

topics.title: Independent Pronouns
topics.short: Independent pronouns stand alone, often first in a sentence: jnk "I", ntk "you", ntf "he", nts "she".

topics.title: The Simple Prepositions
topics.short: m "in, from, as", n "to, for", r "to, toward", ḥr "on", ḫr "with, near (a person)", ḥnꜥ "with", jn "by", mj "like".

topics.title: Prepositions with Pronouns
topics.short: Prepositions take suffix pronouns: n=f "to him", ḥr=s "on it", ḥnꜥ=j "with me"; m becomes jm before a suffix: jm=f "in it".

topics.title: Compound Prepositions
topics.short: Prepositions combine with nouns: m-bꜣḥ "in the presence of", m-ḫt "after", ḥr-ḥꜣt "before", r-gs "beside".

topics.title: The Adverbial Sentence
topics.short: A subject followed by a prepositional phrase or adverb makes a sentence: z m pr "the man is in the house".

topics.title: jw and mk
topics.short: Statements often begin with jw (marking the sentence as a statement of fact) or mk "look!"; mk takes a dependent pronoun: mk wj m pr "look, I am in the house".

topics.title: The Nominal Sentence
topics.short: Two nouns side by side can say "A is B", and an independent pronoun can lead: jnk zꜣ=k "I am your son".

topics.title: Sentences with pw
topics.short: pw "this" makes a sentence "it is A" or "A is B": zꜣ=j pw "he is my son".

topics.title: The Adjectival Sentence
topics.short: An adjective first, then its subject, makes a sentence: nfr sw "he is good"; nfr pr=f "his house is good".

topics.title: Numerals
topics.short: Numbers are written by repeating signs: the stroke 1, hobble 10, coil 100, lotus 1,000, finger 10,000, tadpole 100,000, and Heh 1,000,000.

topics.title: Counting Things
topics.short: Numbers follow the noun they count: zꜣ 3 "three sons"; ordinals like "second" use -nw: snnw "second".

topics.title: Writing a Date
topics.short: Dates give the regnal year, the month of a season and the day: ḥꜣt-zp 5 ꜣbd 2 ꜣḫt sw 10 "year 5, month 2 of the Flood, day 10".

topics.title: The Five Royal Names
topics.short: A king had five names: the Horus name, the Two Ladies name, the Golden Horus name, the throne name and the birth name.

topics.title: Cartouches and Their Titles
topics.short: The throne name follows nsw-bjt "King of Upper and Lower Egypt"; the birth name follows zꜣ-rꜥ "son of Ra". Both are in cartouches.

topics.title: Reading Royal Names
topics.short: Read a cartouche sign by sign, remembering honorific transposition: jmn written first in Tutankhamun is read last.

topics.title: The Offering Formula
topics.short: Stelae and tombs begin ḥtp-dj-nsw, "an offering that the king gives", to a god like Osiris or Anubis, for the ka of the dead.

topics.title: Bread, Beer and the Voice Offering
topics.short: The formula continues with the gifts: prt-ḫrw "an invocation offering" of bread and beer, oxen and fowl, linen and alabaster.

topics.title: Titles and Epithets
topics.short: Monuments give titles like sš "scribe", jmj-rꜣ "overseer", ḥm-nṯr "priest" and epithets like mꜣꜥ-ḫrw "true of voice".

topics.title: Verb Roots
topics.short: Egyptian verbs are built on roots of two, three or four consonants: sḏm "hear", ḏd "say", nḏm "be sweet".

topics.title: Verb Classes
topics.short: Verbs fall into classes: strong roots (sḏm), third-weak (mrj "love", jrj "do"), doubled (mꜣꜣ "see"), and causatives in s- (sꜥnḫ "make live").

topics.title: Causative Verbs
topics.short: Adding s- to a root makes a causative "make (something) do": ꜥnḫ "live", sꜥnḫ "make live"; mn "remain", smn "make firm".

topics.title: The Irregular Verbs
topics.short: A few common verbs are irregular: rdj/dj "give", jj/jw "come", jnj "bring", wnn "be, exist".

topics.title: The Verb Forms at a Glance
topics.short: Middle Egyptian has suffix forms (sḏm=f, sḏm.n=f, sḏm.tw=f), the stative, the infinitive, participles and relative forms, and the imperative.

topics.title: Forms of the Infinitive
topics.short: The infinitive is the verb's noun form; third-weak verbs add -t and usually drop the weak j: mrt "to love", jrt "to do"; strong verbs show no ending: sḏm.

topics.title: Using the Infinitive
topics.short: The infinitive acts as a noun: as the object of another verb, after prepositions, and in headings and captions.

topics.title: Subjects and Objects of the Infinitive
topics.short: A noun or suffix after an infinitive can be its object or subject: rdjt=f "his giving" or "giving it".

topics.title: The sḏm=f
topics.short: The sḏm=f is the verb stem plus a subject: sḏm=f "he hears", sḏm z "the man hears".

topics.title: Noun Subjects and Word Order
topics.short: Word order is verb, subject, object, then adverbs: dj nsw ḥtp "the king gives an offering".

topics.title: What the sḏm=f Means
topics.short: The sḏm=f covers general and present action and, after certain words or in wishes, the future or "may he hear".

topics.title: The sḏm=f of Weak Verbs
topics.short: Weak and irregular verbs change in the sḏm=f: jr=f "he does", dj=f "he gives", mꜣꜣ=f "he sees".

topics.title: rdj with the sḏm=f: "Cause That"
topics.short: rdj "give" followed by a sḏm=f means "cause that, let": rdj=f sḏm=j "he let me hear".

topics.title: The sḏm.n=f
topics.short: Adding .n between the stem and the subject makes the sḏm.n=f: sḏm.n=f "he heard".

topics.title: What the sḏm.n=f Means
topics.short: The sḏm.n=f expresses completed action, usually past: rdj.n=f "he gave", or "he has given".

topics.title: jw sḏm.n=f in Narrative
topics.short: jw sḏm.n=f states a past event as a fact, as in biographies: jw jr.n=j "I did".

topics.title: Stative Endings
topics.short: The stative adds endings for its subject: -kj (I), -tj (you), -w or no ending (he), -tj (she), -wjn (we), -tjwnj (you all), -w (they).

topics.title: What the Stative Means
topics.short: The stative describes a state: of intransitive verbs, the state reached ("he has come, he is here"); of transitive verbs, a passive state ("it is sealed").

topics.title: The Stative in Sentences
topics.short: The stative usually follows a noun or pronoun subject, often after jw or mk: mk wj jj.kj "look, I have come".

topics.title: The Stative or the sḏm.n=f?
topics.short: Both can point to the past, but the stative describes a state and its subject comes first, while the sḏm.n=f reports an act with the subject after.

topics.title: Active Participles
topics.short: An active participle means "one who does": sḏm "one who hears", ḏd "one who says"; it agrees like an adjective.

topics.title: Passive Participles
topics.short: A passive participle means "one who is done to": mrr "one who is loved", rdj "what is given".

topics.title: Participles in Phrases
topics.short: Participles agree with the noun they describe, take objects, and can stand alone as nouns: sḏmw "those who hear".

topics.title: Relative Forms
topics.short: A relative form is a verb with its own subject that describes a noun: ḫt rdjt.n=f "the thing that he gave" (with -t, agreeing with the feminine ḫt).

topics.title: The Relative Adjective ntj
topics.short: ntj "who, which" introduces a relative clause: z ntj m pr "the man who is in the house"; jwtj "who is not" is its negative.

topics.title: The sḏm.tw=f Passive
topics.short: Adding .tw makes a passive: sḏm.tw=f "he is heard"; with a noun, rdj.tw ḥtp "an offering is given".

topics.title: Other Ways to Say the Passive
topics.short: The passive sḏm=f, the stative of transitive verbs, and the passive participle all express things done to someone.

topics.title: Negation with n
topics.short: n before a verb form negates it, with a twist: n sḏm=f usually means "he did not hear", and n sḏm.n=f "he cannot hear".

topics.title: nn, "There Is No"
topics.short: nn before a noun means "there is not": nn mw "there is no water"; nn also negates some sentences and the future.

topics.title: The sḏmt=f: "Not Yet" and "Until"
topics.short: The sḏmt=f appears after n and r: n sḏmt=f "he has not yet heard", r sḏmt=f "until he hears".

topics.title: The Negative Verb tm
topics.short: tm "not to be (doing)" negates forms that cannot take n, like infinitives and participles: tm sḏm "not hearing".

topics.title: Do Not!
topics.short: Negative commands use m (the imperative of jmj "not to do"): m sḏm "do not listen".

topics.title: Circumstantial Clauses
topics.short: A clause without an introducing word, after a main clause, often describes circumstances: "when", "while", "as".

topics.title: Conditions with jr
topics.short: jr "if" introduces a condition, often with the sḏm=f or sḏm.n=f: jr sḏm=k "if you listen".

topics.title: Purpose and Result
topics.short: Purpose is shown with r + infinitive "in order to" or with a sḏm=f after another verb: "so that he may hear".

topics.title: The Pseudoverbal Construction
topics.short: A subject followed by ḥr + infinitive means "is doing" and by r + infinitive "is going to do": jw=f ḥr sḏm "he is hearing".

topics.title: Clauses After Indefinite Nouns
topics.short: After a noun without "the", a plain clause can describe it, with no ntj: z sḏm=f "a man who hears".

topics.title: Emphatic Forms: A Debated Idea
topics.short: Some forms put the stress on an adverb ("it was in the house that he heard"); scholars debate how many such forms exist and how to name them.

topics.title: The Imperative
topics.short: The imperative gives commands, usually the bare stem; jmj "give!" and mj "come!" are irregular.

topics.title: Questions
topics.short: jn (or jn jw) asks a yes-no question; question words include zj "who?", jḫ "what?" and tnj "where?".

topics.title: Particles
topics.short: Small words color a sentence: mk "look", jsṯ "now", ḥꜣ "would that", ḥm "indeed", js "for, as".

topics.title: jn and the Cleft Sentence
topics.short: jn + noun + participle stresses who did it: jn nsw rdj "it is the king who gives".

topics.title: Reading a Middle Kingdom Stela
topics.short: A stela starts with the offering formula, names the gods, lists the gifts, then names the owner and his titles.

topics.title: Families on Stelae
topics.short: Stelae list relatives with "his son", "his daughter", "born of" (jr.n, ms.n) and their epithets.

topics.title: Tomb Autobiographies
topics.short: Officials told their lives in set phrases: "I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked."

topics.title: Sinuhe: The Opening
topics.short: The Tale of Sinuhe begins with his titles and the death of King Amenemhat I.

topics.title: Sinuhe: The Flight
topics.short: Sinuhe overhears news of the king's death, panics and flees toward the east, a scene told with vivid verbs.

topics.title: The Eloquent Peasant
topics.short: A peasant robbed on his way to market pleads for justice in fine speeches, which delight the king.

topics.title: The Rosetta Stone in Hieroglyphs
topics.short: The hieroglyphic section of the Rosetta Stone names King Ptolemy V with long royal titles in cartouches.

topics.title: From Transliteration to Good English
topics.short: A good translation keeps the meaning and the tone, not the word order: jw=j jj.kj becomes "I have come", not "is I come".

topics.title: Using a Sign List
topics.short: Gardiner's sign list sorts signs into lettered groups (A men, B women, G birds, M plants, N sky and earth...) and numbers them.

topics.title: Using a Dictionary
topics.short: Middle Egyptian dictionaries list words in transliteration order, ꜣ j y ꜥ w b p f m n r h ḥ ḫ ẖ z s š q k g t ṯ d ḏ.

topics.title: Many Gods, Many Forms
topics.short: Egyptians worshiped many gods; one god could appear in several forms, and several gods could share one role.

topics.title: Recognizing the Gods
topics.short: Gods are known by their heads, crowns and emblems: Amun's two tall plumes, Osiris's crook and flail, Isis's throne sign, Maat's feather.

topics.title: Gods and Their Cities
topics.short: Each great god had a home city: Ptah at Memphis, Ra at Heliopolis, Amun at Thebes, Thoth at Hermopolis, Osiris at Abydos, Hathor at Dendera.

topics.title: Divine Families
topics.short: Gods were grouped in families of three: Amun, Mut and Khonsu at Thebes; Osiris, Isis and Horus; Ptah, Sekhmet and Nefertem at Memphis.

topics.title: The Osiris Myth
topics.short: In the myth, Seth killed his brother Osiris; Isis restored him, and their son Horus won the throne, while Osiris ruled the dead.

topics.title: Amun-Ra and Combined Gods
topics.short: Gods could be joined into one, like Amun-Ra, king of the gods in the New Kingdom, joining the hidden Amun and the sun god Ra.

topics.title: The Heliopolis Account
topics.short: At Heliopolis, Atum rose from the waters of Nun and created Shu and Tefnut, who gave birth to Geb (earth) and Nut (sky): the first gods of the Nine (the Ennead).

topics.title: The Memphis Account
topics.short: At Memphis, Ptah created the world by thought and word; the text survives on the Shabaka Stone (c. 710 BC), and its date of composition is debated.

topics.title: The Hermopolis Account
topics.short: At Hermopolis, creation began with eight gods (the Ogdoad), four pairs standing for waters, endlessness, darkness and hiddenness.

topics.title: The First Mound
topics.short: The accounts share an image: a mound rising from the waters at the first moment, recalled by the benben stone and by temple floors.

topics.title: Maat and Isfet
topics.short: Maat was the right order of the world, truth and justice; isfet was disorder. Keeping maat was the duty of gods, kings and people.

topics.title: The King Between Gods and People
topics.short: The king was Horus on earth and son of Ra; he stood between the gods and the people, offering to the gods for everyone.

topics.title: The King Offers to the Gods
topics.short: Temple walls show the king offering to the gods in every scene, though priests did the daily work in his name.

topics.title: The Sed Festival
topics.short: The sed festival renewed the king's strength, traditionally after thirty years of rule and then every few years.

topics.title: Cult Temples and Memorial Temples
topics.short: Cult temples housed a god; memorial (mortuary) temples kept up the cult of a dead king, like those on the west bank at Thebes.

topics.title: The Plan of a Temple
topics.short: From the river: quay, avenue of sphinxes, pylon, open court, hypostyle hall, offering hall and sanctuary.

topics.title: The Temple as the World
topics.short: The temple pictured the world at creation: the pylon the horizon, the columns a papyrus marsh, the sanctuary the first mound, rising and darkening inward.

topics.title: The Daily Ritual
topics.short: Each morning priests opened the shrine, woke, washed, dressed and fed the god's statue, then sealed it again.

topics.title: Priests
topics.short: Priests served in shifts; ranks included the ḥm-nṯr ("god's servant"), the wꜥb ("pure one") and the lector priest who read the rituals.

topics.title: Karnak and Luxor
topics.short: Karnak, the temple of Amun at Thebes, grew for two thousand years; an avenue of sphinxes joins it to Luxor Temple.

topics.title: The Opet Festival
topics.short: In the Opet festival, Amun's statue traveled in its sacred boat from Karnak to Luxor Temple, renewing the king's rule.

topics.title: The Beautiful Festival of the Valley
topics.short: Each year Amun crossed the Nile to the temples of the west bank, and families feasted at the tombs of their dead.

topics.title: Beliefs About the Afterlife
topics.short: Egyptians believed death led to a new life, if the body was kept, the name remembered and offerings continued.

topics.title: The Ka, the Ba and the Akh
topics.short: A person had several parts: the ka (life force, which received offerings), the ba (shown as a bird with a human head, free to move), the akh (the transfigured spirit), the name and the shadow.

topics.title: The Judgment of the Dead
topics.short: The heart was weighed against the feather of Maat before Osiris; the dead declared they had not done wrongs, and a monster waited for those who failed.

topics.title: The Duat and the Sun's Night Journey
topics.short: The Duat was the realm of the dead, through which the sun god sailed each night to be reborn at dawn.

topics.title: The Field of Reeds
topics.short: The blessed dead hoped to live in the Field of Reeds, a perfect Egypt where crops grew tall; shabti figures would do their work.

topics.title: Offerings for the Dead
topics.short: Families and priests brought food and drink to a tomb's false door and said the offering formula, so the dead would be fed.

topics.title: Why Mummify?
topics.short: Egyptians preserved the body so the ka and ba could return to it; dry desert graves had first shown them that bodies could last.

topics.title: How Bodies Were Preserved
topics.short: Embalmers removed the internal organs, dried the body with natron salt for about forty days, then wrapped it in linen with amulets; the whole process took about seventy days.

topics.title: Coffins, Canopic Jars and Masks
topics.short: Organs went into four canopic jars guarded by the Four Sons of Horus; the body lay in nested coffins, sometimes with a mask over the face.

topics.title: The Pyramid Texts
topics.short: The oldest religious texts, spells carved inside pyramids from Unas (end of the 5th Dynasty) on, to help the king rise to the sky.

topics.title: The Coffin Texts
topics.short: In the Middle Kingdom, spells were painted inside the coffins of officials, so non-royal people could use them too.

topics.title: The Book of the Dead
topics.short: From the New Kingdom, spells for the journey through the afterlife were written on papyrus rolls placed in the tomb; Egyptians called them "spells for going forth by day".

topics.title: Books of the Underworld
topics.short: New Kingdom royal tombs show the sun's night journey hour by hour, in books like the Amduat ("What Is in the Underworld").

topics.title: Mastaba Tombs
topics.short: Early elite tombs were mastabas: low, flat-topped buildings over a burial shaft, with a chapel for offerings.

topics.title: The Pyramid Complex
topics.short: A pyramid stood in a complex: a valley temple by the river, a covered causeway, and a mortuary temple against the pyramid.

topics.title: Rock-Cut Tombs
topics.short: From the Middle Kingdom, many tombs were cut into cliffs, as at Beni Hasan; New Kingdom kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings.

topics.title: Why Tombs Were Decorated
topics.short: Scenes of farming, feasting and offering were meant to provide for the dead forever, not only to record their lives.

topics.title: Composite Views
topics.short: Artists drew each part from its most typical view: the face in profile, the eye from the front, shoulders from the front, legs in profile.

topics.title: The Grid and the Canon of Proportions
topics.short: Artists drew figures on a grid: a standing figure was 18 squares from the soles to the hairline, and a later grid used 21 squares.

topics.title: Size Shows Importance
topics.short: The most important figure is the largest: the king larger than his enemies, a tomb owner larger than his servants.

topics.title: Colors and Their Meanings
topics.short: Colors carried meaning: black for fertile soil and rebirth, green for growth, red for energy or danger, gold for the flesh of the gods.

topics.title: Registers and Ground Lines
topics.short: Scenes run in horizontal bands (registers), each with its own ground line; figures face the way the text runs.

topics.title: Kinds of Statues
topics.short: Common types are the seated statue, the standing striding statue (left foot forward), the scribe statue, the block statue and the pair statue.

topics.title: Raised and Sunk Relief
topics.short: Raised relief cuts away the background; sunk relief cuts the figure into the wall and suits bright sun outdoors.

topics.title: Painting and Pigments
topics.short: Painters used mineral colors, including the first known synthetic pigment, Egyptian blue, on plaster or stone.

topics.title: The Art of the Amarna Age
topics.short: Under Akhenaten, art changed: long faces, rounded bodies, family scenes, and the Aten's rays ending in hands.

topics.title: Household Gods
topics.short: At home, people turned to protectors like Bes and Taweret, especially for childbirth and children.

topics.title: Amulets
topics.short: People wore amulets for protection: the wedjat eye, the scarab, the ankh, the djed pillar and the tyet knot.

topics.title: Oracles and Letters to the Dead
topics.short: People asked gods questions through oracles at festivals and wrote letters to dead relatives asking for help.

topics.title: The Aegean World
topics.short: Crete, the Cyclades and mainland Greece, linked by the sea, in the Bronze Age (about 3000 to 1100 BC).

topics.title: The Minoans of Crete
topics.short: Crete's Bronze Age civilization, named by Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos; we do not know what they called themselves.

topics.title: Knossos and the Cretan Palaces
topics.short: Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros: big buildings around a central court that stored goods, held workshops and kept records.

topics.title: The Mycenaeans
topics.short: Greek speakers of the mainland from about 1600 BC, with palaces at Mycenae, Pylos, Thebes and Tiryns; by about 1450 BC Greek speakers ran Knossos too.

topics.title: Dating the Aegean Bronze Age
topics.short: Periods named from pottery styles (Early, Middle and Late Minoan; Helladic on the mainland), tied to years by radiocarbon and by links to Egypt.

topics.title: The End of the Palaces
topics.short: Around 1200 BC the mainland palaces were destroyed, Pylos by fire, and writing disappeared from Greece for about four centuries.

topics.title: Word Signs, Syllables and Letters
topics.short: Three ways to write: a sign for a word (logogram), a sign for a syllable (syllabogram), or a sign for a single sound (a letter of an alphabet).

topics.title: How a Syllabary Works
topics.short: One sign per syllable: a vowel alone (a) or a consonant plus a vowel (ka, ke, ki, ko, ku), so the signs fill a grid of consonants and vowels.

topics.title: Cretan Hieroglyphs
topics.short: Crete's earliest script, used mostly on seals from about 2100 or 1900 BC to about 1700 BC; it overlapped with Linear A and is still unread.

topics.title: A Family of Aegean Scripts
topics.short: Linear A gave rise to Linear B; on Cyprus, Cypro-Minoan and then the Cypriot syllabary, which wrote Greek and was read in the 1870s.

topics.title: Then Came the Alphabet
topics.short: After the palaces fell no one wrote in Greece for about four centuries; around 800 BC Greeks borrowed the Phoenician letters and added vowels.

topics.title: Arthur Evans at Knossos, 1900
topics.short: Evans began digging at Knossos in March 1900, found thousands of clay tablets, named Linear A and Linear B, and believed their language was not Greek.

topics.title: Carl Blegen at Pylos
topics.short: In 1939 Blegen found the archive room of the palace at Pylos on the first day of digging; after the war, in 1952, his team found many more tablets.

topics.title: Clay, Fire and Survival
topics.short: The tablets were sun-dried clay meant for one season's records; the fires that destroyed the palaces baked them and saved them.

topics.title: Numbering the Signs
topics.short: Emmett Bennett sorted the signs into a standard list; scholars still name a sign by its number, like *08, and write an unread sign that way.

topics.title: Alice Kober's Triplets
topics.short: In the 1940s Alice Kober showed that Linear B words change their endings, using sets of three related forms, without guessing any sounds.

topics.title: Building the Grid
topics.short: Michael Ventris placed signs in a grid so that signs in one row shared a consonant and signs in one column a vowel, before knowing any of the sounds.

topics.title: The Breakthrough: Cretan Place Names
topics.short: Ventris tried known Cretan place names on words found only at Knossos: ko-no-so (Knossos), a-mi-ni-so (Amnisos) and tu-ri-so (Tylissos), and the grid gave Greek.

topics.title: Greek, 1952
topics.short: Ventris announced on BBC radio on 1 July 1952 that Linear B was Greek; with John Chadwick he published the case in 1953.

topics.title: The Tripod Tablet Confirms It
topics.short: On Pylos tablet Ta 641, read in 1953, the words read by Ventris's values describe the pictured vessels: ti-ri-po beside a tripod, and cups with four, three or no handles.

topics.title: The Five Vowel Signs
topics.short: a, e, i, o and u: five signs that stand for a vowel alone, the first column of the grid.

topics.title: The d, k, m, n and p Rows
topics.short: Each row is one consonant with the five vowels: da de di do du, ka ke ki ko ku, and so on.

topics.title: The Other Rows: j, q, r, s, t, w, z
topics.short: The rest of the grid: q for sounds like kw, r for both r and l, z for a sound like dz, and the glides j and w; some rows have gaps.

topics.title: Special Signs
topics.short: Signs beyond the basic grid: a2 (ha), a3 (ai), au, pu2 (phu), ra2, ra3, ro2, ta2, and signs for clusters like dwe, dwo, nwa, pte, twe and two.

topics.title: Signs Still Unread
topics.short: About fifteen rare signs, such as *18, *47 and *63, have no agreed value; a few, like *65 (perhaps ju) and *79 (perhaps zu), have proposed values.

topics.title: Every Sign Ends in a Vowel
topics.short: Linear B can only write syllables that end in a vowel, so Greek words full of consonant clusters and final consonants must be bent to fit.

topics.title: Missing Consonants
topics.short: Final consonants, and l, m, n, r and s before another consonant, are not written: ka-ko is khalkos (bronze), pa-ta is panta (all), pe-mo is sperma (seed).

topics.title: Clusters and Empty Vowels
topics.short: Other consonant clusters are split with a vowel borrowed from the next syllable: ko-no-so for Knossos, ti-ri-po for tripos, a-re-ka-sa-da-ra for Alexandra.

topics.title: One Sign, Several Sounds
topics.short: r stands for r and l; p, k and q signs each cover a voiced, voiceless and aspirated sound; only d and t are kept apart; h is usually not written.

topics.title: Diphthongs and Glides
topics.short: Between vowels the glides j and w often appear (i-je-re-u, hiereus, priest); the u of a diphthong is written (au, eu), but the i of ai, ei, oi is often left out.

topics.title: Logograms
topics.short: Signs for things (man, woman, horse, tripod, wheat, wine) that stand before a number and say what is counted; they are not read as part of a sentence.

topics.title: Male and Female Animals
topics.short: Small marks show the sex of animals: a ram has two short bars across its stem, a ewe a forked stem; scholars write them OVISm and OVISf.

topics.title: Aegean Numbers
topics.short: Strokes for ones, bars for tens, circles for hundreds, circles with rays for thousands; you add them up, and the order of the groups does not change the value.

topics.title: Weights and Measures
topics.short: Dry goods: a unit, then T (a tenth), V (a sixth of T) and Z (a quarter of V); liquids: a unit, S (a third), V and Z; weights from the talent (L) down.

topics.title: Pages, Leaves and Labels
topics.short: Page-shaped tablets for lists, palm-leaf tablets for single entries, clay labels for baskets, sealings, and words painted on jars.

topics.title: Scribes and Their Hands
topics.short: Each scribe's handwriting can be recognized; scholars count about 66 hands at Knossos and 45 at Pylos and number them.

topics.title: Reading a Tablet Line
topics.short: Most lines follow one pattern: a word or name, then a logogram, then a number; a word divider separates words.

topics.title: Mycenaean Words and Their Descendants
topics.short: ti-ri-po is tripous (tripod), di-pa is depas (cup), e-ra-wo is elaion (oil), wa-na-ka is anax (lord): many Mycenaean words live on in later Greek.

topics.title: Endings You Can See
topics.short: Some endings show through the spelling: -o-jo for the genitive of o-stems (te-o-jo, of the god), -e and -i for datives (di-we, to Zeus), -pi for an instrumental plural.

topics.title: Places on the Tablets
topics.short: ko-no-so (Knossos), pa-i-to (Phaistos), a-mi-ni-so (Amnisos), ku-do-ni-ja (Kydonia, modern Chania), pu-ro (Pylos) and te-qa (Thebes) are named on the tablets.

topics.title: Gods on the Tablets
topics.short: po-se-da-o (Poseidon), di-we and di-wo (Zeus), e-ra (Hera), di-wo-nu-so (Dionysus), e-ma-a2 (Hermes) and a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja (Mistress Athena) appear by name.

topics.title: The Palace Economy
topics.short: The tablets track what came in and went out: flocks and wool, oil and perfume, rations for workers, bronze for smiths, chariots and armor.

topics.title: The Wanax and the Lawagetas
topics.short: The wa-na-ka (wanax) ruled the palace state; the ra-wa-ke-ta (lawagetas) ranked next; a qa-si-re-u (later basileus, king) was a lesser local official.

topics.title: Offerings to the Gods
topics.short: Tablets list offerings of oil, honey and gold vessels to gods; Pylos tablet Tn 316 records gold vessels and people brought to Zeus, Hera and others.

topics.title: What the Tablets Don't Tell
topics.short: No poems, laws, letters or histories survive in Linear B; the tablets record one season's business, so much about these people remains unknown.

topics.title: Linear A: Where and What
topics.short: The Minoan script, used about 1800 to 1450 BC: about 1,400 short inscriptions, most from Hagia Triada, Zakros, Chania and Phaistos.

topics.title: Signs Shared with Linear B
topics.short: Many Linear A signs look like Linear B signs, so scholars read them with the Linear B values by convention; this is a working guess about sounds.

topics.title: Linear A Numbers and Fractions
topics.short: Linear A counts with the same decimal marks as Linear B and also has fraction signs; J as one half is widely accepted, while values for the others are proposed.

topics.title: Ku-ro, the Total
topics.short: The word read ku-ro stands before a number that equals the sum of the list above it, so it is widely accepted to mean "total"; ki-ro also recurs in lists, its meaning uncertain.

topics.title: The Libation Formula
topics.short: Stone offering tables from sanctuaries repeat a set of words, such as a-sa-sa-ra-me (also ja-sa-sa-ra-me), i-pi-na-ma and si-ru-te; their meanings are unknown.

topics.title: Why Linear A Can't Be Read Yet
topics.short: The texts are few and short, the Minoan language matches no known language, and there is no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone.

topics.title: How to Judge a Decipherment Claim
topics.short: A good decipherment makes testable predictions, reads the whole corpus the same way, fits place names and new finds, and convinces specialists.

topics.title: Linear A and Linear B Side by Side
topics.short: The same sign shapes, different languages: what we know about each script, what we don't, and why Linear B could be read when Linear A cannot.

topics.title: Good and Bad: bene- and mal-
topics.short: bene- means well and mal- means badly: two small parts that unlock a family of words.

topics.short: Words for warm hearts and cold ones.

topics.short: Words for good manners and bad ones.

topics.title: Agreeing and Disagreeing
topics.short: Words for coming together and pulling apart.

topics.title: Plenty and Scarcity
topics.short: Words for having lots, and for having little.

topics.title: Belief, Trust and Truth: cred, fid and ver

topics.title: Honest and Dishonest

topics.title: Words of Praise

topics.title: Sad
topics.short: Words for sorrow, gloom and longing.

topics.title: Belief and Doubt
topics.short: Words for believing, supposing and doubting.

topics.title: Changeable
topics.short: Words for people and things that change without warning.

topics.title: Making Things Worse

topics.title: Laws and Rules

topics.title: Ordinary and Overused
topics.short: Words for the everyday and the worn out.

topics.title: Looking and Seeing: spec and vid
topics.short: spec, spic and vid, vis mean look and see.

topics.title: Brave and Fearful
topics.short: Words for courage and for its lack.

topics.title: Strict and Lenient
topics.short: Words for firm rules and loose ones.

topics.title: Words of Blame

topics.title: Angry and Hateful
topics.short: Words for anger, from annoyance to hatred.

topics.title: Noticing and Understanding
topics.short: Words for paying attention and taking things in.

topics.title: How Often
topics.short: Words for now and then, again and again, and without end.

topics.title: Helping Along
topics.short: Words for making things easier and helping them grow.

topics.title: Who Rules
topics.short: Words for kinds of power and government.

topics.title: Unusual
topics.short: Words for the odd, the out of place and the never seen before.

topics.title: Speaking and Saying: loqu and dict
topics.short: loqu and locut mean speak; dict means say.

topics.title: Proud and Humble
topics.short: Words for people who think too much of themselves, and for those who don't.

topics.title: Right and Wrong
topics.short: Words for honorable conduct and dishonorable conduct.

topics.title: Arguing a Case
topics.short: Words for making a claim and answering one.

topics.title: Calm
topics.short: Words for peace of mind and steady nerves.

topics.title: Comparing and Contrasting
topics.short: Words for likeness and difference.

topics.title: Beginnings
topics.short: Words for starting, and for things just begun.

topics.title: Getting in the Way
topics.short: Words for slowing things down and blocking them.

topics.title: Guilt and Innocence
topics.short: Words for blame, punishment and pardon.

topics.title: Big and Small
topics.short: Words for the enormous and the tiny.

topics.title: Turning, Throwing and Pulling: vert, ject and tract
topics.short: vert means turn, ject means throw and tract means pull.

topics.title: Careful and Careless
topics.short: Words for doing things with great care, and with too little.

topics.title: Real and Fake
topics.short: Words for the real thing and for imitations.

topics.title: Tricky Twins
topics.short: Pairs of words that look or sound alike but mean different things.

topics.title: Fear and Worry
topics.short: Words for fear, from a twinge of doubt to dread.

topics.title: Learners and Experts
topics.short: Words for beginners, dabblers and masters.

topics.title: Peaks and Endings
topics.short: Words for high points, low points and endings.

topics.title: Calming Things Down
topics.short: Words for soothing feelings and settling quarrels.

topics.title: Fighting and Making Peace
topics.short: Words for conflict and for ending it.

topics.title: Everywhere
topics.short: Words for what is found all around.

topics.title: Words of Time: chron, temp and ann
topics.short: chron (Greek) and temp (Latin) mean time; ann and enn mean year.

topics.title: Friendly and Aloof
topics.short: Words for warm company and for keeping apart.

topics.title: Models and Examples
topics.short: Words for the best examples and the patterns others follow.

topics.title: Clear and Unclear
topics.short: Words for ideas that are easy to follow and ideas that are not.

topics.title: Puzzled
topics.short: Words for being confused, and for the puzzles that confuse us.

topics.title: Dreamers and Doers
topics.short: Words for big dreams and practical plans.

topics.title: Growing and Shrinking
topics.short: Words for growth and decline.

topics.title: Stirring Things Up
topics.short: Words for starting trouble and spurring action.

topics.title: Giving In
topics.short: Words for yielding, surrendering and agreeing to go along.

topics.title: Important and Trivial
topics.short: Words for what matters most and what hardly matters.

topics.title: Not: in-, im- and ir-
topics.short: The prefix in- often means not, and changes to im- or ir- to fit the next sound.

topics.title: Stubborn and Yielding
topics.short: Words for holding firm and for giving way.

topics.title: Self-Control and Indulgence
topics.short: Words for holding back and for giving in to pleasure.

topics.title: Joking and Mocking
topics.short: Words for humor, gentle and sharp.

topics.title: Bored and Interested
topics.short: Words for dull hours and fascinating ones.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Arguments
topics.short: Words for arguments that hold up and arguments that fall apart.

topics.title: Before and After
topics.short: Words for what comes first and what follows.

topics.title: Stopping and Holding Back
topics.short: Words for discouraging, limiting and stopping.

topics.title: Judging Fairly
topics.short: Words for fair judgment and for bias.

topics.title: Hard and Easy
topics.short: Words for tasks that are hard, risky, useless or too easy.

topics.title: Feeling, Loving and Humankind: path, phil and anthrop
topics.short: path means feeling, phil means love and anthrop means human being.

topics.title: Wise and Foolish
topics.short: Words for good sense and for the lack of it.

topics.title: Insults and Slights
topics.short: Words for putting people down.

topics.title: Loud and Angry Words
topics.short: Words for noise and for heated speech.

topics.title: Lazy and Sleepy

topics.title: Inborn and Acquired
topics.short: Words for what we are born with and what we pick up.

topics.title: Waiting and Hurrying

topics.title: Coaxing and Forcing
topics.short: Words for getting people to do things, gently or roughly.

topics.title: Insiders and Outsiders
topics.short: Words for shutting people out and for narrow or wide horizons.

topics.title: Too Much
topics.short: Words for more than enough.

topics.title: Flocks, Peace and Pleasing: greg, pac and plac
topics.short: greg means flock; pac means peace and plac means please.

topics.title: Spenders and Savers
topics.short: Words for how people handle money.

topics.title: Tricks and Schemes
topics.short: Words for tricksters and their plots.

topics.title: Slippery Speech
topics.short: Words for dodging, hinting and misleading.

topics.title: Regret and Shame
topics.short: Words for being sorry and for being embarrassed.

topics.title: Obvious and Seeming
topics.short: Words for what is plain to see and what only appears so.

topics.title: Luck and Chance
topics.short: Words for good luck, bad luck and pure chance.

topics.title: Destroying
topics.short: Words for tearing down and wiping out.

topics.title: Secret and Hidden
topics.short: Words for secrets, stealth and things out of sight.

topics.title: Showy and Plain
topics.short: Words for beauty, show and plainness.

topics.short: omni and pan mean all, ambi means both, eu means good and hyper means over.

topics.title: Flatterers and the Bold
topics.short: Words for bowing too low and for standing too tall.

topics.title: Leanings and Likings

topics.title: Rare Words for Praise and Blame

topics.title: Deep and Shallow Thinking

topics.title: Old and New

topics.title: Taking and Giving Up
topics.short: Words for seizing things and for letting them go.

topics.title: Rebels and Factions
topics.short: Words for those who break from the group, and for groups that split.

topics.title: Harmful and Wholesome
topics.short: Words for what harms and what does good.

topics.title: Prefix, Root and Suffix
topics.short: Most long words are built from parts: a prefix in front, a root in the middle and a suffix at the end.

topics.title: Latin and Greek: Where the Parts Come From
topics.short: Many English words come from Latin, often by way of French, and many learned and scientific words come from Greek.

topics.title: Not: in-, un- and non-
topics.short: in-, un- and non- turn a word into its opposite; in- changes to im-, il- and ir- to fit the next sound.

topics.title: Without: a- and an-
topics.short: In words from Greek, a- (an- before a vowel) means without or not.

topics.title: Good and Bad: bene- and mal-
topics.short: bene- means well and mal- means badly.

topics.title: Good and Bad in Greek: eu- and dys-
topics.short: eu- means good or well and dys- means bad or difficult, in words from Greek.

topics.title: Wrongly and Apart: mis- and dis-
topics.short: mis- means wrongly; dis- means apart, away or not.

topics.title: Before and After: pre-, ante- and post-
topics.short: pre- and ante- mean before; post- means after.

topics.title: Under and Over: sub-, super-, hypo- and hyper-
topics.short: sub- and hypo- mean under; super- and hyper- mean over or beyond.

topics.title: Between, Within and Around: inter-, intro-, circum- and peri-
topics.short: inter- means between, intro- and intra- mean within, and circum- and peri- mean around.

topics.title: Across and Through: trans-, per- and dia-
topics.short: trans- means across or beyond; per- and dia- mean through.

topics.title: Out and In: ex-, e-, in- and en-
topics.short: ex- and e- mean out; in-, im-, en- and em- mean in or into.

topics.title: Back, Again and Down: re- and de-
topics.short: re- means back or again; de- means down, away or completely.

topics.title: Together: con-, com- and syn-
topics.short: con- (Latin) and syn- (Greek) mean with or together.

topics.title: Against: contra-, anti- and ob-
topics.short: contra-, counter-, anti- and ob- all carry the idea of against.

topics.title: Away, Toward and Forward: ab-, ad- and pro-
topics.short: ab- means away, ad- means toward and pro- means forward.

topics.title: How Many: mono-, uni-, di- and poly-
topics.short: Number prefixes come in Greek and Latin pairs: mono- and uni- (one), di- and bi- (two), poly- and multi- (many).

topics.title: All and Both: omni-, pan- and ambi-
topics.short: omni- (Latin) and pan- (Greek) mean all; ambi- means both.

topics.title: Prefixes That Change Shape
topics.short: Many prefixes change their last letter to match the root that follows: in- to im-, con- to col-, ad- to ac-, sub- to sup-.

topics.title: Say, Speak and Call: dict, loqu, voc, nounce and mand
topics.short: dict means say, loqu means speak, voc means call, nounce means announce and mand means order.

topics.title: Look and See: spec, spic, vid and vis
topics.short: spec and spic mean look; vid and vis mean see.

topics.title: Believe, Trust, True and Know: cred, fid, ver and sci
topics.short: cred means believe, fid means trust, ver means true and sci means know.

topics.title: Go and Step: ced, cess, gress and grad
topics.short: ced, ceed and cess mean go or yield; gress and grad mean step.

topics.title: Throw and Send: ject, mit and miss
topics.short: ject means throw; mit and miss mean send or let go.

topics.title: Lead, Pull and Shut: duc, tract and clud
topics.short: duc means lead, tract means pull and clud and clus mean shut.

topics.title: Turn: vert and vers
topics.short: vert and vers mean turn.

topics.title: Peace, Pleasing and War: pac, plac and bell
topics.short: pac means peace, plac means please or calm and bell means war.

topics.title: Flocks, Friends and Hearts: greg, am, cord and sent
topics.short: greg means flock, am means love or friend, cord means heart and sent means feel.

topics.title: Hold, Hang, Carry and Pour: ten, pend, fer and fund
topics.short: ten means hold, pend means hang or weigh, fer means carry and fund and fus mean pour.

topics.title: Run, Follow, Walk and Flee: cur, sequ, ped and fug
topics.short: cur means run, sequ means follow, ped means foot and fug means flee.

topics.title: Light and Heavy: luc, lev and grav
topics.short: luc means light (brightness), lev means light (not heavy) and grav means heavy.

topics.title: Life, Food and Sleep: viv, vor and somn
topics.short: viv and vit mean life, vor means eat and somn means sleep.

topics.title: Time: chron, temp, ann and nov
topics.short: chron (Greek) and temp (Latin) mean time, ann and enn mean year, and nov means new.

topics.title: Feeling, Love and Humankind: path, phil, miso and anthrop
topics.short: path means feeling, phil means love, miso means hate and anthrop means human being.

topics.title: Word and Writing: log and graph
topics.short: log means word, reason or study; graph and gram mean write or draw.

topics.title: Rule: -cracy, -archy and auto-
topics.short: -cracy and -crat mean rule or power, -archy and -arch mean rule or chief, and auto- means self.

topics.title: Birth, Kind and Form: gen and morph
topics.short: gen means birth, kind or produce; morph means form or shape.

topics.title: Adjective Endings: -ous, -ive, -ible and -ic
topics.short: Endings like -ous (full of), -ive (tending to), -ible and -able (able to be) and -ic (having to do with) make adjectives.

topics.title: Noun Endings: -ity, -tion, -ance, -ism and -ist
topics.short: Endings like -ity, -tion, -ance and -ence name a quality or an act; -ism names a belief and -ist a person.

topics.title: Verb Endings: -ate, -ify and -ize
topics.short: Endings like -ate, -ify and -ize make verbs that mean to make or to act.

topics.title: Standard Error and Error Bars
topics.short: The standard error of a mean is SE = s/√n. Error bars of ±2 SE give roughly a 95% confidence interval; when such bars for two groups do not overlap, the difference is likely real.

topics.title: Null and Alternative Hypotheses
topics.short: The null hypothesis says there is no effect or no difference; the alternative says there is. A test asks how likely data this extreme would be if the null were true.

topics.title: Chi-Square Goodness of Fit
topics.short: χ² = Σ (observed − expected)² / expected. Compare it with the critical value for (categories − 1) degrees of freedom at p = 0.05: larger means reject the expected ratio.

topics.title: Levels of Protein Structure
topics.short: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence; secondary is α-helices and β-sheets held by backbone hydrogen bonds; tertiary is the overall fold from R-group interactions; quaternary is several chains together.

topics.title: Amino Acid R Groups
topics.short: Amino acids differ only in their R groups: nonpolar, polar, acidic (negative) or basic (positive). Where each kind sits, inside the fold or on the surface, sets how a protein folds.

topics.title: The Direction of DNA and RNA
topics.short: Each strand has a 5′ end (phosphate) and a 3′ end (hydroxyl). The two strands of DNA run antiparallel, and nucleotides are always added to the 3′ end.

topics.title: Surface Area to Volume
topics.short: For a cube of side s, surface area is 6s² and volume s³, so SA:V = 6/s. Cells stay small, flatten, or fold their membranes to keep SA:V high enough for exchange.

topics.title: Water Potential
topics.short: Water moves from higher to lower water potential: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp. Solute potential is Ψs = −iCRT (R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K)); adding solute makes Ψ more negative.

topics.title: Membrane Potential
topics.short: Pumps and channels make an uneven spread of ions: the sodium-potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP, and K⁺ leaks out, leaving the inside negative (about −70 mV in a resting neuron).

topics.title: Compartmentalization
topics.short: Membranes divide eukaryotic cells into compartments with different conditions, so incompatible reactions can run at once: lysosome enzymes work at pH 5 inside, while the cytoplasm stays near pH 7.

topics.title: Free Energy and Coupled Reactions
topics.short: Reactions with ΔG < 0 (exergonic) release free energy and can happen on their own; ΔG > 0 (endergonic) need an input. Cells couple endergonic steps to ATP hydrolysis so the total ΔG is negative.

topics.title: Enzyme Kinetics
topics.short: Rate rises with substrate concentration and levels off when the enzymes are saturated (Vmax). Doubling the enzyme doubles Vmax; temperature and pH move the curve.

topics.title: Competitive and Noncompetitive Inhibition
topics.short: A competitive inhibitor blocks the active site, and enough substrate outcompetes it. A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape, lowering Vmax no matter how much substrate.

topics.title: The Light Reactions
topics.short: In the thylakoids, photosystem II splits water (releasing O₂) and passes electrons down a chain that pumps H⁺; photosystem I re-energizes them to make NADPH; ATP synthase makes ATP as H⁺ flows back out.

topics.title: The Calvin Cycle
topics.short: In the stroma, the enzyme rubisco fixes CO₂ onto RuBP; ATP and NADPH reduce the products to G3P. Three CO₂ give one G3P for the cell, using 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.

topics.title: C4 and CAM Plants
topics.short: When stomata close in hot, dry weather, rubisco fixes O₂ instead of CO₂ (photorespiration). C4 plants like corn separate fixation in space; CAM plants like cactuses separate it in time, taking in CO₂ at night.

topics.title: Glycolysis and the Krebs Cycle
topics.short: Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate (net 2 ATP, 2 NADH). Pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle release the carbons as CO₂ and load electrons onto NADH and FADH₂.

topics.title: Oxidative Phosphorylation
topics.short: NADH and FADH₂ give electrons to the chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane; it pumps H⁺ into the intermembrane space. H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase makes most of the ATP; O₂ takes the spent electrons and forms water.

topics.title: How Cells Signal
topics.short: Cells signal by direct contact (gap junctions, surface molecules), locally (paracrine signals and synapses), or over long distances (hormones carried in the blood).

topics.title: Reception, Transduction and Response
topics.short: A ligand binds a receptor (on the surface, or inside for steroid hormones); a relay of proteins, often kinases adding phosphates and second messengers like cAMP, passes and amplifies the signal; the cell responds.

topics.title: Amplification and Changes in Pathways
topics.short: Each activated enzyme in a cascade activates many of the next, so one ligand can trigger millions of product molecules. A mutated receptor or relay protein can block a response or switch it on for good.

topics.title: Feedback in Living Systems
topics.short: Negative feedback holds a variable near a set point (blood glucose, body temperature); positive feedback drives a change to completion (blood clotting, fruit ripening with ethylene). Disrupting either shows in the data.

topics.title: Regulating the Cell Cycle
topics.short: Cyclins rise and fall through the cycle and switch on cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) that push the cell past checkpoints. Proteins like p53 halt the cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger apoptosis.

topics.title: Linked Genes
topics.short: Genes close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together. A dihybrid test cross then gives mostly parental types and a few recombinants made by crossing over.

topics.title: Recombination Frequency and Gene Maps
topics.short: Recombination frequency = recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring. 1% equals one map unit; genes far apart recombine more, so frequencies give the order of genes on a chromosome.

topics.title: Nondisjunction
topics.short: If a pair of homologs (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) fails to separate, some cells made get an extra chromosome (n + 1) and others are missing one (n − 1).

topics.title: Inheritance Outside the Nucleus
topics.short: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own genes. They are usually passed down from one parent only, most often the mother, so these traits do not show Mendelian ratios.

topics.title: Environment and Phenotype
topics.short: The same genotype can show different phenotypes in different conditions: hydrangea flower color follows soil pH, and Himalayan rabbits grow dark fur where their body is cooler.

topics.title: Replication in Detail
topics.short: Helicase opens the fork, primase lays an RNA primer, DNA polymerase extends 5′ to 3′: the leading strand continuously, the lagging strand in Okazaki fragments that ligase joins.

topics.title: Transcription and RNA Processing
topics.short: RNA polymerase binds a promoter and builds RNA 5′ to 3′. In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA gets a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail, and introns are spliced out; alternative splicing makes several proteins from one gene.

topics.title: Translation in Detail
topics.short: The small ribosomal subunit finds the start codon; tRNAs enter the A site, the peptide moves from the P site, and empty tRNAs leave from the E site. A release factor ends the chain at a stop codon.

topics.title: Operons: lac and trp
topics.short: In bacteria, the lac operon is inducible: lactose inactivates the repressor, so genes are on only when lactose is present. The trp operon is repressible: tryptophan activates the repressor and shuts the genes off.

topics.title: Gene Regulation in Eukaryotes
topics.short: Transcription factors bind promoters and enhancers; packing matters too: acetylating histones opens chromatin (more expression), methylating DNA usually closes it. These epigenetic marks can pass to daughter cells.

topics.title: Gene Expression and Specialization
topics.short: Different cell types switch on different sets of genes using different transcription factors, which is why a muscle cell and a nerve cell with the same genome make different proteins.

topics.title: Mutations and Their Effects
topics.short: Read a mutation's effect from the codon table: silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift. Its effect on the organism depends on where it falls and on the environment, and mutations are the raw material of variation.

topics.title: Sizing DNA on a Gel
topics.short: Distance moved is roughly linear in the logarithm of fragment size, so read an unknown band against the ladder: between the 1,000 and 500 base-pair bands means between those sizes.

topics.title: Transformation and DNA Sequencing
topics.short: In bacterial transformation, cells take up a plasmid; an antibiotic-resistance gene lets only transformed cells grow on selective plates. Sequencing reads the order of bases, as in reading fragments by their ends.

topics.title: Hardy-Weinberg Problems
topics.short: From one known frequency find the rest: q² from the recessive phenotype, q = √q², p = 1 − q, carriers = 2pq. Compare observed genotypes with expected ones to test for equilibrium.

topics.title: Genetic Drift
topics.short: Drift is a random change in allele frequency, strongest in small populations. A bottleneck (most die by chance) or a founder effect (a few start a new population) can change frequencies sharply.

topics.title: Molecular Clocks
topics.short: If differences in a gene build up at a roughly steady rate, the number of differences estimates how long ago two lineages split, once the rate is calibrated with fossils.

topics.title: Building Trees from Data
topics.short: Build a tree from a table of traits or sequence differences: the pair with the fewest differences shares the most recent ancestor. Parsimony picks the tree that needs the fewest changes.

topics.title: Patterns of Speciation and Extinction
topics.short: Speciation may be gradual or come in bursts after long stable periods (punctuated equilibrium). Adaptive radiation fills open niches quickly, often after mass extinctions; extinction is part of life's history.

topics.title: Early Earth and the Origin of Life
topics.short: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, and fossil microbes date back about 3.5 billion years. Experiments show simple organic molecules form under early-Earth conditions; how the first cells arose is still an open question, with hypotheses such as an "RNA world".

topics.title: Responses to the Environment
topics.short: Organisms respond to cues: plants by tropisms and photoperiod, animals by kinesis (changing speed) and taxis (moving toward or away), and by signals such as alarm calls and the honeybee's waggle dance.

topics.title: Energy Budgets and Metabolism
topics.short: Endotherms spend much of their energy keeping warm, so they need more food per gram than ectotherms; smaller endotherms have higher metabolic rates per gram. Net intake goes to growth and offspring.

topics.title: Primary Productivity
topics.short: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is all the energy producers capture; net primary productivity NPP = GPP − R (respiration). Ecologists measure it with oxygen or carbon changes in light and dark bottles.

topics.title: Population Growth Equations
topics.short: Exponential growth: dN/dt = rN. Logistic growth: dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, which slows growth as N nears K. Calculate rates at a given N and read the S-curve.

topics.title: Measuring Diversity
topics.short: Simpson's diversity index D = 1 − Σ(n/N)² runs from 0 (one species) toward 1 (many even species). It rewards both richness and evenness.

topics.title: Community Structure and Trophic Cascades
topics.short: Communities are shaped from the top down (predators) and the bottom up (nutrients). Keystone species, ecosystem engineers like beavers, and invasive species can restructure them.

topics.title: Disruptions to Ecosystems
topics.short: Invasive species, habitat loss, pollution, disease and changes in climate can change populations fast. A population with more genetic variation is more likely to have individuals that survive a change.

topics.title: Hypotheses and Controlled Experiments
topics.short: A hypothesis is a testable explanation that makes a prediction. A controlled experiment changes one independent variable, measures a dependent variable, holds the rest constant, and repeats trials.

topics.title: Reading Graphs and Data
topics.short: Read a graph by its axes and units first, then the trend; compare groups by their means and spread, and tell correlation from cause.

topics.title: Scientific Theories
topics.short: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation that ties together many facts and observations, like the cell theory and the theory of evolution. A law describes a pattern; a theory explains it.

topics.title: The Elements and Bonds of Life
topics.short: Living things are built mostly of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, with phosphorus and sulfur. Atoms share electrons in covalent bonds; ionic bonds and weak hydrogen bonds hold molecules to each other.

topics.title: The Properties of Water
topics.short: Water is polar, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds. That gives cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, a high specific heat, its power as a solvent, and ice that floats.

topics.title: Acids, Bases and pH
topics.short: pH measures how acidic a solution is: 7 is neutral, lower is acidic, higher is basic. Each step of 1 is a tenfold change, and buffers keep the pH of living things steady.

topics.title: Monomers and Polymers
topics.short: Large biological molecules are chains of small units. Dehydration synthesis joins monomers and releases water; hydrolysis splits polymers by adding water.

topics.title: Carbohydrates
topics.short: Sugars (monosaccharides like glucose) are quick energy; polysaccharides store energy (starch in plants, glycogen in animals) or build structure (cellulose in plant cell walls).

topics.title: Lipids
topics.short: Fats, oils, phospholipids and steroids do not mix with water. Fats store energy compactly, phospholipids build membranes, and steroids include cholesterol and some hormones.

topics.title: Proteins
topics.short: Proteins are chains of amino acids (20 kinds) folded into precise shapes. The shape decides the job: enzymes, structure, transport, signals and defense.

topics.title: Nucleic Acids
topics.short: DNA and RNA are chains of nucleotides, each a sugar, a phosphate and a base. DNA stores genetic information; RNA helps use it to build proteins.

topics.title: Enzymes
topics.short: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. The substrate fits the active site; the enzyme is not used up and can work again and again.

topics.title: Temperature, pH and Enzymes
topics.short: Each enzyme works best at an optimal temperature and pH. Too far away, the enzyme's shape changes (it denatures) and it stops working.

topics.title: Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
topics.short: Prokaryotic cells (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have both. All cells have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

topics.title: The Endomembrane System
topics.short: A protein made for export follows a path: ribosomes on the rough ER, then a vesicle to the Golgi apparatus, then a vesicle to the cell membrane, where it is released.

topics.title: Where Mitochondria and Chloroplasts Came From
topics.short: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria taken in by an ancient cell. Evidence: they have their own circular DNA and ribosomes, two membranes, and divide like bacteria.

topics.title: The Cell Membrane
topics.short: The membrane is a double layer of phospholipids (water-loving heads out, water-fearing tails in) with proteins floating in it: the fluid mosaic model.

topics.title: Diffusion and Concentration Gradients
topics.short: Particles spread from higher to lower concentration until evenly mixed. Small nonpolar molecules like oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse straight through the membrane.

topics.title: Osmosis and Tonicity
topics.short: Water moves across a membrane toward the side with more solute. In a hypotonic solution a cell gains water; in a hypertonic one it loses water; in an isotonic one there is no net change.

topics.title: Channels, Carriers and Pumps
topics.short: Ions and polar molecules cross through proteins. Facilitated diffusion goes down the gradient with no energy; active transport, like the sodium-potassium pump, uses ATP to move against it.

topics.title: Endocytosis and Exocytosis
topics.short: Cells take in large particles by wrapping them in membrane (endocytosis) and release large molecules by fusing vesicles with the membrane (exocytosis). Both use energy.

topics.title: ATP: The Cell's Energy Currency
topics.short: ATP releases energy when its last phosphate is removed, becoming ADP. Cells couple that release to work, and recharge ADP back to ATP with energy from food.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.short: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. In the chloroplast, the light-dependent reactions split water and make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle uses them to build sugar from CO₂.

topics.title: What Limits Photosynthesis
topics.short: The rate of photosynthesis rises with light, carbon dioxide and temperature until something else becomes the limiting factor, and falls at high temperature as enzymes denature.

topics.title: Cellular Respiration
topics.short: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP. Glycolysis (cytoplasm) splits glucose; the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain (mitochondria) release the rest, about 30 ATP per glucose in all.

topics.title: Fermentation
topics.short: Without oxygen, cells keep glycolysis running by fermentation: muscle cells make lactic acid; yeast make ethanol and carbon dioxide, which makes bread rise. Only 2 ATP per glucose.

topics.title: Photosynthesis, Respiration and the Carbon Cycle
topics.short: Photosynthesis pulls CO₂ from the air into sugars; respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns it. Their balance, along with burning and the ocean, sets the carbon dioxide in the air.

topics.title: Chromosomes and Their Numbers
topics.short: A body cell of a species has a set number of chromosomes in matching (homologous) pairs: 46 in humans, so the diploid number is 2n = 46 and the haploid number n = 23. A copied chromosome is two sister chromatids joined at a centromere.

topics.title: The Cell Cycle
topics.short: A cell spends most of its life in interphase (G1 growth, S DNA copying, G2 preparation), then divides in the mitotic phase. Checkpoints decide whether it goes on.

topics.title: Mitosis
topics.short: In prophase chromosomes condense; in metaphase they line up in the middle; in anaphase sister chromatids pull apart; in telophase two nuclei form. Cytokinesis splits the cell into two identical cells.

topics.title: Controlling the Cell Cycle
topics.short: Proteins at checkpoints let the cycle continue only when the cell is ready and its DNA is intact. When those controls fail, cells can divide without limit, which is what happens in cancer.

topics.title: Meiosis
topics.short: Meiosis is two divisions that turn one diploid cell into four haploid cells. Meiosis I separates homologous pairs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

topics.title: How Meiosis Makes Variation
topics.short: Crossing over swaps pieces between homologs, and independent assortment lines each pair up on its own: with n pairs there are 2ⁿ ways to sort the chromosomes, so every cell made is unique.

topics.title: Mitosis and Meiosis Compared
topics.short: Mitosis: one division, two identical diploid cells, for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, four different haploid cells, with crossing over and independent assortment.

topics.title: Mendel's Experiments
topics.short: Mendel crossed true-breeding pea plants: the F1 all showed one trait, and the F2 showed both in about a 3:1 ratio. He explained it with paired factors, now called genes, that separate (segregate).

topics.title: Monohybrid Crosses
topics.short: For one gene, write each parent's gametes, fill the Punnett square, and read the genotype ratio (1:2:1 for Aa × Aa) and the phenotype ratio (3:1).

topics.title: The Test Cross
topics.short: To learn whether a dominant-looking organism is AA or Aa, cross it with a recessive (aa) one: any recessive offspring show it was Aa.

topics.title: Probability Rules for Genetics
topics.short: For independent events, multiply (the product rule): the chance of aa and bb is ¼ × ¼. For outcomes that can happen in different ways, add (the sum rule).

topics.title: Dihybrid Crosses
