topics.short: For two genes on different chromosomes, AaBb × AaBb gives four gamete types each and a 16-box square with a 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio.

topics.title: Incomplete Dominance and Codominance
topics.short: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is in between (red × white snapdragons give pink); in codominance both alleles show fully (red and white hairs in a roan coat).

topics.title: Multiple Alleles: Blood Types
topics.short: The ABO blood type gene has three alleles: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant and both dominant to i. Six genotypes give four blood types: A, B, AB and O.

topics.title: Polygenic Traits and the Environment
topics.short: Traits like human height and the color of wheat kernels are shaped by many genes and the environment, giving a smooth range (a bell-shaped curve) instead of a few clear types.

topics.title: X-Linked Traits
topics.short: Genes on the X chromosome show a special pattern: XY individuals have one X, so a single recessive allele shows. Red-green color blindness is a common example.

topics.title: Reading Pedigrees
topics.short: A pedigree traces a trait through a family. Two unaffected parents with an affected child show a recessive trait; a dominant trait does not skip generations.

topics.title: The Structure of DNA
topics.short: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. Sugars and phosphates form the backbone; bases pair in the middle, A with T and G with C, by hydrogen bonds.

topics.title: DNA Replication
topics.short: Helicase unzips the helix; DNA polymerase adds matching nucleotides to each old strand. Each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one new (semiconservative).

topics.title: Transcription
topics.short: In the nucleus, RNA polymerase reads a gene's template strand and builds a matching mRNA: A in DNA pairs with U in RNA, T with A, G with C, C with G.

topics.title: Translation
topics.short: At the ribosome, each three-base codon of mRNA is matched by a tRNA anticodon carrying an amino acid. The ribosome links the amino acids into a protein until it reaches a stop codon.

topics.title: Reading the Genetic Code
topics.short: Use a codon table to translate mRNA: start at AUG (methionine), read three bases at a time, and stop at UAA, UAG or UGA. 64 codons code for 20 amino acids.

topics.title: Mutations
topics.short: A substitution can be silent (same amino acid), missense (a different one) or nonsense (a stop). An insertion or deletion shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it.

topics.title: Turning Genes On and Off
topics.short: Every cell has the same DNA, but each cell type uses different genes. Proteins that bind DNA switch genes on and off, as when bacteria make lactose-digesting enzymes only when lactose is present.

topics.title: PCR: Copying DNA
topics.short: The polymerase chain reaction copies a chosen piece of DNA by cycles of heating (separate strands), cooling (primers bind) and warming (polymerase builds). Each cycle doubles it: 2ⁿ copies after n cycles.

topics.title: Gel Electrophoresis
topics.short: DNA is negatively charged, so in a gel it moves toward the positive end. Shorter pieces move farther; comparing bands with a ladder of known sizes gives each piece's length.

topics.title: Recombinant DNA
topics.short: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences; ligase joins pieces, so a gene can be put into a plasmid and taken up by bacteria, which then make the protein, such as human insulin.

topics.title: Natural Selection
topics.short: Evolution by natural selection follows from variation, heritability, more offspring than can survive, and differences in survival and reproduction. Over generations, helpful heritable traits become more common.

topics.title: Directional, Stabilizing and Disruptive Selection
topics.short: Directional selection shifts the average one way; stabilizing selection favors the middle; disruptive selection favors both extremes. Read each from how a trait's graph changes.

topics.title: Evolution in Action
topics.short: Antibiotic and pesticide resistance and the changing beaks of Galápagos finches after a drought show natural selection measured within a few generations.

topics.title: Evidence: Fossils and Anatomy
topics.short: Transitional fossils (early whales with legs, Tiktaalik), homologous structures, and vestigial structures such as a whale's hip bones point to common ancestry.

topics.title: Evidence: DNA and Proteins
topics.short: Species that share a more recent common ancestor have more similar DNA and protein sequences. Counting differences in a sequence lets us compare relatedness.

topics.title: Reading Phylogenetic Trees
topics.short: A phylogenetic tree shows common ancestry: each branch point is a common ancestor. Relatedness is read from the most recent shared branch point, not from how close the tips are on the page.

topics.title: Building Cladograms
topics.short: Group organisms by shared derived traits: the trait shared by all but one marks the first branch, and each newer trait marks a smaller group nested inside.

topics.title: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
topics.short: In a population that is not evolving, allele frequencies p + q = 1 stay constant and genotype frequencies are p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Find q from the share of recessive individuals: q = √(q²).

topics.title: Mutation, Drift, Gene Flow and Selection
topics.short: Allele frequencies change through mutation, genetic drift (chance, strongest in small populations, as in bottlenecks and founder effects), gene flow (migration) and natural selection.

topics.title: How New Species Form
topics.short: A species splits when populations stop exchanging genes: a barrier divides them (geographic isolation), or they come to live in different habitats or flower or reproduce at different seasons. In plants, a doubled chromosome set can make a new species in one generation.

topics.title: Exponential and Logistic Growth
topics.short: With unlimited resources a population grows exponentially (a J-curve); as resources run short, growth slows toward the carrying capacity K (an S-curve, logistic growth).

topics.title: Density-Dependent and Independent Factors
topics.short: Density-dependent factors like food, disease and predation hit harder as a population grows crowded; density-independent factors like floods, fires and frosts hit regardless of size.

topics.title: Niches and Community Interactions
topics.short: Each species has a niche, its role and needs. Two species cannot share exactly the same niche for long (competitive exclusion); predation, mutualism and parasitism shape communities too.

topics.title: Energy Flow and Biomass
topics.short: Energy enters as sunlight captured by producers and flows up the trophic levels, with roughly 10% passed on at each step. Biomass and numbers usually shrink up the pyramid too.

topics.title: The Carbon, Nitrogen and Phosphorus Cycles
topics.short: Carbon cycles through photosynthesis, respiration, the ocean and fossil fuels; nitrogen through fixation, nitrification and denitrification by bacteria; phosphorus slowly through rock, soil and water, with no gas phase.

topics.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Conditions
topics.short: Where oxygen runs short, as in waterlogged soil or deep mud, some microbes use fermentation or other pathways, which changes how carbon and nitrogen cycle there.

topics.title: Stability, Disturbance and Change
topics.short: Ecosystems hold fairly steady when conditions are steady, and recover from small disturbances. Large changes, like a new predator or a changed climate, can shift them to a new state.

topics.title: Keystone Species and Trophic Cascades
topics.short: A keystone species has a much larger effect than its numbers suggest: removing sea otters let sea urchins boom and strip kelp forests, a trophic cascade.

topics.title: Group Behavior
topics.short: Herding, flocking, schooling and cooperative hunting can improve survival: more eyes watch for predators, and individuals cut their own risk.

topics.title: Biodiversity and Human Impact
topics.short: Biodiversity is measured by richness (how many species) and evenness (how balanced). Habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and overharvesting reduce it; conservation solutions are judged by evidence and trade-offs.

topics.title: Homeostasis and Feedback
topics.short: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment within a narrow range. In negative feedback a sensor detects a change and effectors push it back; positive feedback amplifies a change until an event ends it, as when blood clots.

topics.title: Controlling Body Temperature
topics.short: When the body is too warm, the brain triggers sweating and wider skin blood vessels; when too cold, shivering and narrower skin vessels. Each is negative feedback.

topics.title: Blood Sugar: Insulin and Glucagon
topics.short: After a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, which helps cells take up glucose and the liver store it, lowering blood sugar. Between meals, glucagon tells the liver to release glucose.

topics.title: Interacting Body Systems
topics.short: Cells form tissues, organs and organ systems that work together: oxygen taken in by the respiratory system is carried by the circulatory system to cells, controlled by the nervous and endocrine systems.

topics.title: The Path of Blood
topics.short: Blood takes two loops: right side of the heart → lungs → left side → body → back to the right side. Valves keep it moving one way.

topics.title: Gas Exchange in the Lungs
topics.short: In the alveoli, oxygen diffuses from air into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. Huge surface area, thin walls and steady blood flow keep the gradients steep.

topics.title: Digestive Enzymes and Absorption
topics.short: Enzymes break food into absorbable units: amylase splits starch, proteases split proteins, lipase splits fats. Villi in the small intestine absorb them into the blood and lymph.

topics.title: Neurons and Signals
topics.short: A neuron receives signals at its dendrites and sends an electrical impulse along its axon. At a synapse, chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) carry the signal to the next cell.

topics.title: The Immune System
topics.short: Innate defenses (skin, inflammation, cells that engulf germs) act fast against anything foreign. Adaptive defenses (B cells making antibodies, T cells) target one invader and leave memory cells; vaccines work by producing that memory without the illness.

topics.title: The Kidneys and Water Balance
topics.short: Nephrons filter blood, reabsorb what the body needs (water, glucose, salts) and leave the wastes in urine. A hormone, ADH, makes the kidneys keep more water when the body is short of it.

topics.title: Water Balance in Plants
topics.short: Guard cells swell and open stomata when water is plentiful and shrink to close them when it is short, balancing carbon dioxide intake against water loss.

topics.title: Living or Not Living?
topics.short: Living things grow, need food, water and air, and can make new living things like themselves. A rock or a toy car does none of these.

topics.title: What Living Things Need
topics.short: Every living thing needs water, air, food (plants make their own) and a place to live with enough room.

topics.title: Once Living: Logs, Leaves and Shells
topics.short: A fallen leaf, a log, a seashell and an apple core were part of living things once. A rock, a coin and a cloud never were.

topics.title: Living Things Grow and Change
topics.short: A kitten grows into a cat and a seed grows into a tree. Living things start small and grow, and many change shape as they grow.

topics.title: What Plants Need
topics.short: Plants need light, water, air, room to grow and nutrients from the soil. Without light or water, a plant wilts and can die.

topics.title: Parts of a Plant
topics.short: Most plants have roots, a stem, leaves and, at some time, flowers. Each part has its own job.

topics.title: What Roots Do
topics.short: Roots hold a plant in the ground and take in water and nutrients from the soil.

topics.title: What Stems and Leaves Do
topics.short: The stem holds the plant up and carries water from the roots to the leaves. Leaves catch sunlight and make the plant's food.

topics.title: Flowers, Fruits and Seeds
topics.short: Flowers make seeds. A fruit is the part of a plant that holds the seeds, so apples, tomatoes, peppers and pumpkins are all fruits.

topics.title: Bees, Butterflies and Pollen
topics.short: Bees, butterflies, birds and the wind carry pollen from flower to flower, and that helps flowers make seeds.

topics.title: How Seeds Travel
topics.short: Seeds travel away from their parent plant: blown by the wind, carried by water, stuck to fur, eaten in fruit by animals, or popped out of a pod.

topics.title: A Seed Starts to Grow
topics.short: A seed holds a tiny plant and food for it. With water and warmth, it sprouts: a root grows down and a shoot grows up toward the light.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Plant
topics.short: Seed, sprout, young plant, adult plant with flowers, then fruit with new seeds, and the cycle starts again.

topics.title: Plants Make Their Own Food
topics.short: Green leaves use sunlight, air and water to make sugar, the plant's food. Animals cannot do this; they must eat.

topics.title: Plant Parts We Eat
topics.short: We eat roots (carrots), stems (potatoes), leaves (lettuce), flowers (broccoli), fruits (apples) and seeds (peas and corn).

topics.title: What Animals Need
topics.short: Animals need food, water, air and shelter, a safe place to rest and raise their young.

topics.title: Plant-Eaters, Meat-Eaters and Both
topics.short: Herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat other animals, and omnivores eat both.

topics.title: Body Parts That Help
topics.short: Beaks, claws, fins, wings, tails and teeth each help an animal get food, move or stay safe.

topics.title: Fur, Feathers, Scales and Skin
topics.short: Mammals have hair or fur, birds have feathers, fish and reptiles have scales, and amphibians have smooth, moist skin.

topics.title: How Animals Move
topics.short: Animals walk, run, hop, fly, swim, crawl and slither, and their bodies are shaped for the way they move.

topics.title: Young Animals and Their Parents
topics.short: Many young animals look like their parents; others look very different at first. Many parents feed and protect their young.

topics.title: Mammals
topics.short: Mammals have hair or fur, breathe air, and feed their babies milk. Dogs, mice, people, bats and whales are mammals.

topics.title: Birds
topics.short: Birds have feathers, a beak and two legs, and they hatch from eggs with hard shells. Not every bird can fly.

topics.title: Fish
topics.short: Fish live in water, breathe with gills, swim with fins, and most have scales.

topics.title: Reptiles
topics.short: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and breathe air. Snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles are reptiles, and most hatch from eggs laid on land.

topics.title: Amphibians
topics.short: Amphibians have smooth, moist skin. Most start life in water with gills and live on land as adults. Frogs, toads and salamanders are amphibians.

topics.title: Insects
topics.short: Insects have six legs and three body parts, and many have wings. Ants, bees, beetles and butterflies are insects; spiders are not.

topics.title: Sorting Animals into Groups
topics.short: Look for clues, such as fur, feathers, scales, moist skin, gills or six legs, to put an animal in its group.

topics.title: What Is a Habitat?
topics.short: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives and finds the food, water and shelter it needs.

topics.title: Forests, Grasslands, Deserts and Icy Places
topics.short: Forests have many trees, grasslands are wide and grassy, deserts get very little rain, and polar places are cold and icy. Each has its own plants and animals.

topics.title: Ponds, Rivers and Oceans
topics.short: Ponds and lakes hold still fresh water, rivers flow, and oceans are salty. Different plants and animals live in each.

topics.title: Made for Their Home
topics.short: A polar bear's thick fur, a camel's wide feet and a cactus's spines all help them live where they live.

topics.title: Animal Homes
topics.short: Birds build nests, bees build hives, rabbits dig burrows, spiders spin webs and beavers build lodges.

topics.title: Living Things Change Their Surroundings
topics.short: Beavers dam streams, squirrels bury nuts that grow into trees, roots crack sidewalks, and people build roads and plant gardens.

topics.title: Energy Starts with the Sun
topics.short: Plants use sunlight to make food. Animals get their energy by eating plants, or by eating animals that ate plants.

topics.title: Food Chains
topics.short: A food chain shows who eats whom: grass, then a rabbit, then a fox. Each arrow points from the food to the animal that eats it.

topics.title: Producers and Consumers
topics.short: Plants are producers because they make food. Animals are consumers because they eat to get their food.

topics.title: Decomposers
topics.short: Worms, mushrooms and tiny bacteria break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Butterfly
topics.short: A butterfly starts as a tiny egg, hatches as a caterpillar, makes a chrysalis, and comes out as a butterfly.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Frog
topics.short: A frog starts as an egg in the water, hatches as a tadpole with a tail and gills, grows legs, loses its tail, and becomes a frog.

topics.title: The Life Cycle of a Chicken
topics.short: A chick grows inside an egg, hatches, grows feathers as a young chicken, and becomes a grown hen or rooster.

topics.title: Comparing Life Cycles
topics.short: Some young look like small adults and just grow (a chick, a kitten); others change shape completely as they grow (a butterfly, a frog).

topics.title: Our Five Senses
topics.short: We see with our eyes, hear with our ears, smell with our nose, taste with our tongue and feel with our skin.

topics.title: How Animals Use Their Senses
topics.short: An owl's big eyes see at night, a dog's nose follows smells, a bat hears echoes, and a cat's whiskers feel the way.

topics.title: Observing Like a Scientist
topics.short: Scientists use their senses and tools like a magnifying glass and a ruler to observe. An observation is what you notice; a guess is what you think might be true.

topics.title: Trees Through the Seasons
topics.short: Many trees grow new leaves in spring, are full and green in summer, turn colors and drop leaves in fall, and stand bare in winter. Evergreens keep their needles.

topics.title: Animals in Winter
topics.short: In winter some animals migrate to warmer places, some hibernate, and others stay active with thick fur and stored food.

topics.title: Getting Ready for Winter
topics.short: In fall, squirrels store nuts, birds gather to fly south, and many animals grow thicker coats or eat extra food.

topics.title: Caring for a Pet
topics.short: A pet needs food, fresh water, a clean home, exercise, gentle hands and visits to the vet.

topics.title: Caring for a Plant
topics.short: A potted plant needs the right amount of water (not too much), light, a pot with holes for drainage, and room to grow.

topics.title: Caring for Nature
topics.short: Watch wild animals without touching or chasing them, leave nests alone, put rocks back the way you found them, and keep trash out of nature.

topics.title: The Characteristics of Life
topics.short: Living things are made of cells, use energy, grow and develop, respond to their surroundings, keep their insides steady, and produce offspring.

topics.title: Fair Tests: Variables and Controls
topics.short: In a fair test you change one thing (the independent variable), measure one thing (the dependent variable), and keep everything else the same, with a control group to compare against.

topics.title: Using a Microscope
topics.short: A light microscope magnifies with two lenses: total magnification is the eyepiece power times the objective power, so 10× and 40× give 400×.

topics.title: Measuring with a Microscope
topics.short: Estimate a cell's size by how many fit across the field of view, and use micrometers: 1 millimeter = 1,000 micrometers (µm).

topics.title: The Cell Theory
topics.short: All living things are made of one or more cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and every cell comes from a cell that already existed.

topics.title: One Cell or Many
topics.short: Unicellular organisms, like bacteria and amoebas, live as a single cell that does every job. Multicellular organisms, like trees and people, are built of many specialized cells.

topics.title: Membrane, Cytoplasm and Nucleus
topics.short: Every cell has a cell membrane that controls what enters and leaves and cytoplasm inside. Cells of plants, animals and fungi also keep their DNA in a nucleus.

topics.title: Organelles and Their Jobs
topics.short: Mitochondria release energy from food, ribosomes build proteins, the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus make and ship materials, and vacuoles and lysosomes store and break things down.

topics.title: Plant Cells and Animal Cells
topics.short: Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole; animal cells have none of these. Both have a membrane, a nucleus and mitochondria.

topics.title: Why Cells Are Small
topics.short: As a cell grows, its volume grows faster than its surface, so a big cell could not move food in and wastes out fast enough. Small cells have more surface for their size.

topics.title: Diffusion and Osmosis
topics.short: Particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are less crowded (diffusion). Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane, toward the side with more dissolved material.

topics.title: Cells, Tissues, Organs and Systems
topics.short: Similar cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs work together in organ systems, and systems make up an organism.

topics.title: From Domain to Species
topics.short: Scientists group living things in ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Each rank holds fewer kinds of organisms that share more traits.

topics.title: Scientific Names
topics.short: Every species has a two-part scientific name, genus then species, like Canis lupus for the gray wolf. The genus starts with a capital, and the whole name is written in italics.

topics.title: Dichotomous Keys
topics.short: A dichotomous key identifies an organism by a series of either-or choices about traits you can observe, leading step by step to its name.

topics.title: Three Domains and the Kingdoms
topics.short: Life is grouped into three domains, Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Eukarya includes protists, fungi, plants and animals.

topics.title: Bacteria
topics.short: Bacteria are single cells with no nucleus. They live almost everywhere, and most are harmless or helpful: they break down dead matter, make yogurt and live in our gut.

topics.title: How Bacteria Multiply
topics.short: A bacterium splits into two, then those two split, and so on. With food and warmth the number doubles each generation: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

topics.title: Viruses
topics.short: A virus is genetic material in a protein coat. It is not a cell; it can make copies of itself only inside a living host cell.

topics.title: Protists
topics.short: Protists are mostly single-celled organisms with a nucleus: animal-like amoebas and paramecia, plant-like algae that photosynthesize, and fungus-like water molds.

topics.title: Fungi
topics.short: Fungi, including yeasts, molds and mushrooms, absorb food from what they grow on. Many are decomposers, and yeast makes bread rise.

topics.title: Helpful and Harmful Microbes
topics.short: Microbes make foods like cheese and bread, recycle nutrients and live in our bodies; a few cause disease. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, and washing hands with soap removes many germs.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.short: In chloroplasts, plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, giving off oxygen. The sugar stores the energy and builds the plant's body.

topics.title: Cellular Respiration
topics.short: Cells release the energy in sugar by combining it with oxygen, giving off carbon dioxide and water. Every living cell does it, plants included, day and night.

topics.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration Together
topics.short: The outputs of photosynthesis (sugar and oxygen) are the inputs of respiration, and the outputs of respiration (carbon dioxide and water) are the inputs of photosynthesis.

topics.title: How Water and Food Move in a Plant
topics.short: Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots; phloem carries sugar from the leaves to where it is used or stored. Water evaporates from leaves through tiny pores called stomata.

topics.title: How Plants Respond
topics.short: Plants grow toward light (phototropism), roots grow down with gravity (gravitropism), and vines curl around what they touch (thigmotropism).

topics.title: Mosses, Ferns, Conifers and Flowering Plants
topics.short: Mosses have no tubes for water and stay small; ferns have tubes but no seeds; conifers make seeds in cones; flowering plants make seeds inside fruits.

topics.title: Flowers, Pollination and Seeds
topics.short: A flower's stamens make pollen. Pollination carries pollen to the pistil, and then a seed forms; the part around the seeds grows into the fruit. Animals and wind help.

topics.title: What Affects How a Plant Grows
topics.short: A plant's growth depends on its genes and its surroundings: light, water, nutrients, temperature and space. The same seeds grow differently in different conditions.

topics.title: Animals With and Without Backbones
topics.short: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not. More than nine in ten known animal species are invertebrates.

topics.title: Invertebrate Groups
topics.short: Sponges, cnidarians (jellyfish), worms, mollusks (snails, octopuses), arthropods (insects, spiders, crabs) and echinoderms (sea stars) are the major invertebrate groups.

topics.title: Vertebrate Groups
topics.short: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals differ in coverings, how they breathe, and whether they keep a steady body temperature.

topics.title: Body Adaptations
topics.short: Adaptations are inherited traits that help an organism survive where it lives, such as a duck's webbed feet, a hawk's hooked beak, or camouflage.

topics.title: Behavior: Instinct and Learning
topics.short: Some behaviors are instincts, done right the first time without learning, like a spider spinning a web. Others are learned, like a crow learning which trash cans hold food.

topics.title: Endotherms and Ectotherms
topics.short: Birds and mammals are endotherms: they make heat inside and keep a fairly steady body temperature. Fish, amphibians and reptiles are ectotherms: their temperature follows their surroundings.

topics.title: Living and Nonliving Parts
topics.short: An ecosystem is the living (biotic) parts, like plants, animals and microbes, together with the nonliving (abiotic) parts, like sunlight, water, soil, air and temperature.

topics.title: Organisms, Populations and Communities
topics.short: An organism is one living thing; a population is all of one species in an area; a community is all the populations together; an ecosystem adds the nonliving parts.

topics.title: Producers, Consumers and Decomposers
topics.short: Producers make their own food from sunlight; consumers eat other organisms; decomposers break down dead matter and wastes and return nutrients to the soil.

topics.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
topics.short: A food web is many food chains linked together. Arrows point from the food to the eater, the direction energy and matter move.

topics.title: When One Population Changes
topics.short: If one population in a food web grows or shrinks, others change too: lose the foxes, and rabbits may boom and then overeat the grass.

topics.title: Energy Pyramids
topics.short: Only about 10% of the energy at one level of a food chain is stored in the next level; the rest is used for living and lost as heat. That is why there are fewer top predators.

topics.title: Competition, Predation and Symbiosis
topics.short: Species compete for the same resources, predators eat prey, and in symbiosis two species live closely: both benefit (mutualism), one benefits without harm (commensalism), or one benefits at the other's cost (parasitism).

topics.title: The Carbon Cycle
topics.short: Carbon moves from the air into plants by photosynthesis, into animals by eating, and back to the air by respiration, decomposition and burning.

topics.title: The Nitrogen Cycle
topics.short: Air is mostly nitrogen, but plants cannot use it directly. Bacteria in soil and in root nodules turn it into forms plants can absorb; decomposers and other bacteria return it to the soil and air.

topics.title: Biomes
topics.short: Biomes are large regions with a similar climate and similar kinds of life: tropical rainforest, desert, grassland, deciduous forest, taiga and tundra.

topics.title: Ecological Succession
topics.short: After a disturbance, communities change in a series of stages. Primary succession starts on bare rock with no soil; secondary succession starts where soil remains, as after a fire.

topics.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
topics.short: Biodiversity is the variety of life. Healthy ecosystems provide clean water, fertile soil, pollination and food, and more diverse ecosystems often recover better after disturbances.

topics.title: People and Ecosystems
topics.short: Habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and overharvesting can harm ecosystems, and solutions such as protected areas, cleanup and careful harvesting are weighed by what they cost and what they protect.

topics.title: How Populations Grow
topics.short: A population grows when more individuals are added (by birth or arrival) than are lost (by death or leaving). With plenty of resources it can grow faster and faster.

topics.title: Limiting Factors and Carrying Capacity
topics.short: Food, water, space, shelter, disease and predators limit a population. The largest population an environment can support over time is its carrying capacity.

topics.title: Predators and Prey
topics.short: When prey are plentiful, predators thrive and increase; then prey fall, and predators follow with a lag. The two populations rise and fall in turns.

topics.title: Counting a Population
topics.short: Ecologists estimate a population by counting in a few sample squares (quadrats) and scaling up: average count per square × number of squares in the whole area.

topics.title: Bones and the Skeleton
topics.short: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs (the skull guards the brain), works with muscles to move, and makes blood cells in the bone marrow. An adult has 206 bones.

topics.title: Muscles
topics.short: Skeletal muscles move bones, smooth muscle moves food and blood through organs, and cardiac muscle pumps the heart. Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs.

topics.title: Digestion
topics.short: Food travels from the mouth through the esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. Teeth and stomach break it up; enzymes break it into small molecules the small intestine absorbs.

topics.title: The Heart and Blood
topics.short: The heart pumps blood through arteries (away from the heart), capillaries (where exchange happens) and veins (back to the heart). Blood carries oxygen, nutrients and wastes.

topics.title: Breathing and Gas Exchange
topics.short: The diaphragm pulls air into the lungs. In tiny air sacs (alveoli), oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out.

topics.title: Nerves, Senses and the Brain
topics.short: Sense organs detect stimuli, nerves carry signals to the brain and spinal cord, and the brain sends signals out to muscles. A reflex is a fast response routed through the spinal cord.

topics.title: The Body's Defenses
topics.short: Skin and mucus keep most germs out. White blood cells attack germs that get in, and some remember a germ so the body can respond faster the next time.

topics.title: Removing Wastes
topics.short: The kidneys filter wastes from the blood and make urine, the lungs remove carbon dioxide, and the skin releases some water and salt in sweat.

topics.title: Systems Working Together
topics.short: During exercise, muscles need more oxygen and sugar, so breathing and heart rate rise, and the body sweats to shed heat. No system works alone.

topics.title: Inherited and Acquired Traits
topics.short: Inherited traits, like eye color, are passed from parents through genes. Acquired traits, like a scar, a skill or a language, come from experience and are not passed on.

topics.title: DNA, Genes and Chromosomes
topics.short: DNA carries the instructions for building an organism. A gene is a section of DNA with the instructions for one protein, and DNA is packed into chromosomes in the nucleus.

topics.title: Genes Make Proteins, Proteins Make Traits
topics.short: A gene is a recipe for a protein, and proteins do the work of the cell: some make pigment, some build structures, some speed up reactions. That is how genes shape traits.

topics.title: One Parent or Two: Copies and Mixes
topics.short: Offspring of one parent, like a bacterium that splits, a yeast that buds or a plant grown from a cutting, get an exact copy of its genes. Offspring of two parents get half their genes from each, so they vary.

topics.title: Alleles: Dominant and Recessive
topics.short: Each gene comes in versions called alleles. You have two alleles for each gene, one from each parent. A dominant allele shows its trait even with one copy; a recessive one shows only with two copies.

topics.title: Genotype and Phenotype
topics.short: Your genotype is your pair of alleles (TT, Tt or tt); your phenotype is the trait that shows (tall or short). Two alleles alike is homozygous; two different is heterozygous.

topics.title: Punnett Squares
topics.short: A Punnett square shows every way the parents' alleles can combine. Put one parent's alleles across the top and the other's down the side, then fill each box.

topics.title: Chances from a Punnett Square
topics.short: Each box of a Punnett square is an equally likely outcome, so a box count gives a probability: 1 of 4 boxes is a 25% chance for each offspring.

topics.title: Mutations
topics.short: A mutation is a change in DNA. It can be harmful, helpful or neutral, depending on how it changes a protein and on the environment.

topics.title: Selective Breeding and Genetic Engineering
topics.short: People choose which plants and animals have offspring to shape traits over generations (selective breeding), and can move a gene into another organism (genetic engineering), as when bacteria make insulin.

topics.title: The Fossil Record
topics.short: Fossils in rock layers, oldest at the bottom, show that life has changed over Earth's history: many species have gone extinct, and simpler forms appear before more complex ones.

topics.title: Comparing Body Structures
topics.short: Homologous structures, like the arm of a person, the flipper of a whale and the wing of a bat, have the same bones arranged in the same way, a sign of a shared ancestor.

topics.title: Natural Selection
topics.short: Individuals vary; some variations are inherited; more young are born than can survive; those with helpful traits survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common.

topics.title: Changes in Populations Over Time
topics.short: Data show natural selection at work: the dark form of the peppered moth rose and then fell as soot came and went, and bacteria exposed to antibiotics become resistant.

topics.title: Kinds of Constitutional Argument
topics.short: Constitutional arguments draw on text, history (original understanding), structure (relations among institutions), precedent (doctrine), consequences (prudence) and national values (ethos); Philip Bobbitt called these the modalities of constitutional argument.

topics.title: Originalism
topics.short: Originalists hold that the Constitution's meaning was fixed when each provision was adopted, today usually as its original public meaning; advocates say this keeps judges bound by law rather than preference and leaves change to the amendment process.

topics.title: Living Constitutionalism
topics.short: Living constitutionalists hold that the Constitution's broad principles are applied to new conditions over time, often through precedent built case by case; advocates say this is how the common law and the Constitution have in fact developed and keeps it workable.

topics.title: Precedent in Constitutional Cases
topics.short: Stare decisis is weaker in constitutional cases because only an amendment or the Court can correct an error; the Court weighs the quality of the reasoning, workability, consistency with related decisions, changed facts and reliance before overruling.

topics.title: Marbury v. Madison
topics.short: In Marbury v. Madison (1803) Chief Justice Marshall held that Marbury had a right to his commission and a legal remedy, but that the Court could not issue a writ of mandamus in its original jurisdiction because that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional; courts must not enforce laws contrary to the Constitution.

topics.title: Review of State Courts and Judicial Supremacy
topics.short: Martin v. Hunter's Lessee (1816) upheld Supreme Court review of state court rulings on federal law; Cooper v. Aaron (1958), unanimous, held that state officials are bound by the Court's interpretation of the Constitution in Brown.

topics.title: Congress and the Courts' Jurisdiction
topics.short: Article III lets Congress make "Exceptions" to the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction and create (or not create) lower courts; in Ex parte McCardle (1869) the Court accepted Congress's repeal of its jurisdiction over a pending appeal; how far this power goes is debated.

topics.title: Standing in Constitutional Cases
topics.short: Standing applies to constitutional claims too: taxpayers generally lack standing to challenge federal spending (Frothingham, 1923), with a narrow Establishment Clause exception (Flast v. Cohen, 1968) that Hein (2007) limited to congressional appropriations.

topics.title: The Political Question Doctrine
topics.short: Baker v. Carr (1962) held malapportionment claims justiciable and listed six markers of a political question; Nixon v. United States (1993) left Senate impeachment trial procedures to the Senate; Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) held partisan gerrymandering claims beyond federal courts.

topics.title: A Government of Enumerated Powers
topics.short: Congress has only the powers the Constitution grants; most are in Article I, Section 8, and others in amendments' enforcement clauses; the Tenth Amendment confirms that other powers are reserved to the states or the people, and there is no general federal police power.

topics.title: McCulloch v. Maryland
topics.short: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) the Court unanimously upheld the Second Bank of the United States as a means "plainly adapted" to Congress's enumerated ends and held that Maryland could not tax it, since "the power to tax involves the power to destroy."

topics.title: Necessary and Proper Today
topics.short: United States v. Comstock (2010) upheld civil commitment of dangerous federal prisoners as a rational means connected to enumerated powers; in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) Chief Justice Roberts wrote that the individual mandate was not a "proper" means under the clause.

topics.title: Gibbons v. Ogden
topics.short: In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) Marshall read "commerce" to include navigation and all commercial intercourse, and "among the several States" to reach commerce that concerns more states than one, so a federal coasting license overrode New York's steamboat monopoly.

topics.title: The Narrow Era (1887 to 1936)
topics.short: The Court separated manufacturing from commerce (United States v. E. C. Knight, 1895), struck down a federal ban on goods made by child labor (Hammer v. Dagenhart, 1918) and struck down New Deal codes and coal regulation (Schechter Poultry, 1935; Carter Coal, 1936), using a direct-indirect effects test.

topics.title: The Turn of 1937
topics.short: NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel (1937) upheld the Wagner Act's reach to a steel company whose labor disputes affected interstate commerce; United States v. Darby (1941) upheld federal wage and hour rules and overruled Hammer v. Dagenhart.

topics.title: Wickard v. Filburn
topics.short: In Wickard v. Filburn (1942) the Court upheld limits on wheat a farmer grew for use on his own farm, because the total (aggregate) effect of many farmers doing the same would substantially affect interstate commerce.

topics.title: The Commerce Power and Civil Rights
topics.short: Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States and Katzenbach v. McClung (both 1964) upheld the Civil Rights Act of 1964's ban on discrimination in public accommodations as regulation of interstate commerce, through interstate travelers and food shipped across state lines.

topics.title: United States v. Lopez
topics.short: In United States v. Lopez (1995), 5 to 4, the Court struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act and named three categories Congress may regulate: the channels of interstate commerce, its instrumentalities and persons or things in it, and activities that substantially affect it; possessing a gun near a school was not economic activity.

topics.title: United States v. Morrison
topics.short: In United States v. Morrison (2000), 5 to 4, the Court struck down the civil remedy in the Violence Against Women Act, holding that gender-motivated violence is not economic activity and that its effects could not be aggregated, and that Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment does not reach private conduct.

topics.title: Gonzales v. Raich
topics.short: In Gonzales v. Raich (2005), 6 to 3, the Court upheld applying the federal Controlled Substances Act to marijuana grown at home for medical use under California law, relying on Wickard because the activity was part of a broader economic market Congress could regulate.

topics.title: NFIB v. Sebelius: Commerce
topics.short: In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) five justices concluded the Commerce Clause did not support the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate, because it compelled people to enter commerce rather than regulating existing activity; the mandate was upheld as a tax.

topics.title: The Taxing Power
topics.short: Congress may tax to raise revenue even if the tax also discourages conduct, but a "tax" that is really a penalty may fail (Bailey v. Drexel Furniture, 1922); NFIB (2012) upheld the mandate's payment as a tax because it was modest, not tied to willfulness and collected by the IRS.

topics.title: The Spending Power
topics.short: Congress may spend for the general welfare, a power not limited to the other enumerated subjects (United States v. Butler, 1936, adopting Hamilton's view over Madison's); Helvering v. Davis (1937) upheld Social Security's old-age benefits.

topics.title: Conditions on Federal Money
topics.short: South Dakota v. Dole (1987) upheld withholding 5 percent of highway funds from states with a drinking age under 21, requiring conditions to be for the general welfare, unambiguous, related to the program and not otherwise unconstitutional, and not coercive; NFIB (2012) held the Medicaid expansion's threat to all existing Medicaid funds coercive.

topics.title: Anti-Commandeering
topics.short: Congress may not compel state legislatures to enact federal programs (New York v. United States, 1992) or order state officers to carry them out (Printz v. United States, 1997), and may not order states to keep their own laws on the books (Murphy v. NCAA, 2018).

topics.title: The Tenth Amendment as a Limit
topics.short: National League of Cities v. Usery (1976) barred federal wage rules for state employees in "traditional governmental functions"; Garcia v. San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority (1985) overruled it, leaving states' protection mostly to the political process.

topics.title: State Sovereign Immunity
topics.short: Chisholm v. Georgia (1793) let a citizen of another state sue Georgia, and the Eleventh Amendment (1795) reversed it; Hans v. Louisiana (1890) barred suits by a state's own citizens; Seminole Tribe (1996) held Congress cannot abrogate immunity under Article I; Ex parte Young (1908) allows suits against state officers for injunctions.

topics.title: Enforcing the Civil War Amendments
topics.short: Congress may enforce the Fourteenth Amendment by "appropriate legislation"; City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) requires "congruence and proportionality" between the injury and the remedy; Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the Voting Rights Act's coverage formula as based on old data.

topics.title: Preemption
topics.short: Valid federal law preempts state law expressly (by its terms) or impliedly, when federal law occupies a field or conflicts with state law (it is impossible to obey both, or state law obstructs federal purposes); there is a presumption against preempting traditional state powers.

topics.title: Discrimination Against Interstate Commerce
topics.short: The Court reads the Commerce Clause to limit states even when Congress is silent: a state law that discriminates against out-of-state commerce is virtually per se invalid unless no other means can serve a legitimate local purpose (City of Philadelphia v. New Jersey, 1978; Maine v. Taylor, 1986).

topics.title: Pike Balancing
topics.short: A nondiscriminatory state law is upheld unless the burden on interstate commerce is "clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits" (Pike v. Bruce Church, 1970); Kassel v. Consolidated Freightways (1981) struck down Iowa's ban on long double-trailer trucks because its slight safety gain did not justify a heavy burden.

topics.title: The Market Participant Exception
topics.short: When a state acts as a buyer or seller rather than a regulator, it may prefer its own residents (Reeves, Inc. v. Stake, 1980); United Haulers (2007) also upheld laws favoring a public waste facility over private ones.

topics.title: Privileges and Immunities of Article IV
topics.short: Article IV's Privileges and Immunities Clause bars states from discriminating against citizens of other states in fundamental matters such as earning a living, unless there is a substantial reason and a close relation to it (Toomer v. Witsell, 1948; Supreme Court of New Hampshire v. Piper, 1985).

topics.title: Youngstown and the Three Zones
topics.short: In Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952), 6 to 3, the Court held that President Truman lacked power to seize the steel mills; Justice Jackson's concurrence set out three zones: presidential power is greatest with Congress's authorization, uncertain in a "zone of twilight" when Congress is silent, and "at its lowest ebb" against Congress's will.

topics.title: Nondelegation and Major Questions
topics.short: Congress may delegate authority to agencies if it lays down an "intelligible principle" (J. W. Hampton, 1928); the Court has struck down delegations to the government only twice (both in 1935); under the major questions doctrine (rooted in FDA v. Brown & Williamson, 2000) agencies need clear authorization for decisions of vast economic and political significance.

topics.title: Bicameralism, Presentment and the Line-Item Veto
topics.short: INS v. Chadha (1983) struck down the one-house legislative veto because lawmaking requires passage by both houses and presentment to the President; Clinton v. City of New York (1998) struck down the Line Item Veto Act for letting the President cancel parts of signed laws.

topics.title: Appointments
topics.short: Principal officers are appointed by the President with Senate consent; Congress may vest the appointment of inferior officers in the President, courts or department heads (Edmond, 1997; Lucia v. SEC, 2018); recess appointments require a recess of at least ten days, presumptively (NLRB v. Noel Canning, 2014).

topics.title: The Removal Power
topics.short: Myers (1926) upheld the President's power to remove executive officers; Humphrey's Executor (1935) allowed limits for multi-member commissions; Morrison v. Olson (1988) upheld the independent counsel; and Seila Law (2020) struck down limits for a single agency director; the Court overruled Humphrey's Executor in 2026.

topics.title: Foreign Affairs
topics.short: United States v. Curtiss-Wright (1936) described broad presidential power in foreign affairs; Dames & Moore v. Regan (1981) upheld executive agreements settling the Iran hostage claims; Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015) held the power to recognize foreign governments belongs to the President alone.

topics.title: War Powers and Detention
topics.short: The Prize Cases (1863) upheld Lincoln's blockade before Congress acted; after 2001, Hamdi v. Rumsfeld (2004) required due process for a citizen held as an enemy combatant, Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006) held military commissions unauthorized, and Boumediene v. Bush (2008) extended habeas corpus to detainees at Guantanamo Bay.

topics.title: Executive Privilege and Presidential Immunity
topics.short: United States v. Nixon (1974) recognized a qualified executive privilege that yields to a criminal trial's need for evidence; Nixon v. Fitzgerald (1982) gave absolute civil immunity for official acts; and Clinton v. Jones (1997) allowed a civil suit about unofficial acts.

topics.title: Rational Basis Review
topics.short: Most laws get rational basis review: a law is upheld if it is rationally related to a legitimate government interest, and the challenger must negate every conceivable basis (Williamson v. Lee Optical, 1955); Carolene Products (1938) and its footnote four suggested closer review for some laws.

topics.title: Intermediate and Strict Scrutiny
topics.short: Intermediate scrutiny requires an important government interest and means substantially related to it; strict scrutiny requires a compelling interest and means narrowly tailored (often, the least restrictive means), with the burden on the government.

topics.title: Choosing the Tier
topics.short: The tier depends on what the law classifies or burdens: race, national origin and fundamental rights trigger strict scrutiny; sex and legitimacy intermediate; most economic and social laws rational basis; some areas use other tests instead, such as the Mathews balance for procedural due process.

topics.title: The Bill of Rights and the States
topics.short: In Barron v. Baltimore (1833) Chief Justice Marshall held that the Bill of Rights limited only the federal government, so Baltimore owed no just compensation under the Fifth Amendment for ruining a wharf.

topics.title: The Slaughter-House Cases
topics.short: In the Slaughter-House Cases (1873), 5 to 4, the Court read the Fourteenth Amendment's Privileges or Immunities Clause narrowly, covering only rights of national citizenship, which left that clause largely unused (Saenz v. Roe, 1999, is a rare exception).

topics.title: Selective Incorporation
topics.short: Through the Due Process Clause the Court has applied most Bill of Rights guarantees to the states, asking whether a right is fundamental to "our scheme of ordered liberty" and "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition" (Duncan v. Louisiana, 1968; McDonald v. Chicago, 2010; Timbs v. Indiana, 2019; Ramos v. Louisiana, 2020).

topics.title: State Action
topics.short: The Fourteenth Amendment limits states, not private persons (the Civil Rights Cases, 1883); private conduct counts as state action when it performs a traditional public function (Marsh v. Alabama, 1946), when courts enforce it (Shelley v. Kraemer, 1948) or when the state is entangled with it (Burton v. Wilmington Parking Authority, 1961).

topics.title: Procedural Due Process
topics.short: When government deprives a person of a protected life, liberty or property interest (Board of Regents v. Roth, 1972), it must give fair procedure; Goldberg v. Kelly (1970) required a hearing before welfare benefits end, and Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) weighs the private interest, the risk of error and the government's interest.

topics.title: The Lochner Era
topics.short: In Lochner v. New York (1905), 5 to 4, the Court struck down a maximum-hours law for bakers as violating liberty of contract; Justice Holmes's dissent said the Constitution "does not enact Mr. Herbert Spencer's Social Statics"; the Court upheld some laws (Muller v. Oregon, 1908) and struck down others (Adkins, 1923).

topics.title: The End of Economic Due Process
topics.short: Nebbia v. New York (1934) and West Coast Hotel v. Parrish (1937), which overruled Adkins, ended close review of economic regulation; since then such laws get rational basis review.

topics.title: Finding Unenumerated Rights: Two Methods
topics.short: Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) asks for a "careful description" of the asserted right and whether it is deeply rooted in the Nation's history and tradition; another approach, from Justice Harlan's dissent in Poe v. Ullman (1961) and used in Obergefell (2015), treats tradition as a living one and reasons from principle.

topics.title: Family and Personal Autonomy
topics.short: The Court has protected parents' rights to direct their children's upbringing (Meyer v. Nebraska, 1923; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 1925; Troxel v. Granville, 2000), extended family living together (Moore v. East Cleveland, 1977) and married couples' use of contraceptives (Griswold v. Connecticut, 1965).

topics.title: The Abortion Cases: Legal History
topics.short: Roe v. Wade (1973) held that due process protects a right to choose abortion, with a trimester framework; Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992) kept Roe's central holding and adopted an "undue burden" test; the Court overruled both in 2022.

topics.title: Liberty, Marriage and the Right to Refuse Treatment
topics.short: Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down bans on interracial marriage; Lawrence v. Texas (2003) struck down a state law criminalizing private conduct between consenting adults of the same sex, overruling Bowers v. Hardwick (1986); Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) held same-sex couples may marry; Cruzan (1990) and Glucksberg (1997) addressed refusing medical treatment and assisted suicide.

topics.title: The Equal Protection Framework
topics.short: Equal protection analysis asks what classification a law makes and then applies the matching tier; the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause imposes the same requirement on the federal government (Bolling v. Sharpe, 1954).

topics.title: Rational Basis in Equal Protection
topics.short: Most classifications get rational basis review and are upheld (Railway Express Agency v. New York, 1949); a few laws have failed it when they rested on animus or irrational prejudice (City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 1985; Romer v. Evans, 1996).

topics.title: Race and Strict Scrutiny
topics.short: Racial classifications get strict scrutiny: Strauder v. West Virginia (1880) struck down excluding Black men from juries; Korematsu (1944) upheld the wartime exclusion order and has since been repudiated; Loving (1967) struck down interracial marriage bans.

topics.title: From Plessy to Brown
topics.short: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld "separate but equal"; the NAACP's cases (Missouri ex rel. Gaines, 1938; Sweatt v. Painter, 1950) found separate graduate schools unequal; Brown v. Board of Education (1954), unanimous, held separate schools "inherently unequal," and Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed."

topics.title: Discriminatory Purpose and Effect
topics.short: A law neutral on its face violates equal protection only if adopted with discriminatory purpose (Washington v. Davis, 1976; Arlington Heights, 1977, listing evidence of purpose); a disparate impact alone is not enough, though some statutes reach impact; Yick Wo v. Hopkins (1886) struck down discriminatory enforcement.

topics.title: Race-Conscious Admissions and Programs
topics.short: Regents v. Bakke (1978) barred quotas but allowed race as one factor; Croson (1989) and Adarand (1995) applied strict scrutiny to all racial classifications, including remedial ones; Grutter v. Bollinger (2003) upheld a holistic program and Gratz v. Bollinger (2003) struck down automatic points; the Court rejected race-conscious admissions programs in 2023.

topics.title: Sex Discrimination
topics.short: Reed v. Reed (1971) struck down a preference for men as estate administrators; Frontiero (1973) drew a plurality for strict scrutiny; Craig v. Boren (1976) set intermediate scrutiny; United States v. Virginia (1996) required an "exceedingly persuasive justification" to exclude women from VMI.

topics.title: Other Classifications
topics.short: State laws discriminating against lawfully present noncitizens usually get strict scrutiny (Graham v. Richardson, 1971); classifications by legitimacy get intermediate scrutiny; age (Massachusetts Board of Retirement v. Murgia, 1976), wealth (San Antonio v. Rodriguez, 1973) and disability (Cleburne) get rational basis.

topics.title: Fundamental Rights and Equal Protection
topics.short: Laws burdening fundamental rights unequally get strict scrutiny: Reynolds v. Sims (1964) required "one person, one vote" for state legislatures; Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966) struck down poll taxes in state elections; Shapiro v. Thompson (1969) and Saenz v. Roe (1999) protected the right to travel; Bush v. Gore (2000) ended the Florida recount.

topics.title: From Clear and Present Danger
topics.short: Schenck v. United States (1919) upheld convictions for antidraft leaflets under a "clear and present danger" test; Holmes's dissent in Abrams (1919) and Brandeis's concurrence in Whitney (1927) argued for a narrower test; Dennis v. United States (1951) upheld Communist Party leaders' convictions.

topics.title: Brandenburg v. Ohio
topics.short: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that the government may not punish advocacy of force or lawbreaking unless it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it; it overruled Whitney.

topics.title: Content-Based and Content-Neutral Laws
topics.short: Laws that regulate speech because of its subject or message are content-based and get strict scrutiny (Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 2015); content-neutral laws get intermediate scrutiny; viewpoint discrimination is the most suspect of all.

topics.title: Categories of Unprotected Speech
topics.short: A few narrow categories get little or no protection: incitement, true threats (Virginia v. Black, 2003), fighting words (Chaplinsky, 1942), obscenity (Miller v. California, 1973), defamation and fraud; the Court has refused to add new categories (United States v. Stevens, 2010).

topics.title: Symbolic Speech
topics.short: Conduct meant to communicate can be speech: United States v. O'Brien (1968) upheld a ban on burning draft cards under a four-part test for content-neutral rules; Tinker (1969) protected armbands; Texas v. Johnson (1989) protected flag burning as political expression.

topics.title: New York Times v. Sullivan
topics.short: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for defamation must prove "actual malice" (knowing falsity or reckless disregard for the truth); Gertz v. Robert Welch (1974) let states set a lower standard for private figures.

topics.title: Prior Restraint
topics.short: Orders that stop speech before it happens bear a heavy presumption against validity: Near v. Minnesota (1931) struck down a law allowing newspapers to be shut down; New York Times Co. v. United States (1971), the Pentagon Papers case, refused to block publication.

topics.title: Public Forums
topics.short: Streets and parks are traditional public forums; government may open designated or limited forums; in nonpublic forums restrictions need only be reasonable and viewpoint-neutral (Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association, 1983).

topics.title: Time, Place and Manner
topics.short: In public forums, content-neutral rules on time, place and manner are valid if narrowly tailored to a significant government interest and leaving open ample alternative channels (Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 1989); they need not be the least restrictive means.

topics.title: Students, Public Employees and Government Speech
topics.short: Tinker (1969) protects student speech unless it would substantially disrupt school; Bethel (1986), Hazelwood (1988) and Morse (2007) define limits; public employees' speech as citizens on public concerns is protected (Pickering, 1968) but not speech made pursuant to official duties (Garcetti v. Ceballos, 2006).

topics.title: Campaign Finance and Speech
topics.short: Buckley v. Valeo (1976) upheld limits on contributions but struck down limits on independent expenditures; Citizens United v. FEC (2010), 5 to 4, held corporations and unions may spend independently on elections; disclosure rules have mostly been upheld.

topics.title: Compelled Speech and Association
topics.short: Government may not compel people to salute the flag (West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943, overruling Gobitis) or display a state motto (Wooley v. Maynard, 1977); NAACP v. Alabama (1958) protected the privacy of membership lists; Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian, and Bisexual Group of Boston (1995) and Boy Scouts of America v. Dale (2000) protected a parade's message and a group's expressive association.

topics.title: The Establishment Clause
topics.short: Everson v. Board of Education (1947) applied the Establishment Clause to the states, invoking Jefferson's "wall of separation," while upholding bus fare reimbursement for students at religious schools.

topics.title: Establishment Tests
topics.short: Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971) asked about secular purpose, primary effect and excessive entanglement; the Court also used endorsement and coercion tests (Lee v. Weisman, 1992) and, for legislative prayer and old monuments, history and tradition (Marsh v. Chambers, 1983); the Court said in 2022 that it no longer applies the Lemon test.

topics.title: Prayer in Public Schools
topics.short: Engel v. Vitale (1962) struck down a state-composed prayer; Abington v. Schempp (1963) struck down school-sponsored Bible reading; Lee v. Weisman (1992) and Santa Fe v. Doe (2000) struck down prayers at graduation and football games; private prayer by students is protected.

topics.title: Public Aid and Religious Schools
topics.short: Zelman v. Simmons-Harris (2002) upheld vouchers chosen by parents; Trinity Lutheran (2017) and Espinoza (2020) held that a state that funds private schools or programs may not exclude religious ones because they are religious.

topics.title: Free Exercise
topics.short: Sherbert v. Verner (1963) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) applied strict scrutiny to burdens on religion; Employment Division v. Smith (1990) held neutral, generally applicable laws need no exemption; Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah (1993) struck down laws that targeted a faith and were not generally applicable.

topics.title: RFRA
topics.short: Congress answered Smith with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993), restoring strict scrutiny for substantial burdens on religion; City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) held it invalid as applied to states, but it binds the federal government (Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, 2014).

topics.title: Heller and McDonald
topics.short: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), 5 to 4, held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms, struck down a handgun ban and said some longstanding regulations remain lawful; McDonald v. Chicago (2010) incorporated the right against the states.

topics.title: Limits on the Second Amendment Right
topics.short: Heller (2008) called longstanding prohibitions presumptively lawful (possession by felons and the mentally ill, carrying in sensitive places, conditions on commercial sale) and protected arms in common use, not dangerous and unusual ones; Caetano v. Massachusetts (2016) applied Heller to stun guns; since 2022 the Court has judged gun laws by the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation rather than by tiers of scrutiny.

topics.title: What Is a Search?
topics.short: Under Katz v. United States (1967) a search occurs when government intrudes on a reasonable expectation of privacy; United States v. Jones (2012) revived a trespass test for physical intrusions; Carpenter v. United States (2018) required a warrant for historical cell-site location records.

topics.title: Warrants and Their Exceptions
topics.short: Searches generally need a warrant based on probable cause, but there are exceptions: consent, plain view, search incident to arrest (Chimel, 1969), the automobile exception (Carroll, 1925), exigent circumstances, and brief stops and frisks on reasonable suspicion (Terry v. Ohio, 1968).

topics.title: The Exclusionary Rule
topics.short: Evidence from unconstitutional searches is generally excluded at trial: Weeks (1914) in federal court, Mapp v. Ohio (1961) in state courts; exceptions include good-faith reliance on a warrant (United States v. Leon, 1984), independent source and inevitable discovery.

topics.title: Miranda v. Arizona
topics.short: Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires police to warn a person in custody before interrogation of the right to remain silent and to a lawyer; Dickerson v. United States (2000) held Miranda is a constitutional rule Congress cannot overrule by statute.

topics.title: Self-Incrimination and Double Jeopardy
topics.short: No one may be compelled to be a witness against himself in a criminal case; double jeopardy bars a second prosecution for the same offense by the same sovereign after acquittal or conviction, though separate sovereigns (state and federal) may each prosecute (Gamble v. United States, 2019).

topics.title: The Right to Counsel
topics.short: Powell v. Alabama (1932) required counsel in a capital case; Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), overruling Betts v. Brady, required states to provide counsel to poor defendants charged with felonies; Strickland v. Washington (1984) set the test for ineffective assistance: deficient performance and prejudice.

topics.title: Juries and Confrontation
topics.short: Duncan v. Louisiana (1968) incorporated the jury trial right for serious crimes; Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) required unanimous juries in state felony trials; Batson v. Kentucky (1986) barred race-based jury strikes; Crawford v. Washington (2004) requires that testimonial statements be tested by cross-examination.

topics.title: The Eighth Amendment
topics.short: The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail and fines and cruel and unusual punishments: Furman v. Georgia (1972) halted death sentences under existing laws, Gregg v. Georgia (1976) upheld revised procedures, and the Court has barred the death penalty for people with intellectual disabilities (Atkins, 2002) and for those under 18 at the time of the crime (Roper, 2005); Timbs (2019) incorporated the Excessive Fines Clause.

topics.title: Takings
topics.short: The Fifth Amendment requires just compensation when property is taken for public use; Kelo v. City of New London (2005), 5 to 4, held economic development a public use; regulations can be takings if they go "too far": Penn Central (1978) balances factors, and Lucas (1992) treats a total loss of economic value as a taking.

topics.title: Voting Rights Law
topics.short: Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act bars voting practices that result in denying or abridging the vote on account of race; Thornburg v. Gingles (1986) set the preconditions for vote dilution claims; Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the preclearance coverage formula; Rucho (2019) left partisan gerrymandering claims to the political process and state courts.

topics.title: Why We Have Government
topics.short: Governments keep order, provide security and public goods, protect rights and settle disputes; the Preamble lists six purposes, from "a more perfect Union" to "the Blessings of Liberty."

topics.title: Forms of Government
topics.short: Governments differ by who rules: one person (monarchy, dictatorship), a few (oligarchy) or the people (democracy, direct or representative); a republic is governed by elected representatives, and authoritarian and totalitarian states allow no real opposition.

topics.title: Natural Rights and the Social Contract
topics.short: Hobbes argued people accept government to escape a "war of all against all"; Locke held that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property and may replace a government that violates them; Montesquieu urged separating powers.

topics.title: Models of Democracy
topics.short: Political scientists describe participatory democracy (broad participation by citizens), pluralist democracy (groups compete for influence) and elite democracy (a few well-informed leaders and groups decide); each can be seen in American institutions.

topics.title: Limited Government and the Rule of Law
topics.short: Under the rule of law, laws are public, apply equally to everyone, including officials, and are enforced by fair procedures; limited government means a constitution sets what officials may and may not do.

topics.title: English and Colonial Roots
topics.short: American government drew on Magna Carta (1215), the English Bill of Rights (1689), the Mayflower Compact (1620), colonial charters and assemblies, and the idea that the people's representatives must consent to taxes.

topics.title: The Ideas of the Declaration
topics.short: The Declaration of Independence (1776) states that people have unalienable rights, that governments get "their just powers from the consent of the governed," and that the people may alter or abolish a government that destroys those ends; its grievances accuse the King.

topics.title: The Articles of Confederation
topics.short: The Articles (1781 to 1789) left power with the states: Congress could not tax, regulate trade between states or enforce laws; there was no executive or national court; laws needed nine states and amendments all thirteen.

topics.title: The Convention and Its Compromises
topics.short: The 1787 Convention settled conflicts by compromise: the Great Compromise (a House by population, a Senate with two per state), the Three-Fifths Compromise, the slave trade clause (no ban before 1808) and the Electoral College.

topics.title: The Federalist and the Anti-Federalists
topics.short: In Federalist No. 10 Madison argued a large republic controls factions; in No. 51 that "ambition must be made to counteract ambition"; Brutus No. 1 warned that a large republic would be too distant from the people and that the national government's powers would swallow the states.

topics.title: Ratification and the Bill of Rights
topics.short: The Constitution took effect when nine states ratified (1788); several states ratified only with calls for amendments, and the First Congress proposed the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791.

topics.title: The Preamble
topics.short: The Preamble begins "We the People" and lists six goals: union, justice, domestic tranquility, the common defense, the general welfare and the blessings of liberty.

topics.title: Article I: The Legislative Branch
topics.short: Article I creates Congress, sets the House and Senate's makeup, lists its powers in Section 8 (taxing, borrowing, commerce, coining money, declaring war and more, ending with the Necessary and Proper Clause), and limits Congress and the states in Sections 9 and 10.

topics.title: Article II: The Executive Branch
topics.short: Article II vests "the executive Power" in a President, sets qualifications and the Electoral College, and names powers: commander in chief, treaties (with two-thirds of the Senate), appointments (with Senate consent), pardons and the duty to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed."

topics.title: Article III: The Judicial Branch
topics.short: Article III creates the Supreme Court, lets Congress create lower courts, gives judges tenure "during good Behaviour" and pay that cannot be cut, lists the kinds of cases federal courts hear, guarantees jury trials for crimes and defines treason.

topics.title: Articles IV to VII
topics.short: Article IV: full faith and credit, privileges and immunities, new states and a republican form of government; Article V: amendments; Article VI: the Supremacy Clause, oaths and no religious test for office; Article VII: ratification by nine states.

topics.title: Separation of Powers
topics.short: The Constitution gives lawmaking to Congress, carrying out the laws to the President and deciding cases to the courts, so no one branch holds all power.

topics.title: Checks and Balances
topics.short: Each branch can check the others: the veto and the override, Senate confirmation of judges, judicial review, impeachment, Congress's control of money, and the President's power to nominate judges.

topics.title: Amending the Constitution
topics.short: Amendments are proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention called by two-thirds of the states, never yet used) and ratified by three-fourths of the states (38 of 50), through legislatures or conventions; there are 27 amendments.

topics.title: Dividing Power: Federal, State and Shared
topics.short: Federalism divides power: the national government has enumerated (delegated) powers such as coining money and war; the Tenth Amendment reserves other powers to the states or the people; both share concurrent powers such as taxing and making courts.

topics.title: Supremacy and Necessary and Proper
topics.short: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) the Court held that the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose reasonable means, such as a national bank, and that under the Supremacy Clause a state may not tax a federal bank.

topics.title: The Commerce Power
topics.short: Congress may regulate commerce "among the several States"; the Court read the power broadly for decades (Gibbons v. Ogden, 1824; the New Deal cases) and then set limits in United States v. Lopez (1995), which struck down a federal ban on guns near schools.

topics.title: Grants and Mandates
topics.short: Washington shapes state policy with money: categorical grants (for specific purposes, with conditions), block grants (broad purposes, more state choice) and mandates (federal requirements, some unfunded); conditions on grants are a main tool, within limits the Court has set.

topics.title: Relations Among the States
topics.short: Article IV requires states to give full faith and credit to each other's public acts and court judgments, to give citizens of other states the same basic privileges and immunities, and to return people charged with crimes (extradition); states may also make compacts with Congress's consent.

topics.title: The House and the Senate
topics.short: The House has 435 members, elected every two years, at least 25 years old and seven years a citizen; the Senate has 100 members, two per state, six-year terms with a third elected every two years, at least 30 and nine years a citizen.

topics.title: Apportionment and Redistricting
topics.short: After each census the 435 House seats are divided among the states by population (every state gets at least one); states then draw districts, which must have nearly equal populations (Wesberry v. Sanders, 1964), after Baker v. Carr (1962) let courts hear such claims; drawing them for party or group advantage is called gerrymandering.

topics.title: The Powers of Congress
topics.short: Congress's enumerated powers include taxing, spending, borrowing, regulating commerce, coining money, declaring war and raising armies; each house has its own powers: the House starts revenue bills and impeaches, the Senate tries impeachments, confirms appointments and approves treaties.

topics.title: Leaders of Congress
topics.short: The Speaker of the House, chosen by the House, leads it; majority and minority leaders and whips organize each party; the Vice President is President of the Senate and votes only to break ties, with the President pro tempore presiding in his or her absence.

topics.title: Committees
topics.short: Most work happens in committees: standing (permanent, by subject), select or special (temporary), joint (both houses) and conference (to settle differences between House and Senate versions of a bill); committees hold hearings and mark up bills.

topics.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
topics.short: A bill is introduced, sent to committee, debated and passed by one chamber, then the other; differences are resolved; the President signs it, vetoes it (Congress may override by two-thirds of each house) or lets it become law without a signature after ten days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is in session.

topics.title: House Rules and the Senate Filibuster
topics.short: The House Rules Committee sets limits on debate and amendments; in the Senate debate is unlimited unless 60 senators vote for cloture, so a minority can block many bills by filibuster; budget reconciliation and nominations have special rules.

topics.title: The Budget and Oversight
topics.short: Congress controls spending: discretionary spending is set each year by appropriations, while mandatory spending (Social Security, Medicare, interest) runs under existing laws; Congress oversees agencies through hearings, investigations and funding; "pork barrel" and logrolling describe trading support for projects.

topics.title: How Members Represent
topics.short: Members may act as delegates (vote as constituents want), trustees (use their own judgment) or politicos (mix the two); divided government, partisanship and the pull of reelection shape their choices.

topics.title: Qualifications, Terms and Succession
topics.short: A President must be a natural-born citizen, at least 35 and a resident for 14 years; the Twenty-second Amendment limits a President to two elected terms; the Vice President comes first in the line of succession, then the Speaker and the President pro tempore; the Twenty-fifth Amendment covers disability.

topics.title: The President's Formal Powers
topics.short: The Constitution makes the President commander in chief and gives the powers to veto, to pardon, to make treaties and appoint officers with the Senate's consent, to receive ambassadors and to give Congress information on the State of the Union.

topics.title: Informal Powers and Tools
topics.short: Presidents also use powers not listed in the Constitution: executive orders, executive agreements with other countries, signing statements, the "bully pulpit" and party leadership.

topics.title: The Federal Bureaucracy
topics.short: The executive branch includes 15 Cabinet departments, independent agencies (such as NASA), independent regulatory commissions (such as the Federal Reserve Board, the SEC) and government corporations (such as the U.S. Postal Service); most employees are hired through a merit civil service.

topics.title: Holding the Bureaucracy Accountable
topics.short: Agencies write rules under authority Congress delegates; Congress checks them with hearings, budgets and new laws; the President appoints and directs leaders; courts review whether rules follow the law; iron triangles link agencies, committees and interest groups.

topics.title: Impeachment
