topics.short: The House may impeach (formally accuse) by majority vote for "Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors"; the Senate tries the case, and conviction takes two-thirds; Presidents Andrew Johnson (1868), Bill Clinton (1998) and Donald Trump (2019) were impeached and acquitted; Richard Nixon resigned (1974) before a House vote.

topics.title: War Powers
topics.short: Congress declares war and funds the military; the President commands it; Congress has declared war only eleven times in five wars, and the War Powers Resolution (1973) requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours and to end action within 60 days (plus 30) without its approval.

topics.title: The Federal Court System
topics.short: There are 94 district courts (trials), 13 courts of appeals (12 regional circuits plus the Federal Circuit) and the Supreme Court; federal courts hear cases about federal law and the Constitution, cases between states, and certain cases between citizens of different states.

topics.title: How the Supreme Court Decides
topics.short: Parties ask the Court to hear a case by a petition for certiorari; it takes a case when four justices agree (the rule of four); after briefs and oral argument the justices vote, and opinions are written for the majority, with concurring and dissenting opinions.

topics.title: Judicial Review and Marbury v. Madison
topics.short: In Marbury v. Madison (1803) the Court held that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional, establishing that federal courts may refuse to enforce laws that conflict with the Constitution.

topics.title: Choosing Federal Judges
topics.short: The President nominates federal judges and the Senate confirms them by majority vote; they serve "during good Behaviour" (for life, unless impeached and removed), which is meant to make them independent of politics.

topics.title: Ways of Reading the Constitution
topics.short: Judges differ in method: originalists read the text as understood when it was adopted; living constitutionalists read its principles in light of changing conditions; judicial restraint favors deferring to elected branches and precedent, while "activism" is a label critics use for decisions they think go too far.

topics.title: Checks on the Courts
topics.short: The other branches check the courts by appointing and confirming judges, passing new laws after a statutory ruling, proposing amendments, setting the courts' size and some of their jurisdiction, and by how they carry out rulings; the courts have no army or budget of their own.

topics.title: The Bill of Rights, One by One
topics.short: Match each of the first ten amendments to what it protects: the First (religion, speech, press, assembly, petition) to the Tenth (powers reserved to the states or the people).

topics.title: Incorporation: Rights Against the States
topics.short: At first the Bill of Rights limited only the national government (Barron v. Baltimore, 1833); through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause the Court has applied most of its protections to the states one by one, from Gitlow v. New York (1925) to McDonald v. Chicago (2010).

topics.title: Freedom of Religion
topics.short: The Establishment Clause bars government from establishing religion: Engel v. Vitale (1962) struck down a state-written prayer in public schools; the Free Exercise Clause protects religious practice: Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) let Amish families end formal schooling after eighth grade.

topics.title: Freedom of Speech
topics.short: Speech is broadly protected but not unlimited: Schenck v. United States (1919) used a "clear and present danger" test; Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected students' armbands; Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) protects advocacy unless it is aimed at and likely to produce imminent lawless action.

topics.title: Freedom of the Press
topics.short: In New York Times v. United States (1971) the Court refused to stop newspapers from publishing the Pentagon Papers, applying a heavy presumption against prior restraint; New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) requires public officials suing for libel to prove "actual malice."

topics.title: The Right to Keep and Bear Arms
topics.short: In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) the Court held the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense; McDonald v. Chicago (2010) applied it to the states; the Court has said the right has limits.

topics.title: Rights of the Accused
topics.short: The Fourth, Fifth, Sixth and Eighth Amendments protect people suspected or accused of crimes: Mapp v. Ohio (1961) applied the exclusionary rule to the states; Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) guaranteed a lawyer for poor defendants charged with felonies; Miranda v. Arizona (1966) required warnings before custodial questioning.

topics.title: Privacy and Unenumerated Rights
topics.short: The Ninth Amendment says listing some rights does not deny others; the Court has recognized rights not named in the text through the Due Process Clause, and it disagrees about how to identify them: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965) and Roe v. Wade (1973) recognized such rights, Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) asked whether a right is deeply rooted in history and tradition, and the Court overruled Roe in 2022.

topics.title: Equal Protection
topics.short: The Fourteenth Amendment forbids states to deny "the equal protection of the laws"; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) allowed "separate but equal," and Brown v. Board of Education (1954) held that separate schools are "inherently unequal."

topics.title: Civil Rights Laws
topics.short: Congress used its powers to ban discrimination: the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (public places, employment), the Voting Rights Act of 1965, Title IX of the Education Amendments (1972, sex discrimination in schools receiving federal funds) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990).

topics.title: Widening the Vote
topics.short: Amendments expanded voting: the Fifteenth (race, 1870), Seventeenth (direct election of senators, 1913), Nineteenth (sex, 1920), Twenty-third (D.C. electors, 1961), Twenty-fourth (no poll taxes in federal elections, 1964) and Twenty-sixth (age 18, 1971).

topics.title: Majority Rule and Minority Rights
topics.short: Democracy rests on majority rule and on protecting minority rights; courts, the Bill of Rights, federalism and supermajority rules protect minorities, and debates over affirmative action, voting districts and religious exemptions show how hard the balance can be.

topics.title: Becoming a Citizen
topics.short: People born in the U.S. (and most born abroad to citizen parents) are citizens; others may naturalize, generally after five years as a permanent resident (three if married to a citizen), at age 18 or older, by passing English and civics tests and taking the Oath of Allegiance.

topics.title: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizens
topics.short: Citizens have the right to vote, run for most offices and serve on juries; responsibilities include obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on a jury when called and, for men 18 to 25, registering with the Selective Service; civic habits such as staying informed are encouraged but not required.

topics.title: Voting and Turnout
topics.short: Citizens 18 and older may vote where they are registered; turnout is higher in presidential years than midterms and rises with age, education and interest; rules on registration, voting by mail and identification vary by state.

topics.title: How Political Views Form
topics.short: Family, school, faith, peers, media and events shape political views; Americans also hold broad shared values (liberty, equality, democracy, individualism, the rule of law) and differ in ideology: liberals, conservatives and libertarians, each describing itself in its own terms.

topics.title: Public Opinion and Polls
topics.short: Polls estimate public opinion from a random sample; a good sample is random and large enough, questions are worded neutrally, and every poll has a margin of error (about plus or minus 3 points for 1,000 people).

topics.title: Interest Groups and the Media
topics.short: Interest groups lobby officials, file lawsuits and support candidates through PACs; the media report, set agendas and frame issues; concerns include unequal access, bias claims from all sides and the spread of false information.

topics.title: Political Parties
topics.short: Parties recruit candidates, organize voters and run the government; the U.S. has a two-party system, encouraged by single-member districts with winner-take-all rules; third parties raise issues but rarely win.

topics.title: Primaries, Caucuses and Conventions
topics.short: Parties choose presidential nominees through state primaries and caucuses that award delegates; closed primaries admit only party members, open primaries any registered voter; delegates nominate at the national convention.

topics.title: The Electoral College
topics.short: Each state has electors equal to its House seats plus two senators, and D.C. has three (538 in all); a candidate needs 270; 48 states give all their electors to the statewide winner, while Maine and Nebraska also award electors by district; if no one has a majority, the House chooses, one vote per state delegation.

topics.title: Money in Campaigns
topics.short: Federal law limits and discloses contributions to candidates (FECA, 1971; BCRA, 2002); Buckley v. Valeo (1976) treated spending as protected speech; Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held the government may not limit independent spending by corporations and unions, which led to super PACs.

topics.title: Congressional Elections
topics.short: Most House members who seek reelection win, thanks to name recognition, fundraising and district lines (the incumbency advantage); the President's party usually loses seats in midterm elections.

topics.title: State Government
topics.short: Every state has its own constitution, a governor, a legislature (all bicameral except Nebraska's) and courts; states run elections, schools, most criminal law, licenses and roads.

topics.title: Local Government
topics.short: Counties, cities and towns, school districts and special districts (water, fire, transit) provide many services; cities may use a mayor-council or a council-manager form; local governments get their powers from their state.

topics.title: Initiative, Referendum and Recall
topics.short: Many states let voters propose laws or amendments by petition (the initiative), approve or reject laws (the referendum) and remove officials before their terms end (the recall); there is no national initiative or referendum.

topics.title: Tribal Nations
topics.short: There are 575 federally recognized tribes (as of 2026); they are sovereign nations with their own governments and courts, in a government-to-government relationship with the United States set by the Constitution, treaties and federal law.

topics.title: Citizenship Test: Government
topics.short: Practice questions like those on the naturalization civics test about principles of American democracy, the system of government, and rights and responsibilities.

topics.title: Citizenship Test: History and Symbols
topics.short: Practice questions like those on the naturalization civics test about colonial times and independence, the 1800s, recent American history, geography, symbols and holidays.

topics.title: History Detectives
topics.short: We learn about the past from sources: things people made and left behind, and words they wrote. Archaeologists dig them up; historians read and compare them.

topics.title: Counting the Years: BC and AD
topics.short: Years before the birth of Jesus are counted backward and marked BC; years after are counted forward and marked AD. There is no year 0: 1 BC is followed by AD 1.

topics.title: The First Farmers
topics.short: For most of the human story, people hunted animals and gathered wild plants. About 12,000 years ago, people in the Middle East began to plant seeds and tame animals, and villages grew.

topics.title: Mesopotamia: Cities, Writing and Laws
topics.short: Between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, the Sumerians built the first cities, invented writing on clay tablets (cuneiform) and used the wheel. King Hammurabi of Babylon wrote down a famous set of laws.

topics.title: Ancient Egypt: Gift of the Nile
topics.short: The Nile flooded each year and left rich soil, so Egypt could grow plenty of food. Pharaohs ruled for about 3,000 years; Egyptians built pyramids, wrote in hieroglyphs and made mummies.

topics.title: The Indus Valley and Ancient India
topics.short: Along the Indus River, people built planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro with straight streets and drains. Later, the emperor Ashoka ruled much of India and carved messages of kindness on stone pillars.

topics.title: Ancient China: Dynasties, the Great Wall and Silk
topics.short: China's history is counted in dynasties, ruling families. The Shang wrote on bones; Confucius taught about respect and good government; the first emperor joined walls together; the Han traded silk on the Silk Road and made paper.

topics.title: Athens and Sparta
topics.short: Ancient Greece was made of city-states. In Athens, citizens voted on laws themselves, the first democracy. Sparta trained its boys to be soldiers. Together they turned back the Persians.

topics.title: Greek Thinkers and Alexander the Great
topics.short: Socrates asked questions, Plato wrote them down, and Aristotle studied almost everything. Aristotle taught Alexander, who built a huge empire and spread Greek ideas as far as India.

topics.title: Rome: From a Village to a Republic
topics.short: Legend says Romulus founded Rome in 753 BC. In 509 BC the Romans sent away their king and made a republic, where elected leaders and a senate governed. Rome slowly took over Italy and the lands around the Mediterranean.

topics.title: The Roman Empire
topics.short: In 27 BC Augustus became the first Roman emperor. For about 200 years the empire was mostly at peace. Romans built roads, aqueducts and arches, and their language, Latin, lives on in many words we use.

topics.title: Judaism, Hinduism and Buddhism
topics.short: Three of the world's oldest faiths: Jews worship one God and follow the Torah; Hindus follow ancient teachings from India called the Vedas; Buddhists follow the teachings of the Buddha about ending suffering.

topics.title: The Beginning of Christianity
topics.short: Jesus of Nazareth taught in Judea about 2,000 years ago. Christians believe he is the Son of God, who died and rose again. His followers spread the faith around the Roman Empire, and in time it became the empire's main religion.

topics.title: Rome Falls in the West, Byzantium Lives On
topics.short: The Western Roman Empire ended in AD 476. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, lasted almost 1,000 years more as the Byzantine Empire, with its great church, the Hagia Sophia, and the laws of Justinian.

topics.title: The Rise of Islam and a Golden Age of Learning
topics.short: Muslims believe that God sent messages to Muhammad, beginning about AD 610, and that the Quran holds those messages. Islam spread quickly, and cities such as Baghdad and Córdoba became centers of science, medicine and books.

topics.title: Castles, Knights and Monasteries
topics.short: In medieval Europe, kings gave land to lords, who were protected by knights and fed by peasants who farmed the land. Monks in monasteries copied books by hand. Charlemagne, crowned emperor in AD 800, encouraged schools.

topics.title: The Vikings
topics.short: From Scandinavia, Viking sailors raided, traded and settled across Europe in fast longships. They settled Iceland and Greenland, and about AD 1000 Leif Erikson reached North America.

topics.title: Inventions of China and the Samurai of Japan
topics.short: Under the Tang and Song dynasties, China invented or improved printing, gunpowder, the magnetic compass and paper money. In Japan, an emperor reigned, while from 1192 shoguns and their samurai warriors held power.

topics.title: Kingdoms of Africa
topics.short: Africa had rich kingdoms: Aksum in the east, Ghana and Mali in the west, where gold was traded for salt, and Great Zimbabwe in the south. Mansa Musa of Mali was one of the richest rulers who ever lived.

topics.title: The Maya, the Aztecs and the Incas
topics.short: In the Americas, the Maya built stone cities and wrote in glyphs; the Aztecs built Tenochtitlan on a lake; the Incas ran a mountain empire joined by thousands of miles of roads.

topics.title: The Renaissance
topics.short: Renaissance means rebirth. Beginning in Italian cities such as Florence in the 1400s, artists and scholars studied the books and art of Greece and Rome and made new art, like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo.

topics.title: The Printing Press and the Reformation
topics.short: About 1450, Johannes Gutenberg printed books with movable metal type. Books became cheaper and ideas spread fast. In 1517 Martin Luther's writings began the Reformation, which divided Western Christians into Catholics and Protestants.

topics.title: The Age of Exploration
topics.short: Sailors crossed the oceans: Zheng He sailed from China to Africa, Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, and Magellan's crew sailed all the way around the world. Plants, animals and diseases crossed with them.

topics.title: The Scientific Revolution
topics.short: Copernicus said the Earth goes around the Sun; Galileo looked through a telescope and saw moons circling Jupiter; Newton explained gravity. People began testing ideas with careful experiments.

topics.title: The American Revolution
topics.short: Thirteen British colonies in North America declared independence on July 4, 1776, won the war, and wrote the Constitution in 1787. George Washington became the first president.

topics.title: The French Revolution and Napoleon
topics.short: In 1789 the people of France rose up against their king, demanding "liberty, equality, fraternity." The revolution brought new rights and a time of fear and war; then Napoleon made himself emperor, until his defeat at Waterloo in 1815.

topics.title: Steam and Factories: The Industrial Revolution
topics.short: Beginning in Britain in the 1700s, machines driven by water and steam began to do work once done by hand. Factories, railways and big cities grew, and so did new problems, like children working long hours.

topics.title: The Long Fight to End Slavery
topics.short: Slavery is very old, but in the 1700s and 1800s people began to fight to end it. Britain ended its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its empire in the 1830s; the United States ended slavery in 1865.

topics.title: An Age of Inventions
topics.short: In about 100 years, inventors gave the world the telegraph, the telephone, the electric light, the car and the airplane. Marie Curie discovered new elements and won two Nobel Prizes.

topics.title: Two World Wars
topics.short: Two terrible wars were fought by many nations: World War I (1914 to 1918) and World War II (1939 to 1945). Afterward, countries formed the United Nations to try to keep the peace.

topics.title: The World from 1945 to 2000
topics.short: After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union competed in a long Cold War and a race to space; people walked on the Moon in 1969. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, and computers and the World Wide Web changed daily life.

topics.title: What Law Is
topics.short: Law is the set of rules a government makes and enforces through courts and officials; it overlaps with morality and custom but differs from them in how it is made and enforced.

topics.title: Sources of American Law
topics.short: American law comes from constitutions, statutes passed by legislatures, regulations written by agencies, court decisions (case law), treaties and local ordinances, and they rank in an order of authority: the federal Constitution first.

topics.title: Federal and State Law
topics.short: Under the Supremacy Clause valid federal law overrides conflicting state law (preemption); otherwise states make most law, and each state has its own constitution, statutes and courts.

topics.title: Public and Private Law
topics.short: Public law governs the relation between government and people (constitutional, administrative, criminal law); private law governs relations among people and organizations (contracts, torts, property, family).

topics.title: Civil and Criminal Cases
topics.short: In a criminal case the government prosecutes and must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; in a civil case a plaintiff sues for a remedy such as money and usually must prove the claim by a preponderance of the evidence; one act can lead to both.

topics.title: The Common Law Tradition
topics.short: The common law grew from English judges' decisions, case by case; the U.S. inherited it (Louisiana's private law draws on the civil law tradition), while civil law systems in much of Europe and Latin America start from comprehensive codes.

topics.title: Stare Decisis
topics.short: Stare decisis ("to stand by things decided") means courts follow precedent: lower courts must follow higher courts in their system (vertical), and courts usually follow their own earlier rulings (horizontal), for stability, fairness and efficiency.

topics.title: Binding and Persuasive Authority
topics.short: A decision binds the courts below it in the same system; decisions from other states, other circuits or lower courts are only persuasive, and so are secondary sources such as treatises and law reviews.

topics.title: Holding and Dicta
topics.short: The holding is the rule of law necessary to decide the case on its facts; dicta are statements in the opinion that were not necessary to the decision, and they do not bind later courts.

topics.title: Distinguishing and Overruling
topics.short: A court may distinguish a precedent by showing material facts differ, or overrule its own precedent; the Supreme Court weighs factors such as the quality of the earlier reasoning, workability, consistency with other decisions, later developments and reliance.

topics.title: The Federal Courts
topics.short: Article III courts include 94 district courts, 13 courts of appeals and the Supreme Court; their judges have life tenure; Congress has also created specialized courts and judges without life tenure, such as bankruptcy and magistrate judges.

topics.title: State Courts
topics.short: Most states have trial courts, an intermediate appellate court and a highest court (usually called the supreme court, though in New York the trial court is the Supreme Court and the highest court is the Court of Appeals); state courts hear the great majority of cases.

topics.title: Jurisdiction
topics.short: A court needs subject-matter jurisdiction (federal courts hear federal-question cases and diversity cases between citizens of different states over $75,000) and personal jurisdiction over the defendant (enough contacts with the state that suit there is fair).

topics.title: Trial Courts and Appellate Courts
topics.short: Trial courts find facts and apply law, with witnesses, evidence and often a jury; appellate courts review the record for legal error, reviewing questions of law de novo and deferring on facts (clear error) and many trial rulings (abuse of discretion).

topics.title: The Path of a Civil Case
topics.short: A civil case moves from complaint and answer through motions to dismiss, discovery and summary judgment to trial, verdict, judgment and appeal; most cases settle or end on motions before trial.

topics.title: The Path of a Criminal Case
topics.short: A criminal case moves from investigation and arrest to charging (by a grand jury indictment for federal felonies, or an information), arraignment and plea, pretrial motions, plea bargaining or trial, verdict, sentencing and appeal; most convictions come from guilty pleas.

topics.title: Case Names and Parties
topics.short: A case name lists the parties ("Smith v. Jones"); at trial they are plaintiff and defendant (or the government and the defendant in criminal cases), on appeal appellant and appellee, and at the Supreme Court petitioner and respondent.

topics.title: Reading a Citation
topics.short: A citation such as Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954) gives the volume (347), the reporter (U.S. Reports), the first page (483) and the year; F.3d and F.4th report the courts of appeals, F. Supp. the district courts.

topics.title: The Parts of an Opinion
topics.short: An appellate decision may include a syllabus (a summary that is not part of the opinion), the opinion of the Court, concurring opinions (agreeing with the result, often for other reasons), dissents and, when no reasoning wins a majority, a plurality opinion.

topics.title: Briefing a Case
topics.short: A student case brief records the facts, the procedural history, the issue (question presented), the holding, the reasoning and the disposition, and often notes concurrences and dissents.

topics.title: IRAC
topics.short: IRAC organizes legal analysis: state the Issue, the Rule, the Application of the rule to the facts and the Conclusion; the Application, where facts are matched to the rule's elements, does the work.

topics.title: What Appellate Courts Do
topics.short: An appellate court may affirm (leave the decision in place), reverse (overturn it), vacate (set it aside) or remand (send it back for more proceedings), often reversing or vacating and remanding together.

topics.title: Rules as Syllogisms
topics.short: Applying a rule is a deductive argument: the rule is the major premise, the facts are the minor premise and the result follows; most disputes are over which rule applies or what the facts are.

topics.title: Reasoning by Analogy
topics.short: Lawyers argue that a case is like a precedent in the ways that matter (analogizing) or unlike it (distinguishing); the key is identifying which facts are material to the rule's purpose.

topics.title: Rules and Standards
topics.short: A rule draws a bright line ("speed limit 65"); a standard calls for judgment ("drive reasonably for conditions"); rules are predictable but can misfit cases, while standards fit cases better but are less predictable.

topics.title: Elements, Factors and Balancing Tests
topics.short: Some legal tests list elements, all of which must be proven; others list factors to weigh, none decisive by itself; a balancing test weighs interests against each other.

topics.title: Burdens and Standards of Proof
topics.short: The burden of proof says which party must prove a point (production and persuasion); the standard says how sure the factfinder must be: preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not), clear and convincing evidence, or beyond a reasonable doubt.

topics.title: Text and Ordinary Meaning
topics.short: Courts begin with the statute's text, read in its ordinary meaning at the time it was enacted and in the context of the whole statute; textualists hold that the enacted words are the law.

topics.title: Purpose
topics.short: Purposivists read a statute in light of the problem it was meant to solve and its evident purpose, especially when the words are unclear or a literal reading would defeat the statute's aims.

topics.title: Legislative History
topics.short: Legislative history includes committee reports, floor statements and earlier drafts; its supporters say it reveals what Congress meant, and its critics say only the enacted text was voted on and history can be selective.

topics.title: Textual Canons
topics.short: Textual canons are rules of thumb about language: expressio unius (listing some implies excluding others), ejusdem generis (a general word after a list takes the list's kind), noscitur a sociis (a word is known by its neighbors), the rule against surplusage and the whole-act rule.

topics.title: Substantive Canons
topics.short: Substantive canons reflect legal values: the rule of lenity (read unclear criminal laws in the defendant's favor), constitutional avoidance (prefer a reading that avoids constitutional doubts) and clear-statement rules (Congress must speak clearly to, for example, override state sovereign immunity).

topics.title: Courts and Agency Interpretations
topics.short: Under Skidmore (1944) an agency's reading gets weight by its power to persuade; under Chevron (1984) courts deferred to reasonable agency readings of ambiguous statutes, and Mead (2001) limited when Chevron applied; the Court overruled Chevron in 2024.

topics.title: The Schools Compared
topics.short: Textualism prizes fidelity to the enacted words, predictability and the legislature's role; purposivism prizes making statutes work as intended; most judges use text, structure, purpose, history and canons in some mix.

topics.title: Cases and Controversies
topics.short: Article III limits federal courts to actual "Cases" and "Controversies": they decide real disputes between adverse parties and do not give advisory opinions.

topics.title: Standing
topics.short: To have standing a plaintiff must show (1) an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized and actual or imminent, (2) caused by the defendant's conduct and (3) likely to be redressed by a favorable ruling (Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 1992).

topics.title: Ripeness and Mootness
topics.short: A case is not ripe if the harm is too speculative or the dispute not yet concrete; it is moot if events end the dispute, unless an exception applies, such as a wrong "capable of repetition, yet evading review" or a defendant's voluntary stop that could be resumed.

topics.title: Political Questions
topics.short: Courts decline questions the Constitution commits to another branch or that lack judicially manageable standards (Baker v. Carr, 1962, listing the factors); examples include Senate impeachment trials (Nixon v. United States, 1993) and partisan gerrymandering claims in federal court (Rucho v. Common Cause, 2019).

topics.title: Contracts
topics.short: A contract is an enforceable promise; it generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration (a bargained-for exchange), and remedies for breach usually aim to give the injured party the benefit of the bargain.

topics.title: Torts
topics.short: A tort is a civil wrong; negligence requires a duty, a breach of that duty, causation (actual and proximate) and damages; intentional torts include battery, assault and trespass; strict liability applies to a few activities.

topics.title: Criminal Law
topics.short: Most crimes require a guilty act (actus reus) and a guilty mind (mens rea); the Model Penal Code ranks mental states as purposely, knowingly, recklessly and negligently; defenses include self-defense and insanity.

topics.title: Administrative Law
topics.short: Agencies make rules, adjudicate cases and enforce laws under statutes; the Administrative Procedure Act (1946) requires notice-and-comment rulemaking for most rules and lets courts set aside agency action that is "arbitrary, capricious" or contrary to law.

topics.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
topics.short: A primary source was made at the time by someone who saw or took part (a letter, a law, a photo); a secondary source was made later by someone studying it (a textbook, a history book).

topics.title: Reading a Source: HIPP
topics.short: Ask four questions of any source: its Historical situation, Intended audience, Purpose and Point of view; each one shapes what the source says and leaves out.

topics.title: Dates, Centuries and Periods
topics.short: The 1700s are the 18th century; historians group years into periods (such as 1754 to 1800) around big turning points, and a timeline shows what came before what.

topics.title: Causes, Effects and Change Over Time
topics.short: Big events usually have several causes, long-term and short-term, and several effects; historians also ask what changed and what stayed the same.

topics.title: The First Peoples of the Americas
topics.short: People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago, by land across Beringia, along the Pacific coast, or both; the exact dates and routes are still studied and debated.

topics.title: Native Cultures Across North America
topics.short: By 1491 Native societies across North America had adapted to very different lands: maize farming and irrigation in the Southwest, hunting and farming on the Plains, fishing in the Northwest, mixed farming and villages in the East.

topics.title: Cities, Confederacies and Pueblos
topics.short: Some Native societies built large towns and alliances: Cahokia, a Mississippian city near present-day St. Louis; the Ancestral Puebloans of the Four Corners; the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy of the Northeast.

topics.title: Why Europeans Explored
topics.short: Portugal and Spain sought sea routes to Asian trade, new wealth, the spread of Christianity and national glory; Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided claims between Spain and Portugal.

topics.title: The Columbian Exchange
topics.short: After 1492 plants, animals, people and diseases crossed the Atlantic both ways: horses, wheat and cattle to the Americas; maize, potatoes and tomatoes to Europe, Africa and Asia; and diseases such as smallpox that killed a large share of Native peoples.

topics.title: The Spanish Empire in the Americas
topics.short: Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec (1521) and Inca empires; Spain ruled through the encomienda system and missions, founded St. Augustine (1565), and debated how Native peoples should be treated.

topics.title: Jamestown and the Chesapeake
topics.short: Jamestown (1607) survived hard early years and grew rich on tobacco; Virginia set up the House of Burgesses in 1619, the same year the first recorded Africans arrived in the colony.

topics.title: Pilgrims and Puritans in New England
topics.short: The Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact (1620) and founded Plymouth; Puritans founded Massachusetts Bay (1630); dissenters such as Roger Williams (Rhode Island, 1636) and Anne Hutchinson were banished.

topics.title: The Middle Colonies
topics.short: New York (Dutch New Netherland until 1664), New Jersey, Pennsylvania (founded by William Penn, a Quaker, in 1681) and Delaware were the most diverse colonies, with wheat farms, ports and wide religious toleration.

topics.title: The Southern Colonies
topics.short: Maryland (1634) was a refuge for English Catholics; the Carolinas grew rice and indigo on plantations worked by enslaved Africans; Georgia (1732) was the last of the thirteen.

topics.title: Comparing the Colonial Regions
topics.short: Compare New England (towns, trade, fishing, small farms), the Middle colonies (wheat, ports, diversity) and the South (cash crops, plantations, slavery) and explain why geography and settlers made them differ.

topics.title: Slavery in the Colonies
topics.short: Enslaved Africans were carried across the Atlantic in the Middle Passage; colonial slave codes made slavery lifelong and inherited through the mother; enslaved people resisted, as in the Stono Rebellion of 1739.

topics.title: Colonists and Native Nations in Conflict
topics.short: As colonies spread, wars broke out: the Pequot War (1636 to 1638), King Philip's (Metacom's) War (1675 to 1676), Bacon's Rebellion against Virginia's governor (1676) and the Pueblo Revolt against Spain (1680).

topics.title: Mercantilism and the Navigation Acts
topics.short: Under mercantilism, colonies existed to enrich the mother country; the Navigation Acts (from 1651) made colonists ship key goods only on English ships to English ports, though Britain enforced them loosely for decades ("salutary neglect").

topics.title: The Great Awakening and the Enlightenment
topics.short: The First Great Awakening (1730s and 1740s, Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield) brought revival preaching and new churches; Enlightenment ideas of reason and natural rights (John Locke) spread through books, Benjamin Franklin and colonial colleges.

topics.title: Colonial Self-Government
topics.short: Colonists grew used to governing themselves through elected assemblies such as the House of Burgesses, New England town meetings and colonial legislatures that controlled taxes; the Zenger trial (1735) defended printing criticism of officials.

topics.title: The French and Indian War
topics.short: Britain and France fought for North America from 1754 to 1763 (part of the Seven Years' War); Britain won Canada and the land east of the Mississippi, but its war debt and the Proclamation of 1763 set the stage for conflict with the colonists.

topics.title: New Taxes and Colonial Protest
topics.short: To pay the war debt, Parliament passed the Sugar Act (1764), Stamp Act (1765) and Townshend Acts (1767); colonists answered with the Stamp Act Congress, boycotts and the cry "no taxation without representation."

topics.title: The Road to Revolution
topics.short: Tension grew from the Boston Massacre (1770) to the Tea Act and Boston Tea Party (1773), the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts (1774) and the First Continental Congress (1774).

topics.title: Lexington, Concord and Common Sense
topics.short: Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775; the Second Continental Congress made George Washington commander; Thomas Paine's Common Sense (January 1776) argued for full independence.

topics.title: The Declaration of Independence
topics.short: Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776, and adopted the Declaration on July 4; written mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it states a theory of government by consent, lists grievances against the King and declares the colonies free.

topics.title: Patriots, Loyalists and Neutrals
topics.short: Colonists divided: Patriots backed independence, Loyalists stayed loyal to Britain, many stayed neutral; Dunmore's Proclamation (1775) offered freedom to enslaved people who joined the British, and most Native nations sided with Britain.

topics.title: Winning the War
topics.short: Key moments: Washington's victory at Trenton (1776), the American win at Saratoga (1777) that brought the French alliance (1778), the hard winter at Valley Forge (1777 to 1778) and the British surrender at Yorktown (1781).

topics.title: The Treaty of Paris, 1783
topics.short: In the Treaty of Paris (1783) Britain recognized American independence, with borders at the Mississippi River in the west, Canada in the north and Spanish Florida in the south.

topics.title: What the Revolution Changed
topics.short: The Revolution brought new state constitutions with bills of rights, the gradual abolition of slavery in Northern states (beginning with Pennsylvania in 1780), Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom (1786) and new ideas about women as "republican mothers."

topics.title: The Articles of Confederation
topics.short: The Articles (in force 1781) set up a weak national government: one vote per state in Congress, no executive or national courts, no power to tax, nine states to pass key laws and all thirteen to amend.

topics.title: The Land Ordinance and the Northwest Ordinance
topics.short: The Land Ordinance of 1785 surveyed western land into square townships; the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 set out how territories become states equal to the old ones and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory.

topics.title: Shays' Rebellion
topics.short: In 1786 and 1787 indebted Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays closed courts to stop foreclosures; the weak national government could do little, which convinced many leaders to strengthen it.

topics.title: The Constitutional Convention
topics.short: In 1787 delegates in Philadelphia replaced the Articles; the Great (Connecticut) Compromise blended the Virginia Plan (seats by population) and the New Jersey Plan (equal seats), and other compromises dealt with slavery and the presidency.

topics.title: Federalists, Anti-Federalists and Ratification
topics.short: Federalists (Madison, Hamilton, Jay, writing as "Publius" in The Federalist) defended the Constitution; Anti-Federalists (such as "Brutus" and the "Federal Farmer") feared a distant, too-strong government without a bill of rights; New Hampshire's ratification in June 1788 made nine states.

topics.title: The Bill of Rights
topics.short: James Madison drafted amendments in the First Congress (1789); ten were ratified in 1791 as the Bill of Rights, protecting freedoms such as speech, religion, the press and fair trials from the national government.

topics.title: Washington Sets the Pattern
topics.short: Washington (1789 to 1797) formed the first Cabinet, backed Alexander Hamilton's plan (paying state war debts, a national bank, tariffs), put down the Whiskey Rebellion (1794), kept the country neutral in Europe's wars, and stepped down after two terms.

topics.title: The First Political Parties
topics.short: Disputes over Hamilton's plans and the French Revolution split leaders into Federalists (Hamilton, Adams: a strong national government, commerce, ties to Britain) and Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison: strict reading of the Constitution, farmers, sympathy for France).

topics.title: John Adams and the Election of 1800
topics.short: Under John Adams came the XYZ Affair, an undeclared naval war with France, and the Alien and Sedition Acts (1798), which Jefferson and Madison opposed in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions; in 1800 power passed peacefully from one party to the other.

topics.title: Jefferson and the Louisiana Purchase
topics.short: In 1803 Jefferson bought Louisiana from France for about $15 million, roughly doubling the country's size, and sent Lewis and Clark (1804 to 1806) to explore it, though he doubted the Constitution clearly allowed the purchase.

topics.title: The Marshall Court
topics.short: Chief Justice John Marshall (1801 to 1835) strengthened the courts and the national government: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review, McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) upheld the national bank, Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) read the commerce power broadly.

topics.title: The War of 1812
topics.short: Over British impressment of sailors, trade limits and support for Native resistance in the West, the U.S. went to war with Britain (1812 to 1815); the British burned Washington, Fort McHenry held, and the Treaty of Ghent restored prewar borders.

topics.title: Good Feelings, Missouri and the Monroe Doctrine
topics.short: Under Monroe one party dominated; Henry Clay's "American System" proposed a bank, tariffs and roads and canals; the Missouri Compromise (1820) balanced slave and free states and drew the 36°30' line; the Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned Europe against new colonies in the Americas.

topics.title: The Market Revolution
topics.short: Canals (the Erie Canal, 1825), steamboats and railroads tied regions into a national market; textile mills (Lowell) grew in the North, while the cotton gin (1793) and world demand spread cotton and slavery across the Deep South.

topics.title: Jacksonian Democracy
topics.short: Most states dropped property rules for white men voting; Andrew Jackson (1829 to 1837) used the spoils system, vetoed the Second Bank's recharter (1832) and faced down South Carolina in the Nullification Crisis (1832 to 1833); Democrats and Whigs formed the second party system.

topics.title: Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears
topics.short: The Indian Removal Act (1830) led to the forced removal of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Choctaw and Seminole nations west of the Mississippi; despite Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Cherokee were forced out in 1838 and 1839 on the Trail of Tears, and thousands died.

topics.title: Revival and Reform
topics.short: The Second Great Awakening (about 1800 to the 1840s) inspired reform movements: temperance, public schools (Horace Mann), better care for the mentally ill (Dorothea Dix), prison reform and utopian communities.

topics.title: The Abolition Movement
topics.short: Abolitionists such as William Lloyd Garrison (The Liberator, 1831), Frederick Douglass, Sojourner Truth and the Grimké sisters demanded an end to slavery; Nat Turner's revolt (1831) and the Underground Railroad showed enslaved people's resistance.

topics.title: Seneca Falls and Women's Rights
topics.short: At Seneca Falls, New York, in 1848 Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott and others issued the Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, which demanded rights for women including the vote.

topics.title: Manifest Destiny
topics.short: The idea that the United States was destined to spread across the continent (named in 1845) drove the annexation of Texas (independent from Mexico since 1836) in 1845 and the Oregon treaty with Britain (1846) at the 49th parallel.

topics.title: The Mexican-American War
topics.short: After a border dispute, the U.S. fought Mexico (1846 to 1848); in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo Mexico ceded California and the Southwest; the Wilmot Proviso to ban slavery in that land passed the House but failed in the Senate.

topics.title: How the Country Grew
topics.short: Match each addition to its year and how it came: the 1783 treaty lands, Louisiana (1803), Florida (1819), Texas (1845), Oregon (1846), the Mexican Cession (1848), the Gadsden Purchase (1853), and later Alaska (1867) and Hawaii (1898).

topics.title: Gold, Immigrants and Nativism
topics.short: The California Gold Rush (1849) drew people from around the world; Irish (after the 1845 famine) and German immigrants poured into the North; nativists formed the anti-immigrant American ("Know-Nothing") Party.

topics.title: The Compromise of 1850
topics.short: California joined as a free state; New Mexico and Utah would decide slavery by popular sovereignty; the slave trade (not slavery) ended in the District of Columbia; a stronger Fugitive Slave Act angered the North, and Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) moved many readers.

topics.title: Kansas-Nebraska and Bleeding Kansas
topics.short: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) let settlers vote on slavery, repealing the Missouri line; violence in "Bleeding Kansas" followed, and opponents of slavery's spread founded the Republican Party (1854).

topics.title: The Dred Scott Decision
topics.short: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) the Supreme Court held 7 to 2 that Black Americans were not citizens who could sue in federal court and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories; the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) overturned the citizenship ruling.

topics.title: Lincoln, John Brown and the Election of 1860
topics.short: Lincoln and Stephen Douglas debated slavery in 1858; John Brown raided Harpers Ferry in 1859; in 1860 Lincoln won the presidency in a four-way race with no electoral votes from the Deep South.

topics.title: Secession and Fort Sumter
topics.short: South Carolina seceded in December 1860, followed by six more Deep South states that formed the Confederacy in February 1861; after Confederates fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861, four more states seceded, while slave-holding border states stayed in the Union.

topics.title: The Union and the Confederacy
topics.short: The Union had far more people, factories and railroads; the Confederacy fought on its own ground with skilled generals; the Union's Anaconda Plan aimed to blockade the coast and seize the Mississippi.

topics.title: Turning Points of the War
topics.short: Key events: Bull Run (1861), Antietam (1862), Gettysburg and the fall of Vicksburg (July 1863), Sherman's capture of Atlanta and March to the Sea (1864), and Lee's surrender at Appomattox (April 1865).

topics.title: Emancipation
topics.short: The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) declared enslaved people free in areas in rebellion and allowed Black men to join the Union army, where about 180,000 served; the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery everywhere in the country.

topics.title: The Home Fronts
topics.short: Both sides drafted soldiers (the New York draft riots, 1863); Lincoln suspended habeas corpus in some areas; Congress passed the Homestead Act, Morrill Land-Grant Act and Pacific Railway Act (1862); women served as nurses and ran farms and businesses.

topics.title: The Gettysburg Address
topics.short: In November 1863 Lincoln dedicated the cemetery at Gettysburg in about 270 words, describing the war as a test of whether a nation "conceived in Liberty" could endure and calling for "a new birth of freedom."

topics.title: Lincoln's Death and Johnson's Plan
topics.short: Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865; Andrew Johnson's lenient plan let Southern states rejoin quickly, and many passed Black Codes limiting freedpeople's rights.

topics.title: Reconstruction Under Congress
topics.short: Congress created the Freedmen's Bureau, passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 over Johnson's veto, imposed the Reconstruction Acts (1867) and impeached Johnson (1868), who was acquitted by one vote; Black men voted and held office, including Senator Hiram Revels.

topics.title: The Reconstruction Amendments
topics.short: The Thirteenth (1865) ended slavery; the Fourteenth (1868) made all persons born here citizens and promised due process and equal protection; the Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote because of race.

topics.title: The End of Reconstruction
topics.short: Violence by the Ku Klux Klan and others, Northern fatigue and the economic panic of 1873 wore Reconstruction down; the Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed 1876 election and federal troops left the last Southern capitals; sharecropping and segregation laws followed.

topics.title: The Transcontinental Railroad
topics.short: The first transcontinental railroad was finished at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869, built largely by Chinese workers from the west and Irish and other workers from the east, and backed by federal land grants and loans.

topics.title: Wars on the Plains
topics.short: As settlers, miners and railroads moved west and the bison herds were destroyed, the U.S. Army fought Plains nations: Sand Creek (1864), the Little Bighorn (1876), and the killing of Lakota people at Wounded Knee (1890); most nations were confined to reservations.

topics.title: Assimilation and the Dawes Act
topics.short: Policy shifted to assimilation: boarding schools such as Carlisle (1879) separated children from their languages and cultures, and the Dawes Act (1887) split reservation land into family plots, with the "surplus" sold; Native landholding fell from about 138 to 48 million acres by 1934.

topics.title: Big Business and Industry
topics.short: Steel (Andrew Carnegie, the Bessemer process), oil (John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil), electricity and the telephone transformed the economy; firms grew by vertical and horizontal integration and trusts, and the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) outlawed combinations in restraint of trade.

topics.title: Workers and Unions
topics.short: Workers faced long hours and dangerous jobs; the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor (1886, Samuel Gompers) organized them; the Haymarket affair (1886), Homestead strike (1892) and Pullman strike (1894) turned violent and set back unions.

topics.title: New Immigrants and Growing Cities
topics.short: From the 1880s, most immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe, many through Ellis Island (opened 1892); cities filled with tenements, political machines such as Tammany Hall, and settlement houses such as Jane Addams's Hull House (1889); the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred most Chinese laborers.

topics.title: Gilded Age Politics and the Populists
topics.short: After President Garfield's assassination, the Pendleton Act (1883) began a merit-based civil service; the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) regulated railroads; struggling farmers formed the People's (Populist) Party (1892); in 1896 William McKinley (gold standard) defeated William Jennings Bryan (free silver).

topics.title: Jim Crow and Plessy v. Ferguson
topics.short: Southern states passed segregation laws and kept Black citizens from voting with poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses; in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) the Supreme Court upheld "separate but equal" 7 to 1, over Justice John Marshall Harlan's dissent; Ida B. Wells campaigned against lynching.

topics.title: Ideas of the Gilded Age
topics.short: People argued over the new wealth: Carnegie's "Gospel of Wealth" (the rich should give it away well), Social Darwinism (competition sorts the fit), the Social Gospel (faith calls for reform), and Booker T. Washington's and W. E. B. Du Bois's different strategies for Black advancement.

topics.title: Becoming a World Power
topics.short: American planters and businessmen in Hawaii helped overthrow Queen Liliuokalani (1893), and the U.S. annexed Hawaii in 1898; the Spanish-American War (1898) brought Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, where a long war against Filipino independence fighters followed (1899 to 1902); Americans debated empire sharply.

topics.title: The Open Door, the Big Stick and the Canal
topics.short: The U.S. sought an Open Door for trade in China (1899); Theodore Roosevelt backed Panama's independence and built the Panama Canal (opened 1914) and added the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) to the Monroe Doctrine; Taft favored "dollar diplomacy."

topics.title: Muckrakers and Reformers
topics.short: Journalists called muckrakers exposed problems: Jacob Riis (city slums), Ida Tarbell (Standard Oil), Upton Sinclair's The Jungle (meatpacking, 1906); Congress passed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act in 1906.

topics.title: The Progressive Presidents
topics.short: Theodore Roosevelt broke up trusts and protected forests and parks; Taft continued antitrust suits; Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act (1913), the Clayton Antitrust Act and the Federal Trade Commission Act (1914).

topics.title: Progressive Amendments and Direct Democracy
topics.short: Four amendments came in seven years: the Sixteenth (income tax, 1913), Seventeenth (senators elected by voters, 1913), Eighteenth (Prohibition, 1919) and Nineteenth (women's suffrage, 1920); many states also adopted the initiative, referendum, recall and direct primary.

topics.title: Winning Women's Suffrage
topics.short: After decades of work by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony and others, Carrie Chapman Catt's NAWSA lobbied state by state while Alice Paul's National Woman's Party picketed the White House; the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in August 1920.

topics.title: The NAACP and the Great Migration
topics.short: The NAACP (1909) fought segregation in court and in public; from about 1910 to 1970 roughly six million Black Southerners moved to cities of the North and West for jobs and to escape Jim Crow.

topics.title: The United States Enters the Great War
topics.short: The U.S. stayed neutral when war began in 1914; German submarine attacks (the Lusitania, 1915; unrestricted warfare, 1917) and the Zimmermann Telegram led Congress to declare war in April 1917.

topics.title: The War at Home and the Peace
topics.short: The government drafted soldiers, ran wartime agencies and limited dissent (the Espionage Act, 1917; Schenck v. United States, 1919); the war ended with the armistice of November 11, 1918; Wilson's Fourteen Points and League of Nations failed to win the Senate's approval of the Treaty of Versailles.

topics.title: The Twenties
topics.short: Cars (the Model T), radio, movies and buying on credit created a mass consumer culture; jazz spread from New Orleans to Chicago and New York; the Harlem Renaissance (Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston) flourished.

topics.title: Conflicts of the Twenties
topics.short: The Red Scare (1919 to 1920), the Sacco and Vanzetti case, immigration quotas (1921, 1924), the Scopes trial (1925), a revived Ku Klux Klan and the struggle to enforce Prohibition showed a country divided over change.

topics.title: The Crash of 1929
topics.short: Stocks crashed in October 1929 (Black Tuesday, October 29); historians and economists weigh several causes of the Depression that followed: speculation and buying on margin, bank failures, a shrinking money supply, overproduction, unequal income and high tariffs.

topics.title: Life in the Great Depression
topics.short: By 1933 about a quarter of workers were unemployed; thousands of banks failed; drought and dust storms drove families from the Plains (the Dust Bowl); Hoover's Reconstruction Finance Corporation lent to banks and businesses, and the Bonus Army was driven from Washington (1932).

topics.title: The New Deal
topics.short: Franklin Roosevelt (from 1933) promised relief, recovery and reform: the CCC, the TVA, the WPA, deposit insurance (FDIC, 1933), the SEC (1934), Social Security and the Wagner Act (1935), and the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938).

topics.title: The New Deal and the Supreme Court
topics.short: The Court struck down parts of the New Deal (Schechter, 1935); Roosevelt's 1937 plan to add justices failed in Congress, but that year the Court began upholding economic regulation (West Coast Hotel v. Parrish; NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin).

topics.title: Judging the New Deal
topics.short: Critics on the left (Huey Long, Father Coughlin) said the New Deal did too little; critics on the right (the American Liberty League) said it did too much; historians and economists still debate how much it helped recovery, while agreeing it changed the federal government's role for good.

topics.title: The Road to War
topics.short: Neutrality Acts (1935 to 1937) kept the U.S. out of foreign wars; after war began in Europe (1939), "cash and carry," Lend-Lease (1941) and the Atlantic Charter moved the country toward the Allies while isolationists argued against it.

topics.title: Pearl Harbor
topics.short: On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the U.S. fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii; Congress declared war on Japan the next day, and Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on December 11.

topics.title: The Home Front
topics.short: Factories switched to war production; millions of women took industrial jobs; rationing, war bonds and scrap drives involved everyone; A. Philip Randolph's planned march won an order against discrimination in defense jobs (1941), and Black Americans pressed a "Double V" for victory abroad and at home.

topics.title: The Incarceration of Japanese Americans
topics.short: Executive Order 9066 (1942) led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them U.S. citizens, to camps; the Supreme Court upheld the removal in Korematsu v. United States (1944); Congress apologized and paid redress in the Civil Liberties Act of 1988.

topics.title: The War in Europe and the Holocaust
topics.short: The Allies fought in North Africa (1942), Sicily and Italy (1943), landed in Normandy on D-Day (June 6, 1944) and turned back Germany's last offensive at the Bulge; Germany surrendered on V-E Day (May 8, 1945); Allied soldiers liberated camps where Nazi Germany had murdered six million Jews and millions of others.

topics.title: The War in the Pacific
topics.short: After the turning point at Midway (June 1942), U.S. forces "island hopped" toward Japan (Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima, Okinawa); atomic bombs struck Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (August 9); Japan announced surrender August 15 and signed it September 2.

topics.title: Planning the Peace
topics.short: At Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July 1945) the Allies planned postwar Europe; the United Nations was founded in 1945, with the U.S. as a permanent member of the Security Council.

topics.title: Containment
topics.short: The U.S. set out to contain Soviet communism: the Truman Doctrine (1947), the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe (1948), the Berlin Airlift (1948 to 1949) and the NATO alliance (1949).

topics.title: The Second Red Scare
topics.short: Fear of Soviet spying (the Hiss and Rosenberg cases) led to loyalty programs, congressional hearings (HUAC) and Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations (1950 to 1954) until the Senate censured him.

topics.title: The Korean War
topics.short: North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950; UN forces led by the U.S. fought North Korean and later Chinese armies; an armistice in 1953 left Korea divided near the 38th parallel, with no peace treaty.

topics.title: The 1950s
topics.short: The GI Bill (1944), suburbs such as Levittown, the baby boom, television and the Interstate Highway Act (1956) reshaped life; the Soviet launch of Sputnik (1957) spurred new spending on science and education.

topics.title: Kennedy, Cuba and the Space Race
topics.short: The Bay of Pigs invasion failed (1961); the Berlin Wall went up (1961); in the Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) the U.S. and the USSR came close to nuclear war before the Soviets removed their missiles; the space race led to Apollo 11's Moon landing (1969).

topics.title: The Vietnam War
topics.short: After the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964), U.S. troops in Vietnam grew to over 500,000; the Tet Offensive (1968) shook public support; protests spread at home (Kent State, 1970); the Paris Peace Accords (1973) ended U.S. combat, and Saigon fell in 1975; Congress passed the War Powers Resolution (1973).

topics.title: The Great Society
topics.short: Lyndon Johnson's Great Society (1964 to 1966) included the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid (1965), federal aid to schools and the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, which ended the national-origins quotas.

topics.title: Nixon, Detente and Watergate
topics.short: Richard Nixon opened relations with China (1972), signed arms limits with the USSR (SALT I, 1972) and created the EPA (1970); the Watergate scandal and United States v. Nixon (1974) led to his resignation on August 9, 1974.

topics.title: The End of the Cold War
topics.short: Ronald Reagan built up defense and called on the Soviets to "tear down this wall" (1987); he and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty (1987); the Berlin Wall fell (November 9, 1989) and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

topics.title: Early Victories
topics.short: Jackie Robinson integrated major league baseball (1947); Truman ordered the armed forces desegregated (1948); Mendez v. Westminster (1947) ended the segregation of Mexican American children in California schools.

topics.title: Brown v. Board of Education
topics.short: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled 9 to 0 that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause, overturning Plessy for schools; resistance followed, and in 1957 Eisenhower sent troops to protect the Little Rock Nine.

topics.title: The Montgomery Bus Boycott
topics.short: After Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955, Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, boycotted the buses for 381 days, led by Martin Luther King Jr.; in 1956 the courts ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.

topics.title: Sit-ins, Freedom Rides and the March on Washington
topics.short: Students sat in at a Greensboro lunch counter (1960) and founded SNCC; Freedom Riders tested bus integration (1961); after the Birmingham campaign (1963) and King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," 250,000 people joined the March on Washington (August 28, 1963).

topics.title: The Civil Rights Laws
topics.short: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in public places and jobs; the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; after the Selma marches, the Voting Rights Act (1965) ended literacy tests and brought federal oversight; the Fair Housing Act followed in 1968.

topics.title: Debates Within the Movement
topics.short: Leaders differed on methods and goals: King's nonviolent integration, Malcolm X's call for self-defense and Black pride, and the Black Power movement (from 1966); King was assassinated in April 1968.

topics.title: Other Movements for Equal Rights
topics.short: Others drew on the movement: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta organized farmworkers (the UFW); the American Indian Movement (1968) pressed for treaty rights; the women's movement won Title IX (1972), though the Equal Rights Amendment was not ratified; the Americans with Disabilities Act passed in 1990.

topics.title: The 1970s
topics.short: An oil embargo (1973) and "stagflation" (high inflation with high unemployment) strained the economy; Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon; Jimmy Carter brokered the Camp David Accords (1978) and faced the Iran hostage crisis (1979 to 1981).

topics.title: The Conservative Resurgence
topics.short: Ronald Reagan won in 1980 and 1984 on lower taxes, less regulation and a stronger defense; supporters credit his policies with the long expansion after 1982, while critics point to larger deficits and widening inequality.

topics.title: A World After the Cold War
topics.short: The U.S. led a coalition in the Gulf War (1991), joined NAFTA (in force 1994), took part in NATO operations in Bosnia (1995) and Kosovo (1999), and faced new questions about its role as the only superpower.

topics.title: Computers, the Internet and a Global Economy
topics.short: Personal computers spread in the 1980s; the World Wide Web (1991) opened the internet to the public; trade and investment linked economies worldwide, and the country debated the gains and costs of globalization.

topics.title: Politics of the 1990s
topics.short: Bill Clinton (1993 to 2001) signed NAFTA and a 1996 welfare reform passed by a Republican Congress; the federal budget ran surpluses from 1998 to 2001; the House impeached Clinton in 1998 and the Senate acquitted him in 1999; the 2000 election was decided after Bush v. Gore.

topics.title: The Nine Periods: Putting It Together
topics.short: Place events from 1491 to 2000 in their AP periods and in order, and explain a cause and an effect that link one period to the next.

topics.title: The American Flag
topics.short: Our flag has 13 stripes for the first 13 colonies and 50 stars for the 50 states today.

topics.title: The Bald Eagle
topics.short: The bald eagle, a big bird of North America, has been on the Great Seal of the United States since 1782 and stands for strength and freedom; in 2024 Congress made it the official national bird.

topics.title: The Liberty Bell
topics.short: The Liberty Bell in Philadelphia is a symbol of freedom; it has a famous crack and its words say to proclaim liberty throughout the land.

topics.title: The Statue of Liberty
topics.short: The Statue of Liberty, a gift from the people of France in 1886, holds up a torch in New York Harbor to welcome people arriving by sea.

topics.title: Our National Anthem
topics.short: Francis Scott Key wrote "The Star-Spangled Banner" in 1814 after he saw the flag still flying over Fort McHenry after a long battle.

topics.title: Our Capital, Washington, D.C.
topics.short: Washington, D.C., is our nation's capital: Congress meets in the Capitol, the President lives and works in the White House, and monuments honor great Americans.

topics.title: Why We Have Rules
topics.short: Rules keep us safe, help us be fair and help us get along, at home, at school and at play.

topics.title: Rules and Laws
topics.short: A law is a rule for everyone in a town, state or country, made by leaders the people choose; laws apply to grown-ups too.

topics.title: Community Helpers
topics.short: Firefighters, police officers, doctors and nurses, teachers, mail carriers and many others help our community, and each has a special job.

topics.title: Leaders and Voting
topics.short: In a vote, each person gets one choice and the choice with the most votes wins; Americans vote to choose leaders like a mayor, a governor and the President.

topics.title: Being a Good Citizen
topics.short: A good citizen follows the rules, tells the truth, helps others, takes care of shared places and, as a grown-up, votes.

topics.title: Independence Day
topics.short: On July 4 we celebrate the birthday of our country: on July 4, 1776, leaders adopted the Declaration of Independence.

topics.title: Thanksgiving Day
topics.short: On the fourth Thursday of November, families give thanks; it remembers the harvest feast of 1621 shared by the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people.

topics.title: Washington's Birthday (Presidents' Day)
topics.short: On the third Monday of February we honor George Washington, the first President, and many people honor all the Presidents.

topics.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
topics.short: On the third Monday of January we honor Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., who led peaceful marches and speeches so that all people would be treated fairly.

topics.title: Memorial Day and Veterans Day
topics.short: Memorial Day (the last Monday of May) remembers service members who died for our country; Veterans Day (November 11) thanks everyone who has served.

topics.title: Juneteenth, Labor Day and Other Holidays
topics.short: Juneteenth (June 19) remembers the end of slavery in Texas in 1865; Labor Day honors workers; other days honor the flag and the Constitution.

topics.title: Holidays Through the Year
topics.short: Put the national holidays in order through the year, from New Year's Day in January to Christmas Day in December.

topics.title: The First Peoples
topics.short: Native Americans lived across North America for thousands of years before Europeans came, in hundreds of nations with their own languages and ways of life.

topics.title: Homes That Fit the Land
topics.short: Native nations built homes from what the land gave them: longhouses of wood and bark, adobe pueblos, tipis on the plains, plank houses by the sea.

topics.title: Corn, Beans and Squash
topics.short: Many Native farmers grew corn, beans and squash together, the "Three Sisters"; corn and other foods first grown in the Americas are now eaten all over the world.

topics.title: Native Nations Today
topics.short: Native nations are still here today, with their own governments, languages and traditions; the federal government recognizes 575 tribes (its January 2026 list).

topics.title: Explorers Cross the Ocean
topics.short: Explorers sailed across the Atlantic Ocean looking for new routes and lands: Leif Erikson about the year 1000, Christopher Columbus in 1492, and many after them.

topics.title: Jamestown, 1607
topics.short: Jamestown, in Virginia, was the first lasting English settlement in America, founded in 1607; the settlers depended on the Powhatan people at first.

topics.title: The Pilgrims and the Mayflower
topics.short: In 1620 the Pilgrims sailed on the Mayflower to find a place to worship in their own way and founded Plymouth Colony; they agreed to make fair laws together.

topics.title: The Harvest Feast of 1621
topics.short: Squanto (Tisquantum) and the Wampanoag helped the Pilgrims plant corn, and in 1621 the Pilgrims and about 90 Wampanoag men led by Massasoit shared a three-day harvest feast.

topics.title: The Thirteen Colonies
topics.short: By 1732 there were thirteen English colonies along the Atlantic coast, from New Hampshire in the north to Georgia in the south.

topics.title: Why the Colonists Broke Away
topics.short: Britain taxed the colonists, who had no vote in Britain's Parliament; many colonists said that was unfair: "no taxation without representation."

topics.title: The Declaration of Independence
topics.short: In 1776 Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence; it says all men are created equal with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

topics.title: George Washington
topics.short: George Washington led the Continental Army in the Revolution and became the first President in 1789; he is called the Father of His Country.

topics.title: Heroes of the Revolution
topics.short: Many people helped win independence: Paul Revere warned of British soldiers, Ben Franklin won help from France, and soldiers and families of every background served.

topics.title: The Constitution: Our Country's Rulebook
topics.short: In 1787 leaders wrote the Constitution, the rulebook for our government; it begins "We the People" and still guides the country today.

topics.title: Three Branches of Government
topics.short: The Constitution splits the work into three branches: Congress makes the laws, the President carries them out, and the courts decide what the laws mean.

topics.title: Lewis and Clark
topics.short: In 1804 Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out to explore the West, helped by Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman, and reached the Pacific Ocean in 1805.

topics.title: Pioneers Head West
topics.short: In the 1840s and after, pioneer families traveled west in covered wagons on trails like the Oregon Trail, a trip of about five months.

topics.title: Slavery and Freedom
topics.short: For more than 200 years many Black people in America were enslaved: they were not free and were forced to work without pay; slavery ended in 1865.

topics.title: Harriet Tubman and Frederick Douglass
topics.short: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and led others to freedom on the Underground Railroad; Frederick Douglass escaped and became a great speaker and writer against slavery.

topics.title: Abraham Lincoln
topics.short: Abraham Lincoln, the 16th President, led the country through the Civil War (1861 to 1865), worked to end slavery and kept the country together.

topics.title: American Inventors
topics.short: Inventors changed how we live: Benjamin Franklin's experiments with electricity, Alexander Graham Bell's telephone (1876), Thomas Edison's light bulb (1879) and the Wright brothers' airplane (1903).

topics.title: Fifty States
topics.short: The country grew from 13 states to 50; the last two, Alaska and Hawaii, became states in 1959, and each state has its own capital city.

topics.title: Clara Barton and Caring for Others
topics.short: Clara Barton cared for wounded soldiers in the Civil War and in 1881 founded the American Red Cross, which still helps people after disasters.

topics.title: Rosa Parks and Dr. King
topics.short: In 1955 Rosa Parks would not give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama; Dr. King helped lead a bus boycott and peaceful marches for equal treatment under the law.

topics.title: Footsteps on the Moon
topics.short: On July 20, 1969, American astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon; Armstrong was the first person to walk on it.

topics.title: Then and Now
topics.short: Put the big events of American history in order, from the first peoples to the Moon landing, and compare life long ago with life today.

topics.title: The Writing Process
topics.short: Writers prewrite, draft, revise, edit and publish, and they go back and forth between the steps as needed.

topics.title: Purpose and Audience
topics.short: Before you write, ask why you are writing and who will read it. Both shape what you say and how you say it.

topics.title: Finding and Narrowing a Topic
topics.short: Brainstorm, list, freewrite or cluster ideas, then narrow the topic to one you can cover well in the space you have.

topics.title: Topic Sentences
topics.short: A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph, usually as the first sentence.

topics.title: Supporting Details
topics.short: Facts, examples, reasons and details support the main idea of the paragraph.

topics.title: Paragraph Unity
topics.short: Every sentence in a paragraph supports its one main idea.

topics.title: Transitions
topics.short: Transitions show how ideas connect: time (then, later), addition (also), contrast (however), cause and effect (therefore) and example (for instance).

topics.title: Organizing a Paragraph
topics.short: Arrange details in an order the reader can follow: by time, by place, by importance, or by comparison.

topics.title: Concluding Sentences
topics.short: A concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph’s idea without just repeating the topic sentence.

topics.title: Narrative Writing
topics.short: A narrative tells events in order, from a point of view, with characters, a setting, a conflict and a resolution.

topics.title: Showing and Telling
topics.short: Show a feeling with action, dialogue and sensory details, and tell when a quick summary moves the story along.

topics.title: Descriptive Writing
topics.short: Use precise nouns, strong verbs and sensory details, arranged in a clear order.

topics.title: Expository Writing
topics.short: Expository writing explains or informs, with facts, definitions and examples, in a neutral voice.

topics.title: Ways to Explain
topics.short: Explain by definition, classification, process, compare and contrast, or cause and effect.

topics.title: Facts, Opinions and Claims
topics.short: A fact can be checked. An opinion is a belief or a judgment. A claim is a statement an argument sets out to prove with reasons and evidence.

topics.title: Persuasive Writing
topics.short: Persuasive writing takes a position and gives reasons and evidence to convince a reader.

topics.title: Thesis Statements
topics.short: A thesis states the main point or claim of an essay, in a sentence or two, and the whole essay supports it.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Theses
topics.short: A strong thesis is specific, can be argued or explained, and can be supported in the space you have.

topics.title: Outlining
topics.short: An outline puts the thesis, the main points and their support in order before you draft.

topics.title: Introductions and Hooks
topics.short: An introduction catches interest, gives the reader the context they need, and leads to the thesis.

topics.title: Body Paragraphs
topics.short: Each body paragraph has a topic sentence tied to the thesis, evidence, an explanation of the evidence, and a link to what comes next.

topics.title: Conclusions
topics.short: A conclusion returns to the thesis in new words and shows why it matters, without starting a new argument.

topics.title: The Five-Paragraph Essay
topics.short: An introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion: a starting form that teaches how an essay holds together.

topics.title: Growing Beyond Five Paragraphs
topics.short: Let the argument decide the number and order of paragraphs: longer sections, a paragraph for the other side, and conclusions that do more than restate.

topics.title: Kinds of Evidence
topics.short: Facts, statistics, examples, expert testimony and anecdotes: each kind has strengths and limits.

topics.title: Using Quotations
topics.short: Introduce a quotation, quote the words exactly, cite the source, and explain what the quotation shows.

topics.title: Summarizing
topics.short: A summary gives a source’s main ideas in your own words, much shorter than the original, without your opinions.

topics.title: Paraphrasing
topics.short: A paraphrase restates one passage in your own words and your own sentence structure, about as long as the original, with a citation.

topics.title: Avoiding Plagiarism
topics.short: Give credit for other people’s words and ideas: quotation marks for exact words, and a citation for anything you quote, paraphrase or summarize.

topics.title: Judging Sources
topics.short: Check who wrote it and what they know, the evidence they give, the date, the purpose, and whether other good sources agree.

topics.title: Research Questions
topics.short: Turn a topic into a focused question, find several good sources, and take notes that record where each idea came from.

topics.title: Citation Styles and Their Uses
topics.short: MLA (9th edition, 2021) is used in literature and the humanities, APA (7th edition, 2020) in psychology and the social sciences, and Chicago (18th edition, 2024) in history and publishing.

topics.title: MLA Works Cited Entries
