topics.short: MLA builds each entry from core elements in order: author, title of source, title of container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, publication date, location.

topics.title: MLA In-Text Citations
topics.short: An MLA in-text citation gives the author’s last name and the page, with no comma: (Morrison 45).

topics.title: APA References and Citations
topics.short: APA uses author and date: (Lee, 2020, p. 12) in the text, and reference entries that begin Lee, A. B. (2020).

topics.title: Chicago Notes and Bibliography
topics.short: Chicago’s notes-and-bibliography style uses numbered footnotes or endnotes and a bibliography; Chicago also offers an author-date system.

topics.title: Reading a Citation
topics.short: Pick out the author, the title, the container, the publisher, the date and the pages in a citation in any style.

topics.title: Revising for Ideas and Order
topics.short: Revise by adding, cutting, moving and replacing: check the thesis, the support, the order and the clarity.

topics.title: Giving and Using Feedback
topics.short: Useful feedback is specific, kind and something the writer can act on: name what works, then one or two things to try.

topics.title: Editing and Proofreading
topics.short: Edit for grammar, punctuation, spelling and format. Read slowly and aloud, or on paper, to see what you wrote and not what you meant.

topics.title: Cutting Wordiness
topics.short: Cut words that add nothing: “due to the fact that” → “because,” “in my opinion, I think” → “I think.”

topics.title: Formal Letters
topics.short: A formal letter has the sender’s address, the date, the inside address, a salutation, the body, a closing and a signature, usually in block format.

topics.title: Writing a Clear Email
topics.short: A clear subject line, a greeting, the main point first, short paragraphs, a polite closing and your name.

topics.title: What Is a Sentence?
topics.short: A sentence tells a whole idea: it names who or what, and tells what happens.

topics.title: Words in the Right Order
topics.short: The words of a sentence go in an order that makes sense: usually who or what first, then what happens.

topics.title: Start with a Capital Letter
topics.short: The first word of every sentence begins with a capital letter.

topics.title: Telling Sentences
topics.short: A telling sentence tells something. It ends with a period.

topics.title: Asking Sentences
topics.short: An asking sentence asks something. It ends with a question mark.

topics.title: Exclamations
topics.short: An exclamation shows strong feeling, like surprise, joy or fear. It ends with an exclamation point.

topics.title: Bossy Sentences
topics.short: A command tells someone to do something: “Please shut the door.” It usually ends with a period.

topics.title: Which End Mark?
topics.short: Read the whole sentence. Does it tell, ask or show strong feeling? Then choose the period, question mark or exclamation point.

topics.title: Nouns: Naming Words
topics.short: A noun names a person, a place, an animal or a thing: Grandma, park, puppy, cup.

topics.title: One and More Than One
topics.short: Add -s to most nouns to mean more than one: cats. Add -es after s, x, sh, ch and z: buses, boxes, dishes.

topics.title: Verbs: Action Words
topics.short: A verb tells what someone or something does: run, eat, sing, sleep, think.

topics.title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow
topics.short: Verbs show when something happens: yesterday I walked, today I walk, tomorrow I will walk.

topics.title: Is, Are, Was and Were
topics.short: Use is and was with one; use are and were with more than one, and with you. A verb matches its noun: he hops, we hop.

topics.title: He, She, It and They
topics.short: Pronouns like I, he, she, it, we and they take the place of nouns, so we don’t say the same name again and again.

topics.title: Describing Words
topics.short: Adjectives describe nouns: what color, what size, what shape, how many, and how something looks, sounds or feels.

topics.title: Words for the Five Senses
topics.short: Sense words tell how something looks, sounds, smells, tastes and feels: shiny, crunchy, sweet, soft, loud.

topics.title: Make a Sentence Grow
topics.short: Add describing words and where or when words to a plain sentence: “The dog ran.” → “The little brown dog ran to the lake.”

topics.title: Capital I
topics.short: When you write about yourself, the word I is always a capital letter.

topics.title: Names of People and Pets
topics.short: Names of people and pets begin with capital letters: Sam, Grandma Rose, Dr. Bell, Biscuit.

topics.title: Days, Months and Holidays
topics.short: Days of the week, months and holidays begin with capital letters: Monday, May, Thanksgiving. Seasons do not: spring, summer.

topics.title: Names of Places
topics.short: The name of one special place begins with capitals: Oak Street, Lincoln Park, Texas, the Pacific Ocean.

topics.title: Short Vowel Words
topics.short: In words like cat, bed, pig, hot and bug, one vowel between two consonants usually makes its short sound.

topics.title: Sh, Ch, Th, Wh and Ck
topics.short: Two letters can spell one sound: ship, chip, thin, when, and duck at the end of a short word.

topics.title: The Silent E
topics.short: An e at the end of a short word makes the vowel say its name: cap → cape, kit → kite, hop → hope.

topics.title: Vowel Teams
topics.short: Two letters together often spell one long vowel sound: rain, play, feet, beach, boat, snow.

topics.title: Adding -s, -ed and -ing
topics.short: Add endings to show more than one or when: jumps, jumped, jumping. In short words like hop, double the last letter: hopped, hopping.

topics.title: Tricky Words to Know by Heart
topics.short: Some common words don’t follow the usual patterns: said, was, of, they, could, because, friend. Learn them by heart.

topics.title: Joining with And
topics.short: Use and to join two short sentences that go together: “I have a cat, and she is gray.”

topics.title: Joining with But
topics.short: Use but to join two ideas that are different, or when the second one is a surprise: “I like snow, but my dog does not.”

topics.title: Because and So
topics.short: Because gives a reason. So tells what happened as a result: “I was cold, so I put on a coat.”

topics.title: Commas in a List
topics.short: Put commas between three or more things in a list: “We packed apples, grapes, and cheese.”

topics.title: Who, What and Where
topics.short: A good sentence about a picture tells who is in it, what they are doing, and where.

topics.title: Does It Match the Picture?
topics.short: Choose the sentence that tells what the picture really shows.

topics.title: Stay on Topic
topics.short: All the sentences about one picture or one idea should be about that idea.

topics.title: Tell What It Is About
topics.short: Start with a sentence that names your topic, give some facts, and finish with a sentence that wraps up.

topics.title: The Parts of a Friendly Letter
topics.short: A friendly letter has a date, a greeting, a body, a closing and a signature.

topics.title: Greetings and Closings
topics.short: Start with a greeting like “Dear Grandma,” and end with a closing like “Love,” each with a comma.

topics.title: A Thank-You Note
topics.short: Thank the person, say what you liked about the gift or the kind thing they did, and sign your name.

topics.title: Beginning, Middle and End
topics.short: A story has a beginning (who and where), a middle (what happens) and an end (how it works out).

topics.title: First, Next, Then, Last
topics.short: Time words like first, next, then, after that and last help a reader follow the order.

topics.title: Characters and Setting
topics.short: The characters are who the story is about. The setting is where and when it happens.

topics.title: A Problem and a Fix
topics.short: Many stories have a problem in the middle and a fix at the end.

topics.title: How-To Writing
topics.short: Tell how to do something, with every step in order, so a reader could follow it.

topics.title: I Think, Because
topics.short: An opinion says what you think and gives a reason: “I think dogs are the best pets because they love to play.”

topics.title: Check Your Writing
topics.short: Read your writing back. Check capital letters, spaces between words, end marks, and words spelled the best you can.

topics.title: Fix the Sentence
topics.short: Find and fix every mistake in a sentence: a missing capital, a missing end mark, a wrong word.

topics.title: The Eight Parts of Speech
topics.short: A word’s part of speech names the job it does in a sentence: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction or interjection.

topics.title: Kinds of Nouns
topics.short: Nouns can be common or proper, concrete or abstract, singular or plural, and collective (team, flock).

topics.title: Personal and Possessive Pronouns
topics.short: Personal pronouns change for person (I, you, he), number (I, we) and case (I, me, my). Possessive pronouns show ownership: mine, yours, hers.

topics.title: Other Kinds of Pronouns
topics.short: Reflexive and intensive (myself), demonstrative (this, those), indefinite (someone, all), interrogative (who? which?) and relative (who, which, that) pronouns.

topics.title: Action and Linking Verbs
topics.short: An action verb shows an action. A linking verb (is, seems, becomes, feels) links the subject to a word that renames or describes it.

topics.title: Helping Verbs and Verb Phrases
topics.short: Helping verbs (forms of be, have and do, and modals like can, will, should and might) come before the main verb to make a verb phrase.

topics.title: Adjectives and Articles
topics.short: Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns: which one, what kind, how many. A, an and the are a special kind called articles.

topics.title: Adverbs
topics.short: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. They tell how, when, where, how often and how much.

topics.title: Prepositions
topics.short: A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun, its object, relates to another word: in the box, after lunch, with Sam.

topics.title: Conjunctions
topics.short: Coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equals; subordinating ones (because, although, when, if) start a dependent clause; correlative pairs (either…or) work together.

topics.title: Interjections
topics.short: An interjection shows feeling and stands apart from the rest of the sentence: Wow! Oh, I see. Well, maybe.

topics.title: One Word, Different Jobs
topics.short: Decide a word’s part of speech by the job it does in this sentence, not by the word alone.

topics.title: Complete Subject and Predicate
topics.short: Every sentence splits in two: the complete subject (who or what it is about) and the complete predicate (what is said about it).

topics.title: Simple Subject and Verb
topics.short: The simple subject is the key noun or pronoun in the subject. The simple predicate is the verb, with any helping verbs.

topics.title: Hard-to-Find Subjects
topics.short: Find the subject in questions, in sentences that start with there or here, and in commands, where it is “you,” understood.

topics.title: Four Kinds of Sentences
topics.short: Declarative sentences state, interrogative sentences ask, imperative sentences command, and exclamatory sentences exclaim.

topics.title: Compound Subjects and Verbs
topics.short: Two or more subjects can share one verb (“Ana and Leo sang”), and two or more verbs can share one subject (“Leo sang and danced”).

topics.title: Direct Objects
topics.short: A direct object receives the action of the verb. It answers whom? or what? after an action verb: “Mia kicked the ball.”

topics.title: Indirect Objects
topics.short: An indirect object tells to whom or for whom the action is done: “She gave Sam the map.” It comes between the verb and the direct object.

topics.title: Predicate Nouns and Predicate Adjectives
topics.short: After a linking verb, a predicate noun renames the subject (“Ana became captain”) and a predicate adjective describes it (“Ana is tall”).

topics.title: Object Complements
topics.short: An object complement follows a direct object and renames or describes it: “They named the puppy Biscuit.” “The news made Dad happy.”

topics.title: Prepositional Phrases as Modifiers
topics.short: A prepositional phrase works as an adjective (“the girl with the kite”) or as an adverb (“ran to the park”).

topics.title: Appositives
topics.short: An appositive is a noun or noun phrase that renames the noun beside it: “My aunt, a pilot, flew us home.”

topics.title: Phrases and Clauses
topics.short: A clause has its own subject and verb. A phrase is a group of words without both.

topics.title: Independent and Dependent Clauses
topics.short: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence. A dependent clause begins with a word like because, when or which and can’t stand alone.

topics.title: Participles and Participial Phrases
topics.short: A participle is a verb form used as an adjective: “the barking dog,” “the broken vase,” “Waving her hat, Mia ran.”

topics.title: Gerunds
topics.short: A gerund is an -ing verb form used as a noun: “Swimming is fun.” “She loves baking bread.”

topics.title: Infinitives
topics.short: An infinitive is to plus a verb. It can work as a noun (“To win was her goal”), an adjective (“a book to read”) or an adverb (“came to help”).

topics.title: Adjective Clauses
topics.short: An adjective clause (a relative clause) usually starts with who, whom, whose, which or that, and modifies a noun: “the book that you lent me.”

topics.title: Adverb Clauses
topics.short: An adverb clause starts with a subordinating conjunction (because, when, although, if) and tells when, why, how or under what condition.

topics.title: Noun Clauses
topics.short: A noun clause does a noun’s job, as a subject or an object: “What you said surprised me.” “I know that she left.”

topics.title: Simple and Compound Sentences
topics.short: A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound sentence joins two or more, with a comma and a coordinating conjunction or with a semicolon.

topics.title: Complex Sentences
topics.short: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

topics.title: Compound-Complex Sentences
topics.short: A compound-complex sentence has two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

topics.title: Diagrams: Subject and Verb
topics.short: In a Reed–Kellogg diagram, the subject and the verb sit on a baseline, split by a short line that crosses it.

topics.title: Diagrams: Adjectives and Adverbs
topics.short: Adjectives and adverbs go on slanted lines under the word they modify.

topics.title: Diagrams: Direct and Indirect Objects
topics.short: A direct object follows a short upright line that stops at the baseline. An indirect object sits on a flat line hung under the verb.

topics.title: Diagrams: Complements
topics.short: A predicate noun or adjective follows a line slanted back toward the subject. An object complement follows a line slanted back toward the direct object.

topics.title: Diagrams: Prepositional Phrases
topics.short: A prepositional phrase hangs under the word it modifies: the preposition on a slanted line, its object on a flat line.

topics.title: Diagrams: Compound Parts and Sentences
topics.short: Compound subjects, verbs and objects split into parallel lines joined by a dashed line with the conjunction. A compound sentence stacks two baselines.

topics.title: Diagrams: Appositives and Words Apart
topics.short: An appositive goes in parentheses beside the noun it renames. Interjections and nouns of direct address sit on short lines above the baseline.

topics.title: Diagrams: Participles, Gerunds and Infinitives
topics.short: A participle bends along a curved line under the noun it modifies. A gerund rides a stepped line and an infinitive a bent line (to on the slant); used as nouns, each stands on a forked stand in a noun’s place.

topics.title: Diagrams: Adjective and Adverb Clauses
topics.short: A dependent clause gets its own baseline below. A dotted line joins an adjective clause to its noun at the relative pronoun; an adverb clause hangs from the word it modifies, with the conjunction on the dotted line.

topics.title: Diagrams: Noun Clauses
topics.short: A noun clause sits on a stand in the place a noun would go: subject, direct object or object of a preposition.

topics.title: Sitting to Write
topics.short: Sit tall and back in the chair, feet flat on the floor, with both arms resting on the table.

topics.title: Holding the Pencil
topics.short: Hold the pencil with the thumb and pointer finger, let it rest on the middle finger, a little way up from the point, and hold it lightly.

topics.title: Placing the Paper
topics.short: Keep the paper in front of you and hold it still with your other hand. For cursive, tilt it: top to the left for a right hand, top to the right for a left hand.

topics.title: The Lines We Write On
topics.short: Letters sit on the baseline. Short letters reach the middle line, tall letters reach the top line, and tail letters go below the baseline.

topics.title: The Strokes That Make Letters
topics.short: Every print letter is made of a few strokes: lines down, lines across, slants and circles. Each stroke has a start and a direction.

topics.title: Start at the Top
topics.short: Most strokes start at the top and go down. Tall letters like b, h, k, l and t start at the top line; short letters start at the middle line.

topics.title: Stick Letters: l, i and t
topics.short: l, i and t are made of straight lines: down from the top, then a dot or a cross.

topics.title: Circle Letters: c, o, a, d, g and q
topics.short: Start just below the middle line and curve back around, the way c begins. a, d, g and q add a line down.

topics.title: Down, Up and Over: r, n, m, h, b and p
topics.short: Pull down, then go back up the line and over the hump: r, n, m and h. b and p add a round bump.

topics.title: Slant Letters: v, w, x, y, z and k
topics.short: These letters use slanted lines: down to the right, down to the left, or both.

topics.title: Special Letters: e, f, j, s and u
topics.short: e starts across the middle; f starts with a hook near the top; j has a tail and a dot; s curves back and forth; u goes down, around and up.

topics.title: Tall, Short and Tail Letters
topics.short: Tall letters (b d f h k l t) reach the top line, short letters stay below the middle line, and tail letters (g j p q y) go down below the baseline.

topics.title: Capitals with Straight Lines
topics.short: E, F, H, I, L and T are made of lines down and across. Every capital starts at the top line and reaches the baseline.

topics.title: Capitals with Slants
topics.short: A, K, M, N, V, W, X, Y and Z use slanted lines from the top line to the baseline.

topics.title: Capitals with Curves
topics.short: B, C, D, G, J, O, P, Q, R, S and U use curves; B, D, P and R start with a line down.

topics.title: b, d, p and q
topics.short: b starts with a tall line and then the bump; d starts with a c and then the tall line. p and q go below the baseline.

topics.title: Letters Close Together
topics.short: Letters in a word sit close, but not touching.

topics.title: A Finger Space Between Words
topics.short: Leave about one finger’s width between words.

topics.title: Sitting on the Lines
topics.short: Every letter sits on the baseline and stays the right size for its kind.

topics.title: Copying Neatly
topics.short: Copy a sentence letter by letter: check the spaces, the sizes, the capital at the start and the mark at the end.

topics.title: Writing 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4
topics.short: Write each number from the top: 0 curves around, 1 goes straight down, 2 and 3 curve, 4 goes down, across, then down.

topics.title: Writing 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9
topics.short: 5 goes down and around, then gets its hat; 6 curves down into a loop; 7 goes across, then slants down; 8 is an S that comes back up; 9 is a circle and a line.

topics.title: Numbers That Get Flipped
topics.short: 2, 3, 5, 7 and 9 face a certain way. Check each one: 3 and 5 curve to the right; 9 has its circle on the left.

topics.title: What Cursive Is
topics.short: In cursive the letters of a word are joined, so the pencil stays down. People use it to write quickly, to sign their names, and to read old letters and documents.

topics.title: The Basic Cursive Strokes
topics.short: Most cursive letters are built from an undercurve (a swing up like a smile), an overcurve (a hill), a downcurve (like the start of c) and a slant line.

topics.title: The Cursive Slant
topics.short: All cursive letters lean the same way, like rain blowing in the wind.

topics.title: Cursive i, t, u and w
topics.short: These letters start with an undercurve, slant down and swing up. Dot i and cross t after you finish the word.

topics.title: Loop Letters: e, l, h, k, b and f
topics.short: Swing up into a loop: small for e, tall for l, h, k, b and f. f also has a loop below the baseline.

topics.title: The c Family: a, c, d, g, o and q
topics.short: Swing up, curve back around like c, and close the letter at the top. d goes up tall; g and q go below.

topics.title: Hill Letters: n, m, v, x, y and z
topics.short: Start with an overcurve, a hill, then slant down. m has three hills’ worth of strokes, n two.

topics.title: Cursive r, s, p and j
topics.short: r and s go up to a point a little above the middle line; p and j go down below the baseline.

topics.title: Tricky Connectors: b, o, v and w
topics.short: b, o, v and w end up at the middle line, not on the baseline, so the next letter joins with a little bridge along the top.

topics.title: Cursive Capitals A, C, E and O
topics.short: These capitals start near the top with a curve around to the left.

topics.title: Cursive Capitals H, K, M, N, U, V, W, X, Y and Z
topics.short: Many of these start with a small hook and a hill at the top, then slant down.

topics.title: Cursive Capitals B, F, P, R and T
topics.short: Start with a slant down, then come back up for the bumps of B, P and R; F and T start with a wavy top.

topics.title: Cursive Capitals D, G, I, J, L, Q and S
topics.short: These capitals have shapes of their own: I and J start with a swing up from the middle; L and S loop; cursive Q looks like a 2.

topics.title: Joining Letters
topics.short: Each letter ends with an exit stroke that becomes the next letter’s entry stroke, so the pencil stays down through the word.

topics.title: Capitals That Join and Capitals That Don’t
topics.short: Some cursive capitals join the next letter (A, C, E, H, K, M, N, U and others); some usually stand alone (B, D, O, P, S, V, W and others).

topics.title: Spacing Joined Words
topics.short: End a word with its exit stroke, lift the pencil, and start the next word about one small o’s width away.

topics.title: Writing Sentences in Cursive
topics.short: Start with a cursive capital, join the letters of each word, space the words, and end with a mark.

topics.title: Checking Letter Shapes
topics.short: Look for closed tops (a, d, g, o), clear loops (e, l), round hills (n, m) and even slant.

topics.title: Signing Your Name
topics.short: A signature is your name in your own handwriting, usually in cursive. Write it the same way each time and keep it readable.

topics.title: Reading Cursive Letters
topics.short: Match each cursive letter to its print letter, especially the ones that look different: cursive r, s, z, G, I, J and Q.

topics.title: Reading Cursive Words
topics.short: Read a cursive word letter by letter at first, then as a whole.

topics.title: Reading Old Handwriting
topics.short: Old letters and documents use cursive styles of their time, sometimes with the long s (ſ), which looks much like f but has no crossbar, or only a nub on the left.

topics.title: What Rhetoric Is
topics.short: Rhetoric is the art of using language to inform, persuade or move an audience. Aristotle defined it as the ability to see, in any case, the available means of persuasion.

topics.title: The Rhetorical Situation
topics.short: The writer, the audience, the purpose, the context (the occasion and the need that calls for the text) and the message shape every choice a writer makes.

topics.title: Ethos: The Speaker’s Character
topics.short: Ethos persuades through the character the speaker shows: good sense, good character and goodwill toward the audience.

topics.title: Pathos: The Audience’s Emotions
topics.short: Pathos persuades by putting the audience in a frame of mind, through stories, images and word choice.

topics.title: Logos: The Reasoning
topics.short: Logos persuades through the argument itself: evidence, examples and reasoning that show a claim is true or likely.

topics.title: Identifying Appeals
topics.short: Most passages blend the appeals. Decide which one each sentence leans on most, and how they work together.

topics.title: Kairos: The Right Moment
topics.short: Kairos is the fitting moment: an argument works when it suits its time, place and audience.

topics.title: Kinds of Claims
topics.short: Claims of fact (is it so?), of value (is it good or bad?) and of policy (what should we do?).

topics.title: Patterns of Reasoning
topics.short: Arguments reason from examples (induction), from general principles (deduction), from cause and effect, from comparison and from analogy.

topics.title: The Toulmin Model
topics.short: Stephen Toulmin’s model: a claim, the grounds (data) offered for it, and the warrant that links them, with backing, a qualifier and a rebuttal.

topics.title: Finding Unstated Warrants
topics.short: State the general principle an argument takes for granted, then ask whether the audience would accept it.

topics.title: Qualifiers and Limits
topics.short: Words like usually, most and probably make a claim match its evidence.

topics.title: Weighing Evidence
topics.short: Good evidence is relevant, sufficient, accurate, current where that matters, and fairly represented.

topics.title: Counterarguments
topics.short: State the strongest opposing view fairly, in terms its supporters would accept, before you answer it.

topics.title: Concession and Rebuttal
topics.short: Concede what is true in the other view, then rebut what you can: “Granted, …; but …”

topics.title: The Classical Arrangement
topics.short: The classical oration: introduction (exordium), background (narratio), the claim and its parts (partitio), proof (confirmatio), answers to objections (refutatio) and conclusion (peroratio).

topics.title: Fallacies in Arguments
topics.short: Spot common fallacies in real writing, by the Logic Ladder’s names: attacking the person, straw man, false dilemma, hasty generalization, slippery slope and others.

topics.title: A Defensible Thesis
topics.short: An argument’s thesis takes a position that reasonable people could dispute, and that you can defend with evidence.

topics.title: The Argument Essay
topics.short: A defensible thesis, a line of reasoning, evidence with commentary, and an answer to the other side, in an order that builds.

topics.title: Line of Reasoning and Commentary
topics.short: Commentary explains how each piece of evidence supports the claim, and the reasons build on each other in a logical order.

topics.title: Rhetorical Analysis
topics.short: Rhetorical analysis explains how a writer’s choices serve a purpose for an audience. It doesn’t argue whether you agree.

topics.title: Choices and Effects
topics.short: Name a choice (a story, a contrast, a repetition), then explain its effect on the audience and how it serves the purpose.

topics.title: Common Rhetorical Devices
topics.short: Anaphora, antithesis, parallelism, rhetorical questions, analogy, understatement and other patterns writers use on purpose.

topics.title: Tone and Shifts in Tone
topics.short: Tone is the writer’s attitude, shown by diction and sentence structure. Analysis often turns on where the tone shifts.

topics.title: A Thesis for Rhetorical Analysis
topics.short: Name the writer, the purpose and the main strategies, and say how they serve the purpose.

topics.title: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay
topics.short: Organize by the writer’s strategies or by the text’s sections, with short quotations and commentary on each.

topics.title: Reading Sources Together
topics.short: Find where sources agree, where they disagree, and where they answer different questions.

topics.title: Working Sources into Your Sentences
topics.short: Use signal phrases, partial quotations, brackets for changes and ellipses for cuts, so sources fit your sentences smoothly.

topics.title: The Synthesis Essay
topics.short: Use several sources to support your own argument, with citations. The sources serve your claim; they don’t make it for you.

topics.title: Diction
topics.short: Choose words for precision, connotation and the right level of formality.

topics.title: Concision
topics.short: Omit needless words: cut redundancy, empty phrases, and weak openings like “There is” and “It is.”

topics.title: Active and Passive Voice, Used Well
topics.short: Prefer the active voice when the doer matters. Use the passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant, or to keep the focus on what was acted on.

topics.title: Sentence Variety
topics.short: Vary sentence length and structure: short sentences for emphasis, longer ones for connected ideas.

topics.title: Emphasis and Word Order
topics.short: Put the words you most want remembered at the end of a sentence, where readers give them the most weight.

topics.title: Old Information Before New
topics.short: Begin a sentence with what the reader already knows and end with what is new, so each sentence hands off to the next.

topics.title: Formal and Informal Register
topics.short: Match the register to the audience: contractions, slang, and person (I, you, one) all signal formality.

topics.title: Figures of Speech
topics.short: Metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole and understatement, chosen for their effect.

topics.title: Classic Style Advice
topics.short: Strunk’s Elements of Style (1918) gave rules like “Omit needless words” and “Use the active voice.” Know what the advice is for and when good writers break it.

topics.title: Reading a Prompt
topics.short: Find the task word (analyze, argue, explain), the subject, and any limits before you plan.

topics.title: Timed Writing
topics.short: Read the prompt closely, plan for a few minutes, write a clear thesis, and save time to reread.

topics.title: The College Application Essay
topics.short: A personal essay shows who you are through a specific story and what you made of it, in your own voice.

topics.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
topics.short: A singular subject takes a singular verb (“The dog barks”); a plural subject takes a plural verb (“The dogs bark”).

topics.title: Agreement Past a Phrase in Between
topics.short: The verb agrees with its subject, not with a noun in a phrase that comes between them: “The box of crayons is on the shelf.”

topics.title: Agreement with Compound Subjects
topics.short: Subjects joined by and usually take a plural verb. With or or nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

topics.title: Indefinite Pronouns and Collective Nouns
topics.short: Each, everyone and nobody take singular verbs; both and many take plural ones; some, all and most depend on the noun they refer to. In American English a collective noun like team usually takes a singular verb.

topics.title: Agreement When the Subject Comes Last
topics.short: In questions and in sentences that start with there or here, find the subject after the verb: “There are two reasons.”

topics.title: Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement
topics.short: A pronoun agrees in number and person with the noun it stands for (its antecedent): “The girls packed their bags.”

topics.title: Singular They and Generic Pronouns
topics.short: For a person whose gender is unknown or not the point, writers choose he or she, rewrite in the plural, or use singular they. Style guides differ on which they prefer.

topics.title: Clear Pronoun Reference
topics.short: Each pronoun should point to one clear noun. “When Ana called Mia, she was upset.” Who was upset?

topics.title: Subject and Object Pronouns
topics.short: Use I, he, she, we and they as subjects; use me, him, her, us and them as objects.

topics.title: Pronouns in Pairs
topics.short: To choose the pronoun in a pair, take out the other person: “Sam and I went” (I went); “for Sam and me” (for me); “between you and me.”

topics.title: Who and Whom
topics.short: Who is a subject, like he; whom is an object, like him. Choose by the pronoun’s job in its own clause.

topics.title: Myself and the Other -self Words
topics.short: Use myself when I is already the subject (“I made it myself”) or for emphasis, not in place of I or me.

topics.title: The Simple Tenses
topics.short: The simple past, present and future: I walked, I walk, I will walk.

topics.title: Irregular Verbs
topics.short: Many common verbs make their past forms in their own ways: go, went, gone; see, saw, seen; bring, brought, brought.

topics.title: Progressive Tenses
topics.short: A form of be plus an -ing verb shows an action in progress: I am reading, I was reading, I will be reading.

topics.title: Perfect Tenses
topics.short: A form of have plus a past participle shows an action finished before some time: I have eaten, I had eaten, I will have eaten.

topics.title: Keeping Tenses Consistent
topics.short: Stay in one tense unless the time really changes.

topics.title: Lie and Lay, Sit and Set, Rise and Raise
topics.short: Lay, set and raise take an object (you lay the book down); lie, sit and rise don’t (you lie down).

topics.title: Active and Passive Voice
topics.short: In the active voice the subject acts (“Sam threw the ball”). In the passive voice the subject receives the action (“The ball was thrown by Sam”).

topics.title: Verb Mood
topics.short: The indicative states and asks, the imperative commands, and the subjunctive states wishes and conditions that aren’t true: “If I were you…”

topics.title: Comparing with Adjectives and Adverbs
topics.short: Use -er or more to compare two and -est or most for three or more; a few change form: good, better, best.

topics.title: Adjective or Adverb?
topics.short: Good is an adjective and well is usually an adverb (“She did well”). After a linking verb, use an adjective (“I feel bad”).

topics.title: Double Negatives
topics.short: Standard English uses one negative word per idea: “I don’t have any,” not “I don’t have none.”

topics.title: Misplaced Modifiers
topics.short: Put a modifier next to the word it describes. Only, just and almost go right before the word they limit.

topics.title: Dangling Modifiers
topics.short: An opening phrase must describe the subject that comes right after it: “Walking home, I saw a fox,” not “Walking home, a fox appeared.”

topics.title: Commas in a Series
topics.short: Use commas between three or more items in a series. Style guides differ on the comma before the last and (the serial, or Oxford, comma).

topics.title: Commas in Dates, Places and Direct Address
topics.short: Use commas in dates (May 4, 2025), between a city and its state (Akron, Ohio), after yes and no, and around the name of someone you speak to (“Thanks, Sam.”).

topics.title: Commas in Compound Sentences
topics.short: Put a comma before and, but, or, so or yet when it joins two independent clauses.

topics.title: Commas After Openers
topics.short: Use a comma after an opening dependent clause or a long opening phrase: “When the bell rang, we left.”

topics.title: Commas Between Adjectives
topics.short: Use a comma between coordinate adjectives (“a long, cold winter”) but not between cumulative ones (“a big red barn”).

topics.title: Commas Around Extra Information
topics.short: Set off information the sentence could do without: “My brother, who lives in Ohio, is visiting.” Don’t set off information that identifies which one.

topics.title: Semicolons
topics.short: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses, and separates items in a list when the items already have commas.

topics.title: Colons
topics.short: A colon comes after a complete sentence to introduce a list, an explanation or a quotation.

topics.title: Apostrophes for Possession
topics.short: Singular: the dog’s bone. Plural ending in s: the dogs’ bones. Other plurals: the children’s books.

topics.title: Apostrophes in Contractions
topics.short: In a contraction the apostrophe stands for missing letters: do not → don’t, it is → it’s.

topics.title: Quotation Marks and Dialogue
topics.short: Put a speaker’s exact words in quotation marks. In American style, periods and commas go inside the closing mark.

topics.title: Titles: Italics or Quotation Marks
topics.short: Italicize the titles of long works (books, films, newspapers); put the titles of short works (poems, articles, songs, chapters) in quotation marks.

topics.title: Dashes, Parentheses and Ellipses
topics.short: Dashes set off a sharp break or something to stress; parentheses set off quieter extras; an ellipsis (…) marks words left out of a quotation, or a pause.

topics.title: Hyphens
topics.short: Hyphenate a compound modifier before a noun (“a well-known author”), but usually not after it (“the author is well known”), and numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine.

topics.title: Sentence Fragments
topics.short: A fragment is a piece of a sentence punctuated as a whole one: it lacks a subject, a verb, or an independent clause (“Because it rained.”).

topics.title: Run-On Sentences
topics.short: A run-on, or fused sentence, runs two independent clauses together with no punctuation between them: “I ran I won.”

topics.title: Comma Splices
topics.short: A comma alone can’t join two independent clauses: “It rained, we stayed inside” is a comma splice.

topics.title: Five Ways to Fix a Run-On
topics.short: Use a period, a comma and a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, a subordinating word, or (when the second part explains the first) a colon.

topics.title: Parallel Lists
topics.short: Items in a list or a series take the same grammatical form: “hiking, swimming, and biking.”

topics.title: Parallel Pairs and Comparisons
topics.short: Words joined by both…and, either…or, not only…but also, and comparisons with than or as need matching forms.

topics.title: Capitalization Rules
topics.short: Capitalize proper nouns and proper adjectives, titles right before a name, and the names of regions, but not compass directions or titles used alone.

topics.title: Capitalizing Titles
topics.short: Capitalize the first and last words and the important words of a title. Style guides differ on short words in the middle.

topics.title: Sound-Alike Words
topics.short: Its and it’s, there, their and they’re, your and you’re, to, too and two, and then and than sound alike but mean different things.

topics.title: Affect, Effect and Other Tricky Pairs
topics.short: Affect and effect, accept and except, fewer and less, imply and infer, lose and loose, complement and compliment.

topics.title: Standard Written Forms
topics.short: Write could have (not could of), supposed to, a lot, regardless and all right: the forms that formal writing expects.

topics.title: Rules That Aren’t Rules
topics.short: Splitting an infinitive, ending a sentence with a preposition and starting one with And or But are not grammar errors, though some readers still object. Know the range.

topics.title: Absolute and Relative Location
topics.short: Absolute location is an exact address or coordinates; relative location describes a place by what is around it.

topics.title: Site and Situation
topics.short: A place's site is its own physical features (a hill, a harbor, a river crossing); its situation is how it connects to places around it.

topics.title: Formal, Functional and Perceptual Regions
topics.short: A formal region shares a trait (like a language); a functional region is tied to a central point (like a TV market); a perceptual region exists in people's minds (like "the South").

topics.title: Scales of Analysis
topics.short: The same question can be studied at the global, national, regional or local scale, and the pattern can look different at each one.

topics.title: Distance Decay and Time-Space Compression
topics.short: Interaction falls off with distance (distance decay), but faster travel and communication make far places feel closer (time-space compression).

topics.title: Density, Concentration and Pattern
topics.short: Density is how many per area, concentration is how close together they are, and pattern is their arrangement (clustered, dispersed, linear).

topics.title: Geographic Data
topics.short: Geographers use numbers from censuses and satellites (quantitative data) and words and pictures from interviews and fieldwork (qualitative data).

topics.title: Choosing a Thematic Map
topics.short: Choropleth maps shade areas by a rate, dot maps show where things are, graduated symbols show amounts, isolines join equal values, and cartograms resize places by a number.

topics.title: People and Environment
topics.short: Environmental determinism said the environment sets how people live; possibilism says it offers choices; today geographers study how people and environments shape each other, and what makes use sustainable.

topics.title: Where People Live
topics.short: Most people live in East Asia, South Asia and Europe, on low, well-watered land near coasts and rivers; dry, cold and high places have few people.

topics.title: Three Kinds of Density
topics.short: Arithmetic density is people per total land; physiological density is people per farmland; agricultural density is farmers per farmland.

topics.title: Birth Rates, Death Rates and Natural Increase
topics.short: The crude birth and death rates count births and deaths per 1,000 people a year; the rate of natural increase is their difference, as a percent.

topics.title: Fertility, Infant Mortality and Life Expectancy
topics.short: The total fertility rate is the average number of children per woman; about 2.1 replaces the population; infant mortality and life expectancy measure health.

topics.title: Doubling Time
topics.short: A population growing at r percent a year doubles in about 70 ÷ r years (the rule of 70).

topics.title: Reading Population Pyramids
topics.short: A population pyramid shows how many males and females are in each age group; its shape tells the story of births, deaths and migration.

topics.title: Pyramid Shapes
topics.short: A wide base means fast growth, straight sides mean slow or no growth, and a narrow base means a shrinking, aging population.

topics.title: The Dependency Ratio
topics.short: The dependency ratio compares people under 15 and over 64 with people aged 15 to 64, who are most likely to work.

topics.title: The Demographic Transition Model
topics.short: As countries develop, death rates fall first and birth rates later, moving through stages from high birth and death rates to low ones.

topics.title: The Epidemiological Transition
topics.short: As countries develop, the main causes of death shift from infectious diseases and famine to chronic diseases such as heart disease and cancer.

topics.title: Malthus and His Critics
topics.short: Thomas Malthus (1798) argued that population would outgrow food; critics point to rising farm output and falling birth rates; neo-Malthusians warn about resources.

topics.title: Population Policies
topics.short: Pronatalist policies encourage births (as in France, and in Singapore since 1987), antinatalist policies discourage them (as in China from 1980 to 2015), and immigration policies shape who arrives.

topics.title: Women, Education and Fertility
topics.short: Where more girls finish school and more women work for pay, families tend to have fewer children, later.

topics.title: Kinds of Migration
topics.short: Migration can be internal or international, voluntary or forced; chain migration follows family and friends; step migration happens in stages.

topics.title: Push and Pull Factors
topics.short: Push factors drive people away (war, few jobs, drought); pull factors draw them (jobs, safety, family); intervening obstacles stand in between.

topics.title: Ravenstein's Laws of Migration
topics.short: Ernst Ravenstein (1880s) observed that most migrants move short distances, long-distance migrants head for big cities, and each flow produces a counterflow.

topics.title: Refugees, Asylum Seekers and Internally Displaced People
topics.short: A refugee has fled their country and cannot safely return; an asylum seeker has asked for protection but awaits a decision; internally displaced people fled but stayed inside their country.

topics.title: Effects of Migration
topics.short: Migration brings remittances home and workers to new places, and can mean a brain drain from the sending country and a gain for the receiving one.

topics.title: Culture Traits, Folk and Popular Culture
topics.short: A culture trait is one part of a culture, such as a food or a holiday; folk culture is local and traditional, popular culture spreads widely and changes fast.

topics.title: Cultural Landscapes
topics.short: The cultural landscape is the visible mark people leave on the land: buildings, fields, signs and places of worship.

topics.title: How Things Spread
topics.short: Relocation diffusion moves with people; expansion diffusion spreads outward as contagious (person to person), hierarchical (big places first) or stimulus (the idea changes as it spreads).

topics.title: Language Families
topics.short: Languages that share an ancestor form a family; Indo-European has the most speakers, then Sino-Tibetan; others include Afro-Asiatic, Niger-Congo and Austronesian.

topics.title: Branches of Indo-European
topics.short: Indo-European branches include Germanic (English, German), Romance (Spanish, French), Balto-Slavic (Russian, Polish) and Indo-Iranian (Hindi, Persian).

topics.title: Lingua Franca, Pidgins and Creoles
topics.short: A lingua franca is a shared language for trade or work; a pidgin is a simple mix for contact; a creole is a pidgin that became a mother tongue.

topics.title: Universalizing and Ethnic Religions
topics.short: Universalizing religions, such as Christianity, Islam and Buddhism, seek members everywhere; ethnic religions, such as Hinduism and Judaism, are tied to one people and place.

topics.title: Where Religions Began and Spread
topics.short: Christianity, Judaism and Islam began in Southwest Asia, Hinduism and Buddhism in South Asia; they spread by trade, migration, missionaries and empires.

topics.title: When Cultures Meet
topics.short: Acculturation is adopting traits while keeping one's culture, assimilation is merging into the larger culture, and syncretism blends two cultures into something new.

topics.title: Globalization and Culture
topics.short: Global media, trade and travel spread popular culture, which can push out local traditions and also lead people to protect and revive them.

topics.title: States, Nations and Nation-States
topics.short: A state is a country with its own government and borders; a nation is a people who share a culture and identity; a nation-state is where the two match.

topics.title: Multinational States and Stateless Nations
topics.short: A multinational state holds several nations; a stateless nation, such as the Kurds, has no state of its own; a multistate nation lives across several states.

topics.title: Sovereignty and Territoriality
topics.short: Sovereignty is a state's right to govern its territory without outside control; territoriality is people's urge to claim and defend space.

topics.title: Kinds of Boundaries
topics.short: Boundaries can follow physical features, cultural lines or straight geometric lines, and can be drawn before settlement (antecedent), after it (subsequent) or imposed from outside (superimposed).

topics.title: Boundary Disputes
topics.short: Disputes can be over where a line is (definitional or locational), how it works (operational) or the resources it divides (allocational).

topics.title: Boundaries at Sea
topics.short: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a country controls its territorial sea to 12 nautical miles and has rights to fish and minerals in an exclusive economic zone out to 200.

topics.title: Shapes of States
topics.short: States can be compact (Poland), elongated (Chile), prorupted (Thailand), perforated (South Africa) or fragmented (Indonesia).

topics.title: Unitary and Federal States
topics.short: A unitary state concentrates power in the central government (France, Japan); a federal state shares power with states or provinces (the United States, India).

topics.title: Forces That Unite and Divide
topics.short: Centripetal forces, such as a shared language or national symbols, pull a state together; centrifugal forces, such as regional differences, can pull it apart and lead to devolution.

topics.title: Organizations Above the State
topics.short: Supranational organizations, such as the UN, the European Union, NATO, the African Union and ASEAN, link states for trade, defense or cooperation.

topics.title: Electoral Districts
topics.short: Legislative districts are redrawn after each census; gerrymandering draws them to favor one group, by packing its opponents' voters into a few districts or cracking them across many.

topics.title: Where Farming Began
topics.short: Farming began about 10,000 to 12,000 years ago in several hearths, including the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica and the Andes.

topics.title: Agricultural Revolutions
topics.short: The first came with farming itself; the second, in Britain in the 1700s, brought new tools and crop rotations; the Green Revolution (1940s-1970s) brought high-yield seeds, fertilizer and irrigation.

topics.title: Intensive and Extensive Farming
topics.short: Intensive farming puts much labor or capital on small plots (market gardens, rice paddies); extensive farming uses large areas with little input (ranching, nomadic herding).

topics.title: Subsistence and Commercial Farming
topics.short: Subsistence farmers grow food mainly for their own families; commercial farmers grow crops and animals to sell.

topics.title: Farming and Climate
topics.short: Plantations grow in the tropics, Mediterranean farms grow grapes and olives, dairy farms sit near cities, grain grows on the plains, and herders live in dry lands.

topics.title: The von Thünen Model
topics.short: Von Thünen (1826) showed farm uses forming rings around a market town: perishable goods and dairy closest, then forest, grains, and ranching farthest out.

topics.title: Rural Settlements and Survey Patterns
topics.short: Rural settlements can be clustered, dispersed or linear; land was divided by metes and bounds, the rectangular township-and-range survey, or long lots.

topics.title: Debates About Food
topics.short: People debate genetically modified crops, organic farming, large and small farms, and food deserts; geographers lay out the evidence and the trade-offs.

topics.title: Urbanization
topics.short: Urbanization is the growth in the share of people living in cities; it is fastest today in Africa and Asia.

topics.title: Why Cities Grow Where They Do
topics.short: Cities grow at good sites (harbors, river crossings, defensible hills) with good situations (crossroads of trade).

topics.title: Central Place Theory
topics.short: Christaller (1933) showed how towns serve the area around them: a good's threshold is the market it needs, and its range is how far people will travel for it.

topics.title: The Rank-Size Rule and Primate Cities
topics.short: In many countries the nth largest city has about 1/n the people of the largest; a primate city is more than twice as large as the next.

topics.title: Models of North American Cities
topics.short: The concentric zone model (Burgess), the sector model (Hoyt) and the multiple nuclei model (Harris and Ullman) each describe how a city's land uses are arranged.

topics.title: Models of Cities Around the World
topics.short: The Latin American city model has a wealthy spine and outer squatter settlements; models of African and Southeast Asian cities show colonial and market districts.

topics.title: Urban Challenges and Responses
topics.short: Cities face sprawl, traffic, housing costs, informal settlements and segregation; responses include public transit, new urbanism, smart growth and redevelopment, each with debated effects.

topics.title: Sectors of the Economy
topics.short: The primary sector takes from the earth (farming, mining), the secondary makes things, the tertiary provides services, and the quaternary and quinary handle information and top decisions.

topics.title: The Spread of Industry
topics.short: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s and spread to Europe, North America and Japan, and later to East Asia and beyond.

topics.title: Weber's Least Cost Theory
topics.short: Alfred Weber (1909) argued factories locate to keep transport and labor costs lowest; bulk-reducing industries locate near raw materials, bulk-gaining near markets.

topics.title: Measuring Development
topics.short: GDP and GNI per capita measure income; the Human Development Index (UNDP) combines life expectancy, schooling and income; other indexes measure gender equality.

topics.title: Theories of Development
topics.short: Rostow's stages of growth (1960) see every country on one path; Wallerstein's world-systems theory sees a core, semi-periphery and periphery linked by trade; dependency theory stresses unequal ties.

topics.title: Trade and Globalization
topics.short: Countries trade by comparative advantage; supply chains, outsourcing and special economic zones spread production around the world, with gains and costs.

topics.title: Sustainable Development
topics.short: Sustainable development meets today's needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs; the UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals (2015) set targets for 2030.

topics.title: What Is a Map?
topics.short: A map is a drawing of a place as if you were looking down on it from the sky.

topics.title: A Bird's-Eye View
topics.short: From above, a table looks like a rectangle and a ball looks like a circle; match each thing to its top view.

topics.title: A Map of a Room
topics.short: A map of a room shows where the bed, the table and the door are, drawn smaller than the real room.

topics.title: Map Symbols
topics.short: A symbol is a small picture or shape on a map that stands for a real thing, like a tree, a house, a road or a school.

topics.title: The Map Key
topics.short: The key (also called the legend) is the box that tells what each symbol on the map means.

topics.title: Colors on a Map
topics.short: On many maps blue means water, green means parks, forests or low land, and brown or tan means mountains or dry land.

topics.title: The Parts of a Map
topics.short: Most maps have a title, a key, a compass rose and a scale: together they say what, where and how far.

topics.title: Where Is It?
topics.short: Words like left, right, above, below, next to, between, near and far tell where things are.

topics.title: North, South, East and West
topics.short: The four cardinal directions are north, south, east and west; on most maps north is at the top.

topics.title: The Compass Rose
topics.short: A compass rose shows the directions on a map; going clockwise from the top they are north, east, south and west.

topics.title: Following Directions on a Map
topics.short: Follow steps like "go 2 blocks north, then 3 blocks east" to find where you end up.

topics.title: In-Between Directions
topics.short: Northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest are halfway between the cardinal directions.

topics.title: The Sun Shows the Way
topics.short: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so morning sunlight comes from the east.

topics.title: Using a Compass
topics.short: A compass needle turns to point north; once you know north, you can find every other direction.

topics.title: Finding a Square on a Grid
topics.short: A grid map has letters along one edge and numbers along another, so every square has a name like B3.

topics.title: Name the Square
topics.short: Look at where a thing is on a grid map, then name its square with its letter and number.

topics.title: Routes on a Map
topics.short: A route is the way you travel from one place to another; on a map you can trace it and count the blocks.

topics.title: How Far? The Scale Bar
topics.short: A scale bar shows how far a length on the map is in real life, like 1 inch for 1 mile.

topics.title: An Address
topics.short: An address tells exactly where a home is: a house number, a street, a town or city, a state and a ZIP code.

topics.title: Places Inside Places
topics.short: Your home is in a neighborhood, in a town or city, in a state, in a country, on a continent, on planet Earth.

topics.title: City, Suburb and Country
topics.short: A city is a big, busy town; a suburb is a town of homes near a city; rural places have farms, fields and few houses.

topics.title: The United States and Its States
topics.short: The United States is a country made of 50 states; each state has its own shape on the map.

topics.title: Capital Cities
topics.short: A capital is the city where a country's or a state's government meets; Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States.

topics.title: Our Neighbors: Canada and Mexico
topics.short: The United States is in North America; Canada is to the north and Mexico is to the south.

topics.title: Land and Water
topics.short: Earth has land and water; about 71 out of every 100 parts of its surface are water, mostly ocean.

topics.title: Mountains, Hills and Valleys
topics.short: A mountain is very high land, a hill is lower and rounder, and a valley is the low land between them.

topics.title: Plains and Plateaus
topics.short: A plain is wide, flat, low land; a plateau is flat land high up, with steep sides.

topics.title: Islands and Peninsulas
topics.short: An island is land with water all around it; a peninsula has water on three sides and joins the mainland on one.

topics.title: Oceans, Lakes and Rivers
topics.short: An ocean is a huge body of salt water; a lake has land all around it; a river is water flowing across the land.

topics.title: A River's Journey
topics.short: A river starts at its source, flows downhill, gets help from smaller rivers called tributaries, and ends at its mouth.

topics.title: Bays, Gulfs and Coasts
topics.short: A coast is where land meets the sea; a bay is part of the sea that curves into the land, and a gulf is a very large bay.

topics.title: Opposite Pairs
topics.short: Some land and water shapes are opposites: an island and a lake, a peninsula and a bay, an isthmus and a strait.

topics.title: Deserts, Forests and Grasslands
topics.short: A desert gets very little rain, a forest is covered with trees, and a grassland is wide open land covered with grass.

topics.title: The Globe
topics.short: A globe is a small, round model of Earth that shows land and water in their true shapes.

topics.title: Globe or Flat Map?
topics.short: A flat map is easy to carry and shows the whole world at once, but it stretches some places; a globe does not.

topics.title: The Seven Continents
topics.short: The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.

topics.title: Find the Continents
topics.short: Find each continent on a world map by its shape and its place: Asia is the biggest, Australia the smallest, Antarctica at the bottom.

topics.title: The Five Oceans
topics.short: The five oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic and Southern; the Pacific is the biggest and the Arctic the smallest.

topics.title: Animals Around the World
topics.short: Many animals live wild on only one continent: kangaroos in Australia, emperor penguins on Antarctica, giraffes in Africa.

topics.title: The Equator
topics.short: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth, halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole.

topics.title: The North and South Poles
topics.short: The North Pole is the farthest point north on Earth, in the Arctic Ocean; the South Pole is the farthest south, on Antarctica.

topics.title: Halves of the World
topics.short: The equator cuts Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres; another line splits it into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.

topics.title: Where Is the United States?
topics.short: The United States is in North America, between Canada and Mexico, with the Atlantic Ocean to the east and the Pacific to the west.

topics.title: Fifty States and a Capital
topics.short: The country has 50 states and the District of Columbia; 48 states touch one another, and Alaska and Hawaii stand apart.

topics.title: U.S. Territories
topics.short: Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa are U.S. territories, not states.

topics.title: Regions of the United States
topics.short: The U.S. Census Bureau groups the states into four regions: the Northeast, the Midwest, the South and the West.

topics.title: State Postal Codes
topics.short: Each state has a two-letter postal code, such as CA for California, TX for Texas and NY for New York.

topics.title: States of the Northeast
topics.short: Find the nine states of the Northeast: the six New England states and New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania.

topics.title: Capitals of the Northeast
topics.short: Match each Northeastern state with its capital, such as Albany for New York and Boston for Massachusetts.

topics.title: States of the Midwest
topics.short: Find the twelve Midwestern states, from Ohio in the east to North Dakota, Nebraska and Kansas in the west.

topics.title: Capitals of the Midwest
topics.short: Match each Midwestern state with its capital, such as Springfield for Illinois and Saint Paul for Minnesota.

topics.title: States of the South Atlantic
topics.short: Find the South Atlantic states, from Delaware and Maryland down the coast to Florida, plus West Virginia and Washington, D.C.

topics.title: Capitals of the South Atlantic
topics.short: Match each South Atlantic state with its capital, such as Tallahassee for Florida and Raleigh for North Carolina.

topics.title: States of the South Central
topics.short: Find the eight South Central states: Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama and Mississippi, and Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas.

topics.title: Capitals of the South Central
topics.short: Match each South Central state with its capital, such as Austin for Texas and Nashville for Tennessee.

topics.title: States of the Mountain West
topics.short: Find the eight Mountain states: Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico.

topics.title: Capitals of the Mountain West
topics.short: Match each Mountain state with its capital, such as Denver for Colorado and Carson City for Nevada.

topics.title: States of the Pacific
topics.short: Find the five Pacific states: Washington, Oregon, California, Alaska and Hawaii.

topics.title: Capitals of the Pacific
topics.short: Match each Pacific state with its capital, such as Sacramento for California and Juneau for Alaska.

topics.title: All Fifty States
topics.short: Find any state on the map of the whole country, and name a state from its place or its shape.

topics.title: All Fifty Capitals
topics.short: Name the capital of any state, or the state that a capital belongs to.

topics.title: Neighboring States
topics.short: Name the states that share a border with a state; Tennessee and Missouri each touch eight others, and Maine touches only one.

topics.title: Landform Regions
topics.short: From east to west: the Coastal Plain, the Appalachian Mountains, the Central Lowland, the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the high basins and plateaus, and the Pacific mountains.

topics.title: Mountain Ranges
topics.short: The Appalachians run near the East Coast; the Rockies run from New Mexico to Montana and on into Canada; the Sierra Nevada and the Cascades rise near the Pacific.

topics.title: Highest and Lowest Places
topics.short: Denali in Alaska is the highest peak in North America (20,310 feet); Badwater Basin in Death Valley is the lowest point (282 feet below sea level).

topics.title: The Continental Divide
topics.short: Along the high Rockies runs the Continental Divide: rain on its west side flows toward the Pacific, rain on its east side toward the Atlantic and the Gulf.

topics.title: Major Rivers
topics.short: Find the Mississippi, Missouri, Ohio, Colorado, Columbia and Rio Grande rivers and the states they pass through.

topics.title: The Mississippi River System
topics.short: The Missouri, Ohio and Arkansas rivers flow into the Mississippi, and the Tennessee flows into the Ohio; the Mississippi carries all their water to the Gulf.

topics.title: The Great Lakes
topics.short: The five Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario ("HOMES"); Lake Michigan is the only one entirely inside the United States.

topics.title: Coasts, Bays and Peninsulas
topics.short: Find the Atlantic, Gulf and Pacific coasts, Chesapeake Bay, Cape Cod, the Florida Peninsula, Puget Sound and San Francisco Bay.

topics.title: Deserts of the United States
topics.short: The four big deserts are the Mojave, the Sonoran, the Chihuahuan and the Great Basin, all in the West and Southwest.

topics.title: Alaska and Hawaii
topics.short: Alaska is the largest state, with glaciers, mountains and tundra; Hawaii is a chain of volcanic islands in the middle of the Pacific.

topics.title: What Is a National Park?
topics.short: National parks protect special places for everyone; Yellowstone (1872) was the first, and the National Park Service has run the parks since 1916.

topics.title: National Parks of the West
topics.short: Find Yellowstone, Yosemite, the Grand Canyon, Zion, Glacier, Rocky Mountain, Olympic, Denali and other parks of the West.

topics.title: National Parks of the Middle and East
topics.short: Find the Great Smoky Mountains, Acadia, the Everglades, Shenandoah, Mammoth Cave, Big Bend and other parks east of the Rockies.

topics.title: Famous Landmarks
topics.short: Match landmarks to their states: the Statue of Liberty (New York), Mount Rushmore (South Dakota), the Golden Gate Bridge (California), the Gateway Arch (Missouri).

topics.title: U.S. Time Zones
topics.short: The 50 states span six time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific, Alaska and Hawaii-Aleutian; it gets earlier as you go west.

topics.title: What Time Is It There?
topics.short: Count the zones between two places and add hours going east or subtract going west.

topics.title: Daylight Saving Time
topics.short: In most states, clocks move ahead an hour in spring and back in fall; Hawaii and most of Arizona stay on standard time all year.

topics.title: Climate Regions
topics.short: Hot, humid summers in the Southeast; cold winters in the North; dry lands in the Southwest; mild, rainy winters on the Pacific coast; tropical Hawaii; cold Alaska.

topics.title: Where Storms Strike
topics.short: Hurricanes strike the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, tornadoes are most common on the Great Plains and in the South, and earthquakes are most common in the West and Alaska.

topics.title: The Largest Cities
topics.short: New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston and Phoenix are the largest U.S. cities by population (2020 Census).

topics.title: Most and Fewest People
topics.short: California, Texas, Florida, New York and Pennsylvania have the most people; Wyoming has the fewest (2020 Census).

topics.title: Crowded and Uncrowded
topics.short: Population density is people per square mile: New Jersey is the most crowded state and Alaska the least.

topics.title: What Grows Where
topics.short: Iowa and Illinois lead in corn, Kansas and North Dakota in wheat, Texas in cotton, Idaho in potatoes, and California in fruits and vegetables.

topics.title: The First Thirteen States
topics.short: The thirteen original states were the colonies along the Atlantic coast; Delaware was the first to approve the Constitution, in 1787.

topics.title: Land Added to the Country
topics.short: The Louisiana Purchase (1803), Florida (1819), Texas (1845), the Oregon Country (1846), the Mexican Cession (1848), Alaska (1867) and Hawaii (1898).

topics.title: When the States Joined
topics.short: Put states in order of joining: Delaware first (1787) and Hawaii last (1959); many Western states joined around 1890.

topics.title: Parallels and Meridians
topics.short: Parallels (lines of latitude) run east and west around the globe; meridians (lines of longitude) run north and south from pole to pole.

topics.title: Latitude
topics.short: Latitude tells how many degrees north or south of the equator a place is, from 0° at the equator to 90° at each pole.

topics.title: Longitude
topics.short: Longitude tells how many degrees east or west of the prime meridian (through Greenwich, England) a place is, up to 180°.

topics.title: Reading Coordinates
topics.short: Give a place's location as latitude first, then longitude: Washington, D.C., is at about 39° N, 77° W.

topics.title: Find a Place by Its Coordinates
topics.short: Go to the latitude line, then along it to the longitude line, and name the city or country where they meet.

topics.title: The Tropics and the Polar Circles
topics.short: The Tropic of Cancer (about 23.4° N), the Tropic of Capricorn (23.4° S), the Arctic Circle (66.6° N) and the Antarctic Circle (66.6° S).

topics.title: Coordinates and Hemispheres
topics.short: The letters in a place's coordinates tell its two hemispheres: 34° S, 151° E (Sydney) is in the Southern and Eastern Hemispheres.

topics.title: Degrees and Minutes
topics.short: A degree has 60 minutes, so 40° 30′ is 40.5°; GPS often writes south and west as negative numbers.

topics.title: How Far Is a Degree?
topics.short: One degree of latitude is about 111 km (69 miles) everywhere; a degree of longitude shrinks from 111 km at the equator to nothing at the poles.

topics.title: Why Flat Maps Stretch
topics.short: You cannot flatten a ball without stretching or tearing it, so every flat world map changes some sizes, shapes, distances or directions.

topics.title: The Mercator Projection
topics.short: Mercator keeps shapes and directions true in small areas, which made it good for sailing, but it makes lands near the poles look far too big.

topics.title: Equal-Area Maps
topics.short: Equal-area projections, such as Gall-Peters, Mollweide and Equal Earth, show every country at its true size compared with others, but bend shapes.

topics.title: Compromise Maps
topics.short: Robinson and Winkel tripel maps keep nothing perfectly but stretch everything only a little; many atlases use them for world maps.

topics.title: Seeing Distortion with Circles
topics.short: Draw same-size circles all over the globe and project them: where the circles grow, the map enlarges areas; where they squash, it bends shapes.

topics.title: Map Scale
topics.short: A scale such as 1:100,000 means 1 unit on the map stands for 100,000 of the same unit on the ground.

topics.title: Kinds of Maps
topics.short: Political maps show borders and cities, physical maps show landforms, and thematic maps show one topic, such as rainfall or population.

topics.title: GPS, GIS and Satellite Images
topics.short: GPS finds your position from satellite signals, satellites photograph Earth, and a GIS stacks map layers to answer questions.

topics.title: Why We Have Time Zones
topics.short: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, 15° each hour, so noon moves west around the world; time zones are about 15° wide.

topics.title: Time Around the World
topics.short: Use UTC offsets to find the time somewhere else: subtract your offset to get UTC, then add the other place's offset.

topics.title: The International Date Line
topics.short: The date line runs near 180° longitude; crossing it going west, you skip ahead one day; going east, you go back one day.

topics.title: The Continents Compared
topics.short: Asia is the largest continent in area and people; Australia is the smallest; Antarctica has no permanent residents.

topics.title: Oceans and Seas
topics.short: Find the oceans and major seas: the Mediterranean, Caribbean, Arabian, South China, North, Black, Red and Bering Seas.

topics.title: Great Rivers of the World
topics.short: Find the Nile, Amazon, Yangtze, Mississippi, Congo, Ganges, Mekong, Danube and Volga, and the continents they flow through.

topics.title: Mountains of the World
topics.short: The Himalayas hold Mount Everest (8,849 m, the highest); the Andes are the longest range above sea level; find the Rockies, Alps, Urals and Atlas too.

topics.title: Deserts of the World
topics.short: The Sahara is the largest hot desert; the Atacama is the driest place outside the poles; Antarctica is the largest desert of all.

topics.title: Lakes and Waterfalls
topics.short: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake by area, Lake Baikal the deepest, Lake Superior the largest freshwater lake by area; Angel Falls is the tallest waterfall.

topics.title: Islands and Peninsulas
topics.short: Greenland is the largest island; find New Guinea, Borneo, Madagascar and Great Britain, and the Arabian, Iberian, Scandinavian, Italian and Korean peninsulas.

topics.title: Straits and Canals
topics.short: Straits such as Gibraltar, the Bosporus, Hormuz, Malacca and Bering, and the Panama and Suez Canals, link seas and carry much of the world's shipping.

topics.title: What Controls Climate
topics.short: Latitude, height above sea level, nearness to the ocean, ocean currents, winds and mountains together set a place's climate.

topics.title: World Climate Zones
topics.short: Geographers group climates into five main types: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar (the Köppen groups A to E), plus highland climates in mountains.

topics.title: Reading a Climograph
topics.short: A climograph shows a place's average temperature (a line) and rainfall (bars) for each month; use it to tell the climate and the hemisphere.

topics.title: Biomes of the World
topics.short: A biome is a large region with similar climate, plants and animals: tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, grassland, temperate forest, Mediterranean, taiga and tundra.

topics.title: Matching Biomes and Climates
topics.short: Temperature and rainfall decide the biome: hot and wet makes rainforest, hot with a dry season savanna, cold and dry tundra.

topics.title: How Many Countries?
topics.short: There are 193 UN member states and 2 observer states (the Holy See and Palestine); places like Taiwan and Kosovo govern themselves but are not UN members.

topics.title: Landlocked Countries
topics.short: A landlocked country has no coast on the open ocean; Kazakhstan is the largest, and Bolivia and Paraguay are the two in South America.

topics.title: Countries of North and Central America
topics.short: Find Canada, the United States, Mexico and the seven countries of Central America, from Guatemala and Belize to Panama.

topics.title: Capitals of North and Central America
topics.short: Match each country with its capital, from Ottawa and Mexico City to Panama City.

topics.title: Countries of the Caribbean
topics.short: Find the thirteen island countries of the Caribbean, from Cuba, Jamaica and the Bahamas to Trinidad and Tobago.

topics.title: Capitals of the Caribbean
topics.short: Match each Caribbean country with its capital, such as Havana (Cuba), Kingston (Jamaica) and Nassau (Bahamas).

topics.title: Countries of South America
topics.short: Find the twelve countries of South America; Brazil is the largest and touches every country except Chile and Ecuador.

topics.title: Capitals of South America
topics.short: Match each South American country with its capital, such as Brasília (Brazil) and Buenos Aires (Argentina).

topics.title: Physical Features of the Americas
topics.short: The Rockies and Andes run down the west side, the Amazon drains the largest rainforest, and plains such as the Great Plains and the Pampas lie in the middle.

topics.title: Countries of Northern Europe
topics.short: Find the ten countries of Northern Europe: the United Kingdom and Ireland, the Nordic countries and the Baltic states.

topics.title: Capitals of Northern Europe
topics.short: Match each country of Northern Europe with its capital, such as Oslo (Norway) and Stockholm (Sweden).

topics.title: Countries of Western Europe
topics.short: Find the nine countries of Western Europe, from France and Germany to the tiny states of Monaco and Liechtenstein.

topics.title: Capitals of Western Europe
topics.short: Match each country of Western Europe with its capital, such as Berlin (Germany) and Bern (Switzerland).

topics.title: Countries of Southern Europe
topics.short: Find the countries of Southern Europe, from Portugal and Spain through Italy to Greece and the Balkans.

topics.title: Capitals of Southern Europe
topics.short: Match each country of Southern Europe with its capital, such as Lisbon (Portugal) and Belgrade (Serbia).

topics.title: Countries of Eastern Europe
topics.short: Find the ten countries of Eastern Europe, from Poland and Czechia to Ukraine and Russia.

topics.title: Capitals of Eastern Europe
topics.short: Match each country of Eastern Europe with its capital, such as Warsaw (Poland) and Kyiv (Ukraine).

topics.title: Physical Features of Europe
topics.short: Find the Alps, Pyrenees, Carpathians and Urals, the North European Plain, the Danube and Rhine, and the Iberian, Italian, Balkan and Scandinavian peninsulas.

topics.title: North Africa: Countries and Capitals
topics.short: Find Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Sudan and their capitals, and Western Sahara, a disputed territory.

topics.title: Countries of West Africa
topics.short: Find the sixteen countries of West Africa, from Senegal and Mali to Nigeria, the most populous country in Africa.

topics.title: Capitals of West Africa
topics.short: Match each West African country with its capital, such as Abuja (Nigeria) and Accra (Ghana).

topics.title: Countries of Central Africa
topics.short: Find the nine countries of Central Africa, including the two Congos, Cameroon, Chad and Angola.

topics.title: Capitals of Central Africa
topics.short: Match each Central African country with its capital, such as Kinshasa (DR Congo) and Luanda (Angola).

topics.title: Countries of East Africa
topics.short: Find the countries of East Africa, from Ethiopia and Kenya to Tanzania, Madagascar and the island nations of the Indian Ocean.

topics.title: Capitals of East Africa
topics.short: Match each East African country with its capital, such as Nairobi (Kenya) and Addis Ababa (Ethiopia).

topics.title: Southern Africa: Countries and Capitals
topics.short: Find South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Lesotho and Eswatini and their capitals; South Africa has three capital cities.

topics.title: Physical Features of Africa
topics.short: Find the Sahara, the Sahel, the Nile and Congo rivers, the Great Rift Valley, Mount Kilimanjaro, Lake Victoria and the Kalahari.

topics.title: Countries of Southwest Asia
topics.short: Find the countries of Southwest Asia, from Türkiye and the countries of the Caucasus to Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states.

topics.title: Capitals of Southwest Asia
topics.short: Match each country of Southwest Asia with its capital, such as Ankara (Türkiye) and Riyadh (Saudi Arabia).

topics.title: Countries of Central and South Asia
