topics.short: Find the five "-stan" countries of Central Asia, and Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and the Maldives.

topics.title: Capitals of Central and South Asia
topics.short: Match each country with its capital, such as New Delhi (India) and Islamabad (Pakistan).

topics.title: East Asia: Countries and Capitals
topics.short: Find China, Japan, Mongolia, North Korea and South Korea and their capitals, and Taiwan, which governs itself.

topics.title: Countries of Southeast Asia
topics.short: Find the eleven countries of Southeast Asia, on the mainland (such as Thailand and Vietnam) and on islands (such as Indonesia and the Philippines).

topics.title: Capitals of Southeast Asia
topics.short: Match each country of Southeast Asia with its capital, such as Bangkok (Thailand) and Hanoi (Vietnam).

topics.title: Physical Features of Asia
topics.short: Find the Himalayas, the Plateau of Tibet, Siberia, the Gobi and Arabian deserts, and the Yangtze, Ganges, Mekong, Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

topics.title: Countries of Oceania
topics.short: Find Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and the island countries of Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.

topics.title: Capitals of Oceania
topics.short: Match each country of Oceania with its capital, such as Canberra (Australia) and Wellington (New Zealand).

topics.title: Australia's Land and Antarctica
topics.short: Find the Outback, the Great Dividing Range, the Great Barrier Reef, the Southern Alps and Antarctica, a continent with no countries, set aside for science.

topics.title: Eight Billion People
topics.short: The world has about 8.2 billion people (UN, 2025); most live in Asia, and growth is slowing.

topics.title: The Most Populous Countries
topics.short: India (about 1.45 billion in 2024) and China (about 1.42 billion) have the most people, followed by the United States, Indonesia and Pakistan (UN World Population Prospects 2024).

topics.title: The Largest Countries by Area
topics.short: Russia is by far the largest country, then Canada; the United States and China come next, and their order depends on how water and disputed land are counted; then Brazil and Australia.

topics.title: Crowded Places
topics.short: Population density is the number of people per square kilometer: divide the people by the land area.

topics.title: The World's Largest Cities
topics.short: Jakarta, Dhaka and Tokyo are the largest cities in the UN's 2025 count; lists differ because they draw city edges differently.

topics.title: Formal Analysis: Describe, Analyze, Interpret
topics.short: Formal analysis looks at how a work is made, its line, color, light, composition and scale, before asking what it means.

topics.title: Subject, Genre and Style
topics.short: The subject is what a work shows; genres group subjects (portrait, landscape, still life, history painting, genre scene); style is how it is shown.

topics.title: Fresco, Tempera, Oil and More
topics.short: True fresco is painted into wet plaster; egg tempera dries fast in fine strokes; oil paint dries slowly and allows glazes and blending.

topics.title: Carving, Modeling and Casting
topics.short: Sculptors carve (take away from stone or wood), model (build up clay or wax) or cast (pour metal into a mold). Relief stays attached to a background; sculpture in the round does not.

topics.title: Patrons and Context
topics.short: Most art before modern times was commissioned: rulers, churches, guilds and families paid for it and often set its subject, size and materials.

topics.title: Dating and Attribution
topics.short: Dates and artists come from documents, signatures, style and science. "c." means about; "attributed to" means scholars think so but it is not certain.

topics.title: Cave Paintings
topics.short: Paleolithic people painted animals deep in caves: Chauvet more than 30,000 years ago and Lascaux about 17,000 years ago, with mineral pigments and charcoal.

topics.title: Carved Figures
topics.short: Small carvings in ivory, bone and stone are among the oldest art. The Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel, carved from mammoth ivory, is about 40,000 years old.

topics.title: Stonehenge and the Megaliths
topics.short: Neolithic people raised huge stones into circles and tombs. Stonehenge was built in stages from about 3000 to 1500 BC.

topics.title: Mesopotamia: Ziggurats and Steles
topics.short: Sumer and Babylon built mud-brick ziggurats and carved steles; the Stele of Hammurabi (about 1750 BC) shows the king before the god Shamash above his laws.

topics.title: Assyria, Babylon and Persia
topics.short: Assyrian palaces had guardian lamassu and carved reliefs; Babylon's Ishtar Gate (about 575 BC) glowed with glazed brick; Persepolis shows rows of tribute bearers.

topics.title: The Rules of Egyptian Art
topics.short: Egyptian artists showed people in composite view (head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders from the front), used hierarchical scale, and laid out figures on a grid.

topics.title: Pyramids and the Old Kingdom
topics.short: The pyramids of Giza (about 2600 to 2500 BC) were royal tombs. The Great Sphinx, probably made for King Khafre, guards the way to his pyramid.

topics.title: Temples and the New Kingdom
topics.short: New Kingdom pharaohs built great temples like Karnak and Hatshepsut's at Deir el-Bahari; the Amarna period brought the bust of Nefertiti, and Tutankhamun's tomb its gold mask.

topics.title: Minoan and Mycenaean Art
topics.short: Minoan Crete built palaces like Knossos and painted lively sea creatures on pottery; Mycenae is known for walls of huge stones and gold masks.

topics.title: Greek Vases: Black-Figure and Red-Figure
topics.short: In black-figure, figures are painted black on the red clay; in red-figure, about 530 BC on, the background is painted black and figures stay red, so details can be painted with a brush.

topics.title: The Doric, Ionic and Corinthian Orders
topics.short: Doric columns have plain cushion capitals and no base; Ionic capitals have scrolls (volutes); Corinthian capitals have acanthus leaves.

topics.title: The Parthenon
topics.short: Built on the Athenian Acropolis from 447 to 432 BC, the Parthenon is a Doric temple to Athena, designed by Iktinos and Kallikrates with sculpture overseen by Phidias.

topics.title: Greek Sculpture: Archaic to Classical
topics.short: Greek sculpture moved from the stiff, smiling figures of the Archaic period to the natural poses of the Classical, like the bronze Charioteer of Delphi.

topics.title: Contrapposto and the Hellenistic Age
topics.short: Contrapposto puts the weight on one leg so hips and shoulders tilt; Hellenistic sculpture after 323 BC added drama and motion, as in the Winged Victory of Samothrace.

topics.title: Roman Arches, Concrete and Domes
topics.short: Romans used the round arch, the vault and concrete to build aqueducts like the Pont du Gard, the Colosseum and the domed Pantheon.

topics.title: Roman Portraits and Wall Painting
topics.short: Republican portraits show age and wrinkles (verism); wall paintings at Pompeii and the Villa of Livia open walls into gardens and views.

topics.title: Early Christian Art and the Basilica
topics.short: After AD 313, Christians built basilicas, long halls with an apse at one end, borrowed from Roman public buildings.

topics.title: The Mosaics of Ravenna
topics.short: At San Vitale in Ravenna (about AD 547), glittering mosaics of glass and stone show the emperor Justinian and the empress Theodora with their courts.

topics.title: Hagia Sophia
topics.short: Built in Constantinople in five years, AD 532 to 537, by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, Hagia Sophia set a huge dome on pendentives over a square plan.

topics.title: Icons
topics.short: An icon is a holy image painted on wood, often in egg tempera with gold. Icons follow set types, so faces and poses repeat across centuries.

topics.title: The Mosque and Its Parts
topics.short: A mosque's prayer hall faces Mecca; the qibla wall holds the mihrab niche, the minbar is the pulpit, and a minaret calls to prayer. The Dome of the Rock (691) is among the oldest Islamic monuments.

topics.title: Geometry, Arabesque and Calligraphy
topics.short: Islamic art is famous for interlaced geometric patterns, arabesque (flowing vine scrolls) and calligraphy, the most honored art.

topics.title: Córdoba and the Alhambra
topics.short: In Spain, the Great Mosque of Córdoba (begun 785) has rows of striped double arches; the Alhambra palaces of Granada (mostly 14th century) have carved stucco and muqarnas vaults.

topics.title: Carpets, Lamps and Books
topics.short: Luxury arts carried Islamic design across the world: knotted carpets like the Ardabil carpet (1539–40), enameled glass mosque lamps and illustrated manuscripts.

topics.title: Illuminated Manuscripts
topics.short: Monks copied and decorated books by hand. The Book of Kells (about 800) and the Lindisfarne Gospels (about 715) fill pages with knotwork and interlace.

topics.title: Romanesque Churches
topics.short: Romanesque churches (about 1000 to 1150) have thick walls, round arches, barrel vaults and small windows, and carved portals for pilgrims.

topics.title: Gothic Cathedrals
topics.short: Gothic builders, from about 1140, combined pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses to raise tall, thin walls filled with glass.

topics.title: Stained Glass
topics.short: Pieces of colored glass held in lead strips filled Gothic windows with light and stories; Chartres and the Sainte-Chapelle (1240s) are famous for it.

topics.title: Books of Hours and the Late Middle Ages
topics.short: Wealthy owners ordered prayer books with calendar pictures, like the Limbourg brothers' Très Riches Heures (about 1412 to 1416) for the Duke of Berry.

topics.title: Chinese Landscape Painting
topics.short: Song dynasty painters such as Fan Kuan (about 1000) and Guo Xi (1072) painted towering mountains in ink on silk, on hanging scrolls and handscrolls.

topics.title: Bronzes, Clay Soldiers and Porcelain
topics.short: Shang dynasty ritual bronzes (about 1600 to 1046 BC), the Terracotta Army of the first emperor (about 210 BC) and Ming blue-and-white porcelain span three thousand years.

topics.title: Buddhist Art Across Asia
topics.short: Buddhist art spread from India across Asia: stupas, robed Buddha figures from Gandhara and Mathura, and temples like Japan's Byōdō-in (1053).

topics.title: Heian Japan and the Tale of Genji
topics.short: Heian court art includes the Phoenix Hall of the Byōdō-in and the 12th-century Tale of Genji handscrolls, seen from above with the roofs "blown off."

topics.title: Temples of South and Southeast Asia
topics.short: Hindu temples rise like sacred mountains: the Brihadishvara at Thanjavur (completed 1010) and Angkor Wat in Cambodia (12th century).

topics.title: Nok, Ife, Benin and Great Zimbabwe
topics.short: Nok terracottas (more than 2,000 years old), the naturalistic Ife heads (12th to 15th centuries), Benin's brass plaques and Great Zimbabwe's stone walls show many African traditions.

topics.title: Olmec, Maya and Aztec
topics.short: The Olmec carved colossal basalt heads (about 1200 to 900 BC); the Maya built Palenque and wrote in glyphs; the Aztec carved the great Sun Stone (about 1502 to 1520).

topics.title: The Andes and Ancient North America
topics.short: The Inca fitted stones without mortar at Machu Picchu (about 1450); the Moche made portrait vessels; Ancestral Puebloans built Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde (about 1190 to 1260).

topics.title: Giotto and the New Naturalism
topics.short: In the Arena Chapel in Padua (about 1305), Giotto painted solid, weighty figures with real feeling, a break from flat Byzantine style.

topics.title: Linear Perspective
topics.short: Brunelleschi showed how lines going back meet at one vanishing point (about 1415 to 1420), Alberti wrote the method down (1435), and Masaccio used it in paint.

topics.title: Brunelleschi's Dome
topics.short: Filippo Brunelleschi raised the dome of Florence Cathedral from 1420 to 1436 without full wooden centering, using a double shell and herringbone brick.

topics.title: Early Renaissance Sculpture and Painting
topics.short: Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise, Donatello's bronze Gattamelata, Fra Angelico's Annunciation and Piero della Francesca's portraits brought the new realism to Florence and beyond.

topics.title: Leonardo da Vinci
topics.short: Leonardo painted the Last Supper (about 1495 to 1498) and the Mona Lisa (begun about 1503), using sfumato, soft smoky transitions without hard outlines.

topics.title: Raphael and Michelangelo
topics.short: Raphael painted calm, graceful portraits and frescoes in Rome; Michelangelo was a sculptor, painter and architect who designed the dome of St. Peter's.

topics.title: Venice: Color and Light
topics.short: Venetian painters such as Giovanni Bellini and Titian built pictures from rich color and oil glazes rather than line, painting on canvas in the damp lagoon air.

topics.title: Van Eyck and Northern Oil Painting
topics.short: Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434) shows what oil glazes could do: tiny details, glowing color and a convex mirror reflecting the room.

topics.title: Dürer and the Print
topics.short: Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg made woodcuts and engravings that sold across Europe, like his Rhinoceros (1515), and watercolors such as the Young Hare (1502).

topics.title: Bruegel and Everyday Life
topics.short: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted peasants, seasons and landscapes, such as Hunters in the Snow and The Harvesters (both 1565).

topics.title: Renaissance Architecture
topics.short: Renaissance architects revived Roman columns, round arches and domes with clear proportions; Palladio's Villa La Rotonda (begun about 1567) was copied for centuries.

topics.title: Mannerism and the Late Renaissance
topics.short: After about 1520, Mannerist artists stretched proportions, crowded space and used cool, strange colors; Bronzino's portraits and El Greco's View of Toledo show the range.

topics.title: What Makes Art Baroque
topics.short: Baroque art (about 1600 to 1750) uses drama, motion, strong light and dark, and diagonal compositions to pull the viewer in; the Catholic Church and kings were its great patrons.

topics.title: Caravaggio and Tenebrism
topics.short: Caravaggio painted ordinary-looking people lit by a sharp beam in deep darkness (tenebrism), as in The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599–1600).

topics.title: Artemisia Gentileschi
topics.short: Artemisia Gentileschi, a follower of Caravaggio, was the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of the Arts of Drawing (1616); her Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting shows her at work.

topics.title: Bernini and Baroque Rome
topics.short: Gian Lorenzo Bernini, sculptor and architect, shaped Rome: his colonnade (1656–1667) wraps St. Peter's Square like open arms.

topics.title: Velázquez and Spain
topics.short: Diego Velázquez, court painter to Philip IV, painted Las Meninas (1656), a puzzle of looking in which the painter, the princess and a mirror all watch us.

topics.title: Rubens and Van Dyck
topics.short: Peter Paul Rubens ran a huge Antwerp workshop and painted with energetic color; his assistant Anthony van Dyck became court painter to Charles I of England.

topics.title: Palaces and Domes
topics.short: Versailles (enlarged from the 1660s) showed royal power in a palace and gardens; Christopher Wren rebuilt St. Paul's Cathedral in London (1675–1710) after the Great Fire.

topics.title: Art for a Market: The Dutch Republic
topics.short: In the 1600s the Dutch Republic had few church commissions and many middle-class buyers, so artists painted portraits, landscapes, still lifes and scenes of daily life to sell.

topics.title: Rembrandt
topics.short: Rembrandt van Rijn painted the group portrait The Night Watch (1642) full of motion and light, and searching self-portraits throughout his life.

topics.title: Vermeer and the Quiet Interior
topics.short: Johannes Vermeer of Delft painted calm rooms lit from a side window, such as The Milkmaid (about 1660; some scholars say a little earlier), using tiny dots of light and costly ultramarine.

topics.title: Judith Leyster and the Genre Scene
topics.short: Judith Leyster, one of the first women in Haarlem's painters' guild, painted lively genre scenes and a famous self-portrait at her easel (about 1630).

topics.title: Landscape and Still Life
topics.short: Jacob van Ruisdael painted skies over flat land and windmills; still lifes of flowers, food and skulls (vanitas) by Rachel Ruysch and Pieter Claesz reminded viewers that life is short.

topics.title: Rococo and the Elegant Portrait
topics.short: Rococo (about 1720 to 1780) brought light pastel color, curving ornament and elegant pleasure; Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun painted Queen Marie Antoinette.

topics.title: Chardin, Canaletto and the Grand Tour
topics.short: Jean-Siméon Chardin painted quiet kitchens and children at play; Canaletto painted precise views of Venice for travelers on the Grand Tour.

topics.title: The Grand Manner Portrait
topics.short: British portraitists such as Thomas Gainsborough (The Blue Boy, about 1770) and Joshua Reynolds posed sitters with dignity, rich fabric and landscape backgrounds.

topics.title: Neoclassicism
topics.short: After the digs at Pompeii, artists such as Jacques-Louis David turned to clear line, calm color and Roman virtue, as in The Oath of the Horatii (1784).

topics.title: Art in Early America
topics.short: John Singleton Copley painted Paul Revere (1768) at his workbench; Gilbert Stuart painted George Washington; Jefferson designed Monticello on Roman and Palladian models.

topics.title: Romanticism and the Sublime
topics.short: Romantic artists (about 1800 to 1850) valued feeling, nature's power and the individual: Caspar David Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog and J. M. W. Turner's storms and sunsets.

topics.title: Constable and Goya
topics.short: John Constable painted the English countryside from close study, as in The Hay Wain (1821); Francisco Goya painted the Spanish court with sharp honesty.

topics.title: The Hudson River School
topics.short: Thomas Cole, Frederic Church and Albert Bierstadt painted American wilderness on a grand scale; Cole's The Oxbow (1836) sets wild hills beside farmland.

topics.title: Realism
topics.short: Realists painted ordinary people and work without idealizing them: Courbet's Stone Breakers (1849), Millet's The Gleaners (1857) and Rosa Bonheur's The Horse Fair (1852–1855).

topics.title: Photography Arrives
topics.short: Louis Daguerre announced the daguerreotype in 1839; by the 1860s photographers such as Julia Margaret Cameron were making photographs as art.

topics.title: American Painting after the Civil War
topics.short: Winslow Homer painted the sea and country life, John Singer Sargent dazzling portraits, and Henry Ossawa Tanner The Banjo Lesson (1893).

topics.title: Ukiyo-e: Japanese Woodblock Prints
topics.short: Edo-period prints of the "floating world" were a team effort: a publisher, a designer such as Hokusai or Hiroshige, a carver and a printer, with one block for each color.

topics.title: Japanese Screens and Castles
topics.short: Folding screens painted on gold leaf, such as Ogata Kōrin's Irises (about 1705), and castles like Himeji (completed 1609) show the splendor of Japan's great families.

topics.title: Ming and Qing China
topics.short: The Ming built the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–1420) and made fine blue-and-white porcelain; literati scholar-painters valued personal brushwork over likeness.

topics.title: Joseon Korea
topics.short: Joseon Korea (1392–1897) prized plain white porcelain such as the round moon jars, and Jeong Seon painted "true-view" landscapes of real Korean mountains.

topics.title: The Mughal Empire
topics.short: Mughal emperors in India sponsored jewel-like manuscript paintings and built the Taj Mahal (1632–1653), Shah Jahan's tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

topics.title: Ottoman and Safavid Splendor
topics.short: The architect Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul (1550–1557) with Iznik tiles; in Isfahan the Safavid Shah Mosque (1611–about 1630) glows with blue tile.

topics.title: Impressionism
topics.short: The Impressionists painted light and modern life with visible broken brushstrokes, often outdoors; their first group show was in Paris in 1874, and Monet's Impression, Sunrise gave them their name.

topics.title: Monet's Series
topics.short: Claude Monet painted the same subject, grainstacks, Rouen Cathedral, water lilies, again and again to show how light and weather change it.

topics.title: Degas, Renoir, Morisot and Cassatt
topics.short: Edgar Degas painted dancers and racehorses, Pierre-Auguste Renoir crowds at leisure, and Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt the lives of women and children.

topics.title: Japonisme
topics.short: After Japan opened to trade in the 1850s, Japanese woodblock prints poured into Europe; their flat color, bold cropping and high viewpoints inspired Degas, Van Gogh and Cassatt.

topics.title: Seurat and Pointillism
topics.short: Georges Seurat placed small dots of pure color side by side for the eye to blend, as in A Sunday on La Grande Jatte (1884–1886).

topics.title: Vincent van Gogh
topics.short: Van Gogh used thick paint (impasto), swirling strokes and strong color to express feeling, as in The Starry Night (1889) and his Sunflowers (1888).

topics.title: Cézanne and Gauguin
topics.short: Paul Cézanne built landscapes and still lifes from patches of color and simple forms, a path toward Cubism; Paul Gauguin used flat, bold color and outlines.

topics.title: Masks, Figures and Textiles in Africa
topics.short: Many African masks and figures were made for performance and ceremony, seen in motion with costume, music and dance; textiles such as Asante kente carry meaning in their patterns.

topics.title: The Benin Bronzes
topics.short: Guilds in the Kingdom of Benin (in today's Nigeria) cast brass plaques and heads for the Oba's palace from the 1500s on; British troops took thousands of them in 1897.

topics.title: Arts of Native North America
topics.short: Northwest Coast carvers made totem poles in formline style; Navajo weavers made striped blankets; Plains artists drew on ledger paper; Pueblo potters made painted and polished pottery.

topics.title: Fauvism and Expressionism
topics.short: Around 1905 the Fauves, led by Henri Matisse, used wild, unnatural color; German Expressionists such as Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Franz Marc used color and distortion to express feeling.

topics.title: Cubism
topics.short: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, from about 1907, broke objects into facets seen from several viewpoints at once; Juan Gris and others carried it on.

topics.title: The First Abstract Paintings
topics.short: Between about 1910 and 1915, Wassily Kandinsky, Kazimir Malevich and others made paintings that show no objects at all, only color, line and shape.

topics.title: Futurism and Dada
topics.short: Italian Futurists (from 1909) glorified speed and machines; Dada artists in Zurich (from 1916) and beyond mocked art itself, as in Marcel Duchamp's Fountain (1917).

topics.title: De Stijl and the Bauhaus
topics.short: Piet Mondrian reduced painting to black lines and primary colors; the Bauhaus school in Germany (1919–1933) joined art, craft and industry in modern design.

topics.title: Surrealism
topics.short: Surrealists, after André Breton's manifesto of 1924, painted dreams and the unconscious: Salvador Dalí's melting watches and René Magritte's puzzles.

topics.title: Modern Architecture
topics.short: Louis Sullivan's skyscrapers ("form follows function"), Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House (1910) and Fallingwater (1935–1939), and Art Deco towers like the Chrysler Building (1930).

topics.title: American Modernism
topics.short: Georgia O'Keeffe painted close-up flowers and desert forms; Edward Hopper lonely city scenes; Harlem Renaissance artists such as Aaron Douglas and, later, Jacob Lawrence told Black American history.

topics.title: Mexican Muralism and Frida Kahlo
topics.short: After the Mexican Revolution, Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painted public murals of Mexican history; Frida Kahlo painted personal self-portraits.

topics.title: Photography as Modern Art
topics.short: Alfred Stieglitz fought for photography as art (The Steerage, 1907); Dorothea Lange's Migrant Mother (1936) made the Great Depression visible.

topics.title: Abstract Expressionism
topics.short: In New York after World War II, Jackson Pollock dripped paint on canvas laid on the floor, and Mark Rothko painted glowing fields of color.

topics.title: Telling the Styles Apart
topics.short: Each period has telltale signs: Gothic pointed arches, Renaissance balance, Baroque drama, Rococo pastels, Neoclassical clarity, Impressionist strokes, Cubist facets.

topics.title: Dating a Work by Its Style
topics.short: Clothes, subject, technique, materials and style narrow a work's date before any document is found.

topics.title: Comparing Two Works
topics.short: Comparing two works side by side, subject, composition, color, technique and purpose, shows what is special about each.

topics.title: The Seven Elements of Art
topics.short: Line, shape, form, space, value, texture and color are the elements of art: the parts every picture is built from.

topics.title: Line as an Element
topics.short: A line is a mark longer than it is wide. Lines can be actual or implied, and they can outline, show direction and suggest movement or calm.

topics.title: Shape and Form
topics.short: Shapes are flat areas, geometric or organic; forms have three dimensions, actual in sculpture or implied by shading in a picture.

topics.title: Space
topics.short: Space is the area around and between things: positive and negative space on the surface, and the illusion of depth in a picture.

topics.title: Value
topics.short: Value is lightness and darkness. It shows form and light and creates contrast, with or without color.

topics.title: Texture: Actual and Implied
topics.short: Actual texture can be touched (thick paint, carved wood); implied texture only looks rough, smooth or soft.

topics.title: Color as an Element
topics.short: Color is what we see when light of different wavelengths reaches our eyes. Artists describe it by hue, value and saturation.

topics.title: Hue, Value and Saturation
topics.short: Hue is the color family (red, blue). Value is how light or dark. Saturation, also called intensity or chroma, is how pure or grayed it is.

topics.title: The Color Wheel
topics.short: The painter's traditional wheel puts red, yellow and blue as primaries, orange, green and violet between them, and six tertiaries in the gaps.

topics.title: Tertiary Colors
topics.short: A tertiary color mixes a primary with the secondary beside it. Its name puts the primary first: red-orange, yellow-green, blue-violet.

topics.title: Tints, Tones and Shades
topics.short: A tint adds white, a shade adds black, and a tone adds gray. Each changes value or saturation but keeps the hue.

topics.title: Monochromatic Color
topics.short: A monochromatic scheme uses one hue with its tints, tones and shades.

topics.title: Complementary Colors
topics.short: Complements sit across from each other on the wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Side by side they make each other look stronger.

topics.title: Analogous Colors
topics.short: Analogous colors sit next to each other on the wheel, such as yellow, yellow-green and green. They look calm and unified.

topics.title: Triadic and Split-Complementary Schemes
topics.short: A triad uses three hues evenly spaced around the wheel (red, yellow, blue). A split-complementary uses one hue and the two on either side of its complement.

topics.title: Warm, Cool and Relative Temperature
topics.short: Reds, oranges and yellows read warm; blues, greens and violets read cool. Temperature is also relative: a red can be warmer or cooler than another red.

topics.title: Colors Change Their Neighbors
topics.short: A color looks different depending on what surrounds it: the same gray looks lighter on black than on white and takes on a hint of the surrounding color's complement.

topics.title: Subtractive Mixing: Paint and Ink
topics.short: Pigments absorb (subtract) some light and reflect the rest. Mixing pigments subtracts more, so mixtures get darker and duller.

topics.title: Additive Mixing: Light
topics.short: Colored lights add together. Red, green and blue light are the additive primaries: red and green light make yellow, and all three make white.

topics.title: Three Sets of Primaries: RYB, CMY and RGB
topics.short: Painters traditionally use red, yellow and blue; printers use cyan, magenta and yellow (plus black); screens and light use red, green and blue.

topics.title: Mixing Neutrals: Browns and Grays
topics.short: Mixing a color with its complement lowers its saturation; in the right amounts complements make rich browns and grays.

topics.title: Print and Screen
topics.short: A screen mixes tiny red, green and blue lights; a printer lays tiny dots of cyan, magenta, yellow and black on white paper.

topics.title: Balance
topics.short: Balance is how visual weight is spread: symmetrical (mirror halves), asymmetrical (unequal things that still feel even) or radial (around a center).

topics.title: Contrast
topics.short: Contrast puts unlike things side by side: light and dark, big and small, smooth and rough, warm and cool.

topics.title: Emphasis
topics.short: Emphasis makes one part stand out as the focal point, through contrast, isolation, placement, detail or lines that lead to it.

topics.title: Movement
topics.short: Movement is the path the eye travels through a work, led by lines, edges, shapes and repeated colors.

topics.title: Pattern
topics.short: A pattern repeats a motif (a shape, line or color) in a regular way across a surface.

topics.title: Rhythm
topics.short: Rhythm is a visual beat made by repeating elements with spacing: regular, alternating, progressive (gradually changing) or flowing.

topics.title: Unity and Variety
topics.short: Unity makes the parts feel like they belong together; variety adds differences to keep it interesting. Good designs balance the two.

topics.title: Proportion and Scale
topics.short: Proportion is the size of parts compared with each other; scale is size compared with something known. Some art uses hierarchical scale: the most important figure largest.

topics.title: Looking Step by Step
topics.short: Describe what you see, analyze how the elements and principles work, interpret what it might mean, then judge with reasons.

topics.title: Triangles, Diagonals and S-Curves
topics.short: Many paintings are built on a simple structure: a stable triangle, an energetic diagonal, a winding S-curve or a circle.

topics.title: Thirds and Focal Points in Paintings
topics.short: Find where the strongest contrast, the lines and the gazes lead; that is the focal point, and its place on the grid shapes the mood.

topics.title: The Value Pattern
topics.short: Squint at a painting and it simplifies into a few big light and dark shapes. That value pattern often carries the composition.

topics.title: Reading Color in Paintings
topics.short: Name the scheme (complementary, analogous, triadic or monochromatic), the temperature and the saturation, and say what they do for the work.

topics.title: What Colors Mean
topics.short: Color meanings come from culture and history, not nature: white is worn for weddings in some places and for mourning in others.

topics.title: Readable Color: Contrast for Text
topics.short: Text needs enough value contrast with its background to read easily; web guidelines ask for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text.

topics.title: Pencil Grades: H, HB and B
topics.short: H pencils are harder and make lighter lines; B pencils are softer and make darker lines. A bigger number means more of either.

topics.title: Paper and Erasers
topics.short: Drawing paper has some tooth to grip graphite. A kneaded eraser lifts tone when you press and dab; a vinyl eraser cleans crisp edges.

topics.title: Holding the Pencil
topics.short: Hold near the point, as for writing, for small, careful details. Hold farther back or overhand, and move from the elbow, for long, loose lines and broad shading.

topics.title: Charcoal, Ink and Colored Pencil
topics.short: Charcoal is soft, dark and smudgy; ink is permanent; colored pencil builds color in light layers.

topics.title: Line Weight and Line Quality
topics.short: Vary the weight of your lines: heavier for near edges and shadow sides, lighter for far edges and lit sides.

topics.title: Contour Drawing
topics.short: A contour line follows the edges of a form slowly, as your eye follows the object, including the edges inside the outline.

topics.title: Blind Contour Drawing
topics.short: Draw a contour while looking only at the object, never at the paper. It trains the eye and hand to move together.

topics.title: Cross-Contour Lines
topics.short: Lines that wrap across a form, like stripes around a ball, show its roundness.

topics.title: Gesture Drawing
topics.short: A gesture drawing takes half a minute to two minutes and catches the movement and weight of a pose, not its details.

topics.title: Positive and Negative Space
topics.short: Positive space is the object; negative space is the space around and between. Drawing the negative shapes helps you see true shapes.

topics.title: From Shapes to Forms
topics.short: A shape is flat; a form has depth. A circle becomes a sphere, a square a cube, a triangle a cone and a rectangle a cylinder.

topics.title: Drawing a Box
topics.short: Draw the nearest corner first. Edges that are parallel on the box either stay parallel or come together as they go back; they never spread apart.

topics.title: Circles in Depth: Ellipses
topics.short: A circle seen at an angle is an ellipse. It looks thinner near eye level and rounder the farther it is above or below eye level.

topics.title: Building Objects from Forms
topics.short: Break a complicated object into simple forms (boxes, cylinders, spheres and cones), draw those lightly, then refine.

topics.title: Value and the Value Scale
topics.short: Value is how light or dark a tone is. A value scale steps evenly from white to black, often in 5, 7 or 9 steps.

topics.title: Hatching
topics.short: Parallel lines make tone. Lines closer together, or heavier, read darker.

topics.title: Cross-Hatching
topics.short: Layers of hatching that cross at an angle build darker values.

topics.title: Stippling
topics.short: Dots make tone: more dots, closer together, read darker.

topics.title: Smooth Tone and Blending
topics.short: Build smooth tone with light, even layers of small strokes; a blending stump or tissue can soften it.

topics.title: Contrast and Key
topics.short: High contrast puts very light next to very dark. A high-key picture is mostly light values; a low-key picture is mostly dark.

topics.title: Where the Light Comes From
topics.short: Choose one light source. Every lit side faces it, and every shadow side and cast shadow points away from it.

topics.title: Highlight, Core Shadow and Reflected Light
topics.short: Light on a round form runs highlight, light, halftone, core shadow and reflected light, and the cast shadow lies on the ground beside it.

topics.title: Cast Shadows
topics.short: A cast shadow falls away from the light. It is darkest and sharpest where the object touches the surface and softens as it goes out.

topics.title: Shading a Sphere
topics.short: Put the values in order around the ball: highlight, light, halftone, core shadow, reflected light, then the cast shadow.

topics.title: Shading a Box: Three Planes
topics.short: Each flat side of a box gets one even value: the side facing the light is lightest and the side turned away is darkest.

topics.title: Proportion: Comparing Sizes
topics.short: Proportion is how sizes compare. Choose one part as your unit and measure the rest in it: "the bottle is three caps tall."

topics.title: Sighting with a Pencil
topics.short: Hold the pencil at arm's length with the elbow straight, close one eye, and mark a length with your thumb to compare it with others.

topics.title: Angles and Plumb Lines
topics.short: Hold the pencil truly vertical or horizontal to judge an edge's angle and to see what lines up above or beside what.

topics.title: The Grid Method
topics.short: Divide the picture and the paper into matching grids and copy one square at a time. Bigger squares on the paper enlarge the drawing.

topics.title: Checking Your Drawing
topics.short: Step back, squint to see the big values, and look at the drawing in a mirror to spot crooked or lopsided shapes.

topics.title: Showing Depth: Overlap, Size and Placement
topics.short: Things in front overlap things behind; farther things look smaller and, below eye level, sit higher on the page.

topics.title: The Horizon Line Is Eye Level
topics.short: In perspective, the horizon line is the viewer's eye level. You see the tops of things below it and the bottoms of things above it.

topics.title: One-Point Perspective
topics.short: Facing a box straight on, its edges that go back from you all meet at one vanishing point on the horizon line.

topics.title: Roads, Rooms and Rails
topics.short: Roads, railroad tracks, hallways and rooms seen straight on narrow toward one vanishing point, and equal spaces look shorter as they go back.

topics.title: Two-Point Perspective
topics.short: Turn the box so a corner faces you. Its edges go back to two vanishing points on the horizon, and vertical edges stay vertical.

topics.title: Three-Point Perspective
topics.short: Looking far up at a tall building or far down from one, the vertical edges also meet, at a third vanishing point above or below.

topics.title: Atmospheric Perspective
topics.short: Faraway things look lighter, bluer, softer and less detailed because of the air between us and them.

topics.title: The Rule of Thirds
topics.short: Divide the picture into thirds both ways; placing the main subject near one of the lines or crossings often looks livelier than dead center.

topics.title: The Focal Point
topics.short: The focal point is where the eye goes first. Artists make it with the strongest contrast, the most detail, isolation or lines that lead to it.

topics.title: Balance
topics.short: Symmetrical balance mirrors the two halves; asymmetrical balance offsets a big, quiet shape with a small, strong one; radial balance spreads from a center.

topics.title: Leading Lines
topics.short: Roads, rivers, fences, gazes and edges lead the eye through a picture, ideally toward the focal point.

topics.title: Thumbnails and Viewfinders
topics.short: Small quick sketches try out several arrangements and crops before the real drawing; a cardboard viewfinder helps choose the view.

topics.title: Setting Up a Still Life
topics.short: Group objects of different heights and sizes, overlap some, leave uneven gaps, and light them from one side.

topics.title: Drawing Texture
topics.short: Texture comes from your marks and the value pattern: short strokes for fur, long ones for wood grain, crisp contrast for rough stone.

topics.title: Shiny and See-Through Things
topics.short: Shiny things show sharp highlights and reflections with strong contrast; glass shows what is behind it, slightly bent, plus a few bright edges.

topics.title: Folds in Cloth
topics.short: Cloth hangs from points of support, and folds spread out from them. Shade each fold like a small cylinder.

topics.title: Proportions of the Head
topics.short: On an adult head seen from the front, the eyes are about halfway down, the face is about five eyes wide, and the nose ends about halfway from the eyes to the chin.

topics.title: Drawing Eyes
topics.short: An eye is a ball in a socket: the lids wrap around it, the upper lid casts a shadow on it, and the upper lid covers part of the iris.

topics.title: The Nose and Mouth
topics.short: Draw the nose with its planes and shadows rather than a hard outline. The corners of the mouth line up roughly below the pupils.

topics.title: Profile and Three-Quarter Views
topics.short: When the head turns, the center line curves around it and the far eye looks narrower; in profile, the ear sits just behind the middle of the head.

topics.title: Expressions
topics.short: Eyebrows, eyelids and mouth change together: raised brows and an open mouth for surprise, lowered brows and a tight mouth for anger.

topics.title: Drawing Hands
topics.short: Start with the mitten shape of the palm and fingers together. The middle finger is about as long as the palm, and the knuckles line up on a curve.

topics.title: Figure Proportions in Heads
topics.short: Artists measure the body in head heights: an adult is about seven and a half heads tall, and a young child only four or five.

topics.title: The Line of Action
topics.short: One curved line through the whole pose shows its movement; the head, chest and hips hang on it.

topics.title: The Mannequin Figure
topics.short: Build the body from simple forms: an egg for the head, boxes for the chest and hips, cylinders for the limbs and balls at the joints.

topics.title: The Clothed Figure
topics.short: Draw the gesture and forms first, then hang the clothes on them. Folds pull from the shoulders, elbows, waist and knees.

topics.title: Warm-Ups
topics.short: A few minutes of straight lines, circles, ellipses and value scales loosens the hand before a drawing.

topics.title: A Sketchbook Habit
topics.short: Short, regular practice adds up: draw a little most days, from life when you can, and date every page.

topics.title: Drawing from Life and from Photos
topics.short: Life drawing shows real depth and light; photos flatten form and can bend near things. Use your own photos or free-to-use ones, and give credit.

topics.title: Straight and Curved Lines
topics.short: A straight line goes one way without bending. A curved line bends, like a smile or a rainbow.

topics.title: Lines That Stand, Lie and Lean
topics.short: A vertical line stands up tall, a horizontal line lies down flat, and a diagonal line leans.

topics.title: Zigzag, Wavy and Spiral Lines
topics.short: A zigzag line has sharp points, a wavy line has smooth bumps, and a spiral winds around and around.

topics.title: Thick and Thin, Light and Dark
topics.short: Press gently for a thin, light line. Press harder, or use a fatter tool, for a thick, dark line.

topics.title: Lines All Around Us
topics.short: Lines are everywhere: stripes on a zebra, rungs on a ladder, waves on the water. Artists notice them and draw them.

topics.title: Circle, Square and Triangle
topics.short: A circle is round with no corners. A square has four equal sides and four corners. A triangle has three sides and three corners.

topics.title: Rectangles, Ovals and More
topics.short: A rectangle is a stretched square, an oval is a stretched circle, and hearts, stars and diamonds are shapes too.

topics.title: Finding Shapes in Things
topics.short: Look at a thing and find its shapes: a wheel is a circle, a door is a rectangle, a roof is a triangle.

topics.title: Neat Shapes and Free Shapes
topics.short: Shapes with straight sides and even curves are geometric. Free, bumpy shapes like leaves, clouds and puddles are organic.

topics.title: Draw a House from Shapes
topics.short: A square or rectangle for the walls, a triangle for the roof, and small rectangles for the door and windows.

topics.title: Draw a Cat from Shapes
topics.short: A circle for the head, two triangles for the ears, an oval for the body, and a curved line for the tail.

topics.title: Draw a Fish and a Bird
topics.short: An oval and a triangle make a fish. An oval body, a circle head, a triangle beak and a curved wing make a bird.

topics.title: Draw a Car or a Train
topics.short: Rectangles for the body and windows and circles for the wheels. The wheels touch the road.

topics.title: Draw Trees and Flowers
topics.short: A tall rectangle trunk and a cloud shape for leaves; a circle center with petals around it for a flower.

topics.title: In Front and Behind
topics.short: When one thing is in front of another, draw the front one whole. The one behind is partly hidden.

topics.title: The Colors of the Rainbow
topics.short: A rainbow always shows its colors in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.

topics.title: The Primary Colors
topics.short: In paint, red, yellow and blue are the primary colors. Many other colors can be mixed from them.

topics.title: Mixing New Colors
topics.short: Mix two primary colors to make a secondary color: red and yellow make orange, yellow and blue make green, red and blue make purple.

topics.title: Warm and Cool Colors
topics.short: Red, orange and yellow look warm, like fire and the sun. Blue, green and purple look cool, like water and leaves.

topics.title: Lighter and Darker Colors
topics.short: Add white to make a color lighter. Add a tiny bit of black to make it darker.

topics.title: The Color Wheel
topics.short: A color wheel puts the colors in a circle. Colors across from each other, like red and green, are opposites, and they make each other look bright.

topics.title: Patterns That Repeat
topics.short: A pattern repeats the same part again and again: red, blue, red, blue.

topics.title: What Comes Next?
topics.short: Find the part that repeats, then use it to tell what comes next.

topics.title: Patterns in Nature
topics.short: Stripes, spots, scales and spirals are patterns on animals and plants.

topics.title: Mirror Halves
topics.short: A thing is symmetrical when one half is a mirror picture of the other half, like a butterfly.

topics.title: Where the Face Parts Go
topics.short: The eyes go about halfway down the head. The nose sits below the eyes, and the mouth below the nose.

topics.title: Happy, Sad and Surprised
topics.short: A mouth that curves up looks happy. A mouth that curves down looks sad. A round open mouth looks surprised.

topics.title: Eyebrows Show Feelings
topics.short: Eyebrows raised high look surprised. Eyebrows that slope down toward the nose look cross.

topics.title: People from Shapes
topics.short: Build a person from shapes: an oval head, a body, and long shapes for arms and legs. Then add clothes.

topics.title: Hair, Hats and Clothes
topics.short: Make each person different with hair, hats, glasses and clothes.

topics.title: Draw It Big
topics.short: Make the main thing big enough to fill the page, not tiny in a corner.

topics.title: Sky and Ground
topics.short: Put the ground along the bottom and the sky above it. The sky comes all the way down to the land.

topics.title: Near and Far
topics.short: Things far away look smaller and sit higher on the page. Near things look bigger and sit lower.

topics.title: Draw What You See
topics.short: Look at the real thing more than at your paper. Notice its shapes before you draw them.

topics.title: Counting the Details
topics.short: Count the legs, petals or windows before you draw, so your drawing has the right number.

topics.title: Bumpy, Smooth and Fuzzy
topics.short: Different marks show how things feel: short lines for fur, dots for sand, long smooth lines for water.

topics.title: Light and Shadow
topics.short: A shadow falls on the side away from the light.

topics.title: An Artist's Tools
topics.short: Crayons, pencils, markers, paint and brushes, clay and scissors each make a different kind of art.

topics.title: Portraits, Landscapes and Still Lifes
topics.short: A portrait shows a person. A landscape shows land and sky. A still life shows things on a table.

topics.title: Pictures and Sculptures
topics.short: A painting or a drawing is flat. A sculpture is solid: you can walk around it.

topics.title: Encode, Store, Retrieve
topics.short: Every memory goes through three stages: you take it in (encode), you keep it (store), and you pull it back out (retrieve).

topics.title: Your Mental Workbench
topics.short: Working memory holds only a few things at once, about four chunks, so new information has to be grouped or practiced to stay.

topics.title: Long-Term Memory
topics.short: Long-term memory holds a huge amount for a long time; the hard part is not space but finding things again.

topics.title: You Can't Remember What You Didn't Notice
topics.short: Encoding starts with attention: what you only half notice is never stored well.

topics.title: Meaning Makes It Stick
topics.short: Facts you understand and connect to what you know are encoded far better than facts you only repeat.

topics.title: Cues: The Way Back In
topics.short: A cue is any hint that leads you back to a memory: a first letter, a place, a picture, a question.

topics.title: The Forgetting Curve
topics.short: Memory fades fastest right after learning and then more slowly; Hermann Ebbinghaus measured this in the 1880s.

topics.title: Reading a Forgetting-Curve Graph
topics.short: On a forgetting-curve graph, time runs left to right and memory runs up; each review is a jump back to the top.

topics.title: Relearning Is Faster
topics.short: Even when you can't recall something, relearning it takes less time than the first learning; Ebbinghaus called this savings.

topics.title: Why Spacing Beats Cramming
topics.short: The same study time spread over several days is remembered far longer than the same time crammed into one sitting.

topics.title: The 1-3-7-21 Schedule
topics.short: A simple starter schedule: learn it, then review on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 21, each time by recalling first.

topics.title: Pick the Next Review Day
topics.short: Find the next review on the 1-3-7-21 schedule by asking which reviews are done and counting from the learning day.

topics.title: The Memory-Work Box
topics.short: A box of index cards with tabs, Daily, Odd/Even, the days of the week and 1 to 31, that spaces reviews out on paper.

topics.title: The Testing Effect
topics.short: Pulling something from memory strengthens it more than reading it again; a quiz is a way to learn, not only a way to check.

topics.title: Why Rereading Fools Us
topics.short: Rereading feels productive because the text looks familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to recall it.

topics.title: Narration: Tell It Back
topics.short: Narration means closing the book and telling back what you just read or heard, in your own words.

topics.title: Blank-Page Recall
topics.short: Write down everything you remember on a blank page, then check and fill the gaps in a different color.

topics.title: Flashcards Done Well
topics.short: Good flashcards ask a question you must answer from memory, in both directions, and keep coming back until they are solid.

topics.title: What a Chunk Is
topics.short: A chunk is a group of items you treat as one unit; chunking lets a small working memory hold more.

topics.title: Chunk a Number
topics.short: Long numbers are easier in groups of three or four, best of all when a group is something you know, like a year.

topics.title: Group a List
topics.short: A long list of words is easier when you sort it into a few groups by kind, then recall group by group.

topics.title: How Many Chunks?
topics.short: Count chunks by dividing the items by the chunk size and rounding up, then compare with the four-chunk workbench.

topics.title: Picture Plus Words
topics.short: Learning with a picture and words together gives a memory two paths back; it helps every learner.

topics.title: Make It Vivid
topics.short: Memorable images are concrete, exaggerated, moving and a little funny, and they connect to the thing you need to recall.

topics.title: Learning Styles: What the Evidence Says
topics.short: There is no good evidence that teaching to a "visual" or "auditory" learning style helps; pictures plus words help everyone.

topics.title: Acronyms
topics.short: An acronym takes the first letter of each item and makes a word or name, like HOMES for the Great Lakes.

topics.title: Acrostic Sentences
topics.short: An acrostic is a sentence whose words start with the same letters as the items, in order.

topics.title: Rhymes, Rhythm and Songs
topics.short: Rhythm and rhyme give words a fixed shape, so a missing word stands out; songs are the oldest memory tool of all.

topics.title: The Keyword Method for New Words
topics.short: To learn a new word, find an English word that sounds like it, then picture the two meanings together.

topics.title: The Memory Palace
topics.short: Place each item along a route through a place you know well; walk the route in your head to recall them in order.

topics.title: Choose a Route
topics.short: A good route has distinct spots in a fixed order that you can walk without thinking, about 5 to 10 per room or area.

topics.title: Place and Walk
topics.short: To recall, walk the route spot by spot; the spot's number tells you the item's position.

topics.title: Sleep On It
topics.short: Sleep helps the brain keep what it practiced; review a little before bed and check in the morning.

topics.title: Mix It Up
topics.short: In review, mixing kinds of problems or subjects feels harder than doing one kind at a time, but it sticks better.

topics.title: Teach Someone
topics.short: Explaining what you learned to someone else is retrieval practice, and it shows you what you really understand.

topics.title: What Fits Which Age
topics.short: Young children do well with songs, chants and picture cards; ages 8 to 11 add chunking, acronyms and a memory box; 12 and up add self-testing and memory palaces.

topics.title: Your First Session
topics.short: Four steps: choose one small thing, encode it with one tool, retrieve it with the book closed, and space it on the calendar.

topics.title: Spot the Weaker Plan
topics.short: Compare two study plans by checking each habit: spaced or crammed, recall or reread, mixed or blocked, rested or tired.

topics.title: Choose the Technique That Fits
topics.short: Match the tool to the material: palaces for order, chunking for numbers, sketches for structure, acronyms for first letters, songs for exact wording, narration for stories.

topics.title: Plan a Memory Session
topics.short: Put it all together: what to learn, which tool, how to recall, when to review, plus sleep and mixing.

topics.title: What a Peg System Is
topics.short: A peg system gives each number a fixed, easy picture; to remember an item at a position, you hang it on that number's peg.

topics.title: Number-Rhyme Pegs
topics.short: Each number from 1 to 10 has a peg word that rhymes with it: one-bun, two-shoe, three-tree, and so on.

topics.title: Number-Shape Pegs
topics.short: Each digit gets a peg that looks like its shape: 2 is a swan, 8 is a snowman, 5 is a hook.

topics.title: Using Pegs for a List
topics.short: With pegs you can recall a list in order, backward, or by position; ten pegs hold ten items.

topics.title: The Ten Sounds
topics.short: The Major System gives each digit a consonant sound: 0 s/z, 1 t/d, 2 n, 3 m, 4 r, 5 l, 6 j/sh/ch, 7 k/g, 8 f/v, 9 p/b.

topics.title: Sounds, Not Spelling
topics.short: Code what you hear: silent letters count for nothing, a double letter that makes one sound is one digit, and c, g, x follow their sound.

topics.title: Digits to Sounds
topics.short: To turn a number into sounds, take each digit in order and write its consonant sound.

topics.title: Words to Digits
topics.short: To read a Major word as a number, say it and turn each consonant sound into its digit.

topics.title: Your 00 to 99 List
topics.short: Most users fix one picture word for every two-digit number, 00 to 99, and learn it as a big peg list.

topics.title: Long Numbers
topics.short: Split a long number into pairs, turn each pair into its list word, and place the pictures along a journey or chain them in a story.

topics.title: Dates and Years
topics.short: A year is four digits: two Major words in one image, tied to the event.

topics.title: A Code for Every Card
topics.short: Before memorizing a deck you fix one image for each of the 52 cards, so seeing a card brings its image at once.

topics.title: Person, Action, Object
topics.short: In PAO, each card or number gets a person, an action and an object; three cards in a row make one picture.

topics.title: Counting Images and Stops
topics.short: Count pictures by dividing items by items per picture, then stops by dividing pictures by pictures per stop, rounding up each time.

topics.title: Building a Long Journey
topics.short: A journey is a memory palace stretched across many rooms or places, with stops in a fixed order, often numbered in fives.

topics.title: Keeping a Journey in Order
topics.short: A journey's power is its order: each stop has a number, so you can recall forward, backward, or from any stop.

topics.title: How Many Stops?
topics.short: Work out how many stops a job needs, and how much a palace of a given size holds.

topics.title: Reusing Palaces
topics.short: A palace can be reused once old images fade; competitors rotate several journeys so lists don't blur together.

topics.title: The Link Method
topics.short: Link each item to the next with a vivid picture, so each one leads to the one after it.

topics.title: The Story Method
topics.short: Turn the list into one short, silly story in which each item causes the next.

topics.title: Which System Fits?
topics.short: Pick by the job: links and stories for short lists, pegs for numbered lists, journeys for long ordered lists, the Major System for numbers, PAO for cards.

topics.title: First-Letter Cues
topics.short: Write just the first letter of each word of a line; reading the letters forces you to recall the words.

topics.title: Learning a Poem Line by Line
topics.short: Build up a poem cumulatively: learn line 1, then lines 1 and 2, then 1 to 3, always reciting from the start before adding.

topics.title: Speaking From a Journey
topics.short: For a speech, memorize the key points in order on a journey, and the opening and closing word for word; speak the rest naturally.

topics.title: Memory Sports
topics.short: In memory competitions people memorize cards, numbers, words, names and faces under time limits, using the systems in this course.

topics.title: What Training Does
topics.short: In a 2017 study, ordinary adults who trained the method of loci for 40 days went from about 26 to about 62 of 72 words, and kept much of the gain four months later.

topics.title: A Sensible Training Plan
topics.short: Train the codes first, then speed: short daily sessions, a timer, a log of your scores, and spaced review of permanent lists.

topics.title: Gilbert: On the Loadstone
topics.short: Experiments with magnets and a small magnetic globe show that the Earth itself is a great magnet.

topics.title: Bacon: The Advancement of Learning
topics.short: A survey of everything people know, what is missing, and why learning is worth the effort.

topics.title: Kepler: The Harmonies of the World
topics.short: Music in the planets' motions, and in the middle of it the third law: periods and distances fit one rule.

topics.title: Kepler: Epitome of Copernican Astronomy
topics.short: A textbook of the new astronomy: ellipses, equal areas in equal times, and a force from the sun.

topics.title: Bacon: Novum Organum
topics.short: A new method for science: clear away the 'idols' of the mind, gather careful observations, and reason up from them.

topics.title: Bacon: New Atlantis
topics.short: Sailors find an island whose wise men run a great house of research for the good of all.

topics.title: Harvey: On the Motion of the Heart and Blood
topics.short: The heart is a pump, and the same blood goes round and round: proved by experiment and simple arithmetic.

topics.title: Descartes: Discourse on the Method
topics.short: Four rules for thinking clearly, 'I think, therefore I am', and a plan for a science built from the ground up.

topics.title: Descartes: The Geometry
topics.short: Algebra meets geometry: lengths become numbers and curves become equations, the road to the graphs every student draws.

topics.title: Galileo: Two New Sciences
topics.short: Three friends talk through the strength of beams and the laws of falling bodies, tested on inclined planes.

topics.title: Harvey: On the Generation of Animals
topics.short: How a chick takes shape day by day inside the egg, and Harvey's claim that all animals begin from an egg.

topics.title: Descartes: Meditations on First Philosophy
topics.short: Six days of thinking: doubt everything, find what can't be doubted, and rebuild knowledge from there.

topics.title: Hobbes: Leviathan
topics.short: Without government, life would be a war of all against all; so people agree to a strong sovereign.

topics.title: Spinoza: Ethics
topics.short: Philosophy set out like Euclid, with definitions and proofs, on God, nature, the emotions and freedom.

topics.title: Pascal: The Scientific Treatises
topics.short: A barometer carried up a mountain, the push of water in a closed vessel, and the triangle of numbers.

topics.title: Pascal: The Provincial Letters
topics.short: Eighteen witty open letters in a religious dispute of his day, which helped shape French prose.

topics.title: Pascal: Pensées
topics.short: Notes for a defense of the Christian faith: the thinking reed, the wager and 'the heart has its reasons.'

topics.title: Milton: Paradise Lost
topics.short: An epic of Satan's rebellion and the fall of Adam and Eve, written by a blind poet to 'justify the ways of God to men.'

topics.title: Milton: Areopagitica and the Poems
topics.short: A famous argument against censoring books before they are printed, with Milton's shorter poems and his drama of Samson.

topics.title: Molière: The Comedies
topics.short: A hypocrite, a miser, a snob and a man who thinks he is sick: comedy that laughs people out of their follies.

topics.title: Racine: Berenice and Phaedra
topics.short: French tragedy at its strictest: one day, one place, and passions that duty can't master.

topics.title: Huygens: Treatise on Light
topics.short: Light as a wave spreading through space, each point sending out its own small wavelets.

topics.title: Newton: The Principia
topics.short: Three laws of motion and one law of gravity explain falling apples, the tides and the orbits of the planets.

topics.title: Newton: Optics
topics.short: White light split by a prism into colors and put back together, and the questions Newton left for later science.

topics.title: Locke: Civil Government and Toleration
topics.short: People have rights to life, liberty and property, government rests on their consent, and belief can't be forced.

topics.title: Locke: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
topics.short: The mind starts as blank paper, and every idea comes from experience: sensation and reflection.

topics.title: Berkeley: The Principles of Human Knowledge
topics.short: To be is to be perceived: a bishop argues there is no matter apart from minds.

topics.title: Hume: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
topics.short: We never see one thing make another happen; we only learn to expect it. What, then, can we know?

topics.title: Kant: The Critique of Pure Reason
topics.short: What can reason know? Kant answers that the mind shapes experience by its own forms of space, time and cause.

topics.title: Kant: The Moral Philosophy
topics.short: Act only on a rule you could want everyone to follow, and treat people always as ends, never only as means.

topics.title: Kant: The Critique of Judgment
topics.short: What happens when we call something beautiful or sublime, and how we judge purpose in living things.

topics.title: Swift: Gulliver's Travels
topics.short: A ship's doctor among tiny people, giants, floating scientists and talking horses, each a mirror for England.

topics.title: Voltaire: Candide
topics.short: A young man taught that all is for the best meets one disaster after another, and ends by tending his garden.

topics.title: Diderot: Rameau's Nephew
topics.short: A philosopher talks in a Paris café with a brilliant, shameless musician who mocks every virtue.

topics.title: Montesquieu: The Spirit of Laws
topics.short: Laws fit a people's climate, customs and government, and freedom needs separate powers that check each other.

topics.title: Rousseau: The Discourses
topics.short: How did inequality begin? Rousseau tells a story of people in a state of nature and the first fence.

topics.title: Rousseau: The Social Contract
topics.short: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains': a government is legitimate only by the general will.

topics.title: Adam Smith: The Wealth of Nations
topics.short: The pin factory and the division of labor, markets and prices, and what makes nations grow rich.

topics.title: The American State Papers
topics.short: The founding documents: a declaration of rights, a first league of states, and the Constitution that replaced it.

topics.title: The Federalist
topics.short: Eighty-five newspaper essays explaining and defending the new Constitution, from factions to the courts.

topics.title: Gibbon: The Decline and Fall, I
topics.short: Rome at its height under the good emperors, and the slow troubles that followed.

topics.title: Gibbon: The Decline and Fall, II
topics.short: The empire in the east, the rise of new powers, and the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

topics.title: Boswell: The Life of Samuel Johnson
topics.short: The great biography: a young Scot follows the dictionary maker for twenty years and writes down his talk.

topics.title: Lavoisier: Elements of Chemistry
topics.short: Careful weighing shows that matter is neither made nor lost, oxygen explains burning, and chemistry gets its new names.

topics.title: Hegel: The Philosophy of Right
topics.short: Freedom made real in law, morality, the family, civil society and the state.

topics.title: Hegel: The Philosophy of History
topics.short: World history read as the story of freedom coming to know itself, from the ancient East to modern Europe.

topics.title: Mill: On Liberty
topics.short: The harm principle: society may limit what you do only to keep you from harming others.

topics.title: Mill: Utilitarianism and Representative Government
topics.short: The greatest happiness of the greatest number, and how a free people can best govern itself.

topics.title: Kierkegaard: Fear and Trembling
topics.short: A meditation on Abraham and Isaac: what faith asks of a person, and why it can't be reduced to ethics.

topics.title: Nietzsche: Beyond Good and Evil
topics.short: An attack on the philosophers' certainties, asking where our ideas of good and evil came from.

topics.title: Tocqueville: Democracy in America
topics.short: A young Frenchman travels the United States and describes how equality shapes its laws, habits and hearts.

topics.title: Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto
topics.short: A short pamphlet that reads history as class struggle; the lesson gives its claims and its critics' replies fairly.

topics.title: Marx: Capital
topics.short: Marx's analysis of commodities, money, labor and the factory system, and how economists have answered it.

topics.title: Faraday: Experimental Researches in Electricity
topics.short: A moving magnet makes a current, lines of force fill space, and the electric motor and dynamo begin.

topics.title: Darwin: The Origin of Species
topics.short: Living things vary, more are born than survive, and natural selection over long ages makes new species.

topics.title: Darwin: The Descent of Man
topics.short: Darwin applies evolution to human beings and adds sexual selection; the lesson also notes where later science disagreed.

topics.title: William James: The Principles of Psychology
topics.short: The stream of consciousness, habit, attention, memory and will, from the founder of American psychology.

topics.title: Goethe: Faust
topics.short: A scholar who has learned everything bargains with the devil for one moment he would wish to last.

topics.title: Jane Austen: Emma
topics.short: A clever young woman plays matchmaker in her village and keeps misreading everyone, herself most of all.

topics.title: Balzac: Cousin Bette
topics.short: A poor relation's quiet jealousy brings down a Paris family, in Balzac's study of money and envy.

topics.title: Melville: Moby-Dick
topics.short: 'Call me Ishmael': a whaling voyage, a captain's hunt for the white whale, and everything about whales.

topics.title: Dickens: Little Dorrit
topics.short: A girl born in a debtors' prison, a man back from abroad, and a London of red tape and false fortunes.

topics.title: Tolstoy: War and Peace
topics.short: Families of Russia live through Napoleon's invasion, and Tolstoy asks what really moves history.

topics.title: George Eliot: Middlemarch
topics.short: A whole English town in one novel, and a young woman who wants to do great good in a small place.

topics.title: Ibsen: The Plays
topics.short: Modern drama begins: ordinary homes where hidden lies and duties finally come to light.

topics.title: Dostoevsky: The Brothers Karamazov
topics.short: Three brothers, their father's murder, and the great arguments about God, freedom and suffering.

topics.title: Twain: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
topics.short: A boy and an escaped slave float down the Mississippi, and Huck decides for himself what is right.

topics.title: Freud: The Interpretation of Dreams
topics.short: Freud's claim that dreams have hidden meanings, its place in history, and what later research found.

topics.title: Freud: The Later Works
topics.short: The unconscious, the id, ego and superego, and Freud's view of civilization, with their critics.

topics.title: William James: Pragmatism
topics.short: An idea's meaning lies in the difference it makes in practice; truth is what works out in experience.

topics.title: Bergson: An Introduction to Metaphysics
topics.short: Two ways of knowing: analysis from outside, and intuition that enters into a thing's living flow.

topics.title: Russell: The Problems of Philosophy
topics.short: Is the table really there? A short, clear tour of what we can know, and why philosophy is worth it.

topics.title: Whitehead: Science and the Modern World
topics.short: How modern science grew from older beliefs about order in nature, and what its picture of the world leaves out.

topics.title: Barth: The Word of God and the Word of Man
topics.short: A Swiss theologian's addresses calling preachers back from their own words to the word of God.

topics.title: Heidegger: What Is Metaphysics?
topics.short: A lecture that asks why there is something rather than nothing, and what our moods reveal.

topics.title: Dewey: Experience and Education
topics.short: Not all experience educates: a short book on what good schooling, old or new, should do.

topics.title: Wittgenstein: Philosophical Investigations
topics.short: Meaning is use: words as tools in 'language games', and many philosophical puzzles as tangles in language.

topics.title: Poincaré: Science and Hypothesis
topics.short: What role do conventions, hypotheses and experiments play in mathematics and physics?

topics.title: Whitehead: An Introduction to Mathematics
topics.short: A short book on why mathematics is about patterns, from variables and functions to the series behind waves.

topics.title: Einstein: Relativity
topics.short: Einstein's own popular explanation: trains, lightning flashes, clocks, and gravity as the shape of space and time.

topics.title: Eddington: The Expanding Universe
topics.short: The galaxies are rushing apart: an astronomer explains the new discovery to general readers.

topics.title: Bohr: Atomic Theory and the Discussion with Einstein
topics.short: The quantum atom, complementarity, and Bohr's long friendly argument with Einstein.

topics.title: Dobzhansky: Genetics and the Origin of Species
topics.short: Darwin's selection joined to Mendel's genes: how variation in populations makes new species.

topics.title: Hardy: A Mathematician's Apology
topics.short: A great mathematician defends pure mathematics for its beauty, and looks back on his life's work.

topics.title: Schrödinger: What Is Life?
topics.short: A physicist asks how living things keep order, and guesses that genes hold a code in a molecule.

topics.title: Planck: Scientific Autobiography
topics.short: The founder of quantum theory looks back on his discovery and on how new ideas win acceptance.

topics.title: Heisenberg: Physics and Philosophy
topics.short: The uncertainty principle and what quantum physics means for old questions about matter.

topics.title: Waddington: The Nature of Life
topics.short: A biologist explains genes, development and evolution, and how a single cell becomes a body.

topics.title: Veblen: The Theory of the Leisure Class
topics.short: Why people buy things to show off: Veblen's idea of 'conspicuous consumption.'

topics.title: Tawney: The Acquisitive Society
topics.short: A historian argues that an economy should serve purposes beyond getting; the lesson gives the replies too.

topics.title: Keynes: The General Theory
topics.short: Why whole economies can stay stuck with high unemployment, and how economists of other schools replied.

topics.title: Frazer: The Golden Bough
topics.short: A vast comparison of myths and customs, and why later anthropologists questioned its method.

topics.title: Weber: Essays in Sociology
topics.short: Politics and science as vocations, authority, bureaucracy and the role of ideas in history.

topics.title: Huizinga: The Waning of the Middle Ages
topics.short: Life, thought and art in 14th- and 15th-century France and the Low Countries, seen as a late autumn.

topics.title: Lévi-Strauss: Structural Anthropology
topics.short: Looking for the hidden patterns, like those of a language, under kinship and myth.

topics.title: Conrad: Heart of Darkness
topics.short: A voyage up the Congo River to find a man named Kurtz, and an indictment of colonial greed.

topics.title: Chekhov: Uncle Vanya
topics.short: On a country estate, people who gave their lives to work wonder what it was for, and go on working.

topics.title: Henry James: The Beast in the Jungle
topics.short: A man waits all his life for something great to happen to him, and misses what was there.

topics.title: Mann: Death in Venice
topics.short: A famous, disciplined writer on holiday loses his self-command in a city under a hidden plague.

topics.title: Proust: Swann in Love
topics.short: A man of taste falls for a woman he doesn't even like, and jealousy and memory take over.

topics.title: Joyce: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
topics.short: Stephen Dedalus grows from a small boy into a young man who chooses art over family, faith and nation.

topics.title: Pirandello: Six Characters in Search of an Author
topics.short: Six characters left unfinished by their author interrupt a rehearsal and demand their story be played.

topics.title: Shaw: Saint Joan
topics.short: Joan of Arc as a farm girl of plain good sense, and the people who tried her, each convinced they were right.

topics.title: Cather: A Lost Lady
topics.short: A boy in a Nebraska railroad town watches a charming woman, and the pioneer era, fade.

topics.title: Kafka: The Metamorphosis
topics.short: Gregor Samsa wakes up as a giant insect, and his family must decide what he still is to them.

topics.title: D. H. Lawrence: The Prussian Officer
topics.short: A young orderly and the officer who torments him, in a story of cruelty and pride before the Great War.

topics.title: T. S. Eliot: The Waste Land
topics.short: A poem of broken voices after the First World War, built from fragments of older poems.

topics.title: Fitzgerald: The Great Gatsby
topics.short: A mysterious rich man throws parties to win back the woman he loved, told by the neighbor who watches.

topics.title: Woolf: To the Lighthouse
topics.short: A family's summers by the sea, ten years apart, told through the flow of their thoughts.

topics.title: Faulkner: A Rose for Emily
topics.short: A Southern town tells the story of the strange old woman it watched for decades.

topics.title: O'Neill: Mourning Becomes Electra
topics.short: Aeschylus' Oresteia retold in New England after the Civil War, a family undone by its past.

topics.title: Hemingway: The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber
topics.short: On an African safari, a man shamed by his fear finds his courage, briefly.

topics.title: Brecht: Mother Courage and Her Children
topics.short: A canteen woman pulls her wagon through the Thirty Years' War, trying to profit from it.

topics.title: Orwell: Animal Farm
topics.short: The animals drive out the farmer, and the pigs slowly become what they replaced.

topics.title: Beckett: Waiting for Godot
topics.short: Two tramps wait by a tree for someone who never comes, and fill the time with talk.

topics.title: Homer: The Iliad
topics.short: The anger of Achilles in the last year of the Trojan War, and what it costs Greeks and Trojans alike.

topics.title: Homer: The Odyssey
topics.short: Odysseus' ten-year voyage home from Troy, and his wife and son holding out for him in Ithaca.

topics.title: Aeschylus: The Oresteia
topics.short: A family curse runs through three plays and ends in a court of law: revenge gives way to justice.

topics.title: Sophocles: Oedipus and Antigone
topics.short: A king hunts for the cause of a plague and finds himself; his daughter defies a king to bury her brother.

topics.title: Euripides: The Plays
topics.short: The most questioning of the three tragedians: war's victims, passion and the gods seen from below.

topics.title: Aristophanes: The Comedies
topics.short: Wild comic fantasies that poke fun at Athens' leaders, poets and philosophers, Socrates included.

topics.title: Herodotus: The Histories
topics.short: The first great history: why Greeks and Persians went to war, with every story he heard along the way.

topics.title: Thucydides: The Peloponnesian War
topics.short: An Athenian general's careful account of the long war between Athens and Sparta, and of power without limits.

topics.title: Plato: The Trial of Socrates
topics.short: Socrates questions a man about holiness, defends his life before a jury, and refuses to escape from prison.

topics.title: Plato: Phaedo
topics.short: Socrates' last day: a conversation about whether the soul outlives the body.

topics.title: Plato: Meno
topics.short: Can virtue be taught? Socrates helps a boy discover a geometry fact he was never told.

topics.title: Plato: Protagoras and Gorgias
topics.short: Socrates against the teachers of persuasion: is it better to suffer wrong than to do it?

topics.title: Plato: Symposium and Phaedrus
topics.short: Speeches at a dinner party on love, climbing from love of one person to love of beauty itself.

topics.title: Plato: The Republic, Books I–V
topics.short: What is justice? Socrates builds a city in words to find out, then looks for justice in the soul.

topics.title: Plato: The Republic, Books VI–X
topics.short: The philosopher-ruler, the divided line, the cave, how cities decline, and the myth of Er.

topics.title: Plato: Theaetetus and Sophist
topics.short: What is knowledge? A young mathematician tries three answers, and Socrates tests each one.

topics.title: Plato: Timaeus and Critias
topics.short: A likely story of how the world was made from shapes and numbers, and the tale of Atlantis.

topics.title: Plato: Statesman, Laws and the Seventh Letter
