topics.short: Plato's last thoughts on ruling and on laws for a real city, and his own story of politics in Sicily.

topics.title: Aristotle: Logic
topics.short: The first full study of reasoning: the syllogism, proof, argument and the tricks of false arguments.

topics.title: Aristotle: Physics
topics.short: Nature, change and its four kinds of cause, place, time, the infinite and the unmoved mover.

topics.title: Aristotle: On the Heavens
topics.short: A round Earth at the center of perfect spheres, the four elements, and weather, comets and rainbows.

topics.title: Aristotle: On the Soul
topics.short: The soul as what makes a living body alive, from plants to people, and how we sense, remember and think.

topics.title: Aristotle: Metaphysics
topics.short: The study of being as being: substance, form and matter, and the first cause of all motion.

topics.title: Aristotle: The Animals
topics.short: The first great work of biology: careful observation of hundreds of animals, and why their parts are as they are.

topics.title: Aristotle: Nicomachean Ethics
topics.short: Happiness as a life of virtue, virtue as a habit between two extremes, and why friends matter.

topics.title: Aristotle: Politics
topics.short: Humans as political animals, the kinds of constitution, and what makes a city good and stable.

topics.title: Aristotle: Rhetoric and Poetics
topics.short: How persuasion works, and what makes a tragedy move us: plot, character and the turn of fortune.

topics.title: Hippocrates: On Medicine
topics.short: Medicine that looks for natural causes, watches the patient closely, and aims to help, or at least to do no harm.

topics.title: Euclid: Elements, Books I–IV
topics.short: Definitions, postulates and proofs: triangles, parallels, the Pythagorean theorem and circles.

topics.title: Euclid: Elements, Books V–X
topics.short: Ratio and proportion, similar figures, prime numbers, the infinitude of primes and incommensurable lengths.

topics.title: Euclid: Elements, Books XI–XIII
topics.short: Solid geometry, the method of exhaustion, and the five regular solids.

topics.title: Archimedes: The Works
topics.short: The law of the lever, why things float, pi trapped between two bounds, and counting the grains of sand to fill the universe.

topics.title: Aquinas: God and Creation
topics.short: Questions about God, the five ways, creation, angels and the human soul, each answered after the objections.

topics.title: Aquinas: Happiness, Virtue and Law
topics.short: What happiness is, how habits become virtues, and the kinds of law, from eternal law to human law.

topics.title: Aquinas: Faith, Hope and Love
topics.short: The virtues of faith, hope and love, and the questions on Christ and the sacraments, as the set selects them.

topics.title: Dante: Inferno
topics.short: Lost in a dark wood, Dante follows Virgil down through the circles of Hell, where each wrong has its fitting place.

topics.title: Dante: Purgatorio
topics.short: Up the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are made new one fault at a time, to meet Beatrice.

topics.title: Dante: Paradiso
topics.short: Through the spheres of heaven to Dante's vision of the Love that moves the sun and all the stars.

topics.title: Chaucer: Troilus and Criseyde
topics.short: A love story set in besieged Troy: trust, fortune and betrayal in Chaucer's longest finished poem.

topics.title: Chaucer: The Canterbury Tales
topics.short: Thirty pilgrims tell stories on the road to Canterbury: knights, millers, a nun's priest and a rooster.

topics.title: Erasmus: The Praise of Folly
topics.short: Folly herself gives a speech in her own honor, mocking the vanity of scholars, rulers and churchmen.

topics.title: Machiavelli: The Prince
topics.short: Advice to a new ruler on how power is won and kept, looking at how people act rather than how they should.

topics.title: Rabelais: Gargantua and Pantagruel
topics.short: Giant comedy about two giants, full of learning and nonsense, with an abbey whose only rule is 'Do what you will.'

topics.title: Montaigne: Essays
topics.short: The man who invented the essay tries out his thoughts on everything, above all on himself.

topics.title: Calvin: Institutes of the Christian Religion
topics.short: A Reformation leader's ordered account of Christian teaching, from knowing God and ourselves to the church.

topics.title: Copernicus: On the Revolutions
topics.short: The sun, not the Earth, at the center: the book that set the planets in a new order.

topics.title: Shakespeare: The Comedies
topics.short: Lovers lost in woods and disguises, fools wiser than lords, and everything set right by the last act.

topics.title: Shakespeare: Romeo and Juliet
topics.short: Two young people from feuding families, and how haste and hatred bring about their deaths.

topics.title: Shakespeare: The History Plays
topics.short: England's kings from Richard II to Richard III: crowns lost and won, and Falstaff in the tavern.

topics.title: Shakespeare: Julius Caesar and the Roman Plays
topics.short: Brutus and the conspirators kill Caesar for the Republic's sake, and the speeches after decide what follows.

topics.title: Shakespeare: Hamlet
topics.short: A prince told by his father's ghost to take revenge, and all the thinking that delays him.

topics.title: Shakespeare: Othello
topics.short: A trusted officer poisons a general's mind with lies, and jealousy does the rest.

topics.title: Shakespeare: King Lear
topics.short: An old king divides his kingdom by who flatters him best, and learns too late which daughter loves him.

topics.title: Shakespeare: Macbeth
topics.short: A brave soldier hears a prophecy, murders his king, and is undone by ambition and guilt.

topics.title: Shakespeare: The Tempest and the Late Plays
topics.short: Lost children found and old wrongs forgiven, ending with a magician who sets his magic aside.

topics.title: Shakespeare: The Sonnets
topics.short: 154 fourteen-line poems about love, friendship, time and whether verse can outlast it.

topics.title: Cervantes: Don Quixote, Part One
topics.short: A country gentleman reads so many romances that he rides out as a knight, with Sancho Panza beside him.

topics.title: Cervantes: Don Quixote, Part Two
topics.short: Now famous from Part One, the knight meets readers of his own story, and Sancho governs an island.

topics.title: Lucretius: On the Nature of Things
topics.short: A poem that explains the world as atoms moving in the void, to free readers from the fear of death and the gods.

topics.title: Virgil: Eclogues and Georgics
topics.short: Shepherds' songs and a long poem on farming: plowing, vines, cattle and bees.

topics.title: Virgil: The Aeneid
topics.short: Aeneas escapes burning Troy and, by duty more than desire, founds the people who will become Rome.

topics.title: Plutarch: Lives of the Greeks
topics.short: Character studies of Greek lawgivers, generals and kings, written to teach by example.

topics.title: Plutarch: Lives of the Romans
topics.short: The heroes and villains of the Roman Republic, paired with Greeks so readers can compare them.

topics.title: Tacitus: The Annals and The Histories
topics.short: A senator's sharp history of the first emperors, from Tiberius to the year of four emperors.

topics.title: Epictetus: Discourses
topics.short: A freed slave teaches that some things are up to us and some are not, and that peace comes from knowing which.

topics.title: Marcus Aurelius: Meditations
topics.short: A Roman emperor's private notebook: reminders to be just, patient and calm, written in army camps.

topics.title: Plotinus: The Enneads
topics.short: Everything flows from the One, and the soul can turn inward and climb back toward it.

topics.title: Nicomachus: Introduction to Arithmetic
topics.short: Even and odd, prime and composite, perfect numbers and figurate numbers: the arithmetic schools taught for a thousand years.

topics.title: Ptolemy: The Almagest
topics.short: The great book of ancient astronomy: an Earth-centered system of circles that predicted the planets for 1,400 years.

topics.title: Galen: On the Natural Faculties
topics.short: How the body grows, takes in food and gets rid of waste, argued from experiments on living things.

topics.title: Augustine: Confessions
topics.short: A life told as a prayer: a restless young man's search, his mother's faith, and his conversion in a garden.

topics.title: Augustine: The City of God
topics.short: Written after Rome was sacked: two cities, one built on love of self and one on love of God, run through all of history.

topics.title: Augustine: On Christian Doctrine
topics.short: How to read and teach the Bible: signs and things, plain and figurative meaning, and the uses of rhetoric.

topics.title: How to Read a Great Book
topics.short: How to choose a book, read it more than once, ask it questions, mark it up, talk about it, and come back to it.

topics.title: The Great Conversation
topics.short: Why people read the great books together, where the idea came from, the case against a fixed list, and how this ladder works.

topics.title: The Syntopicon and Mortimer Adler
topics.short: Who Mortimer Adler was, how his index of great ideas works across the whole set, his other books, and our own idea index.

topics.title: Power Budgets and Battery Life
topics.short: Add up the current of every part; battery life is about capacity ÷ current, less a safety margin.

topics.title: Design, Build, Test, Repeat
topics.short: Change one thing at a time, run several trials, and record the success rate honestly.

topics.title: Robotics Careers and Honest Timelines
topics.short: Most robotics engineers hold an engineering degree; technicians often start with two years of training. A portfolio of finished projects helps at every level.

topics.title: Open and Closed Loops
topics.short: Open loop runs a fixed command; closed loop measures the error, setpoint minus measurement, and corrects it.

topics.title: Proportional Control
topics.short: Command = Kp times the error, limited to what the motor can give.

topics.title: One Step of a PID Controller
topics.short: u = Kp e + Ki (sum of e Δt) + Kd (Δe / Δt), computed fresh every loop.

topics.title: Time Constants
topics.short: A first-order system covers 63% of the way to its new value in one time constant τ, and about 99% in 5τ.

topics.title: Stability and Tuning
topics.short: Too much gain overshoots and can oscillate or diverge; tune P first, then D, then a little I.

topics.title: A Safe Electronics Bench
topics.short: Low-voltage kits, batteries handled by the maker's rules, and a soldering iron that always goes back in its stand.

topics.title: Ohm's Law on a Breadboard
topics.short: Voltage pushes, resistance resists, and current is the result: V = IR.

topics.title: The Resistor Every LED Needs
topics.short: Pick the series resistor from what is left after the LED's forward voltage: R = (V - Vf)/I.

topics.title: Voltage Dividers and Sensors
topics.short: Two resistors in series split a voltage; a light sensor in a divider turns light into volts.

topics.title: Analog Readings
topics.short: An analog-to-digital converter turns 0 to 3.3 V into a whole number from 0 to 1023 (10-bit) or 4095 (12-bit).

topics.title: PWM: Fast Switching for Motors and Lights
topics.short: Switch fully on and off very fast; the fraction of time on, the duty cycle, sets the average voltage.

topics.title: What Makes a Robot
topics.short: A robot senses the world, decides with a program, and acts, over and over.

topics.title: Sensors and Motors
topics.short: Sensors are a robot's senses; motors, servos, lights and speakers are its muscles.

topics.title: A First Circuit
topics.short: Current flows only around a complete loop: battery, switch, resistor and LED.

topics.title: Programs, Steps and Loops
topics.short: A program is a list of steps the robot follows in order; a loop repeats steps.

topics.title: A Cardboard Arm and a Bristlebot
topics.short: A lever arm moves its end farther than your hand, but with less force.

topics.title: Gear Ratios
topics.short: A small gear driving a big one trades speed for torque by the ratio of their teeth.

topics.title: Torque and Choosing a Motor
topics.short: Torque is force times lever arm; a motor must beat the load's torque, m g L, with room to spare.

topics.title: Wheels and Speed
topics.short: Rolling speed is angular speed times radius: v = ωr, and rpm must be turned into radians per second first.

topics.title: Coordinate Frames
topics.short: A point seen by the robot becomes a point on the map by a rotation and a shift.

topics.title: Forward Kinematics of a Two-Link Arm
topics.short: Given the joint angles, the hand is at x = L1 cos θ1 + L2 cos(θ1 + θ2), y = L1 sin θ1 + L2 sin(θ1 + θ2).

topics.title: Inverse Kinematics of a Two-Link Arm
topics.short: Given where the hand should go, the law of cosines gives the elbow angle; there are usually two answers, and sometimes none.

topics.title: Differential Drive
topics.short: Two wheels: v = (vR + vL)/2, ω = (vR − vL)/W, and the turning radius is v / ω.

topics.title: Odometry
topics.short: Update the pose each step: x += d cos θ, y += d sin θ, θ += Δθ.

topics.title: Occupancy Grids
topics.short: Cut the floor into cells: cell = floor(position / cell size); each cell is free, occupied or unknown.

topics.title: Shortest Paths on a Grid
topics.short: Breadth-first search explores in rings and finds the fewest moves; Dijkstra's algorithm does the same with costs.

topics.title: A* Search
topics.short: A* adds a guess of the distance left, f = g + h, so it looks toward the goal first and still finds the shortest path.

topics.title: Drift, Landmarks and SLAM
topics.short: A heading error θ makes the position error grow like d sin θ; seeing known landmarks again pulls the estimate back.

topics.title: Tracing Code by Hand
topics.short: Follow a program one line at a time, writing down every variable, to know what it will do.

topics.title: Decisions from Sensors
topics.short: if, elif and else turn readings into actions; the order of the tests matters.

topics.title: State Machines
topics.short: A robot is always in one state; each input moves it along a rule to the next.

topics.title: Loop Timing
topics.short: A control loop runs at a steady rate: period = 1 / frequency, and all the work must fit inside it.

topics.title: Integers, Overflow and Bit Masks
topics.short: An 8-bit unsigned number wraps from 255 to 0; masks set, clear and test single bits.

topics.title: Nodes and Topics
topics.short: Each job is a node; nodes publish and subscribe to named topics at steady rates.

topics.title: Services and Actions
topics.short: A topic streams, a service asks once and waits for one reply, and an action runs a long task with feedback and can be canceled.

topics.title: Units and Axes: REP 103
topics.short: ROS uses SI units (meters, seconds, radians) and right-handed frames: x forward, y left, z up.

topics.title: Chains of Transforms
topics.short: A point in the camera's frame reaches the map through a chain: camera to base, base to map.

topics.title: How a Simulator Steps Time
topics.short: A simulator advances in fixed steps Δt; the real-time factor is simulated time over wall-clock time.

topics.title: Wheel Encoders
topics.short: Counts divided by counts per turn give turns; turns times the circumference give distance.

topics.title: Ultrasonic Distance
topics.short: Sound goes out and back, so distance = speed of sound times time, divided by 2.

topics.title: Accelerometers and Gyros
topics.short: At rest, an accelerometer's tilt is atan(ax / az); a gyro gives turn rate, which adds up to angle and drifts.

topics.title: Noise and Averages
topics.short: Averaging N independent readings shrinks the noise by the square root of N.

topics.title: The Complementary Filter
topics.short: Trust the gyro over short times and the accelerometer over long times: θ = α(θ + ω Δt) + (1 − α) θ_acc.

topics.title: A Kalman Filter in One Dimension
topics.short: Gain K = P / (P + R); new estimate = old + K (measurement − old); new P = (1 − K) P.

topics.title: Pixels and Image Size
topics.short: An image is a grid of pixels; a color pixel stores three numbers, so a 640 × 480 color frame is 921,600 bytes.

topics.title: Color Thresholding
topics.short: Keep the pixels whose color passes a test, such as red − (green + blue)/2 > T; the rest are background.

topics.title: Finding the Center and Steering
topics.short: The target's center is the average column of the pixels that pass; the steering error is that minus the image center.

topics.title: The Pinhole Camera
topics.short: Image size in pixels = f × real size ÷ distance, so a known size gives the distance.

topics.title: A Lemon Battery, Like Volta's Pile
topics.short: Two different metals in a sour juice make a small voltage; cells in series add their voltages.

topics.title: A Nail Electromagnet, Like Sturgeon's and Henry's
topics.short: Current in a coil makes a magnet; more turns and more current make it stronger, and an iron core multiplies it.

topics.title: A Homopolar Motor, Faraday's 1821 Idea
topics.short: A current crossing a magnetic field feels a push, F = BIL; arranged right, the push keeps a wire spinning.

topics.title: A Hand Generator, Faraday's 1831 Discovery
topics.short: A changing magnetic field through a coil makes a voltage; faster changes and more turns make more.

topics.title: A Telegraph, Like Morse's
topics.short: A key closes a circuit; an electromagnet far away clicks; dots and dashes carry letters.

topics.title: A Glowing Filament, Edison's and Swan's Problem
topics.short: Current heats a thin filament until it glows; in air it burns away, so lamps need a vacuum or a gas without oxygen.

topics.title: A Crystal Radio with No Battery
topics.short: A coil and capacitor pick one station; a diode turns its radio wave back into sound you can hear in a sensitive earphone.

topics.title: A Printing Press, Gutenberg's Way
topics.short: Backward metal letters, set and justified, inked and pressed, print a page the right way round, hundreds of times a day.

topics.title: Archimedes: The Lever and the Crown
topics.short: A Greek of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC) who proved the law of the lever, worked out why things float, and built machines that astonished his city.

topics.title: Hero of Alexandria: Steam, Air and Automatic Machines
topics.short: A teacher in Roman Egypt (about the 1st century AD) who described a spinning steam ball, automatic doors and a coin-operated dispenser.

topics.title: Ibn al-Haytham: Light, Sight and the Dark Room
topics.short: A scholar of Basra and Cairo (c. AD 965–c. 1040) whose Book of Optics showed that we see because light enters the eye, and tested it.

topics.title: Benjamin Franklin: Lightning, the Rod, the Stove and Bifocals
topics.short: Printer, writer and experimenter (1706–1790) who showed lightning is electricity, invented the lightning rod, and never patented his inventions.

topics.title: Alessandro Volta: The Pile of 1800
topics.short: An Italian professor (1745–1827) who stacked zinc, copper and brine-soaked card into the first battery, after a long debate with Galvani about frogs' legs.

topics.title: Michael Faraday: The Motor and the Generator
topics.short: A bookbinder's apprentice (1791–1867) who became the great experimenter of the Royal Institution: the first motor in 1821, induction in 1831.

topics.title: Samuel Morse: The Telegraph and Its Code
topics.short: A painter turned inventor (1791–1872) who, with Alfred Vail and Joseph Henry's science, sent messages along a wire in dots and dashes.

topics.title: Alexander Graham Bell: The Telephone
topics.short: A teacher of deaf students (1847–1922) who turned the shape of a sound wave into a changing current, and patented the telephone in 1876.

topics.title: Thomas Edison: Menlo Park and the Light Bulb
topics.short: An inventor (1847–1931) who made invention a team job at Menlo Park: the phonograph in 1877, then a long-lasting bulb after testing thousands of materials.

topics.title: Nikola Tesla: The Rotating Magnetic Field
topics.short: An engineer (1856–1943) who pictured a motor with no brushes, driven by a magnetic field that turns, and made alternating current practical.

topics.title: The Wright Brothers: Gliders and the Wind Tunnel
topics.short: Wilbur (1867–1912) and Orville (1871–1948) Wright solved control first with wing-warping, then found the tables of lift were wrong and built a wind tunnel in 1901.

topics.title: The Wright Brothers: The 1903 Flyer and After
topics.short: With their own engine and propellers, the Wrights flew four times on December 17, 1903, then spent years learning to fly in circles and for long times.

topics.title: Hawking: A Brief History of Time
topics.short: A chapter-by-chapter guide, in our own words, to Stephen Hawking's 1988 book about space, time, black holes and the beginning of the universe.

topics.title: Hawking: The Universe in a Nutshell
topics.short: A guide to Hawking's 2001 follow-up: relativity, the shape of time, predicting the future and whether time travel is possible.

topics.title: Sagan: Cosmos
topics.short: A guide to the 13 chapters of Carl Sagan's 1980 book, written with the television series: the history of science and our place among the stars.

topics.title: Sagan's Other Books
topics.short: Pale Blue Dot, The Demon-Haunted World, The Dragons of Eden, Contact and more: what each is about and how Sagan taught people to test claims.

topics.title: Gutenberg: Movable Type, Ink and the Press
topics.short: In Mainz around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg put together cast metal letters, an oil-based ink and a screw press, and printed a Bible.

topics.title: Leonardo da Vinci: Notebooks and Flying Machines
topics.short: The painter and engineer (1452–1519) filled notebooks with studies of birds, water and machines; most of his designs were never built in his lifetime.

topics.title: Galileo: The Telescope and the Rolling Ball
topics.short: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) built better telescopes from a rumor, saw the moons of Jupiter, and timed balls rolling down ramps.

topics.title: Newton: Prisms, a New Telescope and the Laws of Motion
topics.short: Isaac Newton (1642–1727) split white light with prisms, built the first working reflecting telescope, and showed that one gravity rules apple and Moon.

topics.title: The Basic Tastes and Aroma
topics.short: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami are tasted on the tongue; most of what we call flavor is aroma, smelled from the back of the mouth.

topics.title: Seasoning: Salt, Acid, Fat and Heat
topics.short: Salt makes food taste more like itself, acid brightens, fat carries flavor, and heat (both chile and cooking) adds depth. Season in layers.

topics.title: Tasting and Adjusting
topics.short: Taste with a clean spoon every time, often; fix flat with salt or acid, too salty with more unsalted base, too sour with sweetness or fat.

topics.title: Herbs, Spices and Aromatics
topics.short: Hardy herbs go in early and tender herbs at the end; toast whole spices to wake them; about 1 part dried herb replaces 3 parts fresh.

topics.title: Seasonality and Sourcing
topics.short: Food tastes best and costs least at the height of its season; menus change with what farms and markets have.

topics.title: Writing a Menu
topics.short: Balance the menu in methods, colors, richness and station load; describe dishes honestly; price from food cost; and look at what sells.

topics.title: The Kitchen and Its Stations
topics.short: A professional kitchen is laid out in stations around the range, ovens, broiler, fryer and cold storage; each machine has one job it does best.

topics.title: Knives and Their Parts, Boards and Steels
topics.short: Four knives do most of the work: chef's, paring, serrated and boning. Know the tip, edge, heel, spine, bolster and tang, and keep the board from sliding.

topics.title: Pans and What They Are Made Of
topics.short: Copper and aluminum spread heat fast, stainless resists acid, cast iron and carbon steel hold heat and season; the shape (sauté, saucepan, rondeau, stockpot, sheet pan) fits the job.

topics.title: Measuring and Hand Tools
topics.short: Scales, thermometers, measuring cups and spoons, ladles and scoops by size, sieves, the chinois, the mandoline with its guard, the spider and the fish spatula.

topics.title: Mixers, Blenders, Processors and Circulators
topics.short: The stand mixer's paddle, whisk and hook; blenders and immersion blenders; the food processor; the combi oven and the immersion circulator.

topics.title: Measuring by Weight
topics.short: Professional recipes are written in grams or ounces because a cup of flour can weigh anywhere from about 120 to 160 grams; tare the scale and weigh.

topics.title: Reading and Scaling a Recipe
topics.short: Read it all twice, find the times and temperatures, then scale with one conversion factor: new yield ÷ old yield.

topics.title: Mise en Place and Working Clean
topics.short: "Everything in its place": read, plan, gather, prep and set up your station before the heat goes on, and clean as you go.

topics.title: Salads and Dressings
topics.short: Wash and dry greens well, dress them just before serving; a vinaigrette is about 3 parts oil to 1 part acid, and emulsified dressings stay mixed.

topics.title: Canapés and Hors d'Oeuvres
topics.short: A canapé is a base, a spread and a topping, small enough for one or two bites; cold food stays at 41°F or below until it is served.

topics.title: Quick Pickles and Refrigerator Pickles
topics.short: Vegetables in a vinegar brine, kept in the refrigerator. Canning for the shelf is a separate skill: use only tested recipes from USDA or extension services.

topics.title: Confit, Pâtés and Terrines
topics.short: Confit is meat cooked slowly in fat; a terrine is a seasoned meat or vegetable mixture cooked in a mold and served cold. Both are kept refrigerated.

topics.title: Charcuterie and Cheese Boards
topics.short: What dry-cured ham and salami are, why their making needs exact curing salts and controlled rooms, and how to build and serve a board of cured meats and cheese.

topics.title: Conduction, Convection and Radiation
topics.short: Pans conduct heat into food, air and liquids carry it by convection, and broilers and grills radiate it; most cooking uses all three.

topics.title: Browning: the Maillard Reaction and Caramelization
topics.short: Above about 280°F to 300°F, proteins and sugars react to make brown color and roasted flavor (Maillard); sugar alone browns as it breaks down (caramelization). Water keeps the surface too cool, so dry the food.

topics.title: Sautéing, Stir-Frying and Pan-Frying
topics.short: Sauté: a little fat, a hot pan, small pieces moving. Pan-fry: more fat, often a breading, cooked on one side and then the other.

topics.title: Deep-Frying and Oil Safety
topics.short: Food submerged in oil at about 325°F to 375°F; dry the food, fry in small batches, and know the fire rules: never water on a grease fire, smother it with a lid, Class K extinguishers in commercial kitchens.

topics.title: Roasting, Grilling and Broiling
topics.short: Roast in hot air, grill over the heat, broil under it; sear, then finish at a lower temperature for large pieces, and use a thermometer.

topics.title: Poaching, Simmering, Boiling and Steaming
topics.short: Poach at about 160°F to 180°F, simmer at about 185°F to 205°F, boil at 212°F at sea level; steam cooks by condensing vapor. Water boils at a lower temperature high in the mountains.

topics.title: Braising and Stewing
topics.short: Brown first, then cook slowly, partly covered in liquid, until tough connective tissue turns to gelatin. Braises use large pieces in a little liquid; stews use smaller pieces covered in liquid.

topics.title: Sous Vide: Precise Low-Temperature Cooking
topics.short: Food sealed in a bag and cooked in a water bath held at an exact temperature. Safety comes from time at temperature: reach a safe minimum temperature, or hold long enough by a published table.

topics.title: The Grip and the Guide Hand
topics.short: Pinch the blade where it meets the handle; curl the guide hand into a claw so the knuckles guide the flat of the blade and the fingertips stay tucked.

topics.title: Slicing, Dicing an Onion and Mincing
topics.short: The rocking cut and the push cut; how to dice an onion with its root holding it together; mincing garlic and herbs.

topics.title: The Classic Cuts and Their Sizes
topics.short: Julienne, batonnet, brunoise and the small, medium and large dice have standard sizes, so food cooks evenly and looks deliberate.

topics.title: Chiffonade, Paysanne, Tourné and Other Shaped Cuts
topics.short: Ribbons of leaves, thin flat squares, rounds, bias and oblique cuts, and the seven-sided tourné.

topics.title: Honing and Sharpening
topics.short: Honing pushes a bent edge back into line; sharpening grinds new metal to make a new edge. Hold a steady angle, about 15 to 20 degrees per side.

topics.title: Whetstones and Knife Care
topics.short: Coarse, medium and fine grits; raising and removing a burr; washing by hand, drying, storing in a block, strip or guard, and never leaving a knife in the sink.

topics.title: Baker's Percentages
topics.short: Every ingredient is written as a percent of the flour's weight: flour is 100%, water 65% means 650 g of water for 1,000 g of flour.

topics.title: Lean Doughs: Flour, Water, Salt and Yeast
topics.short: Mix, knead to build gluten, ferment, shape, proof and bake. Hydration (water as a percent of flour) sets the texture; salt is about 2%.

topics.title: Enriched and Laminated Doughs
topics.short: Butter, eggs, milk and sugar make soft, rich doughs (brioche, challah); folding a sheet of butter into dough again and again makes layers (croissant, puff pastry).

topics.title: Pie Dough, Pâte Sucrée and Pâte à Choux
topics.short: 3-2-1 pie dough (flour, fat, water by weight), sweet tart dough made by creaming, and choux paste cooked on the stove, then beaten with eggs so it puffs in the oven.

topics.title: Custards: Crème Anglaise and Pastry Cream
topics.short: Crème anglaise is milk, yolks and sugar stirred over gentle heat until it coats a spoon (about 170°F to 180°F); pastry cream adds starch and must come to a boil to thicken.

topics.title: Chocolate and Tempering
topics.short: Tempering melts, cools and gently rewarms chocolate so the cocoa butter sets in its stable form: shiny, snapping, not streaky.

topics.title: Sugar Stages and Caramel
topics.short: As syrup cooks, water boils off and the temperature rises: thread, soft ball, firm ball, hard ball, soft crack, hard crack, then caramel.

topics.title: Plated Desserts
topics.short: A main item, a sauce, something crisp, something cold, and a garnish that belongs: contrast in texture, temperature and color.

topics.title: Plate Composition
topics.short: Choose the plate, then build with color, height and texture; leave clear space; odd numbers of pieces look natural; keep the rim clean.

topics.title: Sauce Work and Garnish
topics.short: Pools, dots, swooshes and spoon drags; every garnish should be edible and belong to the dish.

topics.title: The Place Setting: Utensils, Glasses and Plates
topics.short: Forks on the left, knives and spoons on the right, used from the outside in; glasses above the knives; the bread plate at upper left; dessert utensils above the plate.

topics.title: The Courses of a Tasting Menu
topics.short: Many small courses in an order that builds: a small bite from the chef, lighter to richer, savory to sweet, often with cheese before dessert and small sweets at the end.

topics.title: Service Styles: French, Russian, American and Family
topics.short: Plated (American) service comes from the kitchen on the plate; Russian service is served from platters at the table; French (guéridon) service finishes dishes on a cart beside the table; family style passes platters.

topics.title: The Pass: Firing and Calling Tickets
topics.short: The expediter calls each order, the stations answer "heard", courses are fired so they finish together, and every plate is checked before it leaves.

topics.title: The Brigade System
topics.short: Escoffier organized big kitchens into stations under one chef: chef de cuisine, sous-chef, chefs de partie such as saucier and pâtissier, cooks, commis and dishwashers.

topics.title: Kitchen Language
topics.short: Short calls keep people safe and orders moving: "behind", "corner", "hot", "sharp", "heard", "fire", "all day", "86" and "on the fly".

topics.title: Station Setup, Prep Lists and Par Levels
topics.short: A par level is how much you need on hand for a service; the prep list is par minus what you have; a station is set up so every item is in reach.

topics.title: Ordering, Receiving and Inventory
topics.short: Order from pars, check deliveries for temperature, quality and count, rotate stock first in, first out, and count inventory on a schedule.

topics.title: Recipe Costing, Yield Tests and Food Cost
topics.short: Usable cost = purchase cost ÷ yield; add up a recipe, divide by portions, and food cost percent = cost ÷ menu price.

topics.title: Timing a Service
topics.short: Work backward from the time food must leave the pass; know your ticket times; fire long-cooking items first so a table's plates finish together.

topics.title: Cleaning Schedules and Equipment Care
topics.short: Clean as you go, a closing clean every night, and a deep-cleaning schedule; hoods, filters, fryers, ice machines and ovens are cleaned and serviced on the schedule set by the manufacturer and local code.

topics.title: Working Safely: Cuts, Burns, Slips and Lifting
topics.short: Prevention habits: sharp knives used with care, dry towels for hot handles, calls when moving, closed non-slip shoes, spills cleaned at once, and help with heavy pots.

topics.title: What Michelin Stars Mean
topics.short: Anonymous inspectors award one star ("worth a stop"), two ("worth a detour") or three ("worth a special journey") for the food on the plate, judged on five published criteria.

topics.title: Stages, Careers and Certifications
topics.short: Most chefs learn by working, often starting as line cooks; staging (working a short trial), culinary programs, apprenticeships and ACF certification are other steps. Figures from the BLS.

topics.title: Capstone: Cook a Tasting Menu at Home
topics.short: Plan, cost, prep and cook a five-course tasting menu for four to six people, with a timeline that starts three days ahead.

topics.title: Muscle, Connective Tissue and Tenderness
topics.short: Muscles that worked hard (shoulder, leg) have more connective tissue and want slow moist heat; tender ones (loin, rib) want quick dry heat. Slice across the grain.

topics.title: Beef, Pork and Lamb Primal Cuts
topics.short: Butchers split each carcass into primals (beef: chuck, rib, short loin, sirloin, round, brisket, plate, flank), then subprimals and portions.

topics.title: Brines, Marinades and Rubs
topics.short: A brine is salt dissolved in water by weight; it seasons inside and helps meat hold moisture. Marinades flavor the surface. Keep both refrigerated and discard used raw marinade unless boiled.

topics.title: Breaking Down a Chicken
topics.short: Legs off at the joint, thighs from drumsticks, breasts off the bone, wings at the joint: eight pieces, plus a frame for stock. Work clean and sanitize after.

topics.title: Fish: Freshness and Filleting a Round Fish
topics.short: Fresh fish smells like the sea, has firm flesh and bright, clear eyes. A round fish gives two fillets: cut behind the head, then along the backbone.

topics.title: Shellfish Basics
topics.short: Live clams, mussels and oysters have closed shells or close when tapped; discard any that stay open or are cracked; keep shellstock tags 90 days; cook shrimp and lobster until opaque.

topics.title: Doneness, Resting and Carryover Cooking
topics.short: Meat keeps rising in temperature after it leaves the heat, a few degrees for steaks and more for big roasts; pull early, rest, then slice.

topics.title: Eggs: Omelets and Poaching
topics.short: The French omelet is rolled, pale and creamy; the American omelet is folded and lightly browned. Poach in barely simmering water; egg dishes are safe at 160°F.

topics.title: Biological, Chemical and Physical Hazards
topics.short: Germs (bacteria, viruses, parasites), chemicals (cleaners, pesticides, allergens) and objects (glass, bone, metal) can all make food unsafe; bacteria need food, warmth, time and moisture.

topics.title: The Temperature Danger Zone
topics.short: Bacteria grow fastest between 41°F and 135°F, the FDA Food Code's limits for restaurants; USDA tells home cooks 40°F to 140°F. Keep cold food cold and hot food hot.

topics.title: Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures
topics.short: Poultry 165°F; ground meat 160°F (USDA) or 155°F for 17 seconds (Food Code); whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb and fish 145°F; check with a thermometer in the thickest part.

topics.title: Cooling Food Safely
topics.short: The Food Code's two stages: from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F or below within 4 more hours. Shallow pans, ice baths and small portions make it work.

topics.title: Holding, Reheating, Labeling and Date Marking
topics.short: Hold hot food at 135°F or above and cold food at 41°F or below; reheat for hot holding to 165°F within 2 hours; label and date, and use ready-to-eat food within 7 days; first in, first out.

topics.title: Cross-Contamination and Storage Order
topics.short: Keep raw animal foods away from ready-to-eat food: separate boards, clean tools, and a refrigerator stored top to bottom by the temperature each food must be cooked to.

topics.title: The Nine Major Food Allergens
topics.short: Milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame (added in 2023). Cooking does not remove an allergen; separate tools and honest answers do.

topics.title: Handwashing, Gloves and Personal Hygiene
topics.short: Wash hands for at least 20 seconds before work, after raw meat, the restroom, touching your face or trash, and before gloving; gloves don't replace handwashing; sick workers stay home.

topics.title: Cleaning and Sanitizing
topics.short: Cleaning removes dirt and food; sanitizing reduces germs to safe levels on a surface that is already clean. Three-compartment sink: wash, rinse, sanitize, air-dry. Mix sanitizer by the label and check with test strips.

topics.title: HACCP: A Plan for Safe Food
topics.short: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points: seven principles that find where food could become unsafe, set limits there, check them and write it down.

topics.title: Stocks: White, Brown, Fish and Vegetable
topics.short: Bones or vegetables, aromatic mirepoix and cold water, simmered (never boiled) and skimmed: chicken about 3 to 4 hours, beef or veal 6 to 8, fish 30 to 45 minutes.

topics.title: Roux, Slurries and Liaisons
topics.short: Roux is equal weights of fat and flour cooked to white, blond or brown; slurries are starch stirred into cold liquid; a liaison of yolks and cream enriches at the end.

topics.title: The Five Mother Sauces
topics.short: Escoffier's leading sauces: béchamel (milk and roux), velouté (white stock and roux), espagnole (brown stock and brown roux), tomato and hollandaise.

topics.title: Small Sauces: Children of the Mothers
topics.short: Add cheese to béchamel for Mornay, mushrooms and cream to velouté for suprême, shallots and wine to demi-glace for bordelaise, tarragon reduction to hollandaise for béarnaise.

topics.title: Emulsions: Mayonnaise, Hollandaise, Vinaigrette, Beurre Blanc
topics.short: Tiny drops of fat held in water with help from an emulsifier such as egg yolk or mustard; add the fat slowly, and keep warm emulsions warm, not hot.

topics.title: Reductions and Pan Sauces
topics.short: Deglaze the browned bits (fond) with wine or stock, reduce, and finish with cold butter swirled in off the heat (monter au beurre).

topics.title: Clear, Cream and Purée Soups
topics.short: Broths and consommé are clear; cream soups are thickened; purées are thickened by the vegetables or beans themselves; bisques are shellfish soups.

topics.title: Blanching and Shocking
topics.short: Cook green vegetables briefly in plenty of salted boiling water, then plunge them into ice water to stop the cooking and keep the color bright.

topics.title: Glazing, Roasting and Purées
topics.short: Glaze in a little water, butter and sugar until shiny; roast at high heat for browned edges; purée cooked vegetables and pass them through a sieve for smoothness.

topics.title: Potatoes: Starchy and Waxy
topics.short: Starchy potatoes (russets) are fluffy for baking, mashing and frying; waxy ones hold their shape in salads and gratins. Classic fries are cooked twice: low, then high.

topics.title: Rice, Grains and Risotto
topics.short: Absorption, pilaf and pasta methods; risotto adds hot stock a little at a time to short-grain rice while stirring, so the starch makes it creamy.

topics.title: Fresh Pasta from Scratch
topics.short: About 100 grams of flour for each large egg; knead until smooth, rest, roll thin, cut, and cook briefly in plenty of salted boiling water.

topics.title: Beans and Lentils
topics.short: Sort and rinse; soak beans to shorten cooking; boil red kidney beans hard in fresh water to destroy a natural toxin; lentils need no soaking.
